subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to different Committees in India, consider the following details :

Sl. No. | Committee | Objective | Organization under which it was formed
1. | R.N. Malhotra Committee | Comprehensive reforms of Insurance sector in India | Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
2. | L.C. Gupta Committee | Preparing a roadmap for the introduction of derivatives trading in India | Securities and Exchange Board of India
3. | Urjit R. Patel Committee | Preparing a roadmap for reforming bank lending to the Housing sector | Reserve Bank of India
4. | Y.H. Malegam Committee | Preparing a roadmap for reforms in Microfinance sector in India | Reserve Bank of India

In which of the above rows are all the details correctly matched ?

keywords.shortNote: Appointed by the Government of India / Ministry of Finance in 1993 to suggest insurance sector reforms; its recommendations led directly to the creation of IRDA (1999), meaning IRDAI did not yet exist to form it.
keywords.concept: R.N. Malhotra Committee: Appointed by the Government of India / Ministry of Finance in 1993 to suggest insurance sector reforms; its recommendations led directly to the creation of IRDA (1999), meaning IRDAI did not yet exist to form it.

keywords.shortNote: Set up by SEBI in 1996 to develop a regulatory framework for introducing exchange-traded financial derivatives in Indian capital markets.
keywords.concept: L.C. Gupta Committee: Set up by SEBI in 1996 to develop a regulatory framework for introducing exchange-traded financial derivatives in Indian capital markets.

keywords.shortNote: Formed by the RBI in 2013 as the Expert Committee to Revise and Strengthen the Monetary Policy Framework, recommending the flexible inflation targeting (FIT) framework using CPI.
keywords.concept: Urjit R. Patel Committee: Formed by the RBI in 2013 as the Expert Committee to Revise and Strengthen the Monetary Policy Framework, recommending the flexible inflation targeting (FIT) framework using CPI.

keywords.shortNote: Constituent sub-committee set up by the RBI Board in 2010 in the wake of the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis, recommending regulations and establishing the NBFC-MFI regulatory category.
keywords.concept: Y.H. Malegam Committee: Constituent sub-committee set up by the RBI Board in 2010 in the wake of the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis, recommending regulations and establishing the NBFC-MFI regulatory category.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Omits Row 4 (Y.H. Malegam Committee), which is also accurately matched with RBI and microfinance sector reforms.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Row 3 misidentifies Urjit Patel Committee's mandate as housing finance instead of monetary policy framework revision.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Row 1 creates an anachronism (IRDAI was created after Malhotra Committee) and Row 3 misstates Patel Committee's mandate.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both Row 2 (L.C. Gupta under SEBI for derivatives) and Row 4 (Y.H. Malegam under RBI for microfinance) have every column correctly matched.

valueAddition.title: Malhotra Committee & The Genesis of IRDAI
bullets: Mandate: Chaired by former RBI Governor R.N. Malhotra, set up in April 1993 by the Government of India (Ministry of Finance).

Key Recommendations (1994): Opening the insurance sector to private players, allowing foreign equity participation (initially recommended up to 26%), ending the state monopoly of LIC and GIC, and creating an independent statutory insurance regulator.
Chronology Anchor: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDA) was created as an interim body in 1996 and made a statutory autonomous regulator by Parliament through the IRDA Act, 1999.

valueAddition.title: Urjit Patel Committee: Anchor of Inflation Targeting
bullets: Committee Title: Expert Committee to Revise and Strengthen the Monetary Policy Framework (constituted September 2013, reported January 2014).

Key Recommendations: Transition from multiple-indicator approach to Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT); Headline CPI (Combined) as the primary nominal anchor; establishment of a 6-member statutory Monetary Policy Committee (MPC).
Housing Lending Relevance: Bank lending to housing is governed by Priority Sector Lending (PSL) norms and RBI regulatory guidelines on Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratios, not the Urjit Patel Committee.

valueAddition.title: Malegam Committee & Post-Crisis Microfinance
bullets: Context: Constituted in October 2010 following aggressive coercive recovery practices and microfinance crises in Andhra Pradesh.

Outcomes: Established a new institutional class called NBFC-MFI, introduced Qualifying Assets criteria (at least 85% of net assets in qualifying micro-loans), margin caps (10-12%), and a maximum cap on borrower indebtedness.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India / Financial Express
inNews.headline: RBI and Central Government Review Five-Year Flexible Inflation Targeting Framework Anchored in Urjit Patel Committee Architecture
inNews.relevance: Directly links back to the enduring statutory role of the Urjit Patel Committee's recommendations underpinning the RBI Act Section 45ZA inflation band.

statementBreakdown.explanation: The objective is correct (insurance reforms), but the committee was constituted by the Ministry of Finance / Government of India in 1993, not by IRDAI. In fact, IRDA was established pursuant to the Malhotra Committee's recommendations via the IRDA Act, 1999.
SEBI appointed the 24-member committee headed by Dr. L.C. Gupta in November 1996 to formulate a regulatory framework for financial derivatives trading in India, which submitted its report in 1998.

While constituted by the RBI, its objective was not housing sector lending; it was set up to revise and strengthen the Monetary Policy Framework, recommending the 4% +/- 2% CPI inflation target and the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC).
Constituted by the RBI Board under Y.H. Malegam to study issues and concerns in the MFI sector, leading to interest rate caps, margin caps, and a distinct regulatory category for NBFC-MFIs.

rows: Insurance Sector Reforms & privatization (led to IRDA Act 1999)
Derivatives trading and risk management framework
Monetary Policy Framework Revision & Inflation Targeting (FIT)

hook.headline: Did IRDA really create the Malhotra Committee?
hook.teaser: Look at the timeline—how can a regulator create the committee that recommended its creation?

keywords.term: Organization under which it was formed
keywords.calloutNote: Look for chronological paradoxes: a child organization cannot set up its parent committee.
activePhrases: Organization under which it was formed

keywords.calloutNote: Urjit Patel recommended CPI inflation targeting and the MPC, not housing sector lending.
activePhrases: reforming bank lending to the Housing sector
dimmedPhrases: Organization under which it was formed

verdicts.source: Malhotra Committee was set up by the Ministry of Finance in 1993; IRDA was only born in 1999 as a result of its report.
SEBI formed the L.C. Gupta Committee in 1996 to establish the regulatory architecture for equity derivatives.
Urjit Patel Committee revolutionized monetary policy by bringing in CPI-based flexible inflation targeting and the MPC.
Set up by the RBI Board after the 2010 Andhra crisis, establishing the NBFC-MFI regulatory framework.

answer.label: D
answer.text: Only rows 2 and 4 are completely matched; row 1 is an institutional anachronism and row 3 misidentifies the monetary policy mandate.

items.desc: Constituted by the Government of India, leading to the creation of IRDA via the 1999 Act.

items.desc: Set the 4% +/- 2% CPI target and led to the statutory Monetary Policy Committee (MPC).

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements about the Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) in India :
1. NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits.
2. All the NBFCs operating in India have to be registered with the RBI.
3. NBFCs form part of the payment and settlement system and can issue cheque drawn on itself.
4. Deposit insurance facility of Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) is not available to the depositors of deposit taking NBFCs.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: A company registered under the Companies Act engaged in lending, investments, hire-purchase, or leasing, satisfying the 50-50 principal business test under Section 45-I(f) of the RBI Act, 1934.
keywords.concept: Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC): A company registered under the Companies Act engaged in lending, investments, hire-purchase, or leasing, satisfying the 50-50 principal business test under Section 45-I(f) of the RBI Act, 1934.

keywords.shortNote: Demand deposits are repayable on demand via cheques/drafts (savings and current accounts), which NBFCs are statutorily prohibited from accepting; only registered NBFCs-D can accept public term/fixed deposits.
keywords.concept: Demand Deposits vs. Term Deposits: Demand deposits are repayable on demand via cheques/drafts (savings and current accounts), which NBFCs are statutorily prohibited from accepting; only registered NBFCs-D can accept public term/fixed deposits.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statements 1 and 4 are factually and legally correct: NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits, and DICGC insurance does not cover NBFC depositors.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Includes the universal qualifier trap ('All NBFCs') and wrongly places NBFCs inside the payment and settlement system.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks the statutory bar on demand deposits.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Carries both erroneous propositions regarding registration and cheque issuance.

valueAddition.title: Core Distinctions: Commercial Banks vs. NBFCs
bullets: Demand Deposits: Banks accept both demand (current/savings) and time deposits. NBFCs are strictly barred from accepting demand deposits.
Payment System: Banks are part of the Payment and Settlement System and can issue cheques drawn on themselves. NBFCs cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves.
Deposit Insurance: Bank deposits are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank. NBFC deposits receive zero insurance cover from DICGC.

Statutory Reserves: Banks must maintain CRR and SLR. NBFCs-D maintain a required percentage of liquid assets (SLR under Section 45-IB), but are not subject to standard Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) mandates.

valueAddition.title: NBFC Entities Exempted from RBI Registration
bullets: Housing Finance Companies (HFCs): Regulatory oversight shifted back to RBI, but originally regulated by the National Housing Bank (NHB).
Merchant Banking Companies, Stock-Brokers, Venture Capital Funds (VCFs), Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs): Regulated directly by SEBI.
Insurance Companies: Regulated by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI).
Nidhi Companies: Governed by Section 406 of the Companies Act, 2013 and regulated by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA).
Chit Fund Companies: Regulated by respective State Governments under the Chit Funds Act, 1982.

valueAddition.title: Scale-Based Regulatory (SBR) Framework for NBFCs
bullets: Base Layer (NBFC-BL): Non-deposit taking NBFCs below ₹1,000 crore asset size, peer-to-peer (P2P) lending platforms, account aggregators, and non-operative financial holding companies.
Middle Layer (NBFC-ML): All deposit-taking NBFCs (irrespective of asset size), non-deposit taking NBFCs with asset size ≥ ₹1,000 crore, standalone primary dealers, and core investment companies.
Upper Layer (NBFC-UL): Top 10 NBFCs identified based on asset size, interconnectedness, and systemic risk, subjected to bank-like capital and governance regulation.
Top Layer (NBFC-TL): Kept empty by default; populated only if an Upper Layer NBFC poses extreme systemic risk.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India / The Hindu
inNews.headline: RBI Tightens Prudential and Liquidity Risk Norms for Upper Layer NBFCs to Ensure Harmony with Commercial Bank Supervision
inNews.relevance: Directly links to the evolving regulatory parity between Upper Layer NBFCs and commercial banks while reinforcing the enduring statutory differences concerning demand deposits, payment systems, and DICGC coverage.

statementBreakdown.reference: Section 45-I(bb) & Section 45-I(f) of RBI Act, 1934 / RBI NBFC Master Directions
statementBreakdown.explanation: NBFCs lend and make investments and hence their activities are kin to that of banks, but they cannot accept demand deposits (repayable on demand via cheques/withdrawals). Only eligible NBFCs-D can accept term/fixed deposits.

To obviate dual regulation, certain categories of NBFCs regulated by other statutory regulators are explicitly exempted from registration with the RBI: Housing Finance Companies (regulated by RBI/NHB but incorporated under separate frameworks), Merchant Banking companies / Venture Capital / Stock-broking firms (regulated by SEBI), Insurance companies (regulated by IRDAI), Nidhi companies and Chit Fund companies (regulated by Ministry of Corporate Affairs / State Governments).

statementBreakdown.reference: Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 / RBI Core Guidelines
statementBreakdown.explanation: NBFCs do not form part of the Payment and Settlement System and therefore cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves.

statementBreakdown.reference: Section 2(g) & Section 16 of Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) Act, 1961
statementBreakdown.explanation: DICGC insurance coverage (up to ₹5 lakh) is available exclusively to depositors of insured commercial banks and cooperative banks. It is not available to depositors of deposit-taking NBFCs.

visualSuggestion.title: Commercial Banks vs. Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs)

rows: Prohibited (Can only accept time deposits if registered NBFC-D)
Integral part; can issue own cheques
Not a part; cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves
Not available to any NBFC depositor
RBI (Section 45-IA), unless exempted due to other sectoral regulators (SEBI, IRDAI, MCA)

hook.headline: Can an NBFC issue a cheque drawn on itself?
hook.teaser: Four classic textbook traps on NBFCs—notice the absolute word that gives it away.

keywords.term: All the NBFCs operating in India
keywords.calloutNote: Spot the absolute qualifier: SEBI, IRDAI, and MCA regulate their own specialized NBFC classes.
activePhrases: All the NBFCs operating in India have to be registered with the RBI

keywords.term: form part of the payment and settlement system
keywords.calloutNote: NBFCs cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves because they do not participate in the core payment clearing system.
activePhrases: NBFCs form part of the payment and settlement system and can issue cheque drawn on itself
dimmedPhrases: All the NBFCs operating in India have to be registered with the RBI

verdicts.source: NBFCs cannot accept savings or current deposits repayable on demand; only select NBFCs can accept term deposits.
Insurance firms (IRDAI), stock brokers (SEBI), and Nidhi companies (MCA) are NBFCs exempted from registering with RBI.
NBFCs do not participate in the clearing system and cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves.
DICGC protection is restricted exclusively to banking institutions and never covers NBFC deposits.

answer.label: A
answer.text: Statements 1 and 4 are correct; statements 2 and 3 are standard misconceptions about NBFC powers.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your NBFCs & Banking notes

items.title: Principal Business
items.desc: Financial assets must exceed 50% of total assets and financial income must exceed 50% of gross income.

items.title: Exemption Power
items.desc: Empowers RBI to exempt entities regulated by other statutory regulators to avoid dual supervision.

items.title: Four-Tier Scale
items.desc: Regulates NBFCs across Base, Middle, Upper, and Top Layers based on systemic importance.

valueAddition.note: Look at statement 2—whenever an economy question claims 'all entities must register with one single body', search for specialized sector regulators like SEBI or IRDAI.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements about Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) :
1. MPI is calculated using Alkire-Foster methodology.
2. MPI calculated by NITI Aayog has a total of twelve indicators.
3. Maternal Health and Bank Account are common indicators in the MPI of NITI Aayog and MPI of United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: A counting approach developed by Sabina Alkire and James Foster that identifies poor individuals based on overlapping deprivation cutoffs across multiple dimensions.
keywords.concept: Alkire-Foster Methodology: A counting approach developed by Sabina Alkire and James Foster that identifies poor individuals based on overlapping deprivation cutoffs across multiple dimensions.

keywords.shortNote: India's localized multidimensional poverty index prepared by NITI Aayog based on NFHS data under the Global Indices for Reforms and Growth (GIRG) mandate.
keywords.concept: National MPI (India): India's localized multidimensional poverty index prepared by NITI Aayog based on NFHS data under the Global Indices for Reforms and Growth (GIRG) mandate.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are factually accurate, while statement 3 falsely claims Maternal Health and Bank Account are common to both indices.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because statement 3 is incorrect.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Omits statement 2 and includes incorrect statement 3.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Omits statement 1, which is also correct.

valueAddition.title: Alkire-Foster (AF) Counting Methodology
bullets: Dual-Cutoff Approach: Cutoff 1 (Deprivation cutoff, 'z') identifies whether a household is deprived in a specific indicator; Cutoff 2 (Poverty cutoff, 'k') requires a household to be deprived in at least 33.33% (one-third) of the weighted indicators to be classified as multidimensionally poor.

Core Formula: MPI = Headcount Ratio (H) × Intensity of Poverty (A). Headcount (H) measures the proportion of people who are multidimensionally poor, while Intensity (A) measures the average share of weighted deprivations experienced by them.

valueAddition.title: Indicator Architecture: Global MPI (10) vs. National MPI (12)
bullets: Three Equal Dimensions: Health (1/3 weight), Education (1/3 weight), and Standard of Living (1/3 weight).

Global MPI (10 Indicators): Health has 2 indicators (Nutrition, Child Mortality); Education has 2 (Years of Schooling, School Attendance); Standard of Living has 6 (Cooking Fuel, Sanitation, Drinking Water, Electricity, Housing, Assets).

National MPI (12 Indicators): Retains all 10 Global MPI indicators and adds 2 India-specific indicators: (1) Maternal Health (under Health dimension, weight 1/12), and (2) Bank Account (under Standard of Living dimension, weight 1/21).

valueAddition.title: Institutional Architecture of National MPI
bullets: Nodal Implementing Agency: NITI Aayog is the nodal agency for the Multidimensional Poverty Index in India under the Cabinet Secretariat's Global Indices for Reforms and Growth (GIRG) mandate.
Primary Data Source: National Family Health Survey (NFHS), conducted by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) with IIPS Mumbai as the nodal research organization.
Inter-Ministerial Coordination: Driven by the Multidimensional Poverty Index Coordination Committee (MPICC) comprising 12 line ministries/departments to formulate targeted reform action plans.

inNews.source: NITI Aayog / UNDP India / The Hindu
inNews.headline: NITI Aayog reviews sub-national multidimensional poverty trends across 707 districts ahead of SDG 2030 targets
inNews.relevance: Directly highlights the 12-indicator framework of the National MPI and its role in tracking targeted poverty reduction under SDG 1.2 across Indian states and districts.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Both the Global MPI (UNDP/OPHI) and India's National MPI (NITI Aayog) employ the Alkire-Foster (AF) dual-cutoff counting methodology, computing the index as the product of the Headcount Ratio (H) and the Intensity of Poverty (A): MPI = H × A.

NITI Aayog's National MPI comprises 12 indicators distributed across three equally weighted macro dimensions: Health (Nutrition, Child & Adolescent Mortality, Maternal Health), Education (Years of Schooling, School Attendance), and Standard of Living (Cooking Fuel, Sanitation, Drinking Water, Electricity, Housing, Assets, Bank Account).

statementBreakdown.reference: Global MPI vs National MPI Indicator Comparison
statementBreakdown.explanation: Maternal Health and Bank Account are NOT common indicators. They are the two India-specific indicators exclusively added by NITI Aayog to the 10 standard indicators of UNDP's Global MPI to reflect national public policy priorities (e.g., PM Jan Dhan Yojana and institutional deliveries).

visualSuggestion.title: Global MPI (UNDP/OPHI) vs. National MPI (NITI Aayog)

rows: Nutrition, Child & Adolescent Mortality, Maternal Health
Cooking Fuel, Sanitation, Drinking Water, Electricity, Housing, Assets
Cooking Fuel, Sanitation, Drinking Water, Electricity, Housing, Assets, Bank Account

hook.headline: How does India's MPI differ from the Global MPI?

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
As a responsible Government official, you are tasked with resolving the situation through mediation, ensuring a sustainable outcome that balances environmental needs, tribal rights, and urban public health.

Consider the following statements with reference to the above :
1. A successful conflict resolution process must begin with acknowledging the cultural concerns of the protesting tribal community before discussing technical alternatives.
2. The Government should move ahead with the project without delay to address urban health concerns, which outweigh the sentiments of a small group.
3. Creating a multi-stakeholder dialogue platform - including tribal leaders, environmental experts, and municipal representatives - to build mutual understanding and help de-escalate tensions.
4. Conducting an independent Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) and sharing findings transparently with both sides to facilitate evidence-based decision-making.

Which of the statements given above would contribute to the resolution process ?

keywords.shortNote: An evidence-based evaluation tool designed to assess potential socio-cultural and ecological consequences prior to project implementation to balance competing public interests.
keywords.concept: Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA): An evidence-based evaluation tool designed to assess potential socio-cultural and ecological consequences prior to project implementation to balance competing public interests.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Empathy (1), participatory platforms (3), and transparent empirical assessments (4) directly foster sustainable mediation.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 2 promotes unilateral executive bulldozing, which sabotages the mediation mandate.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Includes the coercive approach of statement 2 while omitting key consensus-building mechanisms.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Coercive project execution without grievance redressal undermines the premise of mediation.

valueAddition.title: Administrative Conflict Resolution & Principled Negotiation
bullets: Fisher and Ury's Negotiation Framework: (1) Separate the people from the problem; (2) Focus on underlying interests rather than entrenched positions; (3) Generate options for mutual gain; (4) Insist on using objective criteria (such as independent ESIAs).
Procedural Justice in Administration: Public compliance depends heavily on perceived fairness of the decision-making process, including voice, respect, neutrality, and trustworthy motives.

Utilitarianism vs. Rights-Based Ethics: Crude majoritarianism ('greatest good for greatest number' ignoring constitutional tribal protections) creates systemic alienation; administrative stewardship demands harmonizing development with fundamental rights.

valueAddition.title: Constitutional and Statutory Safeguards for Tribal Communities
bullets: Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act (PESA), 1996: Mandates prior consultation and approval of the Gram Sabha for land acquisition and rehabilitation in Fifth Schedule areas.
Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006: Codifies recognition of individual and community forest rights; Gram Sabha consent is legally required prior to diversion of forest tracts.

Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997) & Niyamgiri Judgment (2013): Reaffirmed that indigenous communities hold sovereign-backed customary and religious rights over local ecology that cannot be summarily brushed aside by executive fiat.

inNews.relevance: Underlines the procedural necessity of Gram Sabha consultations, social impact assessments, and multi-stakeholder mediation in balancing urban needs with tribal rights.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Validating the identity, cultural ties, and socio-economic fears of vulnerable stakeholders builds procedural trust, which is a prerequisite before presenting technical solutions.

Unilaterally overriding minority or indigenous community concerns under a majoritarian utilitarian pretext breaches democratic trust, violates statutory rights, and escalates public conflict rather than resolving it.
Setting up a multi-stakeholder forum brings parity to negotiations, bridges informational gaps, and institutionalizes constructive dialogue across competing groups.
An independent, transparent ESIA provides empirical clarity and scientific legitimacy, grounding subsequent deliberations in verifiable evidence.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Ms. X is a mid-level civil service official working in the urban development department of a major city. Recently, she was involved in approving a contract for a public infrastructure project - a new community park. During the approval process, she received a piece of confidential information indicating that one of the shortlisted contractors had a history of poor workmanship and allegations of corruption in other cities, though nothing had been legally proven. The Head of the Department, Mr. Y, advised her not to disclose this information to the project committee or the public because it could delay the project and damage the city's reputation. However, Ms. X believed that withholding such information compromised transparency and public trust.

What amongst the following should Ms. X do now ?
1. Immediately disclose the information to the project committee and the public
2. Recommend removing the contractor from the shortlist to protect the project's integrity
3. Propose a 'limited disclosure' to an oversight committee, while keeping the information confidential from the public for the time being

Select the answer using the code given below :

keywords.shortNote: The administrative principle requiring unverified allegations to be scrutinized through designated internal oversight channels rather than premature public disclosure or arbitrary penal action.
keywords.concept: Institutional Due Process: The administrative principle requiring unverified allegations to be scrutinized through designated internal oversight channels rather than premature public disclosure or arbitrary penal action.

keywords.shortNote: Rule of law doctrine ensuring no contractor is debarred, blacklisted, or removed without legally substantiated proof and a reasonable opportunity to be heard (audi alteram partem).
keywords.concept: Natural Justice: Rule of law doctrine ensuring no contractor is debarred, blacklisted, or removed without legally substantiated proof and a reasonable opportunity to be heard (audi alteram partem).

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.reference: Includes rash public disclosure (1) and arbitrary debarment (2)
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both actions disregard civil service conduct rules and procedural fairness.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: A limited, confidential disclosure to an oversight mechanism upholds fiduciary responsibility while safeguarding natural justice.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Recommending summary removal without an inquiry or proof constitutes arbitrary administrative action.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: Includes flawed and conflicting courses of action
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 violate basic administrative law and procedural ethics.

valueAddition.title: Ethical Balance in Public Procurement & Whistleblowing
bullets: Presumption of Regularity vs. Fiduciary Duty: Public officials hold a fiduciary duty to protect state funds, but cannot act as vigilantes; allegations must be funneled through formal vigilance mechanisms.

CVC Due Diligence Standards: The Central Vigilance Commission mandates that complaints must be verified for authenticity and substance through confidential preliminary inquiry before taking punitive action against bidders.
Internal Channels First: Administrative ethics requires exhausting internal institutional safeguards (oversight bodies, departmental vigilance, CVC) before any contemplation of public disclosures.

valueAddition.title: Legal Safeguards in Blacklisting & Vendor Debarment
bullets: Erusian Equipment & Chemicals Ltd. v. State of West Bengal (1975): Landmark Supreme Court ruling establishing that blacklisting or debarring a contractor incurs civil consequences and cannot be executed without notice and an opportunity of hearing.
Kulja Industries Ltd. v. Western Hill Telecom (2014): Held that debarment cannot be an arbitrary exercise of power; it requires solid evidentiary foundation and proportionality.
Rule 151 of General Financial Rules (GFR), 2017: Prescribes clear statutory thresholds and departmental review processes before a firm can be debarred from public procurement.

inNews.relevance: Directly guides civil servants on channeling unproven supplier allegations to Independent External Monitors (IEMs) rather than resorting to arbitrary exclusion.

statementBreakdown.reference: Rule 9 of Central Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964
statementBreakdown.explanation: Leaking unverified confidential information to the general public violates official secrecy norms, damages reputations without proof, and breaches civil service conduct rules governing unauthorized communication of official documents.

statementBreakdown.reference: Doctrine of Natural Justice (Audi Alteram Partem) & GFR Rule 151
statementBreakdown.explanation: Debarring or removing a shortlisted contractor solely based on unproven allegations and hearsay violates natural justice. Arbitrary exclusion invites immediate judicial stay and tender cancellation by courts.

Escalating the matter confidentially to a designated oversight or vigilance body balances public integrity with procedural fairness, ensuring rigorous due diligence without causing unwarranted public prejudice or administrative chaos.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
'X' was addressing a seminar on the meaning of the term 'law' as provided under Article 13, Part III of the Constitution of India. 'X' explained that the meaning of the term 'law' in the Constitution of India was very comprehensive. It included ordinances, orders and even rules and regulations. 'Y' pointed out that the term 'law' in Article 13 also included custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law, to which 'X' was not convinced.

Based on the above, select the correct conclusion from the options given below :

options.text: 'X' is correct in the interpretation of law, including the view on non-inclusion of custom.
options.label: a

options.text: The view of 'Y' that 'law' included custom is not correct.
options.label: b

options.text: The views of both 'X' and 'Y' are correct.
options.label: c

options.text: The view of only 'Y' is correct.
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: Constitutional clause defining 'law' broadly to include ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, and customs or usages having the force of law.
keywords.concept: Article 13(3)(a): Constitutional clause defining 'law' broadly to include ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, and customs or usages having the force of law.

keywords.shortNote: Non-legislative executive instruments (rules, regulations, notifications, orders) expressly caught under the Article 13 judicial review net.
keywords.concept: Subordinate Legislation: Non-legislative executive instruments (rules, regulations, notifications, orders) expressly caught under the Article 13 judicial review net.

keywords.shortNote: The power of the Supreme Court (Art 32) and High Courts (Art 226) to strike down any 'law' inconsistent with Fundamental Rights.
keywords.concept: Judicial Review: The power of the Supreme Court (Art 32) and High Courts (Art 226) to strike down any 'law' inconsistent with Fundamental Rights.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.reference: Article 13(3)(a) of the Constitution of India
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because X incorrectly excluded 'custom or usage', directly contradicting the express textual definition of 'law' under Article 13(3)(a).

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because Y's assertion is completely accurate—Article 13(3)(a) explicitly states that 'law' includes 'custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law'.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: Synthesis of X's vs. Y's Stances
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because X and Y hold conflicting positions on the inclusion of custom; since custom is constitutionally included, X's refusal to accept it makes X wrong.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: Article 13(3)(a) of the Constitution of India
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (d) is correct. Only Y holds the legally sound view under the Constitution, as Article 13(3)(a) explicitly includes customs and usages within the definition of 'law'.

valueAddition.title: Textual & Structural Anatomy of Article 13
bullets: Article 13(1) & 13(2) (The Invalidation Clauses): Declare that all pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights become void to the extent of inconsistency (Doctrine of Eclipse / Severability), and prohibit the State from making any post-constitutional law taking away Part III rights.

Article 13(3)(a) (The Definition Clause): Explicitly defines: ''law' includes any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law'.
Article 13(3)(b) ('Laws in force'): Encompasses laws passed by a Legislature or other competent authority before the commencement of the Constitution and not previously repealed.

Article 13(4) vs. Basic Structure: Inserted by the 24th CAA, 1971 to state that Article 13 does not apply to constitutional amendments under Article 368; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) upheld this exclusion but subjected amendments to the Basic Structure doctrine.

valueAddition.title: Dialogue-Based Scenario: Tracking the Negative Elimination
bullets: Personal Law vs. Custom: In State of Bombay v. Narasu Appa Mali (1951), the Bombay High Court held that uncodified personal law is not covered under 'custom or usage' of Article 13; however, the Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed that established customs having the force of law are strictly tested against Part III.

Non-Statutory Inclusions: UPSC frequently tests whether candidates know that 'law' is not limited to parliamentary statutes; it extends downwards to executive notifications and sideways to social customs.

inNews.source: The Hindu / Supreme Court of India
inNews.headline: Supreme Court Invokes Article 13 to Strike Down Discriminatory Customary Inheritance Practices in Tribal Belts
inNews.relevance: Judicial benches examining whether exclusionary customary practices violate Articles 14 and 21 anchor their jurisdiction in Article 13(3)(a), reaffirming that customs having the force of law are directly vulnerable to Part III scrutiny.

analysis.coreTakeaway: Remember: Article 13(3)(a) explicitly defines 'law' to include custom or usage having the force of law; because X rejected custom, X's view is legally flawed, making only Y's assertion correct.

visualSuggestion.title: Components of 'Law' Under Article 13(3)(a)
visualSuggestion.caption: Notice what UPSC did here: the examiner created a seminar dialogue to test whether candidates recognize that unwritten customs and usages are explicitly included in the definition of law.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Which of the following statements with regard to the persons with disabilities in India is/are correct ?
1. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, an Act passed by the Parliament of India in 2018, mandates reservation in education and employment, places a legal duty on Governments to ensure accessibility and non-discrimination.
2. The Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan focuses on achieving universal accessibility for Persons with Disabilities across three key domains - built infrastructure, transport systems and information and communication technology.
3. The National Divyangjan Finance and Development Corporation (NDFDC) is a public sector organisation set up by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs as a not-for-profit company to promote entrepreneurship among Persons with Disabilities (PwDs).

Select the answer using the code given below :

keywords.term: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016
keywords.shortNote: Parliamentary enactment passed in December 2016 replacing the 1995 Act to enforce the UNCRPD mandate.
keywords.concept: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016: Parliamentary enactment passed in December 2016 replacing the 1995 Act to enforce the UNCRPD mandate.

keywords.shortNote: Accessible India Campaign launched in 2015 targeting barrier-free access across built spaces, transportation, and ICT.
keywords.concept: Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan: Accessible India Campaign launched in 2015 targeting barrier-free access across built spaces, transportation, and ICT.

keywords.shortNote: Apex non-profit corporation under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment offering concessional credit to Divyangjan entrepreneurs.
keywords.concept: NDFDC: Apex non-profit corporation under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment offering concessional credit to Divyangjan entrepreneurs.

keywords.shortNote: Directive Principle of State Policy directing public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness, and disablement.
keywords.concept: Article 41: Directive Principle of State Policy directing public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness, and disablement.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (b) is correct. Statement 2 accurately defines the three accessibility pillars of the Abhiyan, while Statements 1 and 3 carry factual year and ministry traps.

valueAddition.title: Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016
bullets: Official Title & Milestones: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016; passed December 2016, enforced on 19 April 2017; replaced Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995.
Constitutional & Global Anchor: Operationalizes the UNCRPD and fulfills Article 41 (State duty for public assistance in disablement) read with Articles 14 and 21.
Key Concrete Mandates: Expanded recognized disabilities from 7 to 21 categories (including acid attack victims, dwarfism, Parkinson's disease, and autism spectrum disorder).
Statutory Thresholds: Mandates minimum 4% reservation in government jobs and 5% reservation in higher educational institutions for persons with benchmark disabilities.

valueAddition.title: Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan (Accessible India Campaign)
bullets: Launch & Administrative Home: Launched on 3 December 2015 (International Day of PwDs) by DEPwD, Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.
Constitutional Mandate Fulfilled: Operationalizes Article 41 (welfare & access) and Article 15 (non-discrimination in public access spaces).

Three Target Verticals: (1) Built environment accessibility (ramps, lifts, braille signage); (2) Transportation system accessibility (railway stations, airports, buses); (3) ICT ecosystem (accessible public websites and digital platforms).
Monitoring Framework: Monitored via the Sugamya Bharat Mobile App and crowd-sourced accessibility audits enforcing Central Public Works Department (CPWD) Harmonised Guidelines.

valueAddition.title: National Divyangjan Finance and Development Corporation (NDFDC)
bullets: Corporate Identity & Locus: Incorporated in January 1997 as an apex Section 8 (not-for-profit) company under DEPwD, Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (not Corporate Affairs).
Constitutional Nexus: Implements economic empowerment goals under Article 41 (Right to work and public assistance) and Article 46 (promotion of educational and economic interests of weaker sections).
Financial Mandate: Provides concessional credit and low-interest self-employment loans channelled via State Channelising Agencies (SCAs), select Public Sector Banks, and Regional Rural Banks.
Capacity Building: Finances specialized entrepreneurship skill training programs and supports marketing infrastructure for Divyangjan micro-enterprises across India.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements about the provisions pertaining to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in India :
1. Provisions regarding the administration of the Tribal Areas in the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram are given in the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution of India.
2. Some tribes of India are entitled to exemption from paying Income Tax on certain incomes.
3. The Constitution of India provides for reservation of seats in Panchayats for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes.

Which one of the following conclusions based on the above statements is correct ?

options.text: There are two correct statements, that include statement 2.
options.label: a

options.text: There are two correct statements, that are statements 1 and 3.
options.label: b

options.text: There is only one correct statement.
options.label: c

keywords.shortNote: Article 244(1) applies the Fifth Schedule to the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in any State other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram, which are governed exclusively under the Sixth Schedule by Article 244(2).
keywords.concept: Fifth Schedule vs. Sixth Schedule (Article 244): Article 244(1) applies the Fifth Schedule to the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in any State other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram, which are governed exclusively under the Sixth Schedule by Article 244(2).

keywords.term: Section 10(26) of the Income Tax Act, 1961
keywords.shortNote: Grants statutory income-tax exemption on income accruing from any source in specified tribal areas, or through dividend/interest on securities, to members of Scheduled Tribes residing in those areas.
keywords.concept: Section 10(26) of the Income Tax Act, 1961: Grants statutory income-tax exemption on income accruing from any source in specified tribal areas, or through dividend/interest on securities, to members of Scheduled Tribes residing in those areas.

keywords.shortNote: Guarantees that not less than one-third of the total number of seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in every Panchayat shall be reserved for women belonging to those communities.
keywords.concept: Article 243D(2): Guarantees that not less than one-third of the total number of seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in every Panchayat shall be reserved for women belonging to those communities.

valueAddition.title: Fifth vs. Sixth Schedule: Core Constitutional Demarcation
bullets: Fifth Schedule Scope (Article 244(1)): Pertains to the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in any State other than the four northeastern States; currently covers Scheduled Areas in 10 States (Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Himachal Pradesh).
Sixth Schedule Scope (Article 244(2) & 275(1)): Pertains strictly to the administration of Tribal Areas in the four northeastern States: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram (AMTM).

Institutional Machinery: Fifth Schedule operates via the Tribes Advisory Council (TAC) and Governor's regulatory notifications; Sixth Schedule establishes Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) and Regional Councils with legislative, judicial, and executive powers.

Applicability of Acts: In the Fifth Schedule, Union/State laws apply automatically unless the Governor directs otherwise; in the Sixth Schedule, Acts of Parliament or State Legislature do not apply to autonomous districts, or apply with exceptions/modifications as specified by the Governor/President.

valueAddition.title: Tax Immunity & Panchayati Raj Reservations for SC/ST
bullets: Section 10(26) Income Tax Immunity: Designed to protect indigenous communities in designated Sixth Schedule areas, Nagaland, Manipur, Tripura, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, and Ladakh; reaffirmed by the Supreme Court in Association of Old Settlers of Sikkim (2023) by extending similar benefit to Sikkimese individuals under Section 10(26AAA).

Vertical & Horizontal Quotas under Article 243D: Article 243D(1) provides vertical reservation for SCs and STs in proportion to their population in the Panchayat area; Article 243D(2) provides a mandatory horizontal reservation ensuring at least one-third of these seats are reserved for SC and ST women.
Offices of Chairpersons: Article 243D(4) similarly reserves the offices of Chairpersons in Panchayats at each level for SCs, STs, and women as the State Legislature may by law provide.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Provisions regarding the administration of tribal areas in the four northeastern States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram (AMTM) are contained in the Sixth Schedule under Article 244(2), whereas the Fifth Schedule applies to Scheduled Areas in any State other than these four States.

Under Section 10(26) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, members of Scheduled Tribes residing in the Sixth Schedule areas, specified regions of the North-East, and Ladakh are exempt from paying tax on income accruing or arising to them from any source in those areas or by way of dividends or interest on securities.

Article 243D(2) explicitly provides that not less than one-third of the total number of seats reserved under clause (1) for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes shall be reserved for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes or, as the case may be, the Scheduled Tribes.

2. Starred questions are those to which a Member desires a written answer.
3. No supplementary question can be asked on an unstarred question.

Which one of the following conclusions based on the above statements is correct ?

options.text: All the three statements are correct.
options.label: a

options.text: There are two correct statements, that include statement 2.
options.label: b

options.text: There is only one correct statement.
options.label: c

keywords.shortNote: The first hour of every parliamentary sitting dedicated to holding the executive accountable through questions posed by MPs to ministers.
keywords.concept: Question Hour: The first hour of every parliamentary sitting dedicated to holding the executive accountable through questions posed by MPs to ministers.

keywords.shortNote: Distinguished by an asterisk (); requires an oral answer on the floor of the House, permitting supplementary questions.
keywords.concept: Starred Question: Distinguished by an asterisk (); requires an oral answer on the floor of the House, permitting supplementary questions.

keywords.shortNote: Requires a written reply laid on the table of the House; does not permit supplementary questions.
keywords.concept: Unstarred Question: Requires a written reply laid on the table of the House; does not permit supplementary questions.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Only Statement 3 is correct (Statements 1 and 2 interchange the definitions of starred and unstarred questions).

valueAddition.title: Taxonomy of Parliamentary Questions
bullets: Starred Questions (*): Printed on green paper in Lok Sabha; requires an oral answer; a maximum of 20 starred questions are included in the list for oral answer per day in Lok Sabha; supplementary questions can be asked.
Unstarred Questions: Printed on white paper in Lok Sabha; requires a written answer; maximum of 230 unstarred questions listed per day; no supplementary questions permitted.

Short Notice Questions: Relates to a matter of urgent public importance; asked with notice shorter than the normal minimum notice period (less than 10 days); answered orally; printed on light pink paper in Lok Sabha.

Questions to Private Members: Asked to a private member under Rule 40 when the subject matter relates to a Bill, Resolution, or matter relating to the business of the House for which that member is responsible; printed on yellow paper in Lok Sabha.

valueAddition.title: Procedural Constraints on Questions
bullets: Notice Window: Generally requires at least 10 to 15 clear days' advance notice to the Secretary-General.
Balloting: Balloting determines priority when notices exceed daily admissible ceilings.
Question Hour Timing: Typically held during the first hour of a sitting (11:00 AM to 12:00 PM in Lok Sabha; 11:00 AM to 12:00 PM in Rajya Sabha as per updated schedule).

1. Although members of this Committee are elected from both Houses of Parliament, the Chairperson of this Committee is appointed by the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
2. Twenty members are elected by the Rajya Sabha and ten members by the Lok Sabha.
3. No Minister, except for the Union Minister of Social Justice and Empowerment, is eligible to be a member of this Committee.
4. Members are elected for a fixed term of two years from the date they enter their office.

Which one of the following conclusions based on the above statements is correct ?

options.text: There is only one correct statement, that is statement 2.
options.label: b

options.text: There are two correct statements, that include statement 1.
options.label: c

keywords.term: Committee on the Welfare of SCs and STs
keywords.shortNote: A joint Parliamentary Standing Committee established in 1968 consisting of 30 members (20 Lok Sabha, 10 Rajya Sabha) to oversee safeguards and welfare programmes for SCs and STs.
keywords.concept: Committee on the Welfare of SCs and STs: A joint Parliamentary Standing Committee established in 1968 consisting of 30 members (20 Lok Sabha, 10 Rajya Sabha) to oversee safeguards and welfare programmes for SCs and STs.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Every single statement contains an explicit factual trap crafted by the examiner.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 2 swaps the quotas: Lok Sabha has 20 members while Rajya Sabha has 10.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect because the appointing authority is the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: All four statements are factually incorrect, making 'There is no correct statement' the right verdict.

valueAddition.title: Committee on SC/ST Welfare: Structural Anatomy
bullets: Genesis: Created in 1968 on the recommendation of the Elayaperumal Committee.
Composition: 30 MPs (20 LS + 10 RS) elected by proportional representation via single transferable vote (PR-STV).
Appointment & Term: Speaker of Lok Sabha appoints the Chairperson; tenure does not exceed one year.
Core Mandate: Scrutinizes annual reports of NCSC (Art. 338) and NCST (Art. 338A), and audits reservation implementation in central services, PSUs, and Union Territories.

statementBreakdown.reference: Rules of Procedure in Lok Sabha / Parliamentary Conventions
statementBreakdown.explanation: The Chairperson of the Committee is appointed by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha from amongst its members, not by the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
The ratio is exactly reversed: 20 members are elected from the Lok Sabha and 10 members are elected from the Rajya Sabha via proportional representation by single transferable vote.
There is an absolute bar on executive participation: no Minister whatsoever is eligible to be elected or continue as a member of the Committee.
Members are elected for a term of one year, not a fixed term of two years; the committee is reconstituted annually.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Which of the following statements about a Zero First Information Report (Zero FIR) under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 is/are correct ?
1. A Zero FIR can be lodged at a police station, even though the place of commission of a cognizable/non-cognizable offence is outside the territorial jurisdiction of that police station.
2. The Officer-in-Charge of the police station where a Zero FIR has been lodged may, with the permission of the competent authority, initiate preliminary enquiry.
3. Under Zero FIR, it is obligatory for the informant to furnish information electronically.

Select the answer using the code given below :

keywords.term: Zero FIR under Section 173(1) of BNSS
keywords.shortNote: Statutory codification mandating registration of information relating to a cognizable offence irrespective of the area where the offence was committed, numbered temporarily as '0' before transfer to the competent police station.
keywords.concept: Zero FIR under Section 173(1) of BNSS: Statutory codification mandating registration of information relating to a cognizable offence irrespective of the area where the offence was committed, numbered temporarily as '0' before transfer to the competent police station.

keywords.shortNote: An FIR (including a Zero FIR) applies exclusively to cognizable offences; non-cognizable offences are recorded separately in the Non-Cognizable Report (NCR) diary under Section 174 of BNSS.
keywords.concept: Cognizable vs. Non-Cognizable Scope: An FIR (including a Zero FIR) applies exclusively to cognizable offences; non-cognizable offences are recorded separately in the Non-Cognizable Report (NCR) diary under Section 174 of BNSS.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Zero FIR does not cover non-cognizable offences, and electronic reporting is not compulsory.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Electronic mode is an option under Section 173, not an obligatory requirement.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 introduces the fatal distractor 'non-cognizable offence'.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Only statement 2 accurately reflects the statutory preliminary enquiry mechanism under Section 173(3) of BNSS.

valueAddition.title: Codification of Zero FIR in BNSS, 2023
bullets: Historical Origin: Originated as an administrative recommendation following the Justice J.S. Verma Committee Report (2013) and Supreme Court directives in Lalita Kumari (2014) to prevent delay in medical care and evidence collection.

Statutory Recognition: Section 173(1) of the BNSS formally codifies Zero FIR into parliamentary statute, stating information regarding a cognizable offence can be lodged 'irrespective of the area where the offence was committed'.

Transfer Protocol: The receiving police station registers it without assigning a regular territorial number (marked as Serial No. '0'), carries out urgent initial steps (medical aid, crime scene preservation), and immediately transfers the file to the jurisdictional station.

valueAddition.title: Key Procedural Shifts under Section 173 of BNSS
bullets: Preliminary Enquiry Window (Sec. 173(3)): For offences punishable with imprisonment of 3 to 7 years, the Officer-in-Charge may, with prior permission of an officer not below DSP rank, conduct a preliminary enquiry within 14 days before proceeding to investigate.
Electronic Communication (e-FIR): Information given electronically is permitted, but the informant must sign it within three days before it is formally registered as an FIR.
Mandatory Copy to Informant: A copy of the FIR must be provided immediately to the informant or the victim free of cost, either physically or electronically.

inNews.source: PIB / Ministry of Home Affairs
inNews.headline: Nationwide integration of CCTNS enables seamless transfer of Zero FIRs across state police borders under BNSS
inNews.relevance: Directly operationalizes Section 173 of the BNSS, facilitating digital cross-jurisdiction transfer of Zero FIRs and mandatory 3-day verification loops.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Section 173(1) explicitly applies to 'every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence'. A Zero FIR cannot be registered for a non-cognizable offence, which is governed by Section 174 (information entered into the diary with informant referred to the Magistrate). Inclusion of 'non-cognizable' invalidates the statement.

Section 173(3) of the BNSS introduces an enabling provision allowing the Officer-in-Charge of a police station, with the prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police, to conduct a preliminary enquiry within fourteen days to ascertain whether a prima facie case exists before proceeding further in cases punishable with imprisonment of 3 to 7 years.

Furnishing information electronically (e-FIR) is an optional and permitted mode, not an obligatory one. Information may be given orally or in writing. When given electronically, it must be taken on record and signed by the informant within three days.

rows: Within territorial jurisdiction of police station
Any police station irrespective of territorial limits
Numbered as '0'; initial urgent steps, then transferred
Entered in station diary; informant referred to Magistrate
Permitted for 3-7 yr offences with DSP nod (14 days)

hook.teaser: Here is the exact criminal law trap UPSC framed in 2026.

keywords.calloutNote: FIRs apply strictly to cognizable offences—non-cognizable crimes are recorded under Section 174 NCR.
activePhrases: cognizable/non-cognizable offence is outside the territorial jurisdiction

keywords.term: obligatory for the informant to furnish information electronically
keywords.calloutNote: Electronic reporting is an optional convenience under Section 173, never a mandatory requirement.
activePhrases: obligatory for the informant to furnish information electronically
dimmedPhrases: cognizable/non-cognizable offence is outside the territorial jurisdiction

verdicts.source: Section 173(1) of BNSS applies strictly to cognizable offences; non-cognizable matters cannot be an FIR.
With DSP permission, a preliminary enquiry within 14 days can be conducted for 3-7 year offences.
Information can be given orally, in writing, or electronically; electronic mode is never obligatory.

answer.label: D
answer.text: Statement 2 only is correct, making (d) the right answer.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your BNSS & Criminal Procedure notes

items.desc: Mandates registering cognizable offence information irrespective of territorial jurisdiction.

stem:
With reference to the organisations under the Government of India, consider the following details :

Sl. No. | Organisation | Function | Controlling Union Ministry
1. | Central Economic Intelligence Bureau (CEIB) | To coordinate between various law enforcement agencies | Ministry of Home Affairs
2. | Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) | To investigate complex corporate frauds | Ministry of Finance
3. | Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) | To preserve values in public life and ensure the health of the national economy | Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions

In how many of the above rows are the given details correctly matched ?

keywords.shortNote: Apex coordinating and intelligence agency for economic offenses, set up in 1985 under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance.
keywords.concept: Central Economic Intelligence Bureau (CEIB): Apex coordinating and intelligence agency for economic offenses, set up in 1985 under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance.

keywords.shortNote: Statutory multi-disciplinary corporate fraud investigation body established under Section 211 of the Companies Act, 2013, under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.
keywords.concept: Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO): Statutory multi-disciplinary corporate fraud investigation body established under Section 211 of the Companies Act, 2013, under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.

keywords.shortNote: Premier investigating agency deriving police powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946, functioning under the DoPT, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.
keywords.concept: Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI): Premier investigating agency deriving police powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946, functioning under the DoPT, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Identifies that only Row 3 has all details (Organisation, Function, and Controlling Union Ministry) correctly matched.

valueAddition.title: Central Economic Intelligence Bureau (CEIB): Institutional Profile
bullets: Establishment: Created in 1985 based on recommendations of the Committee on Economic Intelligence.
Ministry: Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance.
Role: Apex intelligence gathering, coordination, and nodal agency for all economic offenses (tax evasion, trade fraud, customs duty evasion, and hawala).
Inter-Agency Coordination: Manages the Economic Intelligence Council (EIC) chaired by the Union Finance Minister and the Regional Economic Intelligence Committees (REICs).

valueAddition.title: Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO): Statutory Framework
bullets: Genesis: Established in 2003 via executive resolution following the Naresh Chandra Committee and Vittal Committee recommendations; gained statutory backing under Section 211 of the Companies Act, 2013.
Controlling Ministry: Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA).
Multi-Disciplinary Nature: Staffed with experts from forensic auditing, taxation, banking, law, capital markets, and information technology.

Investigation Scope: Cases are assigned exclusively by the Central Government (Section 212) when corporate fraud involves public interest, large-scale financial diversion, or severe inter-departmental complexity.

valueAddition.title: Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI): Legal Foundation & Dual Supervision
bullets: Statutory Root: Derives its investigating authority and jurisdiction from the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946.
Administrative Parent: Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.

Superintendence Split: Under Section 4(1) of the DSPE Act, superintendence over corruption offenses under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 vests in the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC); superintendence in all other matters vests in the Central Government (DoPT).

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements with reference to the Constitution of India :
1. There is no Article in the Constitution of India that specifies that the Constitution of India will be officially called the 'Constitution of India'.
2. There is no Article in the Constitution of India that specifies that the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935 stand repealed.
3. There is no Article in the Constitution of India that mentions 26th January, 1950 as the date of the commencement of the Constitution of India.

Which one of the following conclusions based on the above statements is correct ?

options.text: There are two correct statements that include statement 3.
options.label: c

options.text: There is only one correct statement.
options.label: d

analysis.coreTakeaway: Remember: Part XXII (Articles 393–395) explicitly covers these exact three provisions: Article 393 names the Constitution, Article 394 fixes commencement on 26 January 1950, and Article 395 repeals the British-era Acts.

keywords.shortNote: The official short title of the supreme legal document explicitly designated by Article 393.
keywords.concept: Constitution of India: The official short title of the supreme legal document explicitly designated by Article 393.

keywords.shortNote: British statute creating the Dominions of India and Pakistan, expressly repealed by Article 395.
keywords.concept: Indian Independence Act, 1947: British statute creating the Dominions of India and Pakistan, expressly repealed by Article 395.

keywords.shortNote: Colonial constitutional framework repealed alongside all its amending enactments under Article 395.
keywords.concept: Government of India Act, 1935: Colonial constitutional framework repealed alongside all its amending enactments under Article 395.

keywords.shortNote: The official date of commencement expressly named in Article 394 of the Constitution.
keywords.concept: 26th January, 1950: The official date of commencement expressly named in Article 394 of the Constitution.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because all three stem statements are factually incorrect per Articles 393, 395, and 394.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Since Statements 1, 2, and 3 are all false, the conclusion that 'there is no correct statement' is the winning answer.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because Statement 3 is false, and there are zero correct statements overall.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because not even one statement is correct; all three are contradicted by Part XXII.

valueAddition.title: Part XXII: The Finishing Provisions of the Constitution
bullets: Article 393 (Short Title): Formally declares the official name: 'This Constitution may be called the Constitution of India.'

Article 394 (Two-Stage Commencement): Put 16 transitional provisions into effect immediately on 26 November 1949 (Articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393, and 394 itself), while bringing the remaining provisions into force on 26 January 1950.
Article 395 (Clean Legal Break): Repealed the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935, but specifically preserved the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949.

valueAddition.title: Common Exam Trap: Preamble vs. Article 394
bullets: Notice the trap: The Preamble records 26 November 1949 as the date of adoption, enactment, and giving to ourselves this Constitution.
It is Article 394—not the Preamble—that legally designates 26 January 1950 as the official 'date of commencement' to honor Purna Swaraj Day (1930).
Aspirants often assume basic titling and repeals are outside the text, but Part XXII cleanly severs British parliamentary sovereignty.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 is false. Article 393 explicitly confers the official title: 'This Constitution may be called the Constitution of India.'

statementBreakdown.reference: Article 395 of the Constitution of India

statementBreakdown.reference: Article 394 of the Constitution of India
statementBreakdown.explanation: Statement 3 is false. Article 394 explicitly specifies 26th January, 1950 as the official 'date of commencement of this Constitution'.

valueAddition.title: Operational Formations & Corps Architecture
bullets: Hierarchical Structure: Command (headed by Army Commander / Lt. Gen) → Corps (headed by GOC / Lt. Gen) → Division (headed by GOC / Maj. Gen) → Brigade (headed by Brigadier) → Battalion (headed by Colonel).

Holding vs Strike Corps: Holding (pivot) corps hold ground along borders and absorb enemy offensives (e.g., 14, 15, 16, 3, 4, 33 Corps); Strike corps possess offensive mechanized depth for penetration (e.g., 1, 2, 21, and 17 Mountain Strike Corps).

15 Corps vs 33 Corps: 15 Corps (Chinar Corps) is headquartered at Badami Bagh, Srinagar (guarding the Kashmir Valley and LoC); 33 Corps (Trishakti Corps) is based at Sukna (guarding the Siliguri Corridor and Sikkim LAC).

valueAddition.title: Key Border Corps & Operational Sectors
bullets: 14 Corps (Fire and Fury Corps): Leh (Ladakh) — Karakoram, Siachen Glacier, Kargil, and eastern LAC.
15 Corps (Chinar Corps): Srinagar (J&K) — Kashmir Valley and Line of Control.
16 Corps (White Knight Corps): Nagrota/Jammu (J&K) — Jammu sector and Pir Panjal range.
33 Corps (Trishakti Corps): Sukna/Siliguri (West Bengal) — Sikkim, Doklam plateau, and Siliguri Corridor.
4 Corps (Gajraj Corps): Tezpur (Assam) — Tawang, Kameng, and western Arunachal Pradesh.
3 Corps (Spear Corps): Dimapur (Nagaland) — Nagaland, Manipur, and eastern frontiers.

inNews.source: PIB / Ministry of Defence

statementBreakdown.explanation: 3 Corps (Spear Corps) is headquartered at Rangapahar Military Station, Dimapur (Nagaland), overseeing counter-insurgency and the India-Myanmar border in the Northeast.
4 Corps (Gajraj Corps) is headquartered at Tezpur (Assam), tasked with the defence of the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in the Kameng sector and western Arunachal Pradesh.
14 Corps (Fire and Fury Corps) is headquartered at Leh (Ladakh), responsible for the high-altitude frontier facing China in Eastern Ladakh (LAC) and Pakistan in Siachen/Kargil (LoC).

keywords.concept: Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan (RGSA): A Centrally Sponsored Scheme approved by the CCEA for 2022–23 to 2025–26 to strengthen the governance and administrative capabilities of PRIs around Localization of Sustainable Development Goals (LSDGs).

keywords.shortNote: The framework of thematic convergence translating 17 global SDGs into 9 aggregate village-level themes implemented by Gram Panchayats.

valueAddition.title: Revamped Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan (RGSA): Core Architecture
bullets: Official Title, Enactment & Duration: Approved by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) on 13 April 2022 for implementation from 1 April 2022 to 31 March 2026, with an outlay of ₹5,911 crore.
Predecessor Scheme: Succeeded the original RGSA (implemented from 2018–19 to 2021–22).
Constitutional Mandate: Fulfills the democratic decentralization goals of Part IX (73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992) and Article 40 (Organization of village panchayats).
Financing Pattern: Centrally Sponsored Scheme; Central share is ₹3,700 crore and State share is ₹2,211 crore (60:40 for general States; 90:10 for NE & Himalayan States; 100% for UTs).
Nodal Administrative Machinery: Implemented by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj in collaboration with State Panchayati Raj Departments and State Institutes of Rural Development (SIRDs).

valueAddition.title: Nine Themes of Localization of SDGs (LSDGs) at Panchayat Level
bullets: Theme 1: Poverty-free and enhanced livelihoods village.
Theme 2: Healthy village.
Theme 3: Child-friendly village.
Theme 4: Water-sufficient village.
Theme 5: Clean and green village.
Theme 6: Self-sufficient infrastructure in village.
Theme 7: Socially just and socially secured village.
Theme 8: Village with good governance.
Theme 9: Engendered development in village.

optionBreakdown.label: I
optionBreakdown.explanation: Verbatim from the DAHD RGM framework: Over 80% of low-producing, non-descript indigenous bovine animals in India are owned by small and marginal farmers and landless labourers. Genetically upgrading these animals directly boosts rural women's and marginal households' incomes with minimal feed-cost escalation.

optionBreakdown.label: II
optionBreakdown.explanation: Launched in December 2014 under the National Programme for Bovine Breeding and Dairy Development (NPBBDD), RGM aims to conserve and develop indigenous 'bovine' breeds in a scientific and holistic manner. Crucially, in official veterinary and scheme terminology, 'bovines' encompasses both indigenous cattle (Bos indicus) and buffaloes (Bubalus bubalis).

analysis.valueAddition:
Revised Rashtriya Gokul Mission norms (Central Sector component under Rashtriya Pashudhan Vikas Yojana; ₹3,400 crore outlay for 2021–26, as of October 2026):
• 100% grant-in-aid for central breeding components & nationwide free doorstep Artificial Insemination.
• 50% capital subsidy (up to ₹2 crore) for Breed Multiplication Farms.
• 35% capital subsidy for new Heifer Rearing Centres (15,000 heifers across 30 facilities).
• 3% interest subvention on loans for farmers buying High Genetic Merit (HGM) IVF heifers.
• 'Gokul Grams' operate as integrated cattle centres (40% unproductive + 60% productive stock) on a zero-waste circular model.

stem:
With reference to investments, consider the following :
I. Bonds
II. Hedge Funds
III. Stocks
IV. Venture Capital

How many of the above are treated as Alternative Investment Funds ?

keywords.shortNote: A privately pooled investment vehicle established or incorporated in India that collects funds from sophisticated investors for investing in accordance with a defined investment policy, outside standard retail collective investment schemes.
keywords.concept: Alternative Investment Fund: A privately pooled investment vehicle established or incorporated in India that collects funds from sophisticated investors for investing in accordance with a defined investment policy, outside standard retail collective investment schemes.

keywords.shortNote: A Category I AIF that pools capital primarily to invest in unlisted early-stage startups, emerging technological ventures, or early-growth enterprises.
keywords.concept: Venture Capital Fund: A Category I AIF that pools capital primarily to invest in unlisted early-stage startups, emerging technological ventures, or early-growth enterprises.

keywords.shortNote: A Category III AIF that employs diverse, complex trading strategies including leverage, derivatives, short-selling, and arbitrage to generate absolute returns.
keywords.concept: Hedge Fund: A Category III AIF that employs diverse, complex trading strategies including leverage, derivatives, short-selling, and arbitrage to generate absolute returns.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Identifies only one AIF asset class, missing the second eligible pooled fund.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Exactly two of the four listed instruments—Hedge Funds (II) and Venture Capital (IV)—are treated as Alternative Investment Funds under SEBI regulations.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Incorrectly classifies traditional public capital market instruments (stocks or bonds) as alternative pooled vehicles.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Conflates underlying primary asset classes (stocks and bonds) with specialized private pooled fund vehicles (AIFs).

valueAddition.title: SEBI Three-Tier AIF Classification Architecture
bullets: Category I AIF: Funds investing in startups, early-stage ventures, social ventures, SMEs, and infrastructure that the government or regulators consider socially or economically desirable (e.g., Venture Capital Funds, Angel Funds, Infrastructure Funds).

Category II AIF: Funds that do not undertake leverage or borrowing other than to meet day-to-day operational requirements and do not fall under Category I or III (e.g., Private Equity Funds, Real Estate Funds, Debt Funds).

Category III AIF: Funds that employ diverse or complex trading strategies and may employ leverage, including through investment in listed or unlisted derivatives (e.g., Hedge Funds, Long-Short Equity Funds).

valueAddition.title: AIF Operating Norms in India
bullets: Minimum Ticket Size: Individual investors must commit a minimum investment of ₹1 crore (reduced to ₹25 lakh for employees/directors of the AIF or fund manager, and ₹25 lakh for Angel Funds).
Private Placement Only: AIFs cannot solicit public subscriptions through open advertisements; units must be placed privately with accredited investors, HNIs, and institutional funds.
Cap on Investors: A standard AIF scheme cannot have more than 1,000 investors (capped at 200 investors in the case of Angel Funds).

inNews.source: Securities and Exchange Board of India / Financial Express
inNews.headline: SEBI Mandates Dematerialization and Standardized Valuation Norms for Category I and II Alternative Investment Funds
inNews.relevance: New regulatory directions enforce demat holding for all AIF investments, improving audit transparency and secondary liquidity tracking for domestic venture capital and private equity investors.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Bonds are traditional fixed-income debt securities issued directly by sovereigns or corporations; they are foundational capital market instruments, not pooled alternative investment vehicles.
Hedge funds are explicitly classified under Indian securities regulations as Category III Alternative Investment Funds.
Stocks (equities) represent fractional ownership in a joint-stock company traded on public bourses; they constitute standard public market assets rather than AIF vehicles.
Venture capital funds are formally categorized under SEBI regulations as Category I Alternative Investment Funds, focused on startup and early-stage capital formation.

Hedge funds are formally regulated under SEBI rules as Category III Alternative Investment Funds.
Stocks are standard equity shares traded on public bourses, not private AIF structures.
Venture capital funds are classified by SEBI as Category I Alternative Investment Funds.

answer.label: B
