keywords.shortNote: The obligation of public officials to answer for the execution of their responsibilities, report infractions, and subject administrative actions to statutory oversight and vigilance scrutiny.
keywords.concept: Accountability in Public Administration: The obligation of public officials to answer for the execution of their responsibilities, report infractions, and subject administrative actions to statutory oversight and vigilance scrutiny.

keywords.shortNote: The ethical duty under the Nolan Principles and Second ARC where a public servant resists illicit pressure, halts fraudulent contracts, and exposes malfeasance to protect citizen welfare.
keywords.concept: Public Interest over Vested Interests: The ethical duty under the Nolan Principles and Second ARC where a public servant resists illicit pressure, halts fraudulent contracts, and exposes malfeasance to protect citizen welfare.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: 'Esprit de corps' denotes fostering team spirit, harmony, and mutual unity among colleagues within an organisation, rather than reporting contract irregularities or escalating matters to vigilance bodies.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: 'Equity' focuses on fairness, impartiality, and social justice in the distribution of public services and treatment of citizens, which is not the primary institutional mechanism demonstrated by whistleblowing and contract termination.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: Second ARC (4th Report: Ethics in Governance) & Nolan Committee Standards
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accountability requires public officials to take full responsibility for programme integrity, answer to statutory standards, report lapses to competent vigilance authorities, and subordinate personal/vested pressures to the public interest.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: 'Delegation' involves entrusting operational authority and duties from a superior to a subordinate manager, which is unrelated to halting contracts or reporting misconduct.

valueAddition.title: Nolan Committee's Seven Principles of Public Life
bullets: Selflessness: Holders of public office must act solely in terms of the public interest.
Integrity: Holders of public office must avoid placing themselves under financial or other obligations to outside individuals or organisations.
Objectivity: Decisions regarding public contracts, awards, or recommendations must be based entirely on merit.
Accountability: Public office holders are accountable to the public for their decisions and actions, and must submit themselves to appropriate scrutiny.
Openness: Information should be withheld only when the wider public interest clearly demands it.
Honesty: Duty to declare any private interests relating to public duties and resolve conflicts in a way that protects the public interest.
Leadership: Holders of public office should promote and support these principles by leadership and example.

valueAddition.title: Henri Fayol's Administrative Principles Tested in Options
bullets: Esprit de Corps: Harmony and cohesion among personnel; union is strength.
Equity: Combination of kindliness and justice when dealing with subordinates to elicit loyalty.
Delegation / Authority & Responsibility: Right to give orders paired with the concomitant obligation to assume responsibility.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
With reference to the Indian polity, consider the following statements :
I. An Ordinance can amend any Central Act.
II. An Ordinance can abridge a Fundamental Right.
III. An Ordinance can come into effect from a back date.

Which of the statements given above are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: An Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, meaning it can alter, modify, amend, or repeal any existing Central Act within Parliament's legislative competence.
keywords.concept: Co-extensive Legislative Power (Article 123(2)): An Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, meaning it can alter, modify, amend, or repeal any existing Central Act within Parliament's legislative competence.

keywords.shortNote: Article 123(3) expressly declares that if an Ordinance makes any provision which Parliament would not under this Constitution be competent to enact, it shall be void; Article 13(3)(a) explicitly includes 'ordinance' in the definition of law, making it subject to Fundamental Rights.
keywords.concept: Fundamental Rights Injunction (Article 13(2) & 123(3)): Article 123(3) expressly declares that if an Ordinance makes any provision which Parliament would not under this Constitution be competent to enact, it shall be void; Article 13(3)(a) explicitly includes 'ordinance' in the definition of law, making it subject to Fundamental Rights.

keywords.shortNote: Because an Ordinance possesses the plenary power of a Parliamentary Act, it can be given retrospective effect (come into effect from a back date), subject to Article 20(1) criminal law safeguards.
keywords.concept: Retrospective Operation: Because an Ordinance possesses the plenary power of a Parliamentary Act, it can be given retrospective effect (come into effect from a back date), subject to Article 20(1) criminal law safeguards.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Combines verified Statements I and III while correctly excluding Statement II.

valueAddition.title: Article 123 & 213: Ordinance Scope & Boundaries
bullets: Co-extensiveness: The Ordinance-making power is co-extensive with the legislative powers of Parliament (Union and Concurrent lists, or State list under Arts. 249, 250, 252, 253).

Subordination to Constitution: An Ordinance is subject to all constitutional limitations that circumscribe an Act of Parliament; it cannot amend the Constitution itself, nor can it override Part III (Fundamental Rights).

Temporal Mechanics: Must be laid before both Houses upon reassembly; lapses 6 weeks from the date of reassembly unless approved earlier, or ceases to operate upon resolutions of disapproval passed by both Houses.
Retrospective Legislation: An Ordinance can amend laws retrospectively and validate past acts, subject only to Article 20(1) (Protection in respect of conviction for offences).

valueAddition.title: Landmark Judicial Precedents on Ordinances
bullets: R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970): The President's satisfaction regarding the existence of circumstances warranting immediate action can be challenged in court on grounds of mala fides.
A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982): Reaffirmed that an Ordinance is 'law' under Article 21, but is fully vulnerable to constitutional challenges on Fundamental Rights violations.

D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) & Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017): Re-promulgation of Ordinances without tabling them before the legislature constitutes a fraud on the Constitution and subversion of democratic legislative process.

inNews.relevance: Directly highlights that an ordinance cannot transcend constitutional limitations, abridge Part III rights, or bypass legislative presentation.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Because an Ordinance is co-extensive with an Act of Parliament in terms of legislative capacity, it can amend or repeal any existing Central Act, provided the subject matter lies within the legislative competence of Parliament.

Article 123(3) read with Article 13(2) bars an Ordinance from violating, abridging, or taking away any Fundamental Right. 'Law' under Article 13(3)(a) explicitly includes Ordinances, rendering any infringing provision void.

statementBreakdown.reference: Supreme Court of India (A.K. Roy v. Union of India, 1982)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Like an Act of Parliament, an Ordinance can be promulgated with retrospective effect (i.e., taking effect from a past date), provided it does not violate the constitutional bar on retrospective criminal legislation under Article 20(1).

bullets: Nagaland (16th State, 1963): Carved out of the Naga Hills-Tuensang Area via the State of Nagaland Act, 1962, grounded constitutionally in the 13th Amendment Act, 1962 (Article 371A).
Manipur, Meghalaya & Tripura (1972): Granted full statehood under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971, raising the count of Indian States to 21 on 21 January 1972.
Sikkim (22nd State, 1975): Elevated from 'Associate State' (35th Amendment Act, 1974) to full-fledged statehood via the 36th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1975 (Article 371F).
Mizoram (23rd State, 1987): Elevated from a Union Territory to a full State following the 53rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1986 (Article 371G) and the Mizoram Peace Accord.

Arunachal Pradesh (24th State, 1987): Transitioned from North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA) to Union Territory in 1972, and achieved full statehood via the 55th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1986 (Article 371H).

valueAddition.title: Part C States Transition Matrix (1950 to 1956)
bullets: 1950 Fourfold Classification: Part A (9 Governor's provinces), Part B (9 Princely States with Rajpramukhs), Part C (10 Chief Commissioner's provinces & small Princely States), Part D (Andaman and Nicobar Islands).

Abolition in 1956: The 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956 abolished the distinction between Part A and Part B states, eliminated Part C states, and replaced them with 14 States and 6 Union Territories.

Part C States converted into UTs in 1956: Delhi, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Tripura, and Bilaspur (which merged into Himachal Pradesh in 1954), while Ajmer, Bhopal, Coorg, Kutch, and Vindhya Pradesh were merged into adjoining larger states.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
With reference to India, consider the following :
I. The Inter-State Council
II. The National Security Council
III. Zonal Councils

How many of the above were established as per the provisions of the Constitution of India ?

keywords.shortNote: A constitutional body established under Article 263 by presidential order upon the recommendation of the Sarkaria Commission to investigate, discuss, and deliberate on subjects of common interest between the Union and the States.
keywords.concept: The Inter-State Council: A constitutional body established under Article 263 by presidential order upon the recommendation of the Sarkaria Commission to investigate, discuss, and deliberate on subjects of common interest between the Union and the States.

keywords.shortNote: A non-statutory executive body established in 1998 by an executive order/Cabinet resolution under the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) to advise the Prime Minister on political, economic, energy, and strategic security.
keywords.concept: The National Security Council (NSC): A non-statutory executive body established in 1998 by an executive order/Cabinet resolution under the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) to advise the Prime Minister on political, economic, energy, and strategic security.

keywords.shortNote: Statutory bodies established under Part III (Sections 15–22) of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (along with the North-Eastern Council established under the NEC Act, 1971), not by the Constitution of India.
keywords.concept: Zonal Councils: Statutory bodies established under Part III (Sections 15–22) of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (along with the North-Eastern Council established under the NEC Act, 1971), not by the Constitution of India.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Only one body (The Inter-State Council under Article 263) was established as per the provisions of the Constitution of India.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Incorrectly presumes two bodies are constitutional, typically by confusing the statutory Zonal Councils with constitutional bodies.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Neither the NSC (executive) nor the Zonal Councils (statutory) have any constitutional foundation.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Incorrect because the Inter-State Council is an express constitutional body under Article 263.

valueAddition.title: Inter-State Council (Article 263)
bullets: Constitutional Mandate: Article 263 empowers the President to establish an Inter-State Council if at any time it appears that the public interests would be served by its establishment.

Functions: Inquiring into and advising upon disputes between States (complementary to Article 131), and investigating and discussing subjects of common interest to make policy coordination recommendations.

Composition: Chaired by the Prime Minister; members comprise Chief Ministers of all States, Chief Ministers of UTs with legislative assemblies, Administrators of other UTs, and six Union Cabinet ministers nominated by the PM.

valueAddition.title: Zonal Councils: Statutory Framework
bullets: States Reorganisation Act, 1956: Created five Zonal Councils (Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, Southern).
North-Eastern Council: Created separately by a dedicated Act—the North-Eastern Council Act, 1971 (comprising Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Tripura, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, and Sikkim).
Common Chairman: The Union Home Minister acts as the common Chairman of all five Zonal Councils as well as the North-Eastern Council.
Vice-Chairman: Chief Ministers of the member States within the zone act as Vice-Chairman by annual rotation.

valueAddition.title: National Security Council (NSC) Architecture
bullets: Three-Tier Structure: Strategic Policy Group (SPG), National Security Advisory Board (NSAB), and National Security Council Secretariat (NSCS).
Apex Leadership: Chaired by the Prime Minister; core members include Ministers of Home Affairs, Defence, External Affairs, and Finance, with the NSA as Secretary.
Completely Executive: Originates purely in a government resolution, operating as an apex advisory agency under the PMO.

similarPyq.stem: Consider the following organizations/bodies in India: 1. The National Commission for Backward Classes 2. The National Human Rights Commission 3. The National Law Commission 4. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission. How many of the above are constitutional bodies?

statementBreakdown.explanation: The Inter-State Council is established under Article 263 of the Constitution of India. It was formally set up by a Presidential Order in 1990 pursuant to the recommendations of the Sarkaria Commission (1988).

The National Security Council (NSC) is an executive body created by the Government of India in 1998, presided over by the Prime Minister with the National Security Advisor (NSA) as its secretary. It has neither constitutional backing nor an underlying statutory Act.

Zonal Councils are statutory bodies, not constitutional bodies. They were established under Sections 15 to 22 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, dividing the country into five zones (Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, and Southern).

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements :
I. The Constitution of India explicitly mentions that in certain spheres the Governor of a State acts in his/her own discretion.
II. The President of India can, of his/her own, reserve a bill passed by a State Legislature for his/her consideration without it being forwarded by the Governor of the State concerned.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: Explicit textual recognition that the Governor acts on aid and advice except in so far as he is by or under the Constitution required to exercise functions in his discretion.
keywords.concept: Constitutional Discretion (Article 163(1)): Explicit textual recognition that the Governor acts on aid and advice except in so far as he is by or under the Constitution required to exercise functions in his discretion.

keywords.shortNote: Article 200 empowers the Governor to reserve a State Bill for the consideration of the President; the President cannot unilaterally take cognizance or reserve a State Bill without gubernatorial transmission.
keywords.concept: Reservation of State Bills (Articles 200 & 201): Article 200 empowers the Governor to reserve a State Bill for the consideration of the President; the President cannot unilaterally take cognizance or reserve a State Bill without gubernatorial transmission.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Identifies Statement I as the sole correct statement.

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Discretion: Governor (Art. 163) vs. President (Art. 74)
bullets: Explicit Discretion: Article 163(1) contains express constitutional wording for gubernatorial discretion ('except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to act in his discretion'); Article 74(1) contains no equivalent phrase for the President.

Finality of Discretion: Under Article 163(2), if any question arises whether a matter falls within the Governor's discretion, the decision of the Governor in his discretion shall be final and cannot be called into question.

Special Discretionary Spheres: Includes Article 371A (Nagaland law and order), Article 371J (Kalyana-Karnataka regional board), Paragraph 9(2) of the Sixth Schedule (licensing royalties between district councils and state government), and Sixth Schedule Paragraph 18 (administration of tribal areas in Assam as agent of President).

valueAddition.title: Articles 200 and 201: Procedural Pipeline of State Bills
bullets: Article 200 Gubernatorial Choices: Assent, withhold assent, return for reconsideration (non-money bills), or reserve for the consideration of the President.
Mandatory Reservation: Second proviso to Article 200 makes reservation mandatory if a Bill derogates from the powers of the High Court so as to endanger its constitutional position.

Article 201 Presidential Prerogatives: When a Bill is reserved by the Governor, the President may declare assent, withhold assent, or direct the Governor to return it to the State Legislature. If re-passed by the State Legislature, the President is still not obliged to give assent (unlike the Governor under Article 200).

inNews.relevance: Directly scrutinizes the constitutional boundary between gubernatorial discretion and presidential consideration under Articles 200 and 201.

similarPyq.stem:
Which of the following are the discretionary powers given to the Governor of a State?
1. Sending a report to the President of India for imposing the President's rule
2. Appointing the Ministers
3. Reserving certain bills passed by the State Legislature for consideration of the President of India
4. Making the rules to conduct the business of the State Government
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
(a) 1 and 2 only
(b) 1 and 3 only
(c) 2, 3 and 4 only
(d) 1, 2, 3 and 4
similarPyq.keyTakeaway: Tests the explicit demarcation between the Governor's constitutional discretionary powers (Articles 356, 200) and powers bound by cabinet aid and advice (Articles 164, 166).

statementBreakdown.explanation: Article 163(1) explicitly provides that there shall be a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the Governor, 'except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion'. Article 163(2) further makes the Governor's decision on whether a matter falls in his discretion final.

Under Article 200, the reservation of a State Bill is an act performed exclusively by the Governor. Under Article 201, the President's jurisdiction is triggered only 'when a Bill is reserved by a Governor for the consideration of the President'; the President has no suo motu power to reserve a State Bill.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following pairs :

Provision in the Constitution of India | Stated under
I. Separation of Judiciary from the Executive in the public services of the State | The Directive Principles of the State Policy
II. Valuing and preserving of the rich heritage of our composite culture | The Fundamental Duties
III. Prohibition of employment of children below the age of 14 years in factories | The Fundamental Rights

How many of the above pairs are correctly matched ?

keywords.shortNote: Article 50 directive in Part IV mandating the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services.
keywords.concept: Separation of Judiciary: Article 50 directive in Part IV mandating the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services.

keywords.shortNote: Article 51A(f) civic duty in Part IV-A obligating every citizen to value and preserve the rich heritage of India's composite culture.
keywords.concept: Composite Culture: Article 51A(f) civic duty in Part IV-A obligating every citizen to value and preserve the rich heritage of India's composite culture.

keywords.shortNote: Article 24 fundamental right in Part III prohibiting the employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines, or hazardous occupations.
keywords.concept: Child Labour Prohibition: Article 24 fundamental right in Part III prohibiting the employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines, or hazardous occupations.

keywords.shortNote: The fundamental structural division between enforceable rights (Part III), state governance directives (Part IV), and citizen duties (Part IV-A).
keywords.concept: Tripartite Classification: The fundamental structural division between enforceable rights (Part III), state governance directives (Part IV), and citizen duties (Part IV-A).

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: Synthesis of Pairs I, II & III
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (c) is correct because each of the three constitutional provisions is paired with its precise constitutional chapter (Part IV, Part IV-A, and Part III respectively).

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Trinity: Rights, Directives & Civic Obligations
bullets: Part III (Negative Injunctions & Fundamental Protections): Article 24 provides an absolute prohibition against child labour in hazardous occupations; unlike Article 23, Article 24 does not allow exceptions for compulsory state service.

Part IV (Positive Governance Directives): Article 50 embodies the doctrine of separation of powers, operationalized at the procedural level through the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973 (and subsequently the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023) by separating judicial magistrates from executive magistrates.

Part IV-A (Moral & Civic Obligations): Article 51A(f) imposes a moral obligation on citizens to protect composite culture, introduced on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee via the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

valueAddition.title: Cross-Part Transposition and Overlap Traps
bullets: Child Welfare Across Three Parts: Article 24 prohibits hazardous child labour under 14 (Part III); Article 39(f) directs healthy development opportunities for children (Part IV); Article 45 directs early childhood care (Part IV); and Article 51A(k) mandates parents/guardians to provide education to children aged 6 to 14 (Part IV-A).

Separation of Powers Confusion: Many aspirants mistakenly associate 'Separation of Judiciary' exclusively with the Basic Structure doctrine or judicial independence in Articles 124–147, overlooking that its explicit constitutional command is located in Article 50 of the DPSPs.

Composite Culture vs. Minority Rights: 'Composite culture' in Article 51A(f) is a general civic duty for all citizens, distinct from the distinct linguistic/cultural rights of minorities protected under Articles 29 and 30 in Part III.

inNews.relevance: Joint operations targeting the rehabilitation of rescued child workers and compliance audits under Article 24 and the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act reaffirm the non-negotiable statutory enforcement of Part III rights.

analysis.coreTakeaway: Remember: All three pairs are accurately placed—Article 50 is a DPSP, Article 51A(f) is a Fundamental Duty, and Article 24 is a Fundamental Right against exploitation.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements :
With reference to the Constitution of India, if an area in a State is declared as Scheduled Area under the Fifth Schedule
I. the State Government loses its executive power in such areas and a local body assumes total administration
II. the Union Government can take over the total administration of such areas under certain circumstances on the recommendations of the Governor

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: Under Paragraph 3 of the Fifth Schedule, the executive power of the Union extends to giving directions to the State as to the administration of Scheduled Areas, but does not empower the Union to take over total direct administration.
keywords.concept: Union Directional Control: Under Paragraph 3 of the Fifth Schedule, the executive power of the Union extends to giving directions to the State as to the administration of Scheduled Areas, but does not empower the Union to take over total direct administration.
States in Scheduled Areas

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement I is constitutionally invalid because the State's executive power remains fully operative in Scheduled Areas.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement II is incorrect because the Union possesses only directive powers, not direct takeover or substitution of state administrative authority.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements make extreme assertions of administrative takeover that contradict the constitutional scheme of the Fifth Schedule.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Neither Statement I nor Statement II is correct under the provisions of the Fifth Schedule.

valueAddition.title: Administrative Architecture of the Fifth Schedule
bullets: Declaration & Modification (Para 6): The President of India is empowered to declare an area as a Scheduled Area, increase or alter its boundaries, or rescind such designation, in consultation with the Governor of that State.
Continuity of State Executive Power (Para 2): Executive power of the State continues to apply to Scheduled Areas without interruption.

Governor's Special Legislative Filter (Para 5): The Governor may direct by public notification that any particular Act of Parliament or of the State Legislature shall not apply to a Scheduled Area, or shall apply subject to exceptions and modifications.

Tribes Advisory Council (Para 4): Established in each State having Scheduled Areas, consisting of not more than 20 members (three-fourths of whom must be ST representatives in the State Legislative Assembly) to advise on welfare and advancement of STs.

valueAddition.title: Role of the Union Government in Scheduled Areas
bullets: Directive, Not Substitutive: Paragraph 3 extends the Union's executive power solely to issuing directions to the State Government regarding the administration of Scheduled Areas.

Presidential Oversight via Governor's Reports: The Governor has an obligatory duty to make a report annually, or whenever required by the President, regarding the administrative state of Scheduled Areas.

Contrast with Sixth Schedule: Sixth Schedule areas (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) feature Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) with direct legislative, judicial, and financial self-governance powers, unlike Fifth Schedule areas which remain embedded within normal state departments.

valueAddition.title: PESA Act, 1996 and Fifth Schedule Interplay
bullets: The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) extends Part IX of the Constitution to Fifth Schedule areas with mandatory modifications.

Gram Sabhas are endowed with specific powers over minor forest produce, land alienation prevention, and village dispute resolution, but this does not displace the State Government's sovereign executive administration.

inNews.relevance: Directly highlights the constitutional limits of the Governor's regulatory and modifying powers over parliamentary and state legislation in Fifth Schedule areas.

similarPyq.stem: At the national level, which Ministry is the nodal agency to ensure effective implementation of the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006? (a) Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (b) Ministry of Panchayati Raj (c) Ministry of Rural Development (d) Ministry of Tribal Affairs

statementBreakdown.explanation: Paragraph 2 of the Fifth Schedule explicitly mandates: 'Subject to the provisions of this Schedule, the executive power of a State extends to the Scheduled Areas therein.' The State Government does NOT lose its executive power, nor does any local body assume total administration. While Tribes Advisory Councils (TAC) and Panchayats (under PESA, 1996) have consultative and decentralized roles, normal state administration continues under the Governor's regulatory oversight.

Paragraph 3 provides that the Governor must submit an annual (or required) report to the President regarding the administration of the Scheduled Areas, and the executive power of the Union extends to the giving of directions to the State as to such administration. There is no constitutional provision permitting the Union Government to 'take over the total administration' of Scheduled Areas on the Governor's recommendation (unlike President's Rule under Article 356 for breakdown of constitutional machinery across the entire State).

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following subjects under the Constitution of India :
I. List I-Union List, in the Seventh Schedule
II. Extent of the executive power of a State
III. Conditions of the Governor's office

For a constitutional amendment with respect to which of the above, ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States is required before presenting the bill to the President of India for assent ?

keywords.shortNote: Prescribes an entrenched amendment procedure requiring ratification by resolutions passed by the legislatures of not less than one-half of the States for provisions touching the federal structure.
keywords.concept: Article 368(2) Proviso: Prescribes an entrenched amendment procedure requiring ratification by resolutions passed by the legislatures of not less than one-half of the States for provisions touching the federal structure.

keywords.shortNote: An exhaustive list of constitutional provisions specified under clauses (a) to (e) of the proviso to Article 368(2) that directly govern the federal compact.
keywords.concept: Entrenched Federal Provisions: An exhaustive list of constitutional provisions specified under clauses (a) to (e) of the proviso to Article 368(2) that directly govern the federal compact.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Only Subjects I (Seventh Schedule lists) and II (extent of state executive power) fall squarely within the entrenched federal provisions of the Article 368(2) proviso.

valueAddition.title: Exhaustive Scope of the Proviso to Article 368(2)
bullets: Clause (a) — Executive Election: Manner and election of the President of India (Articles 54 and 55).
Clause (b) — Executive Extent: Extent of the executive power of the Union (Article 73) and of the States (Article 162).
Clause (c) — Higher Judiciary: The Supreme Court (Chapter IV of Part V) and High Courts for the States (Chapter V of Part VI) as well as High Courts for Union Territories (Article 241).

Clause (d) — Legislative Relations & Schedules: Distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States (Chapter I of Part XI), any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule, and the representation of States in Parliament (Fourth Schedule).
Clause (e) — Constituent Power Itself: The provisions of Article 368 itself.

valueAddition.title: Procedural Mechanics of State Ratification
bullets: Form of Approval: Ratification must be through a resolution passed by the State Legislature (or both houses in bicameral states) by a simple majority of members present and voting.
Threshold Requirement: Ratification requires approval from 'not less than one-half of the States' before the bill is presented to the President.
Absence of Time Limit: The Constitution prescribes no statutory time limit within which State Legislatures must ratify or reject an amendment bill.
Irrevocability of Consent: Once a State Legislature passes a ratification resolution, constitutional convention holds that it cannot subsequently withdraw or revoke that ratification.

inNews.source: Supreme Court of India
inNews.headline: Constitution Bench clarifies limits of Parliamentary amending power over federal distribution of tax and regulatory powers in the Seventh Schedule
inNews.relevance: Reiterates the non-negotiable requirement of State ratification under the Article 368(2) proviso whenever legislative entries affecting Union-State fiscal and executive distribution are altered.

similarPyq.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Procedure for Amendment of the Constitution of India?
1. An amendment to the Constitution of India can be initiated by the introduction of a bill in the Lok Sabha only.
2. If such an amendment seeks to make changes in the federal character of the Constitution, the amendment also requires to be ratified by the legislature of not less than half of the States.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 only
(c) Both 1 and 2
(d) Neither 1 nor 2

statementBreakdown.explanation: Clause (c) of the proviso explicitly enumerates 'any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule', meaning an amendment to the Union List (List I), State List (List II), or Concurrent List (List III) mandates prior ratification by not less than half the State Legislatures.

statementBreakdown.reference: Article 368(2) proviso, clause (b) read with Article 162
statementBreakdown.explanation: Clause (b) of the proviso explicitly covers 'the extent of the executive power of the Union and the States' (Articles 73 and 162), mandating ratification by not less than half of the State Legislatures.

Conditions of the Governor's office (Article 158) is not included within the exhaustive list of the proviso to Article 368(2); amending it requires only a special majority of Parliament under Article 368(2) without State ratification.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
With reference to the Indian polity, consider the following statements :
I. The Governor of a State is not answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his/her office.
II. No criminal proceedings shall be instituted or continued against the Governor during his/her term of office.
III. Members of a State Legislature are not liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said within the House.

Which of the statements given above are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: Grants personal immunity to the President and Governors, declaring they shall not be answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of their office.
keywords.concept: Article 361(1): Grants personal immunity to the President and Governors, declaring they shall not be answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of their office.

keywords.shortNote: Imposes an absolute bar on instituting or continuing criminal proceedings against the President or a Governor in any court during their term of office.
keywords.concept: Article 361(2): Imposes an absolute bar on instituting or continuing criminal proceedings against the President or a Governor in any court during their term of office.

keywords.shortNote: Confers parliamentary/legislative immunity on MLAs and MLCs, stating no member of a State Legislature is liable to any court proceedings in respect of anything said or any vote given in the legislature.
keywords.concept: Article 194(2): Confers parliamentary/legislative immunity on MLAs and MLCs, stating no member of a State Legislature is liable to any court proceedings in respect of anything said or any vote given in the legislature.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Confirms that all three statements (I, II, and III) are correct constitutional provisions.

valueAddition.title: Article 361: Four Clauses of Executive Immunity
bullets: Article 361(1) Official Acts: Complete personal immunity from judicial answerability for official actions (government may still be sued under Article 300).
Article 361(2) Criminal Proceedings: Total immunity from criminal prosecutions, FIRs, or trials during the entire duration in office.
Article 361(3) Arrest and Imprisonment: Complete bar on the issuance of any process for arrest or imprisonment by any court during incumbency.
Article 361(4) Civil Proceedings: Civil actions regarding personal acts done before or after entering office can only be instituted after giving a two-month advance written notice.

valueAddition.title: Legislative Speech Immunity: Article 105(2) vs. Article 194(2)
bullets: Scope of Speech: Members enjoy absolute speech freedom inside the legislative floor under Articles 105(2) (MPs) and 194(2) (MLAs/MLCs), subject only to the internal rules of procedure and the Speaker's discipline.

Bribery Carve-out (Sita Soren Judgment, 2024): A 7-judge Constitution Bench overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998), establishing that parliamentary immunity under Articles 105(2) and 194(2) does not shield a lawmaker from criminal prosecution for taking a bribe to make a speech or cast a vote.

inNews.source: Supreme Court of India / The Hindu
inNews.headline: Supreme Court 7-judge Constitution Bench rules parliamentary immunity under Articles 105 and 194 does not protect legislators accepting bribes
inNews.relevance: Directly interprets the constitutional boundaries of speech and voting immunities under Article 194(2).

statementBreakdown.explanation: Article 361(1) explicitly states that the President or the Governor of a State shall not be answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his/her office or for any act done or purporting to be done by him/her in the exercise and performance of those powers and duties.

Article 361(2) explicitly provides that no criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted or continued against the President, or the Governor of a State, in any court during his/her term of office.

Article 194(2) explicitly grants speech immunity, providing that no member of the Legislature of a State shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in the Legislature or any committee thereof.

rows: Absolute bar during term of office (Art. 361(2))
Not a member of the legislative chamber
Permitted only after 2 months' prior written notice (Art. 361(4))
Civil arrest prohibited 40 days before/after sessions (Section 135A, CPC)

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following activities :
I. Production of crude oil
II. Refining, storage and distribution of petroleum
III. Marketing and sale of petroleum products
IV. Production of natural gas

How many of the above activities are regulated by the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board in our country ?

keywords.term: Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB)
keywords.shortNote: A statutory body constituted under the PNGRB Act, 2006 to oversee midstream and downstream activities, explicitly excluding upstream exploration and production.
keywords.concept: Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB): A statutory body constituted under the PNGRB Act, 2006 to oversee midstream and downstream activities, explicitly excluding upstream exploration and production.

keywords.shortNote: Section 1(4) and the Preamble of the PNGRB Act specifically state that the Act applies to refining, processing, storage, transportation, distribution, marketing, and sale, 'excluding production of crude oil and natural gas'.
keywords.concept: Exclusion of Upstream Production: Section 1(4) and the Preamble of the PNGRB Act specifically state that the Act applies to refining, processing, storage, transportation, distribution, marketing, and sale, 'excluding production of crude oil and natural gas'.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Two activities (II and III) are covered, not just one.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Only two activities—refining, storage and distribution (II) and marketing and sale (III)—fall under PNGRB's statutory jurisdiction. Production of crude oil (I) and natural gas (IV) are excluded.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Activities I and IV are upstream operations completely outside PNGRB's statutory remit.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Assuming PNGRB regulates all oil and gas activities from wellhead to retail burner tip is the classic examiner trap.

valueAddition.title: Upstream vs. Downstream Architecture
bullets: Upstream (Exploration & Production): Regulated administratively by the Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH) under MoPNG via the Oilfields (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, not by PNGRB.
Midstream & Downstream (Refining, Pipelines, City Gas Distribution, Retailing): Governed by PNGRB under the 2006 Act to promote competition, common carrier access, and consumer protection.
Statutory Exclusion Clause: Section 1(4) opens with the definitive boundary: '...excluding production of crude oil and natural gas.'

valueAddition.title: Core Powers & Quasi-Judicial Status of PNGRB
bullets: Composition: Chairperson and 4 members (including one Member-Legal) appointed by the Central Government on recommendations of a search committee headed by Member, NITI Aayog.
Bench Strength & Civil Court Powers: PNGRB has civil court powers under CPC, 1908 to settle disputes between entities or between an entity and consumer.
Appellate Mechanism: Appeals against orders or decisions of PNGRB lie directly before the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), not the High Court.

inNews.source: The Hindu
inNews.headline: PNGRB issues unified tariff regulations to accelerate National Gas Grid connectivity
inNews.relevance: Directly illustrates PNGRB exercising its midstream pipeline tariff-determination power under Section 11 to foster competitive gas distribution.

similarPyq.stem:
With reference to the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB), consider the following statements:
1. PNGRB is the first regulatory body set up by the Government of India.
2. One of the tasks of PNGRB is to ensure competitive markets for gas.
3. Appeals against the decisions of PNGRB go before the Appellate Tribunals for Electricity.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

statementBreakdown.explanation: Production of crude oil is an upstream activity explicitly excluded from the jurisdiction of PNGRB; it falls under the purview of the Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH) and the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
Refining, processing, storage, transportation, and distribution of petroleum and petroleum products constitute midstream and downstream operations squarely regulated by PNGRB.

Marketing and sale of petroleum products, including retail service obligations, pipeline access, and consumer protection against restrictive trade practices, fall directly under PNGRB's regulatory mandate.
Just like crude oil, the production (upstream extraction) of natural gas is expressly excluded from the mandate of the PNGRB Act.

verdicts.source: Section 1(4) of the PNGRB Act expressly excludes the production of crude oil from its regulatory domain.
Refining, processing, storage, and pipeline transportation are core activities regulated under the 2006 Act.
Marketing, retail distribution networks, and consumer pricing displays fall directly under PNGRB oversight.
Like crude oil, natural gas extraction and production are governed by the DGH, completely excluding PNGRB.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Only two activities are covered, making (b) the right choice.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Statutory Bodies notes

items.desc: The Act expressly excludes upstream production of crude oil and natural gas.

items.title: Common Carrier Mandate
items.desc: Empowered to declare pipelines common or contract carriers for open third-party access.

items.title: Appeals to APTEL
items.desc: Appeals against PNGRB orders go to the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity, not High Courts.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements with regard to pardoning power of the President of India :
I. The exercise of this power by the President can be subjected to limited judicial review.
II. The President can exercise this power without the advice of the Central Government.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: Empowers the President to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment, or to suspend, remit, or commute sentences across Union offenses, court-martial convictions, and death penalties.
keywords.concept: Article 72: Empowers the President to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment, or to suspend, remit, or commute sentences across Union offenses, court-martial convictions, and death penalties.

keywords.shortNote: The constitutional doctrine permitting courts to strike down executive clemency orders if passed without application of mind, with mala fides, on extraneous grounds, or in violation of fundamental rights.
keywords.concept: Limited Judicial Review of Clemency: The constitutional doctrine permitting courts to strike down executive clemency orders if passed without application of mind, with mala fides, on extraneous grounds, or in violation of fundamental rights.

valueAddition.title: Article 72:
bullets: Aid and Advice: The Constitution Bench in Maru Ram (1980) held that the power under Article 72 is exercisable strictly on the advice of the Union Cabinet, not at the personal discretion of the President.
No Oral Hearing: In Kehar Singh (1989), the Supreme Court ruled that a petitioner has no fundamental right to an oral hearing before the President in clemency proceedings.

Grounds for Judicial Review: In Epuru Sudhakar (2006), the Court held clemency challengeable if passed without application of mind, based on extraneous or political considerations, or infected with mala fides.

Undue Delay as Commutation Ground: In Shatrughan Chauhan (2014), the Court ruled that unexplained, inordinate executive delay in deciding mercy petitions is a supervening circumstance violating Article 21, entitling death-row prisoners to commutation.

valueAddition.title: Article 72 (President) vs. Article 161 (Governor)
bullets: Scope of Offenses: President exercises powers over offenses against Union laws; Governor exercises powers over offenses against State laws.
Court-Martial: President alone can pardon, reprieve, or commute sentences awarded by military courts (Court-Martial); the Governor has zero authority.

Death Sentence: President alone possesses plenary power to pardon a death sentence; following State of Haryana v. Raj Kumar (2021), a Governor can commute or remit death sentences, but cannot grant an absolute pardon.

inNews.source: Supreme Court of India / The Hindu
inNews.headline: Supreme Court reaffirms Epuru Sudhakar principles regarding judicial review of executive clemency under Articles 72 and 161
inNews.relevance: Directly highlights the constitutional boundaries governing judicial review of presidential and gubernatorial clemency orders.

similarPyq.stem:
Which of the following is/are among the discretionary powers of the President of India?
1. Sending back the advice given by Council of Ministers for reconsideration
2. Withholding assent to Bills
3. Reserving Bills for reconsideration of the President
4. Dismissing ministers
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
(a) 1 and 2 only
(b) 1, 2 and 3
(c) 2 and 4
(d) 1, 3 and 4

statementBreakdown.reference: Maru Ram v. Union of India (1980) & Epuru Sudhakar v. Govt. of A.P. (2006)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Pardoning power under Article 72 is subject to limited judicial review; the Supreme Court established that courts can intervene if the order is arbitrary, mala fide, discriminatory, or founded on extraneous considerations.

statementBreakdown.reference: Article 74(1) & Maru Ram v. Union of India (1980)
statementBreakdown.explanation: The President cannot exercise pardoning powers independently or in personal discretion; Article 74(1) binds the President to act strictly on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (communicated through the Ministry of Home Affairs).

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements :
I. On the dissolution of the House of the People, the Speaker shall not vacate his/her office until immediately before the first meeting of the House of the People after the dissolution.
II. According to the provisions of the Constitution of India, a Member of the House of the People on being elected as Speaker shall resign from his/her political party immediately.
III. The Speaker of the House of the People may be removed from his/her office by a resolution of the House of the People passed by a majority of all the then Members of the House, provided that no resolution shall be moved unless at least fourteen days' notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution.

Which of the statements given above are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: Mandates institutional continuity by ensuring the Speaker does not vacate office upon Lok Sabha dissolution until immediately before the first meeting of the newly constituted House.
keywords.concept: Tenure Post-Dissolution (Article 94 Proviso 2): Mandates institutional continuity by ensuring the Speaker does not vacate office upon Lok Sabha dissolution until immediately before the first meeting of the newly constituted House.

keywords.shortNote: Resigning from a political party upon becoming Speaker is a British Westminster convention, not an Indian constitutional requirement; Paragraph 5 of the Tenth Schedule merely protects a Speaker from disqualification if they voluntarily resign, without making it mandatory.
keywords.concept: Party Membership & Tenth Schedule Exemption: Resigning from a political party upon becoming Speaker is a British Westminster convention, not an Indian constitutional requirement; Paragraph 5 of the Tenth Schedule merely protects a Speaker from disqualification if they voluntarily resign, without making it mandatory.

keywords.shortNote: Requires a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Lok Sabha (effective majority), preceded by at least 14 days' advance notice.
keywords.concept: Removal by Effective Majority (Article 94(c)): Requires a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Lok Sabha (effective majority), preceded by at least 14 days' advance notice.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Correctly combines verified Statements I and III while rejecting the false assertion in Statement II.

valueAddition.title: Article 94 & 96: Removal Dynamics of the Speaker
bullets: Majority Required: An 'effective majority' (a majority of all the then members of the House, taking into account current vacancies).
Procedural Safeguard (Article 94 Proviso 1): Mandatory 14 days' advance notice before the resolution can be moved.

Status during Removal Resolution (Article 96(1)): The Speaker cannot preside over the sitting when a resolution for their removal is under consideration, though they have the right to be present, speak, and participate.

Voting Prerogative during Removal (Article 96(2)): Can vote in the first instance on the removal resolution or related proceedings, but possesses no casting vote in the case of an equality of votes (unlike ordinary sittings under Article 100).

valueAddition.title: Speaker's Party Neutrality: Indian vs. British Practice
bullets: British Model: The Speaker formally severs all connections with their political party upon election, resigns from party membership, and contests future elections as an unaffiliated Speaker ('Once a Speaker, always a Speaker').

Indian Model: Speakers remain active members of their political parties. Under Paragraph 5 of the Tenth Schedule, a Speaker is exempt from anti-defection disqualification if they choose to resign from their party, or if they rejoin that political party after ceasing to hold office, but resignation is purely optional.

inNews.source: Lok Sabha Secretariat / The Hindu
inNews.headline: Rules Committee examines constitutional safeguards and presiding protocols under Articles 94 and 96 during no-confidence notices against parliamentary officers
inNews.relevance: Directly reinforces the constitutional stipulations regarding 14 days' notice and effective majority thresholds under Article 94(c).

similarPyq.stem:
Regarding the office of the Lok Sabha Speaker, consider the following statements:
1. He/She holds the office during the pleasure of the President.
2. He/She need not be a member of the House at the time of his/her election but has to become a member of the House within six months from the date of his/her election.
3. If he/she intends to resign, the letter of his/her resignation has to be addressed to the Deputy Speaker.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 and 2 only
(b) 3 only
(c) 1, 2 and 3
(d) None

statementBreakdown.reference: Second Proviso to Article 94, Constitution of India
statementBreakdown.explanation: Article 94 explicitly states in its second proviso: 'Provided further that, whenever the House of the People is dissolved, the Speaker shall not vacate his office until immediately before the first meeting of the House of the People after the dissolution.'

The Constitution of India contains no mandatory provision requiring the Speaker to resign from their political party upon election. Resignation from political affiliation is a British convention ('Once a Speaker, always a Speaker'); in India, Paragraph 5 of the Tenth Schedule merely provides that if the Speaker voluntarily gives up party membership, they will not attract anti-defection disqualification.

statementBreakdown.reference: Article 94(c) and First Proviso, Constitution of India
statementBreakdown.explanation: Article 94(c) provides that the Speaker may be removed by a resolution of the House of the People passed by a majority of all the then members of the House (effective majority). The first proviso to Article 94 mandates that no such resolution shall be moved unless at least fourteen days' notice has been given.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements :
I. If any question arises as to whether a Member of the House of the People has become subject to disqualification under the 10th Schedule, the President's decision in accordance with the opinion of the Council of Union Ministers shall be final.
II. There is no mention of the word 'political party' in the Constitution of India.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: Decisions on disqualification arising out of defection under the Tenth Schedule are rendered exclusively by the Chairman or the Speaker of the House, not by the President.
keywords.concept: Tenth Schedule Adjudication (Paragraph 6(1)): Decisions on disqualification arising out of defection under the Tenth Schedule are rendered exclusively by the Chairman or the Speaker of the House, not by the President.

keywords.shortNote: The President decides disqualification matters arising under Article 102(1) (e.g., office of profit, unsound mind, insolvency) in accordance with the binding opinion of the Election Commission of India, not the Council of Ministers.
keywords.concept: Article 103 (Ordinary Disqualifications): The President decides disqualification matters arising under Article 102(1) (e.g., office of profit, unsound mind, insolvency) in accordance with the binding opinion of the Election Commission of India, not the Council of Ministers.

keywords.shortNote: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 introduced the Tenth Schedule, embedding the term 'political party' multiple times throughout its provisions (Paragraphs 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5).
keywords.concept: Constitutional Recognition of 'Political Party': The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 introduced the Tenth Schedule, embedding the term 'political party' multiple times throughout its provisions (Paragraphs 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5).

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Identifies that both Statement I and Statement II are factually and constitutionally incorrect.

valueAddition.title: Adjudicating Disqualifications: Article 103 vs. Tenth Schedule
bullets: Article 102(1) / Article 191(1) Disqualifications: Office of profit, unsound mind, undischarged insolvent, loss of citizenship, or disqualified by any parliamentary law (RPA, 1951). Decision authority: President (Centre) or Governor (State) acting strictly on the binding advice of the Election Commission of India (Articles 103 & 192).
Article 102(2) / Article 191(2) Disqualifications: Disqualification on grounds of defection under the Tenth Schedule. Decision authority: Speaker or Chairman of the respective House.

Judicial Review (Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu, 1992): The Speaker/Chairman acting under Paragraph 6 acts as a tribunal; the decision is subject to judicial review by High Courts and the Supreme Court on grounds of mala fides, perversity, or violation of natural justice.

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Entrenchment of 'Political Party'
bullets: 1950 Original Constitution: Envisaged parliamentary democracy without formal textual mention of political parties.
52nd Amendment Act (1985): Brought the Anti-Defection Law as the Tenth Schedule, expressly defining and incorporating 'political party', 'original political party', and 'legislature party'.

91st Amendment Act (2003): Inserted Articles 75(1B), 164(1B), and 361B, explicitly disqualifying a member disqualified under the Tenth Schedule from being appointed as a Minister or holding a remunerative political post.

inNews.source: Supreme Court of India / The Hindu
inNews.headline: Supreme Court Constitution Bench scrutinizes reasonable timelines for Speaker's adjudication of Tenth Schedule disqualification petitions
inNews.relevance: Directly highlights the adjudicatory role of the Speaker as a tribunal under Paragraph 6(1) of the Tenth Schedule.

similarPyq.stem:
With reference to the anti-defection law in India, consider the following statements:
1. The law specifies that a nominated legislator cannot join any political party within six months of being appointed to the House.
2. The law does not provide any time-frame within which the presiding officer has to decide a defection case.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 only
(c) Both 1 and 2
(d) Neither 1 nor 2

statementBreakdown.explanation: Questions of disqualification under the Tenth Schedule are decided by the Chairman or the Speaker of the respective House (Paragraph 6(1)). In contrast, questions arising under Article 102(1) are decided by the President according to the opinion of the Election Commission of India (Article 103), not the Council of Ministers.

While absent in the original 1950 text, the term 'political party' was explicitly inserted into the Constitution via the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985 in the Tenth Schedule (and later in the 91st Amendment Act, 2003 under Article 75(1B) and Article 164(1B)).

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements :
I. Panchayats at the intermediate level exist in all States.

valueAddition.title: Part IX: Core Structural Articles & Exam Traps
bullets: Article 243B (Constitution of Panchayats): Mandates a three-tier structure (village, intermediate, and district levels) in every State, but exempts States with a population under 20 lakhs from constituting the intermediate tier.

Article 243C (Composition & Direct Election): All seats in Panchayats at all three levels are filled by direct election from territorial constituencies; Chairpersons at intermediate and district levels are elected indirectly by and from amongst elected members.

Article 243F (Disqualifications for Membership): A person is qualified to contest at 21 years of age, distinguishing local self-government from State Legislative Assemblies (25 years) and Legislative Councils/Rajya Sabha (30 years).

Article 243I (State Finance Commission): Constituted by the Governor every five years; recommends devolution of net proceeds of taxes, duties, tolls, and user charges, as well as grants-in-aid under the Consolidated Fund of the State.

Article 243K (State Election Commission): Vests the superintendence, direction, and control of electoral rolls and conduct of all Panchayat elections in an independent State Election Commissioner appointed by the Governor.

valueAddition.title: Compulsory vs. Voluntary Provisions of the 73rd Amendment Act, 1992
bullets: Compulsory Provisions (Mandatory in all State Acts): Organization of Gram Sabha; 3-tier structure (with population exemption for intermediate tier); direct elections to all seats; 21 years minimum age; reservation for SCs/STs in proportion to population and minimum one-third reservation for women; 5-year fixed tenure; reconstitution within 6 months of premature dissolution; establishment of State Election Commission and State Finance Commission.

Voluntary Provisions (At State Discretion): Voting rights of MPs/MLAs in Panchayats; reservation for backward classes; devolution of powers and responsibilities listed in the Eleventh Schedule (29 functional subjects); financial powers to levy and collect taxes, duties, and tolls.

inNews.source: Press Information Bureau (PIB)
inNews.headline: Ministry of Panchayati Raj reviews implementation of State Finance Commission awards and fiscal transfers to rural local bodies
inNews.relevance: Directly links the mandate of Article 243I to fiscal empowerment and autonomous resource generation across PRIs.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Article 243B(2) explicitly provides that Panchayats at the intermediate level may not be constituted in a State having a population not exceeding twenty lakhs (such as Goa and Sikkim).

Article 243F(1)(a) explicitly stipulates that no person shall be disqualified on the ground that they are less than twenty-five years of age if they have attained the age of twenty-one years; the qualifying age is 21 years, not 30 years.

Under Article 243I(1), the State Finance Commission is constituted by the Governor of the State, not the Chief Minister, and its recommendations encompass all three tiers of Panchayats rather than only the intermediate level.

valueAddition.title: BIMSTEC: Institutional Evolution & Nomenclature
bullets: June 1997 (Bangkok Declaration): Formed as BIST-EC (Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, Thailand Economic Cooperation).
December 1997: Myanmar joined, renaming the grouping to BIMST-EC.
February 2004: Nepal and Bhutan joined as full members.
July 2004 (1st Summit, Bangkok): Rechristened as the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC).
2014: Permanent Secretariat established in Dhaka, Bangladesh (India contributes ~32% of operational costs).

valueAddition.title: Rationalised 7 Pillars & Lead Countries (Colombo Summit 2022)
bullets: Security: Led by India (covers Counter-Terrorism and Transnational Crime, Disaster Management, Energy).
Trade, Investment & Development: Led by Bangladesh.
Environment & Climate Change: Led by Bhutan.
Agriculture & Food Security: Led by Myanmar (covers Agriculture, Fisheries & Livestock).
People-to-People Contact: Led by Nepal (covers Culture, Tourism, People-to-People Contact forums).
Science, Technology & Innovation: Led by Sri Lanka (covers Technology, Health, Human Resource Development).
Connectivity: Led by Thailand.

statementBreakdown.explanation: BIMSTEC comprises exactly seven member states—Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and Thailand—a membership count that remains unchanged through January 2025.
BIMSTEC was founded on 6 June 1997 through the Bangkok Declaration, not the Dhaka Declaration of 1999. The permanent secretariat is located in Dhaka, which examiners frequently use as a trap.
Nepal was not a founding member. The founding members were Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, and Thailand (BIST-EC). Myanmar joined in late 1997, while Nepal and Bhutan joined later in February 2004.

Under the reorganized 7 pillars adopted in 2022, India leads the 'Security' pillar (counter-terrorism, disaster management, energy). Tourism falls under the 'People-to-People Contact' pillar, which is led by Nepal.

IV. Lokpal cannot inquire into the allegations of corruption against a sitting Prime Minister of India.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.concept: Lokpal: India's statutory apex anti-corruption ombudsman established under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 to inquire into corruption allegations against public servants.

optionBreakdown.explanation: Only statement III represents a correct statutory provision of the 2013 Act; statements I, II, and IV are direct statutory traps.

valueAddition.title: Lokpal Institution & Statutory Mandate
bullets: Establishment & Governing Act: Created by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (Act No. 1 of 2014) as a statutory, multi-member body consisting of a Chairperson and up to eight Members.
Composition & Diversity Quota: 50% of the members must be Judicial Members. A minimum of 50% of members must come from among SCs, STs, OBCs, Minorities, and Women.

Selection Committee: Appointed by the President on recommendations of a 5-member committee: Prime Minister (Chairperson), Speaker of the Lok Sabha, Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha (or leader of the single largest opposition party), Chief Justice of India (or nominee SC Judge), and an eminent jurist nominated by the President on the recommendations of the other four.
Tenure & Independence: 5 years or until 70 years of age. Post-tenure restrictions bar diplomatic assignments, reappointment, or contesting elections for 5 years.

valueAddition.title: Powers of Lokpal to Investigate & Inquire
bullets: Preliminary Inquiry Wing (Section 20): Lokpal maintains its own Inquiry Wing, or can direct any investigating agency, including the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) or CBI, to conduct a preliminary inquiry completed normally within 90 days.

Superintendence over CBI (Section 25): Vested with powers of superintendence and direction over the CBI for cases referred by it; investigating officers assigned cannot be transferred without Lokpal's prior concurrence.

Civil Court Powers (Section 27): Possesses powers of a Civil Court under CPC, 1908 for summoning witnesses, examining on oath, discovery and production of documents, and requisitioning public records.

Search, Seizure & Attachment (Sections 28 & 29): Authorized to direct search and seizure operations and provisionally attach properties suspected to be acquired through corruption for up to 90 days pending inquiry.

Recommendation of Transfer or Suspension (Section 32): Empowered to recommend the competent authority to transfer or suspend a public servant facing inquiry to prevent witness tampering or destruction of evidence.

inNews.headline: Lokpal exercises statutory superintendence powers to fast-track high-profile corruption probes
inNews.relevance: Highlights the practical deployment of Sections 20 and 25 of the Lokpal Act governing preliminary inquiry timelines and administrative oversight over the CBI.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Section 1(4) explicitly provides that the Act applies to public servants not only within India but also to public servants posted outside India.

While members cannot be sitting MPs or MLAs, the Chairperson is not restricted to a CJI. A former Chief Justice of India, a former Supreme Court Judge, or an eminent person with 25 years of specialized expertise is eligible.
Section 3(4) explicitly specifies that the Chairperson or a Member shall not be a person of less than forty-five years of age on the date of assuming office.
The Lokpal has statutory jurisdiction over a sitting Prime Minister, subject to specific subject-matter carve-outs and a mandatory two-thirds full bench approval.

stem:
Consider the following airports :
1. Donyi Polo Airport
2. Kushinagar International Airport
3. Vijayawada International Airport

In the recent past, which of the above have been constructed as Greenfield projects ?

keywords.shortNote: An infrastructure project constructed from scratch on previously undeveloped land, lacking any pre-existing civil or operational structures.
keywords.concept: Greenfield Project: An infrastructure project constructed from scratch on previously undeveloped land, lacking any pre-existing civil or operational structures.

keywords.shortNote: An infrastructure project that modifies, modernizes, or expands an existing operational or abandoned facility.
keywords.concept: Brownfield Project: An infrastructure project that modifies, modernizes, or expands an existing operational or abandoned facility.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Donyi Polo (Hollongi) and Kushinagar were developed from the ground up under the Greenfield Airports Policy, whereas Vijayawada is an expansion of an existing wartime airstrip.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Vijayawada is an upgraded brownfield asset.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Vijayawada is brownfield, and Kushinagar was built as a greenfield facility.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Vijayawada Airport is not a greenfield installation.

valueAddition.title: Greenfield vs. Brownfield Infrastructure Matrix
bullets: Greenfield Investment: Creating entirely new production or transport assets from zero on raw land. Offers design flexibility, modern technological optimization, and zero legacy encumbrances, but involves high land acquisition risks, environmental clearances, and longer gestation periods.

Brownfield Investment: Upgrading, refurbishing, or expanding pre-existing functional assets. Involves shorter commissioning lead times and existing market access, but comes with structural limitations, legacy debt, or environmental remediation costs.

Government Policy (Greenfield Airports Policy, 2008): Provides a 2-stage approval process—'Site Clearance' followed by 'In-Principle' approval. The Centre has granted in-principle approval for 21 greenfield airports across India (e.g., Mopa in Goa, Navi Mumbai, Noida/Jewar, Hollongi/Donyi Polo, Kushinagar).

valueAddition.title: Aviation Infrastructure Financing Models in India
bullets: UDAN Scheme (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik): Viability Gap Funding (VGF) model utilized to revive unserved and underserved airstrips (predominantly brownfield airstrip upgrades).

Public-Private Partnerships (PPP): Concession agreements structured on DBFOT (Design, Build, Finance, Operate, and Transfer) principles with revenue-sharing per passenger (e.g., Jewar and Navi Mumbai airports).

Asset Monetization Pipeline (NMP): Leasing operational brownfield airports (e.g., Ahmedabad, Lucknow, Mangaluru, Jaipur, Guwahati, Thiruvananthapuram) under long-term concessions to private operators to fund fresh greenfield capital investments.

stem: With reference to the Indian economy, "Collateral Borrowing and Lending Obligations" are the instruments of :

keywords.shortNote: A standardized, short-term money market repo instrument backed by eligible securities, developed by CCIL to facilitate borrowing and lending among entities without direct access to the interbank call money market.
keywords.concept: Collateralized Borrowing and Lending Obligation: A standardized, short-term money market repo instrument backed by eligible securities, developed by CCIL to facilitate borrowing and lending among entities without direct access to the interbank call money market.

keywords.shortNote: A collateralized repo transaction where a third-party intermediary acts as a custodian and clearing agent between borrowing and lending participants.
keywords.concept: Triparty Repo: A collateralized repo transaction where a third-party intermediary acts as a custodian and clearing agent between borrowing and lending participants.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.reference: Capital Market vs Money Market classification
optionBreakdown.explanation: The bond market trades medium to long-term debt securities (exceeding one year), whereas CBLO is strictly a short-term liquidity management instrument.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: The forex market handles currency exchange and cross-border currency derivatives, not domestic rupee collateralized borrowing.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: CBLO was introduced by the Clearing Corporation of India Limited (CCIL) in 2003 under RBI regulations as a discounted short-term money market instrument with maturities ranging from overnight to one year.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: The stock market facilitates trading in company shares and equity instruments, having no role in institutional overnight rupee collateral borrowing.

valueAddition.title: Collateralized Money Markets
bullets: CBLO was launched by CCIL in 2003 to allow non-bank entities like mutual funds, insurance companies, and corporates to access short-term collateralized liquidity.
In November 2018, the RBI phased out CBLO and fully transitioned it to the Triparty Repo (TREPS) market on the CCIL trading platform.
TREPS operates with central counterparty clearing, meaning CCIL acts as the settlement guarantor against approved government securities collateral.

valueAddition.title: Key Money Market Segments
bullets: Call/Notice/Term Money: Uncollateralized borrowing restricted strictly to scheduled commercial banks and primary dealers.
Triparty Repo (TREPS): Collateralized borrowing open to banks, primary dealers, mutual funds, insurance firms, NBFCs, and corporates.
Commercial Paper (CP) and Certificates of Deposit (CD): Short-term unsecured promissory notes issued by corporates and banks respectively.

subject: Economy
stem: The total fertility rate in an economy is defined as :

options.text: the number of children born per 1000 people in the population in a year.
options.label: a

options.text: the number of children born to a couple in their lifetime in a given population.
options.label: b

options.text: the birth rate minus death rate.
options.label: c

options.text: the average number of live births a woman would have by the end of her child-bearing age.
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: A synthetic demographic measure calculating the average number of children that would be born alive to a woman over her lifetime if she were to pass through her childbearing years (15-49) conforming to the age-specific fertility rates (ASFR) of that given year.
keywords.concept: Total Fertility Rate (TFR): A synthetic demographic measure calculating the average number of children that would be born alive to a woman over her lifetime if she were to pass through her childbearing years (15-49) conforming to the age-specific fertility rates (ASFR) of that given year.

keywords.shortNote: The total fertility rate at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next without migration, internationally benchmarked at roughly 2.1 children per woman.
keywords.concept: Replacement Level Fertility: The total fertility rate at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next without migration, internationally benchmarked at roughly 2.1 children per woman.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: The number of live births per 1,000 mid-year total population in a given year defines the Crude Birth Rate (CBR), not TFR.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fertility metrics are computed per woman relative to age-specific cohorts, not per 'couple'.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Crude birth rate minus crude death rate represents the Rate of Natural Increase (RNI) of a population, expressing natural population growth.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accurately and comprehensively defines Total Fertility Rate as the average number of live births a woman would have during her child-bearing reproductive years.

valueAddition.title: Core Demographic Indicators
bullets: Crude Birth Rate (CBR): Number of live births per 1,000 mid-year population in a given year. It is 'crude' because it includes the entire population regardless of age or sex distribution.
General Fertility Rate (GFR): Number of live births per 1,000 women in the reproductive age group (15-49 years) in a given year.
Total Fertility Rate (TFR): Sum of age-specific fertility rates ($TFR = 5 \times \sum ASFR$ across 5-year age intervals). It removes the confounding effects of the population's age structure.

Net Reproduction Rate (NRR): Number of daughters a woman would bear who survive to their own childbearing age under prevailing fertility and mortality schedules (NRR = 1 signifies exact demographic replacement).

valueAddition.title: India's Demographic Transition & NFHS Trends
bullets: Sub-Replacement Milestone: NFHS-5 recorded India's national TFR dropping to 2.0 (below the replacement threshold of 2.1), with urban areas at 1.6 and rural areas at 2.1.
Demographic Dividend Window: Falling fertility accelerates the decline of the youth dependency ratio, expanding the working-age population cohort (15-64 years) through 2055-2060.

Regional Variations: While northern states (such as Bihar and Uttar Pradesh) hovered around or slightly above replacement levels in earlier surveys, southern and western states have been significantly below replacement level for over two decades.

inNews.source: UN DESA / Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
inNews.headline: SRS Statistical Bulletin highlights continued decline in India's total fertility rate to 1.9 accompanied by rising median population age
inNews.relevance: Directly highlights the economic implications of sub-replacement TFR on future labor supply, social security funding, and the demographic transition model.

statementBreakdown.reference: United Nations Population Division & NFHS Demographic Definitions
statementBreakdown.explanation: Total Fertility Rate (TFR) measures the average number of live births a woman would bear by the end of her reproductive window (conventionally defined as ages 15-49), assuming current age-specific fertility patterns prevail.
