subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. In India, Non-Banking Financial Companies can access the Liquidity Adjustment Facility window of the Reserve Bank of India.
2. In India, Foreign Institutional Investors can hold the Government Securities (G-Secs).
3. In India, Stock Exchanges can offer separate trading platforms for debts.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: A liquidity management tool used by the RBI allowing eligible counterparties to borrow money through repurchase agreements (repos) or park excess funds via reverse repo/SDF, historically restricted to Scheduled Commercial Banks and Primary Dealers.
keywords.concept: Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF): A liquidity management tool used by the RBI allowing eligible counterparties to borrow money through repurchase agreements (repos) or park excess funds via reverse repo/SDF, historically restricted to Scheduled Commercial Banks and Primary Dealers.

keywords.shortNote: Foreign Portfolio Investors are permitted to invest in dated Government Securities and Treasury Bills under designated routes including the Medium-Term Framework (MTF) and the Fully Accessible Route (FAR).
keywords.concept: FII / FPI G-Sec Access: Foreign Portfolio Investors are permitted to invest in dated Government Securities and Treasury Bills under designated routes including the Medium-Term Framework (MTF) and the Fully Accessible Route (FAR).

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: NBFCs cannot access the RBI LAF window; direct access is preserved for Scheduled Commercial Banks and Primary Dealers.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ignores the established statutory eligibility of FIIs/FPIs to hold Indian Government Securities under FAR and VRR.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly treats NBFCs as standard LAF counterparties alongside commercial banks.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statements 2 and 3 are factually sound, while Statement 1 carries a direct institutional ineligibility.

valueAddition.title: Eligible Counterparties for RBI Liquidity Operations
bullets: Standard LAF Counterparties: Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs, excluding Regional Rural Banks) and Standalone Primary Dealers (SPDs) having Current Account and Subsidiary General Ledger (SGL) accounts with the RBI.

Targeted Exceptions: Special targeted windows (such as TLTRO during COVID-19 or liquidity support lines via SIDBI/NABARD) indirectly supported NBFCs, but NBFCs never enjoy direct standing access to standard LAF repo/reverse repo/SDF windows.
Standing Deposit Facility (SDF): Introduced in 2022 under Section 17 of the RBI Act to absorb uncollateralized liquidity, keeping the eligible counterparty list identical to the LAF.

valueAddition.title: Routes for Foreign Investment in Indian Sovereign Debt
bullets: Fully Accessible Route (FAR): Introduced in April 2020, removing foreign investment ceilings on designated benchmark 5-year, 10-year, and 30-year G-Secs, facilitating India's inclusion into global bond indices (e.g., J.P. Morgan GBI-EM, Bloomberg EM Local Currency).
Voluntary Retention Route (VRR): Encourages long-term stable foreign inflows by requiring FPIs to retain at least 75% of their committed investments for a minimum 3-year tenure.
General Route / Medium-Term Framework (MTF): Fixes a quantitative ceiling pegged as a designated percentage of outstanding sovereign stock.

valueAddition.title: Stock Exchange Debt Segments
bullets: Separate Platform Framework: SEBI notified circulars in 2013 allowing stock exchanges to launch a standalone 'Debt Segment' distinct from the Cash Equity and Equity Derivatives segments.
Instruments Traded: Corporate bonds, commercial papers, debentures, Government of India Dated Securities (G-Secs), State Development Loans (SDLs), and Treasury Bills.
Trading Architecture: Operates both an order-driven book (continuous matching for retail investors) and a request-for-quote (RFQ) platform designed for institutional bilateral trades.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India / The Hindu
inNews.headline: Inflows via Fully Accessible Route (FAR) Surge as India Strengthens Sovereign Weight in Global Emerging Market Bond Indices
inNews.relevance: Directly reaffirms statement 2 regarding FPI holdings in sovereign G-Secs, highlighting how the FAR channel enables seamless global institutional participation in Indian government paper.

statementBreakdown.reference: RBI Master Directions – Priority Sector Lending & Financial Markets Operations (LAF Eligibility)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Eligible participants for the RBI's standard Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) repos and Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) windows are restricted to Scheduled Commercial Banks (excluding RRBs) and Standalone Primary Dealers (SPDs). Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) do not have direct access to the LAF window of the RBI.

statementBreakdown.reference: Foreign Exchange Management (Debt Instruments) Regulations / RBI FAR Framework
statementBreakdown.explanation: Registered Foreign Portfolio Investors (formerly FIIs) are permitted to invest in Indian Government Securities (G-Secs) through the General Route, the Voluntary Retention Route (VRR), and the Fully Accessible Route (FAR), which allows investment without any macro ceiling in specified securities.

statementBreakdown.reference: SEBI Guidelines on Dedicated Debt Segment (2013 / NCS Regulations)
statementBreakdown.explanation: SEBI introduced regulatory frameworks permitting recognized stock exchanges like BSE and NSE to establish separate and dedicated debt trading segments for secondary market trading of corporate bonds, debentures, G-Secs, and state development loans.

keywords.concept: Government Securities: Tradeable sovereign debt instruments issued by the Central Government or State Governments acknowledging their public borrowing obligations.

keywords.shortNote: Debt securities issued by private or public corporations to raise medium- to long-term capital from institutional and retail investors.
keywords.concept: Corporate Bonds: Debt securities issued by private or public corporations to raise medium- to long-term capital from institutional and retail investors.

keywords.shortNote: A regulatory initiative launched by the Reserve Bank of India allowing individual retail investors to directly open gilt accounts and trade government securities.
keywords.concept: RBI Retail Direct Scheme: A regulatory initiative launched by the Reserve Bank of India allowing individual retail investors to directly open gilt accounts and trade government securities.

optionBreakdown.label: a

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Omits insurance companies, which constitute one of the largest holding classes in Indian fixed-income markets.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Omits pension funds, which regularly transact in government securities and corporate debentures.

valueAddition.title: Retail G-Sec & Debt Market Access Channels
bullets: RBI Retail Direct enables individual investors to open a Retail Direct Gilt (RDG) Account to bid in primary auctions and trade on NDS-OM.
SEBI created regulatory frameworks for Online Bond Platform Providers (OBPPs) to facilitate transparent retail trading in listed corporate debt.
SEBI reduced the minimum face value for privately placed debt securities issued to retail investors from 1 lakh to 10,000 rupees to deepen liquidity.

bullets: IRDAI mandates life insurers to invest a minimum of 50% of controlled funds in government securities and other approved securities.
PFRDA guidelines allow pension fund managers to allocate up to 50% in Government Securities and up to 45% in corporate debt instruments.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following :
1. Exchange-Traded Funds (ETF)
2. Motor vehicles
3. Currency swap

Which of the above is/are considered financial instruments ?

keywords.shortNote: Any contract that gives rise to a financial asset of one entity and a financial liability or equity instrument of another entity.
keywords.concept: Financial Instrument: Any contract that gives rise to a financial asset of one entity and a financial liability or equity instrument of another entity.

keywords.shortNote: A marketable pooled investment security that tracks an index, commodity, or basket of assets and trades continuously on a stock exchange like an equity share.
keywords.concept: Exchange-Traded Fund (ETF): A marketable pooled investment security that tracks an index, commodity, or basket of assets and trades continuously on a stock exchange like an equity share.

keywords.shortNote: An over-the-counter derivative contract in which two counterparties exchange principal and interest payments in different currencies over an agreed period.
keywords.concept: Currency Swap: An over-the-counter derivative contract in which two counterparties exchange principal and interest payments in different currencies over an agreed period.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Excludes currency swaps, which are classic derivative financial instruments.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly classifies motor vehicles (physical real assets) as financial instruments.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to separate tangible physical property from contractual financial claims.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Correctly pairs ETFs (cash security) and currency swaps (derivative contract) while excluding physical motor vehicles.

valueAddition.title: The Two-Sided Contract Test
bullets: A financial instrument always creates a financial asset for one party and a corresponding financial liability or equity claim for the counterparty.
Physical assets like motor vehicles, real estate, and gold bullion fail this test because ownership confers direct physical utility without a counterparty financial liability.
Derivatives such as forwards, futures, options, and swaps qualify as financial instruments because their value derives from underlying financial variables under a binding contract.

valueAddition.title: Cash Instruments vs. Derivative Instruments
bullets: Cash instruments (shares, bonds, treasury bills, ETFs) have prices determined directly by market demand and supply for the underlying claim.
Derivative instruments (currency swaps, interest rate swaps, index options) derive their payoff strictly from the price movement of an underlying asset or exchange rate.
Both categories fall under the regulatory architecture of SEBI (for exchange-traded securities) or RBI (for OTC interest rate and foreign exchange derivatives).

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
inNews.headline: RBI Introduces USD-INR Forex Swap Facility for External Commercial Borrowings
inNews.relevance: RBI launched a special USD-INR swap window in June 2026 to help banks hedge foreign currency borrowings and manage domestic rupee liquidity through bilateral derivative contracts.

statementBreakdown.explanation: An ETF represents a contractual ownership claim over a pooled portfolio of underlying securities or commodities and is traded directly on stock exchanges, qualifying as a cash market financial instrument.
Motor vehicles are physical, tangible real assets whose value stems from mechanical utility rather than a bilateral financial contract creating a simultaneous financial asset and liability.
A currency swap is a derivative contract obligating two parties to exchange cash flows in two different currencies, creating mutual contractual rights and payment obligations.

Shares, Bonds, ETFs, Options, Currency Swaps

hook.teaser: Notice how UPSC mixes everyday physical property with market contracts to test one basic definition.

keywords.calloutNote: Think of an ETF as a demat unit giving you a contractual claim over a basket of securities on an exchange.
activePhrases: Exchange-Traded Funds (ETF)

keywords.calloutNote: Recall that any derivative contract exchanging cash flows between two parties is a financial instrument.
activePhrases: Currency swap
dimmedPhrases: Exchange-Traded Funds (ETF)

verdicts.source: An ETF is a tradable mutual fund unit backed by underlying securities, making it a standard financial instrument.
A motor vehicle is a tangible physical asset—it gives you transport utility, not a financial claim against a counterparty.
A currency swap is a binding contract to exchange principal and interest in two currencies, which is a textbook derivative instrument.

answer.label: D
answer.text: Both ETFs and currency swaps are contractual financial instruments, leaving motor vehicles out—so 1 and 3 only is the clean answer.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to the sectors of the Indian economy, consider the following pairs :

Economic activity | Sector
1. Storage of agricultural produce | Secondary
2. Dairy farm | Primary
3. Mineral exploration | Tertiary
4. Weaving cloth | Secondary

How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched ?

keywords.shortNote: Activities undertaken by directly exploiting natural resources, including agriculture, dairy farming, forestry, fishing, and mining and quarrying.
keywords.concept: Primary Sector: Activities undertaken by directly exploiting natural resources, including agriculture, dairy farming, forestry, fishing, and mining and quarrying.

keywords.shortNote: Activities that transform natural products into other forms through manufacturing and industrial processing (e.g., spinning yarn, weaving cloth, sugar production).
keywords.concept: Secondary Sector: Activities that transform natural products into other forms through manufacturing and industrial processing (e.g., spinning yarn, weaving cloth, sugar production).

keywords.shortNote: Activities that generate support services rather than physical goods, such as transport, storage, banking, trade, and communication.
keywords.concept: Tertiary Sector: Activities that generate support services rather than physical goods, such as transport, storage, banking, trade, and communication.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Pairs 2 and 4 are both accurately classified.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Dairy farming (Primary) and Weaving cloth (Secondary) are correctly matched; storage is Tertiary and mineral exploration is Primary.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Pairs 1 and 3 are misclassified.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Storage is not secondary and mineral exploration is not tertiary.

valueAddition.title: Three-Sector Classification Framework (MoSPI / CSO)
bullets: Primary Sector (Natural Resource Extraction): Agriculture, forestry, fishing, livestock/dairy, and mining and quarrying (including crude oil and gas extraction).
Secondary Sector (Value Addition & Manufacturing): Manufacturing (registered and unregistered), electricity, gas, water supply, other utility services, and construction.

Tertiary Sector (Services Infrastructure): Trade, repair services, hotels and restaurants, transport, storage, communication, broadcasting, financial services, real estate, professional services, public administration, and defense.

valueAddition.title: Quaternary and Quinary Extensions
bullets: Quaternary Sector: Knowledge-based segment of the services economy focusing on information generation, R&D, software development, data analytics, and financial consultancy.

Quinary Sector: Apex decision-making segment consisting of top executives, policy makers, government officials, research scientists, and legal advisors ('gold collar' professions) shaping strategic direction.

inNews.source: PIB / Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
inNews.headline: MoSPI releases updated National Industrial Classification aligning digital warehousing and mining services with international standard industrial classification
inNews.relevance: Directly reaffirms the sectoral demarcations between extractive operations (Primary), industrial conversion (Secondary), and logistical warehousing (Tertiary).

statementBreakdown.explanation: Storage of agricultural produce (warehousing/cold storage) does not manufacture or transform goods; it provides an essential logistical service to support the primary and secondary sectors, placing it firmly in the Tertiary (Services) sector.
Dairy farming relies directly on biological processes of animals and natural fodder availability to produce raw milk, making it a classic Primary sector economic activity.
Mineral exploration, mining, and quarrying involve direct extraction of earth resources and are categorized under the Primary sector in national accounting, not the Tertiary sector.

Weaving cloth takes raw agricultural or synthetic fibers (like cotton yarn) and processes them through spinning and weaving into fabric, making it a core manufacturing activity of the Secondary sector.

verdicts.source: Storage and cold chains are logistics services, placing them in the Tertiary sector.
Dairy farming relies directly on animal biological processes, making it a Primary activity.
Mining, quarrying, and mineral extraction fall under the Primary sector in national accounting.
Weaving cloth transforms raw yarn into textiles, which is core Secondary manufacturing.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Only two pairs (2 and 4) are correctly matched, making (b) the right answer.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to physical capital in Indian economy, consider the following pairs :

Items | Category
1. Farmer's plough | Working capital
2. Computer | Fixed capital
3. Yarn used by the weaver | Fixed capital
4. Petrol | Working capital

How many of the above pairs are correctly matched ?

keywords.shortNote: Durable physical assets, tools, machines, computers, and buildings that can be utilized repeatedly in production across multiple cycles over many years.
keywords.concept: Fixed Capital: Durable physical assets, tools, machines, computers, and buildings that can be utilized repeatedly in production across multiple cycles over many years.

keywords.shortNote: Raw materials, fuel, inputs, and money in hand that are consumed, exhausted, or transformed completely within a single production cycle.
keywords.concept: Working Capital: Raw materials, fuel, inputs, and money in hand that are consumed, exhausted, or transformed completely within a single production cycle.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Pairs 2 and 4 are both accurately classified.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Computer (Fixed capital) and Petrol (Working capital) are correctly matched; plough is Fixed capital and yarn is Working capital.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Pairs 1 and 3 are inversely swapped.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Plough is durable (fixed) and yarn is an intermediate raw material (working).

valueAddition.title: Four Factors of Production & Physical Capital Breakdown
bullets: Land: Natural gifts including soil, water, forests, and mineral deposits.
Labour: Physical and mental human effort dedicated to economic production.
Physical Capital (Variety of inputs required at every stage):
• Fixed Capital: Durable assets such as tools, machines, buildings, tractors, turbines, and computers that can be reused over many production cycles without being physically consumed in a single use.

• Working Capital: Non-durable circulating capital comprising raw materials (e.g., yarn for weavers, clay for potters), fuels (petrol, diesel, electricity consumed), and cash in hand for day-to-day payments.
Human Capital: The knowledge, skill, training, and enterprise embodied in the workforce that coordinates land, labour, and physical capital to produce an economic output.

valueAddition.title: Accounting & National Income Treatment
bullets: Depreciation (Consumption of Fixed Capital): Fixed capital is subject to annual wear, tear, and obsolescence, which is deducted from Gross Capital Formation to arrive at Net Capital Formation.
Intermediate Consumption: Working capital inputs (raw materials, operating fuel) are treated as intermediate consumption and netted out of gross output to determine Gross Value Added (GVA).

Gross Capital Formation (Investment): Consists of Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) plus net changes in inventories (stocks of raw materials, semi-finished, and finished goods held as working capital).

inNews.source: Ministry of Finance / Economic Survey
inNews.headline: Economic Survey highlights expansion in Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) driven by private corporate capex in hardware and automation
inNews.relevance: Directly links physical capital accumulation (Fixed Capital) to national output expansion and productivity growth.

statementBreakdown.explanation: A farmer's plough is an agricultural tool/implement that can be used across multiple cropping seasons for many years; it is durable and constitutes Fixed capital, not Working capital.
Computers, servers, and generators are durable electronic machinery used over multiple years in business and production operations, categorizing them as Fixed capital.
Yarn is an intermediate raw material that gets woven into cloth and exhausted during that specific production process, making it Working capital, not Fixed capital.
Petrol is an operating consumable fuel that is burnt and exhausted during transport or machine operations in a single run, correctly classifying it as Working capital.

visualSuggestion.title: Physical Capital: Fixed Capital vs. Working Capital

Tagged as working capital because farmers use it daily
Durable electronic machine lasting multiple years
Intermediate raw material exhausted in producing cloth
Tagged as fixed capital because it is core to weaving

hook.teaser: Here is the exact NCERT Class 9 economy trap UPSC tested in Prelims 2024.

activePhrases: Farmer's plough | Working capital

verdicts.source: A plough is a durable tool used over many seasons, categorizing it as Fixed Capital.
Computers and office machinery survive multiple production cycles over several years.
Raw materials like yarn get completely consumed into the final fabric during production.
Operating fuels like petrol are used up in a single operational cycle as working capital.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Only two pairs (2 and 4) are correctly matched, making (b) the correct answer.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to the rule/rules imposed by the Reserve Bank of India while treating foreign banks, consider the following statements :
1. There is no minimum capital requirement for wholly owned banking subsidiaries in India.
2. For wholly owned banking subsidiaries in India, at least 50% of the board members should be Indian nationals.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: A regulatory policy framed by the RBI in November 2013 incentivizing foreign banks to incorporate locally as separate Indian legal entities with near-national treatment, ring-fenced capital, and an independent local board.
keywords.concept: Wholly Owned Subsidiary (WOS) Framework: A regulatory policy framed by the RBI in November 2013 incentivizing foreign banks to incorporate locally as separate Indian legal entities with near-national treatment, ring-fenced capital, and an independent local board.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: No central bank permits a banking subsidiary with zero capital; RBI specifies a ₹500 crore (₹5 billion) capital floor.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: A common trap based on partial reading of Paragraph 8(d). The 50% pool includes PIOs and NRIs, whereas the strict Indian national floor is one-third (and they must be resident in India).

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements distort explicit prudential and governance clauses of the 2013 RBI WOS scheme.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: UPSC Official Answer Key & RBI Master Directions
optionBreakdown.explanation: Neither statement is correct as per the official regulatory architecture established by the RBI.

valueAddition.title: Modes of Foreign Bank Presence in India
bullets: Single Mode of Presence: Foreign banks must choose between the Branch Mode or the Wholly Owned Subsidiary (WOS) Mode. They cannot operate through both simultaneously.

Mandated WOS Conversion: Foreign banks incorporated in jurisdictions where domestic legislation confers a preferential claim to depositors in the home country (over foreign depositors in a resolution) are mandated to operate strictly through a WOS in India.

Near-National Treatment: WOS entities receive treatment at par with domestic private sector banks regarding branch expansion (exempted from annual WTO quota caps, except in locations sensitive from a national security perspective).

valueAddition.title: Corporate Governance & Board Mandates for a WOS
bullets: Professional Specialization: Not less than 51% of the total number of board members must possess specialised knowledge/practical experience as required under Section 10A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

Non-Executive & Independence Ratios: Not less than two-thirds of the board must consist of non-executive directors, and at least one-third must be completely independent of the Indian subsidiary, parent bank, or parent associates.

Nationality Formulation: Not less than 50% of the directors must be Indian nationals / NRIs / PIOs, subject to the condition that at least one-third of the total directors are Indian nationals resident in India.

valueAddition.title: Prudential & Priority Sector Obligations
bullets: Capital Adequacy: Must comply with Basel III capital requirements from day one, maintaining a capital-to-risk weighted assets ratio (CRAR) at par with domestic banks.

Priority Sector Lending (PSL): Must achieve the standard 40% PSL target (computed on Adjusted Net Bank Credit or off-balance sheet equivalents), matching domestic commercial banks after an agreed initial transitional phase.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India / The Economic Times
inNews.headline: RBI Considers Calibrated Incentives to Encourage Remaining Foreign Branch Banks to Voluntarily Transition into Local Wholly Owned Subsidiaries
inNews.relevance: Directly links to the policy trade-off between foreign bank branch networks and locally incorporated WOS units, highlighting ring-fencing of domestic deposits and local board accountability.

statementBreakdown.reference: Paragraph 6(a) of the RBI Scheme for Setting up of WOS by Foreign Banks in India
statementBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 is economically absurd and legally false. The RBI mandates that the initial minimum paid-up voting equity capital for a Wholly Owned Subsidiary (WOS) shall be ₹500 crore (₹5 billion), brought in upfront via free foreign exchange remittance from the parent bank.

statementBreakdown.reference: Paragraph 8(d) of the RBI Scheme for Setting up of WOS by Foreign Banks in India
statementBreakdown.explanation: The rule states: 'not less than 50 per cent directors should be Indian nationals / Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) / Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs), subject to the condition that one-third of the directors are Indian nationals resident in India.' The statement asserts that at least 50% must be Indian nationals, ignoring that PIOs (foreign passport holders) and NRIs count towards the 50% threshold, with only one-third strictly required to be resident Indian nationals.

hook.headline: Can a foreign bank open in India with zero capital?
hook.teaser: One statement is common sense; the other is an ultra-fine statutory wording trap.

keywords.calloutNote: Regulatory common sense: no central bank permits an incorporated bank with zero capital.
activePhrases: There is no minimum capital requirement for wholly owned banking subsidiaries in India

keywords.term: at least 50% of the board members should be Indian nationals
keywords.calloutNote: The 50% quota includes NRIs and PIOs; the strict Indian national requirement is only one-third (and resident in India).
activePhrases: at least 50% of the board members should be Indian nationals
dimmedPhrases: There is no minimum capital requirement for wholly owned banking subsidiaries in India

verdicts.source: RBI mandates an upfront minimum paid-up voting equity capital of ₹500 crore (₹5 billion) for any foreign bank WOS.
The 50% bracket permits NRIs and PIOs; only one-third of the board must strictly be Indian nationals resident in India.

answer.label: D
answer.text: Neither statement is correct; RBI requires ₹500 crore minimum capital, and the 50% board rule includes NRIs and PIOs.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Foreign Banks & RBI Regulations notes

items.title: Minimum Capital
items.desc: Wholly owned subsidiaries must bring ₹500 crore upfront via foreign exchange remittance.

items.title: Resident Directors
items.desc: At least one-third of total directors must strictly be Indian nationals resident in India.

items.title: Branch Freedom
items.desc: WOS gets parity with Indian private banks for domestic branch expansion, bypassing WTO caps.

valueAddition.note: Look at statement 2: UPSC often drops secondary qualifying phrases like 'NRIs / Persons of Indian Origin' to turn a statutory clause into an inaccurate absolute statement.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) rules in India, consider the following statements :
1. CSR rules specify that expenditures that benefit the company directly or its employees will not be considered as CSR activities.
2. CSR rules do not specify minimum spending on CSR activities.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: The statutory obligation under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 requiring qualifying companies to spend at least 2% of their average net profits of the preceding three financial years on social and environmental activities listed in Schedule VII.
keywords.concept: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR): The statutory obligation under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 requiring qualifying companies to spend at least 2% of their average net profits of the preceding three financial years on social and environmental activities listed in Schedule VII.

keywords.shortNote: The legal provision governing CSR applicability, requiring any company with a net worth of Rs. 500 crore or more, turnover of Rs. 1,000 crore or more, or net profit of Rs. 5 crore or more to constitute a CSR Committee and meet mandatory spending norms.
keywords.concept: Section 135 of Companies Act, 2013: The legal provision governing CSR applicability, requiring any company with a net worth of Rs. 500 crore or more, turnover of Rs. 1,000 crore or more, or net profit of Rs. 5 crore or more to constitute a CSR Committee and meet mandatory spending norms.

keywords.shortNote: The exhaustive statutory list of permissible developmental areas—such as eradicating hunger, promoting education, healthcare, environmental sustainability, and contributions to PM CARES or Swachh Bharat Kosh—eligible for CSR expenditure.
keywords.concept: Schedule VII of Companies Act, 2013: The exhaustive statutory list of permissible developmental areas—such as eradicating hunger, promoting education, healthcare, environmental sustainability, and contributions to PM CARES or Swachh Bharat Kosh—eligible for CSR expenditure.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accurately identifies the exclusion of self-serving and employee-centric spending while rejecting the false claim that no minimum spending floor exists.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Contradicts the core 2% minimum profit-spending mandate under Section 135(5) of the Companies Act, 2013.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to catch the blatantly false assertion regarding minimum CSR expenditure.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks Rule 2(1)(d), which bars companies from counting employee welfare or brand-promotion expenses as CSR.

valueAddition.title: Section 135 Applicability Thresholds & The 2% Rule
bullets: A company triggers mandatory CSR compliance if it crosses ANY ONE of three thresholds in the immediately preceding financial year: Net Worth >= Rs. 500 crore, Turnover >= Rs. 1,000 crore, or Net Profit >= Rs. 5 crore.
Qualifying companies must spend at least 2% of their average net profits of the preceding three financial years on Schedule VII activities, giving preference to local areas around their operations.

Following the 2019/2021 amendments, CSR shifted from 'comply or explain' to mandatory transfer: unspent CSR funds not tied to an ongoing project must be transferred to a Schedule VII fund (such as PMNRF or Clean Ganga Fund) within 6 months of the financial year-end.

valueAddition.title: What Never Counts as CSR (Negative List)
bullets: Activities carried out in the normal course of business (except R&D on new vaccines, drugs, or medical devices under specified notifications).
Programs designed exclusively for the benefit of the company's own employees and their families.

Contributions to any political party under Section 182 of the Companies Act, 2013, or activities undertaken outside India (except training of Indian sports personnel representing India internationally).

inNews.source: Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) / Business Standard
inNews.headline: MCA National CSR Data Portal Shows Corporate CSR Outflows Cross Rs. 34,000 Crore Led by Education and Health
inNews.relevance: Ministry of Corporate Affairs disclosures in September 2026 highlighted stronger compliance under mandatory unspent-account transfer rules, with education, healthcare, and rural development absorbing over two-thirds of corporate CSR funds.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Under Rule 2(1)(d) of the CSR Rules, activities undertaken in the normal course of business, activities benefitting employees of the company (as defined under the Code on Wages), and sponsorship activities yielding direct marketing benefits for the company are explicitly excluded from CSR.
Section 135(5) explicitly mandates a minimum annual CSR spending floor of at least 2% of the average net profits made by the company during the three immediately preceding financial years.

hook.teaser: Notice how UPSC pairs a detailed exclusion rule with one blatantly false claim about minimum spending.

keywords.calloutTerm: “benefit the company directly or its employees”
keywords.calloutNote: Under CSR Rules, anything done in normal business or exclusively for your own staff is strictly disqualified from CSR.
activePhrases: benefit the company directly or its employees

keywords.calloutNote: Section 135 of the Companies Act is famous worldwide precisely because it mandates a strict 2% minimum profit spend.
activePhrases: do not specify minimum spending
dimmedPhrases: benefit the company directly or its employees

Section 135(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 specifies a minimum CSR expenditure of 2% of average net profits over the preceding three years.

answer.label: A
answer.text: India made history by mandating a 2% minimum CSR spend while barring employee-only perks—so 1 only is the right answer.

items.desc: CSR applies if Net Worth >= Rs. 500 cr, Turnover >= Rs. 1,000 cr, or Net Profit >= Rs. 5 cr in the previous year.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I: If the United States of America (USA) were to default on its debt, holders of US Treasury Bonds will not be able to exercise their claims to receive payment.
Statement-II: The USA Government debt is not backed by any hard assets, but only by the faith of the Government.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements ?

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
options.label: a

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
options.label: b

options.text: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
options.label: c

options.text: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: Long-term marketable sovereign debt securities issued by the US Department of the Treasury (with maturities of 20 or 30 years) that pay fixed semi-annual interest and are backed unconditionally by the full faith and credit of the US Government rather than specific physical collateral.
keywords.concept: US Treasury Bonds: Long-term marketable sovereign debt securities issued by the US Department of the Treasury (with maturities of 20 or 30 years) that pay fixed semi-annual interest and are backed unconditionally by the full faith and credit of the US Government rather than specific physical collateral.

keywords.shortNote: Public debt obligations not collateralized against tangible state property, meaning bondholders cannot seize physical government assets in the event of a sovereign default.
keywords.concept: Unsecured Sovereign Debt: Public debt obligations not collateralized against tangible state property, meaning bondholders cannot seize physical government assets in the event of a sovereign default.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
optionBreakdown.explanation: Because US Government debt is backed purely by sovereign faith rather than physical hard assets (Statement-II), bondholders have no collateralized property to seize or enforce claims against in a default scenario (Statement-I).

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks that the absence of hard-asset collateral in Statement-II is the exact reason bondholders cannot enforce physical recovery claims in Statement-I.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.text: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly assumes US Treasury bonds are backed by Fort Knox gold or physical federal assets, whereas the US left gold backing behind decades ago.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.text: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to recognize that unlike corporate secured bonds—where creditors can seize mortgaged factories—unsecured sovereign bonds leave holders with no hard-asset claim to execute upon default.

valueAddition.title: Secured Corporate Bonds vs. Unsecured Sovereign Treasury Bonds
bullets: In private corporate lending, a secured bondholder holds a legal lien over specific physical collateral (machinery, real estate, inventory) that can be seized and liquidated through bankruptcy courts if the company defaults.

By contrast, US Treasury bills, notes, and bonds are unsecured obligations backed purely by the 'full faith and credit' of the US Government—meaning investors cannot attach federal buildings, gold reserves, or military assets if a debt-ceiling standoff triggers default.

valueAddition.title: Why Foreign Central Banks (Including RBI) Still Hold US Treasuries as Safe Assets
bullets: Even without hard-asset collateral, US Treasuries serve as the global risk-free benchmark because the US Government holds sovereign taxing power over the world's largest economy and issues debt in the world's primary reserve currency (the US Dollar), reinforced by Section 4 of the 14th Amendment stating that the validity of US public debt shall not be questioned.

inNews.source: US Department of the Treasury / Reuters
inNews.headline: US Federal Public Debt Surpasses USD 38 Trillion as Global Central Banks Rebalance Treasury Holdings
inNews.relevance: October 2026 US Treasury International Capital (TIC) data showed foreign central banks—including the Reserve Bank of India—actively managing US Treasury holdings amid rising federal debt levels and fiscal deficit debates.

statementBreakdown.reference: Sovereign Immunity & Unsecured Treasury Bond Terms
statementBreakdown.explanation: Because US Treasury securities are unsecured sovereign obligations with no pledged physical collateral and sovereign immunity shields federal property from seizure, bondholders have no hard assets to attach or foreclose upon to enforce immediate payment if the US Government defaults.

statementBreakdown.reference: US Department of the Treasury — Full Faith and Credit Standard
statementBreakdown.explanation: US Treasury securities are not backed by gold reserves, land, or any tangible hard assets—they are backed solely by the 'full faith and credit' of the United States Government, which directly explains why bondholders cannot seize assets to recover payment upon default.

answer.label: A
answer.text: Because US debt has no hard-asset backing, bondholders have nothing to seize upon default—so both statements are right and Statement-II explains Statement-I.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I: Syndicated lending spreads the risk of borrower default across multiple lenders.
Statement-II: The syndicated loan can be a fixed amount/lump sum of funds, but cannot be a credit line.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements ?

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
options.label: a

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
options.label: b

options.text: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
options.label: c

options.text: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: A financing arrangement where a group of lenders (the syndicate) jointly pool funds under a unified credit agreement to finance a single large corporate borrower, administered by a designated lead arranger/agent bank.
keywords.concept: Syndicated Lending: A financing arrangement where a group of lenders (the syndicate) jointly pool funds under a unified credit agreement to finance a single large corporate borrower, administered by a designated lead arranger/agent bank.

keywords.shortNote: A flexible borrowing facility allowing the corporate borrower to draw down, repay, and re-borrow funds up to an agreed limit over a specified tenure, frequently structured as a tranche within syndicated facilities.
keywords.concept: Credit Line Facility: A flexible borrowing facility allowing the corporate borrower to draw down, repay, and re-borrow funds up to an agreed limit over a specified tenure, frequently structured as a tranche within syndicated facilities.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Syndicated facilities frequently include revolving credit lines for corporate working capital needs.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks the contractual reality that syndicated loans accommodate both fixed term loans and revolving credit lines.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement-I accurately reflects the core risk-diversification rationale of loan syndication, while Statement-II introduces an artificial technical prohibition on credit lines.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: Statement-I is true and Statement-II is false
optionBreakdown.explanation: Inverts the truth value of both propositions.

valueAddition.title: Structure of a Loan Syndicate
bullets: Lead Arranger / Mandated Lead Arranger (MLA): The primary bank mandated by the corporate borrower to structure the terms, prepare the information memorandum, price the loan, and recruit syndicate participants.
Facility Agent / Administrative Agent: Acts as the intermediary liaison between the borrower and the syndicate members, channeling interest/principal payments and monitoring covenant compliance.

Common Documentation: Unlike bilateral loans, the syndicate operates under a single common loan agreement, ensuring identical covenants, interest benchmarks, and default events for all participant lenders.

valueAddition.title: Syndicated Loan Tranches & Formats
bullets: Term Loan Tranche (Amortising or Bullet): Fixed lump sum drawn upfront or against project construction milestones, repaid according to a predetermined schedule.
Revolving Credit Facility (RCF): A committed credit line drawn, repaid, and redrawn at the borrower's operational discretion to manage seasonal or working capital fluctuations.
Letters of Credit (LC) / Guarantee Tranches: Non-funded syndicated credit lines supporting trade and performance contracts.

valueAddition.title: Consortium Lending vs. Syndicated Lending
bullets: Consortium Lending: Traditional arrangement in Indian public sector banking where banks enter into an inter-creditor agreement with separate individual loan sanctions, often with rigid collective procedural rules.
Loan Syndication: Market-driven, structured approach where the lead arranger sells down loan parts to participants who hold pro-rata exposure under a uniform master agreement.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India / The Hindu BusinessLine
inNews.headline: Indian Corporates Expand Offshore and Domestic Syndicated Credit Lines to Finance Green Energy and Infrastructure Capex
inNews.relevance: Directly links to how large infrastructure projects utilize syndicated multi-tranche facilities—combining long-term debt and revolving credit lines—to distribute balance sheet exposure across banks.

statementBreakdown.reference: Core Principles of Syndicated Finance / LMA Standards
statementBreakdown.explanation: Because a single large loan (e.g. for infrastructure, mining, or major acquisitions) could exceed a single bank's capital exposure limits or risk tolerance, a syndicate disperses the potential credit and default risk among several institutional lenders proportionally.

Statement-II claims that a syndicated loan 'cannot be a credit line'. In standard commercial banking, a syndicated loan can take multiple structural forms: a term loan (fixed lump sum), a revolving credit facility (revolving credit line), a letter of credit facility, or a multi-currency hybrid blend of these structures.

hook.headline: Can a syndicated loan be a credit line?
hook.teaser: Statement-II slips in the word 'cannot'—and that is where the trap snaps shut.

keywords.term: spreads the risk of borrower default
keywords.calloutNote: The fundamental economic goal of syndication is dividing giant credit exposures among multiple banks.
activePhrases: Syndicated lending spreads the risk of borrower default across multiple lenders

keywords.calloutNote: Absolute negative trap: syndicated loans routinely include revolving credit lines.
activePhrases: cannot be a credit line
dimmedPhrases: Syndicated lending spreads the risk of borrower default across multiple lenders

verdicts.source: By pooling many banks into one deal, no single balance sheet carries the entire failure risk of a multi-thousand-crore borrower.
Syndicated loans can be structured as fixed term loans, revolving credit lines, or a hybrid combination of both.

answer.label: C
answer.text: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect because syndicated loans frequently take the form of revolving credit lines.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Corporate Banking notes

items.title: Architect
items.desc: Structures the loan package, drafts terms, and sells participations to syndicate members.

items.title: Unified Contract
items.desc: All member banks lend under identical legal covenants administered by a facility agent.

items.title: Revolving Lines
items.desc: Allows corporate borrowers to tap, repay, and redraw operational funds on tap within the syndicate.

valueAddition.note: Look at Statement-II—examiners frequently insert rigid exclusions ('cannot be X') on versatile financial instruments that actually permit multiple contractual variants.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements in respect of the digital rupee :
1. It is a sovereign currency issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in alignment with its monetary policy.
2. It appears as a liability on the RBI's balance sheet.
3. It is insured against inflation by its very design.
4. It is freely convertible against commercial bank money and cash.

Which of the statements given above are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: The sovereign digital currency issued by the RBI as legal tender under Section 22 of the amended RBI Act, representing a direct liability on the central bank's balance sheet.
keywords.concept: Digital Rupee (e₹): The sovereign digital currency issued by the RBI as legal tender under Section 22 of the amended RBI Act, representing a direct liability on the central bank's balance sheet.

keywords.shortNote: Like physical cash, the digital rupee is non-interest bearing fiat currency whose real purchasing power erodes when prices rise; it carries zero built-in inflation insurance.
keywords.concept: Inflation Neutrality / Inflation Risk: Like physical cash, the digital rupee is non-interest bearing fiat currency whose real purchasing power erodes when prices rise; it carries zero built-in inflation insurance.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Omits statement 4, which correctly captures the 1:1 free convertibility of the digital rupee into cash and bank deposits.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Falsely accepts statement 3, which claims that fiat digital currency is structurally immune to inflation.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Omits statement 1, ignoring the sovereign issuer status of the RBI.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: RBI Concept Note on CBDC & UPSC Answer Key
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statements 1, 2, and 4 are legally and theoretically accurate, while statement 3 introduces an impossible economic assertion regarding automatic inflation insurance.

valueAddition.title: Central Bank Money vs. Commercial Bank Money
bullets: Balance Sheet Placement: Digital Rupee (e₹) sits on the liability side of the RBI balance sheet under Reserve Money (M0), carrying sovereign backing with zero credit/counterparty risk.
Commercial Bank Deposits: Sit as liabilities on commercial banks' balance sheets (forming part of Broad Money, M3) and are subject to commercial credit risk (protected only up to ₹5 lakh by DICGC).
One-to-One Parity: Complete, frictionless two-way convertibility exists between physical banknotes, commercial bank savings accounts, and digital rupee tokens.

valueAddition.title: Design Choice: Why CBDC Cannot Be Inflation-Insured
bullets: Non-Interest Bearing: To preserve credit flow in the economy and prevent 'bank runs' or massive deposit migration from commercial banks to the central bank during crises, the RBI explicitly opted for a non-remunerated (zero-interest) CBDC.

Purchasing Power Link: Because it yields no interest and holds no gold/commodity backing, its real value depreciates at the exact rate of consumer inflation (CPI), identical to a paper ₹100 note in your wallet.
Contrast with Inflation-Indexed Bonds (IIBs): Capital-indexed bonds protect the principal from inflation; sovereign fiat currency never possesses built-in inflation protection.

valueAddition.title: Wholesale (e₹-W) vs. Retail (e₹-R) Ecosystem
bullets: Wholesale CBDC (e₹-W): Operational since November 2022; restricted to settlement of secondary market transactions in Government Securities to eliminate settlement risk without CCIL intermediation.
Retail CBDC (e₹-R): Operational since December 2022; token-based digital legal tender distributed via banking intermediaries to individuals and merchants.
Interoperability with UPI: Facilitated via standardized QR codes, allowing consumers to pay UPI-enabled merchants straight from their CBDC wallet.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India / The Hindu
inNews.headline: RBI Pilots Programmable Purpose-Bound Digital Rupee for Agricultural Subsidies and Direct Benefit Transfers
inNews.relevance: Directly illustrates the sovereign functionality of the Digital Rupee as programmable legal tender, while reaffirming its central bank balance sheet liability status and parity with cash.

statementBreakdown.reference: RBI Concept Note on CBDC (Executive Summary & Section 2.1)
statementBreakdown.explanation: The Digital Rupee is legal tender issued by the central bank as sovereign currency, aligned with the RBI's overarching monetary policy objectives and managed within the national reserve money (M0) framework.

statementBreakdown.reference: Section 22 & Section 34 of the RBI Act, 1934
statementBreakdown.explanation: CBDC constitutes central bank money. Unlike commercial bank deposits (which are liabilities of commercial banks), the digital rupee is a direct liability on the balance sheet of the Reserve Bank of India, precisely like physical currency notes in circulation.

Digital rupee is a digital counterpart of fiat paper currency. It is non-interest-bearing and its purchasing power fluctuates with general price levels. No fiat currency is 'insured against inflation by its very design'—that would require inflation-indexed yields, which CBDC deliberately does not offer to prevent bank disintermediation.

statementBreakdown.reference: RBI Concept Note on CBDC (Section 2.2: Fungibility)
statementBreakdown.explanation: The digital rupee is fully and seamlessly convertible at par (1:1) into physical cash as well as commercial bank deposits through digital token wallets.

visualSuggestion.title: Digital Rupee (e₹) vs. Physical Cash vs. Bank Deposits

rows: Earns nominal interest (may partially offset inflation)

hook.headline: Is the Digital Rupee protected against inflation?
hook.teaser: One impossible economic promise in this question makes elimination instantaneous.

keywords.term: insured against inflation by its very design
keywords.calloutNote: Economic impossibility: Digital Rupee is fiat currency—when inflation rises, its purchasing power falls just like paper cash.
activePhrases: It is insured against inflation by its very design

keywords.term: appears as a liability on the RBI's balance sheet
keywords.calloutNote: Central bank money is a direct sovereign liability of the RBI, unlike bank deposits which are commercial bank liabilities.
activePhrases: It appears as a liability on the RBI's balance sheet
dimmedPhrases: It is insured against inflation by its very design

verdicts.source: Digital Rupee is legal tender issued by the RBI as sovereign currency aligned with its monetary policy.
It forms part of currency in circulation and sits directly on the liability side of the RBI's balance sheet.
CBDC is non-interest-bearing fiat money; it offers zero built-in insurance against price inflation.
The digital rupee converts freely and instantaneously into commercial bank deposits and physical paper cash.

answer.label: D
answer.text: Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct; statement 3 is false because fiat money cannot be insured against inflation by design.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Central Banking & CBDC notes

items.title: Central Bank Money
items.desc: A direct claim on the central bank carrying zero default risk, unlike commercial bank deposits.

items.title: No Bank Disintermediation
items.desc: Intentionally earns 0% interest to prevent deposits from fleeing commercial banks during panic.

items.title: Unified QR Rails
items.desc: Merchants can accept digital rupee tokens seamlessly via existing interoperable UPI QR codes.

valueAddition.note: Spot the conceptual absurdity in Statement 3: no sovereign paper note or fiat digital token is ever 'insured against inflation by design'.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to the 'Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan', consider the following statements :
1. This scheme guarantees a minimum package of antenatal care services to women in their second and third trimesters of pregnancy and six months post-delivery health care service in any government health facility.
2. Under this scheme, private sector health care providers of certain specialities can volunteer to provide services at nearby government health facilities.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: A flagship initiative launched in 2016 by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to provide assured, comprehensive, and quality antenatal care free of cost to pregnant women in their 2nd and 3rd trimesters on the 9th day of every month at designated government health facilities.
keywords.concept: Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA): A flagship initiative launched in 2016 by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to provide assured, comprehensive, and quality antenatal care free of cost to pregnant women in their 2nd and 3rd trimesters on the 9th day of every month at designated government health facilities.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because PMSMA is strictly an antenatal care scheme during pregnancy and does not include a six-month post-delivery healthcare package.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: PMSMA mobilizes volunteer private specialists at public health centres for 2nd and 3rd trimester antenatal check-ups, without extending to six months post-delivery care.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because the 'six months post-delivery health care service' clause in Statement 1 is fabricated.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because voluntary participation by private specialists at government facilities is the core public-private pillar of PMSMA.

valueAddition.title: Operational Architecture & Color-Coded Risk Tracking Under PMSMA
bullets: Fixed Monthly Day & Facility Coverage: Conducted on the 9th day of every month across Primary Health Centres (PHCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs), and District Hospitals; under Extended PMSMA (e-PMSMA), high-risk pregnant women receive up to three additional specialist ANC check-ups plus SMS tracking.

Color-Coded MCP Card Stickers: Green sticker indicates a normal pregnancy with no detected risk factors, whereas a Red sticker flags a High-Risk Pregnancy (HRP) for priority specialist referral and institutional delivery planning.

valueAddition.title: Distinguishing India's Three Core Maternal Health Schemes
bullets: PMSMA (2016): Free specialist antenatal check-ups during 2nd/3rd trimesters via public-private specialist volunteering (no cash transfer, no 6-month post-natal cover).
Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK, 2011): Zero-expense institutional delivery, C-section, drugs, diagnostics, diet, and free transport for pregnant women and sick infants up to 1 year.

Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY): Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) cash incentive of Rs. 5,000 for the first child (and Rs. 6,000 for a second girl child under Mission Shakti) to compensate wage loss.

inNews.source: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) / Press Information Bureau (PIB)
inNews.headline: Over 6.5 crore antenatal check-ups completed under Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan as Extended PMSMA scales high-risk pregnancy tracking
inNews.relevance: October 2026 Health Ministry data showed over 6.5 crore 2nd and 3rd trimester ANC examinations and 65 lakh high-risk pregnancies identified via volunteer private and public specialists under PMSMA.

statementBreakdown.reference: MoHFW PMSMA Guidelines · Antenatal Scope Only (No 6-Month Post-Delivery Package)
statementBreakdown.explanation: While PMSMA guarantees a minimum package of free antenatal care services to pregnant women in their second and third trimesters on the 9th of every month, it does not provide six months of post-delivery healthcare services.

statementBreakdown.reference: PMSMA Volunteer Engagement Model · Private Sector Specialists
statementBreakdown.explanation: Under PMSMA, private sector OB/GYN specialists, radiologists, and physicians are encouraged to volunteer their services on the 9th of every month at nearby government health facilities under the 'IPledgeFor9' initiative.

visualSuggestion.title: Key Maternal Health Schemes Under the National Health Mission

rows: Free specialist ANC check-ups & diagnostics on the 9th of every month with volunteer private doctors
Free institutional delivery, drugs, diagnostics, blood, diet & pick-up/drop transport
Pregnancy through delivery & sick infants up to 1 year
Conditional cash transfer (Rs. 5,000 for 1st child; Rs. 6,000 for 2nd girl child)

hook.headline: Does PMSMA cover six months of post-delivery healthcare in government hospitals?
hook.teaser: Look closely at the second half of Statement 1—one added tail turns a true sentence false.

keywords.calloutNote: PMSMA covers free antenatal care during the 2nd and 3rd trimesters on the 9th of each month—it does not extend to six months post-delivery.
activePhrases: six months post-delivery health care service

keywords.term: private sector health care providers of certain specialities can volunteer
keywords.calloutNote: Private OB/GYNs, radiologists, and physicians volunteer at government health facilities on the 9th of every month under PMSMA.
activePhrases: private sector health care providers of certain specialities can volunteer
dimmedPhrases: six months post-delivery health care service

verdicts.source: PMSMA guarantees 2nd and 3rd trimester antenatal check-ups on the 9th of every month, not six months of post-delivery healthcare.
Private OB/GYN specialists, radiologists, and physicians volunteer at nearby government health facilities under PMSMA.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Only Statement 2 is correct—PMSMA uses volunteer private specialists for 2nd and 3rd trimester antenatal care without a six-month post-delivery package.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Social Sector & Health notes

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to the Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maan-dhan (PM-SYM) Yojana, consider the following statements :
1. The entry age group for enrolment in the scheme is 21 to 40 years.
2. Age specific contribution shall be made by the beneficiary.
3. Each subscriber under the scheme shall receive a minimum pension of ₹ 3,000 per month after attaining the age of 60 years.
4. Family pension is applicable to the spouse and unmarried daughters.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: A voluntary and contributory central sector pension scheme launched in 2019 for unorganised sector workers earning up to ₹15,000 per month.
keywords.concept: Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maan-dhan (PM-SYM): A voluntary and contributory central sector pension scheme launched in 2019 for unorganised sector workers earning up to ₹15,000 per month.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Entry age begins at 18 (not 21), and family pension is restricted strictly to the spouse.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Beneficiaries pay an age-graded contribution (2) and are guaranteed ₹3,000 per month after age 60 (3).

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 3 is an established core guarantee of the scheme.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements 1 and 4 carry factual distractors.

valueAddition.title: PM-SYM Institutional & Financial Architecture
bullets: Target Group: Home-based workers, street vendors, agricultural labourers, construction workers, and domestic helpers in the unorganised sector whose monthly income does not exceed ₹15,000.
Exclusions: Workers covered under EPFO, ESIC, or NPS, and individuals who are income tax payees.
Pension Fund Manager: Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) acts as the Pension Fund Manager and manages disbursement through its network.
Enrollment Channel: Common Services Centres (CSCs) serve as enrollment points using Aadhaar and Jan Dhan/savings bank accounts on auto-debit.

valueAddition.title: Spouse & Exit Provisions
bullets: Spouse Co-Contribution: If both spouses are eligible unorganised workers, both can join separately and receive ₹3,000 each upon reaching 60 years of age.
Death During Receipt: If the subscriber dies while receiving the pension, the spouse is entitled to 50% as family pension (₹1,500/month).

Death Before 60: If the subscriber dies before attaining age 60, the spouse can continue the scheme by paying regular contributions, or exit and claim the accumulated corpus with savings bank interest.
Sibling / Children Rights: If the subscriber dies leaving no spouse, the entire corpus (contributions + interest) is refunded into the Pension Fund, not paid to children.

inNews.source: PIB / Ministry of Labour and Employment
inNews.headline: Labour Ministry links e-Shram portal with PM-SYM to automate pension auto-debit and drive saturation among domestic workers
inNews.relevance: Directly highlights the convergence between universal unorganised worker registries (e-Shram) and contributory social safety nets like PM-SYM.

statementBreakdown.reference: Ministry of Labour & Employment · PM-SYM Operational Guidelines
statementBreakdown.explanation: The prescribed entry age window for enrolment is 18 to 40 years, not 21 to 40 years.

statementBreakdown.reference: Ministry of Labour & Employment · Contribution Chart
statementBreakdown.explanation: Contributions are strictly age-specific on a graduated scale. A subscriber joining at age 18 contributes ₹55 per month, whereas a subscriber joining at age 40 contributes ₹200 per month until reaching age 60.

statementBreakdown.reference: Ministry of Labour & Employment · Pension Rules
statementBreakdown.explanation: Upon attaining the age of 60 years, every enrolled beneficiary receives an assured minimum monthly pension of ₹3,000.

Under PM-SYM rules, family pension is applicable solely to the spouse (50% of the pension amount, i.e., ₹1,500/month). Unmarried daughters or children are not eligible for the family pension under this scheme.

visualSuggestion.title: PM-SYM Feature Verification Matrix

hook.headline: Do unmarried daughters get the PM-SYM family pension?
hook.teaser: It sounds plausible, but here is the exact exclusion trap UPSC set in 2024.

keywords.term: entry age group for enrolment in the scheme is 21 to 40 years
keywords.calloutNote: PM-SYM entry age starts early at 18 years, not 21.
activePhrases: The entry age group for enrolment in the scheme is 21 to 40 years

keywords.calloutNote: Family pension under PM-SYM is strictly confined to the surviving spouse—children are barred.
activePhrases: Family pension is applicable to the spouse and unmarried daughters
dimmedPhrases: The entry age group for enrolment in the scheme is 21 to 40 years

verdicts.source: Enrolment opens at age 18 and closes at age 40 for unorganised workers.
Subscribers pay an age-specific sum ranging from ₹55 (at 18) to ₹200 (at 40) per month.
The scheme assures a guaranteed monthly pension of ₹3,000 upon reaching 60 years.
50% family pension goes solely to the surviving spouse; daughters/children have no claim.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Statements 2 and 3 only are correct, making (b) the right answer.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Social Security Scheme notes

items.title: Entry Window
items.desc: Available to unorganised workers earning up to ₹15,000/month not covered under EPFO/ESIC.

items.title: Central Subsidy
items.desc: Central Government deposits an exact 50:50 matching share alongside the worker's contribution.

items.title: Spouse Benefit Only
items.desc: Family pension is 50% (₹1,500) and payable exclusively to the spouse upon beneficiary demise.

valueAddition.note: Examiners routinely inflate the lower age bound from 18 to 21 and expand family pension recipients beyond the spouse to test fine-print memory.

Consider the following statements :
Statement-I: The Indian Flying Fox is placed under the "vermin" category in the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.

Who was the Provisional President of the Constituent Assembly before Dr. Rajendra Prasad took over ?
(a) C. Rajagopalachari
(b) Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
(c) T.T. Krishnamachari
(d) Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha

analysis.coreTakeaway: Remember: Following the French convention of electing the oldest member as temporary chairman, Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha presided over the opening session on 9 December 1946 until Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946.

keywords.shortNote: Temporary presiding officer appointed to conduct initial proceedings before the formal election of the permanent head.
keywords.concept: Provisional President: Temporary presiding officer appointed to conduct initial proceedings before the formal election of the permanent head.

keywords.shortNote: Sovereign constitution-making body formed under the 1946 Cabinet Mission Plan that first assembled on 9 December 1946.
keywords.concept: Constituent Assembly: Sovereign constitution-making body formed under the 1946 Cabinet Mission Plan that first assembled on 9 December 1946.

keywords.shortNote: Elected as the permanent, full-time President of the Constituent Assembly on 11 December 1946.
keywords.concept: Dr. Rajendra Prasad: Elected as the permanent, full-time President of the Constituent Assembly on 11 December 1946.

keywords.shortNote: Oldest member of the Assembly nominated as temporary/provisional President on J.B. Kripalani's proposal.
keywords.concept: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha: Oldest member of the Assembly nominated as temporary/provisional President on J.B. Kripalani's proposal.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: C. Rajagopalachari served in the Interim Government (Education and Arts) and later became India's first Indian Governor-General, but never held the provisional presidency.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: CAD Vol. V (Drafting Committee Appointment, 29 August 1947)
optionBreakdown.explanation: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee appointed on 29 August 1947, but was not the provisional president of the full Assembly.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: T.T. Krishnamachari served as one of the two Vice-Presidents (alongside H.C. Mukherjee) and on the Drafting Committee, not as provisional president.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, being the oldest member, was appointed provisional President on 9 December 1946 following the French practice until Dr. Rajendra Prasad took over on 11 December 1946.

valueAddition.title: Timeline of Assembly Functionaries (December 1946)
bullets: 9 December 1946: Assembly met for the first time with 211 members (Muslim League boycotted). Acharya J.B. Kripalani invited Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha to take the Chair as temporary President.
11 December 1946: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was unanimously elected as the permanent President.
Dual Vice-Presidents: The Assembly later elected two Vice-Presidents—H.C. Mukherjee (elected January 1947) and V.T. Krishnamachari (elected July 1947).
Constitutional Advisor: Sir B.N. Rau was appointed legal/constitutional advisor to prepare the initial benchmark draft.

valueAddition.title: Common Exam Trap: Sinha vs. Prasad vs. Ambedkar
bullets: Don't confuse the bodies: Dr. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee (7 members), not the Constituent Assembly itself.
Don't confuse temporary with permanent: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha presided for only two days (9–10 December 1946) until regular elections took place on 11 December.
Origin of Rule: The convention of appointing the senior-most/oldest member as pro-tem chair was consciously borrowed from the French National Assembly practice.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
As per Article 368 of the Constitution of India, the Parliament may amend any provision of the Constitution by way of :
1. Addition
2. Variation
3. Repeal

Select the correct answer using the code given below :

keywords.shortNote: Grants constituent power to Parliament to amend by way of addition, variation, or repeal any provision of the Constitution in accordance with the prescribed procedure.
keywords.concept: Article 368(1): Grants constituent power to Parliament to amend by way of addition, variation, or repeal any provision of the Constitution in accordance with the prescribed procedure.

keywords.shortNote: Inserted clause (1) into Article 368 to explicitly clarify that Parliament exercises constituent power to amend any provision by addition, variation, or repeal, overriding the Golaknath ruling.
keywords.concept: 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971: Inserted clause (1) into Article 368 to explicitly clarify that Parliament exercises constituent power to amend any provision by addition, variation, or repeal, overriding the Golaknath ruling.

valueAddition.title: Verbatim Text & Judicial History of Article 368(1)
bullets: Verbatim Clause Phrasing: 'Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.'

Origins in the 24th Amendment Act, 1971: Originally, Article 368 was marginal-headed 'Procedure for amendment of the Constitution'. The 24th Amendment substituted the title to 'Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor' and inserted clause (1) to affirm Parliament's constituent power following I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967).

Substantive Scope: Addition allows inserting new articles or parts (e.g., Article 21A, Part IXA); variation allows modifying phrasing or scope (e.g., changing ages or quotas); repeal allows deleting existing articles or clauses (e.g., Article 31, Article 19(1)(f)).

Substantive Limit (Basic Structure Doctrine): In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Supreme Court affirmed that while Parliament's power under Article 368 encompasses addition, variation, or repeal, it cannot alter, damage, or destroy the basic structure of the Constitution.

valueAddition.title: Article 368 Procedural Guardrails
bullets: Introduction: A constitutional amendment bill can be introduced in either House of Parliament, but not in State Legislatures.
Prior Sanction: Does not require the prior recommendation of the President.
Special Majority: Must be passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
No Joint Sitting: There is no constitutional provision for a joint sitting under Article 108 to resolve a deadlock on an amendment bill.
Presidential Assent: Under the 24th Amendment Act, 1971, the President 'shall give his assent' to the bill, eliminating presidential veto over constitutional amendments.

inNews.source: Supreme Court of India
inNews.headline: Constitution Bench clarifies outer boundaries of constituent power under Article 368 regarding basic structure safeguards
inNews.relevance: Reiterates that while the modes of addition, variation, and repeal are wide, they remain subject to the basic structure limitation.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Article 368(1) explicitly specifies that Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition any provision of the Constitution.
Article 368(1) expressly includes variation as one of the three statutory methods of constitutional amendment.
Article 368(1) explicitly empowers Parliament to amend provisions by way of repeal, as seen in the repeal of Article 31 (Right to Property) by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.

visualSuggestion.title: The Three Modalities of Constitutional Amendment (Article 368)

rows: Inserting new articles, clauses, schedules, or parts into the constitutional text
Insertion of Article 21A (Right to Education) by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002; insertion of Part IXA (Municipalities) by the 74th Amendment Act, 1992
Modifying, amending, or expanding the scope and wording of an existing provision
Substitution of Article 45 wording by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002; changing retirement ages of High Court judges from 60 to 62 years by the 15th Amendment Act, 1963
Formally deleting, rescinding, or expunging an existing provision from the Constitution
Omission of Article 31 and Article 19(1)(f) (Right to Property) by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978; deletion of Part VII (Part B States) by the 7th Amendment Act, 1956

valueAddition.title: North Eastern Council: Statutory Architecture & Key Milestones
bullets: Enactment & Headquarters: Constituted by the North Eastern Council Act, 1971; became operational on 7 November 1972 with permanent headquarters at Shillong, Meghalaya.
Parent Administrative Ministry: Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (MDoNER), established in 2001 and elevated to a full-fledged Union Ministry in 2004.

2002 Statutory Transformations: The North Eastern Council (Amendment) Act, 2002 formally added Sikkim as the 8th member state (joining Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, and Tripura), restructured the apex council, and repositioned the NEC as a regional planning body.

Executive Restructuring (June 2018): The Union Cabinet approved the nomination of the Union Home Minister as ex-officio Chairman and the Minister of State (Independent Charge), MDoNER as Vice-Chairman.
Distinct from Zonal Councils: Zonal Councils were created under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956; the NEC is an independent statutory entity governed by its own dedicated 1971 enactment.

valueAddition.title: Zonal Councils vs. North Eastern Council: Structural Contrast
bullets: Statutory Basis: Five Zonal Councils exist under Part III of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956; NEC exists under the North Eastern Council Act, 1971.
Common Chairperson: Union Home Minister chairs all five Zonal Councils (statutory) as well as the NEC (via 2018 executive order).
Vice-Chairmanship: In Zonal Councils, Chief Ministers of constituent states rotate annually as Vice-Chairman; in the NEC, the Minister of State (IC), MDoNER serves as Vice-Chairman.

Membership Nuance: Zonal Councils include the CM and two other ministers nominated by the Governor from each state; the NEC statutory body uniquely includes both the Governor and Chief Minister of all eight constituent states.
