stem: How many Delimitation Commissions have been constituted by the Government of India till December 2023 ?

keywords.shortNote: A high-powered statutory body set up by the Central Government under an Act of Parliament to redraw territorial constituencies for the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.
keywords.concept: Delimitation Commission: A high-powered statutory body set up by the Central Government under an Act of Parliament to redraw territorial constituencies for the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.

keywords.shortNote: Constitutional provisions mandating readjustment and division of each State into territorial constituencies after each decennial Census by an authority determined by law.
keywords.concept: Article 82 & Article 170: Constitutional provisions mandating readjustment and division of each State into territorial constituencies after each decennial Census by an authority determined by law.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: There have been four nationwide commissions, not just one.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Commissions were set up after the 1951, 1961, 1971, and 2001 Censuses.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Three commissions had already been set up by 1973; the fourth was constituted in 2002.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Till December 2023, Delimitation Commissions have been constituted exactly four times: in 1952, 1963, 1973, and 2002.

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Foundations & Freeze Amendments
bullets: Constitutional Mandates: Article 82 governs readjustment of Lok Sabha seats after each census, while Article 170(3) governs seats in State Legislative Assemblies.

42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976: Froze the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies (as well as inter-state allocation) based on the 1971 Census until the year 2000 to promote family planning.

84th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001: Extended the freeze on the total number of seats and state-wise allocation until the first Census published after 2026 (i.e. post-2026). It also empowered the 2002 Commission to redraw intra-state territorial boundaries based on the 1991 Census.
87th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003: Altered the base census year for intra-state constituency redrawing from the 1991 Census to the 2001 Census without altering total seat numbers.

valueAddition.title: Composition & Finality of Delimitation Orders
bullets: Composition: Chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge, alongside the Chief Election Commissioner (or an Election Commissioner nominated by CEC), and the respective State Election Commissioner as ex-officio members.
Associate Members: Drawn from MPs and MLAs of the relevant states to aid deliberations, but they possess no voting rights.

Immunity from Judicial Review (Article 329(a)): Orders of the Delimitation Commission, once published in the Gazette of India and coming into force, have the full force of law and cannot be questioned in any court of law.

keywords.shortNote: Lists the official languages recognized by the Indian Constitution, expanding from 14 original languages in 1950 to 22 languages through three subsequent constitutional amendments.
keywords.concept: Eighth Schedule: Lists the official languages recognized by the Indian Constitution, expanding from 14 original languages in 1950 to 22 languages through three subsequent constitutional amendments.

keywords.shortNote: Enacted on 31 August 1992 to incorporate Konkani, Manipuri (Meitei), and Nepali into the Eighth Schedule, raising the total count of recognized languages from 15 to 18.
keywords.concept: 71st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992: Enacted on 31 August 1992 to incorporate Konkani, Manipuri (Meitei), and Nepali into the Eighth Schedule, raising the total count of recognized languages from 15 to 18.

keywords.shortNote: Added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali (the 'BDMS' quartet) to the Eighth Schedule, coming into force in January 2004.
keywords.concept: 92nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003: Added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali (the 'BDMS' quartet) to the Eighth Schedule, coming into force in January 2004.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Direct match. Accurately combines verified Statements 1, 2, and 3.

valueAddition.title: Eighth Schedule: Chronological Expansion Milestones
bullets: Original 1950 Roster (14 Languages): Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Kashmiri, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia (originally Oriya), Punjabi, Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, and Urdu.
21st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1967: Added Sindhi as the 15th language.
71st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992: Added Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali (mnemonic: KMN), bringing the total to 18 languages.
92nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003: Added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali (mnemonic: BDMS), expanding the schedule to 22 languages.
96th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011: Substituted 'Odia' for 'Oriya' in the Eighth Schedule without altering the total count.

valueAddition.title: Constitutional & Administrative Significance of the Eighth Schedule
bullets: Article 344(1): Mandates the President to constitute an Official Language Commission representing the diverse languages specified in the Eighth Schedule.
Article 351: Directs the Union to promote the spread of Hindi and enrich its vocabulary by drawing primarily on Sanskrit and secondarily on the languages specified in the Eighth Schedule.

Official Exams & Public Services: Candidates appearing for UPSC Civil Services Examinations are entitled to write answers in any of the 22 Eighth Schedule languages, and Sahitya Akademi awards recognize literature in all 22 languages plus English and Rajasthani.

stem:
Which of the following statements are correct about the Constitution of India ?
1. Powers of the Municipalities are given in Part IX A of the Constitution.
2. Emergency provisions are given in Part XVIII of the Constitution.
3. Provisions related to the amendment of the Constitution are given in Part XX of the Constitution.

Select the answer using the code given below :

keywords.shortNote: Constitutional segment titled 'The Municipalities' inserted via the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, spanning Articles 243P to 243ZG.
keywords.concept: Part IX-A: Constitutional segment titled 'The Municipalities' inserted via the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, spanning Articles 243P to 243ZG.

keywords.shortNote: Segment governing Emergency Provisions across three tiers (Articles 352, 356, and 360) and their statutory fallout.
keywords.concept: Part XVIII: Segment governing Emergency Provisions across three tiers (Articles 352, 356, and 360) and their statutory fallout.

keywords.shortNote: Single-article constitutional segment titled 'Amendment of the Constitution' consisting solely of Article 368.
keywords.concept: Part XX: Single-article constitutional segment titled 'Amendment of the Constitution' consisting solely of Article 368.

keywords.shortNote: Empowers Parliament to exercise constituent power to add, vary, or repeal any provision of the Constitution within the basic structure doctrine.
keywords.concept: Article 368: Empowers Parliament to exercise constituent power to add, vary, or repeal any provision of the Constitution within the basic structure doctrine.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Since Statements 1, 2, and 3 are all factually and textually correct, Option (d) is the correct answer.

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Architecture: Landmark Parts & Amendment History
bullets: 74th Amendment Act, 1992: Inserted Part IX-A and the Twelfth Schedule (18 functional items), converting urban local self-government into an enforceable constitutional mandate.

Minerva Mills Case (1980): The Supreme Court struck down Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 (inserted by the 42nd CAA), reaffirming that Parliament's amending power under Part XX is limited and cannot destroy the Basic Structure.
Single-Article Parts: Part XX (Article 368) is one of the rare constitutional parts comprising just a single Article, alongside Part XVII Chapter IV (Article 351).

valueAddition.title: Common Exam Trap: Roman Numeral Mapping & Adjacent Parts
bullets: Panchayats vs. Municipalities vs. Co-operatives: Notice the suffix sequencing—Part IX is Panchayats, Part IX-A is Municipalities, and Part IX-B (added by 97th CAA 2011) is Co-operative Societies.
Part XVII vs. Part XVIII: Examiners frequently attempt to trap candidates between Part XVII (Official Language, Articles 343–351) and Part XVIII (Emergency, Articles 352–360).
Roman Numeral Confusion: Aspirants under exam fatigue often misread Part XX (20) as Part XXI (21, Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions).

inNews.relevance: While dormant in legislative amendments, the structural layout of the Constitution's Parts remains an evergreen UPSC testing ground to check basic anatomical literacy of the bare text.

options.label: b

options.text: Inter-State quarantine is a Union subject under the Union List.
options.label: c

options.text: Corporation tax is a State subject under the State List.
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: Delineates the distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States across List I (Union List), List II (State List), and List III (Concurrent List).
keywords.concept: Seventh Schedule (Article 246): Delineates the distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States across List I (Union List), List II (State List), and List III (Concurrent List).

keywords.shortNote: A Union subject covering inter-State quarantine and the prevention of the extension from one State to another of infectious or contagious diseases.
keywords.concept: Inter-State Quarantine (Entry 81, List I): A Union subject covering inter-State quarantine and the prevention of the extension from one State to another of infectious or contagious diseases.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Inter-State trade and commerce is an exclusive Union subject under Entry 42 of List I, while trade and commerce within the State falls under Entry 26 of List II (State List), subject to Entry 33 of List III.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Inter-State migration and inter-State quarantine are grouped together as exclusive Union subjects under Entry 81 of the Union List (List I).

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Entry 81 of the Union List explicitly assigns 'Inter-State migration; inter-State quarantine' to the exclusive legislative competence of the Parliament of India.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 85 & Article 366(6)
optionBreakdown.explanation: Corporation tax is an exclusive Union tax head under Entry 85 of List I, defined under Article 366(6) as a tax on income levied on corporate entities.

valueAddition.title: Seventh Schedule: Inter-State Subjects & Boundary Entries
bullets: Entry 42, List I: Inter-State trade and commerce (assigned exclusively to Parliament to ensure a unified national common market).
Entry 81, List I: Inter-State migration; inter-State quarantine (enables uniform federal surveillance and mobility standards during epidemics or demographic shifts).
Entry 56, List I: Regulation and development of inter-State rivers and river valleys to the extent declared by Parliament by law to be expedient in the public interest.
Entry 85, List I: Corporation tax (centralised direct corporate tax base providing revenues divisible under Article 270 on Finance Commission recommendations).

Contrast with State Competence (List II): Intra-state public health and sanitation, hospitals, and dispensaries fall under Entry 6 of List II; intra-state trade and commerce falls under Entry 26 of List II.

valueAddition.title: Taxation Entries Architecture: Separation without Concurrency
bullets: No Concurrent Tax Heads: In the original constitutional design, there were no shared/concurrent taxing powers in List III to prevent double taxation by both tiers of government on the same subject.

GST Breakthrough (101st Amendment Act, 2016): Article 246A introduced a sui generis concurrent legislative competence for Parliament and State Legislatures over goods and services tax, operating outside the standard Seventh Schedule lists.
Residuary Powers (Article 248 & Entry 97, List I): Any tax matter not enumerated in List II or List III vests exclusively with Parliament.

valueAddition.title: Evolution of Privacy Jurisprudence: M.P. Sharma to Puttaswamy
bullets: Early Rejections: In M.P. Sharma (1954, 8-judge bench) and Kharak Singh (1962, 6-judge bench), the Supreme Court declined to recognize a constitutional right to privacy, though Subba Rao, J.'s dissent in Kharak Singh planted the seeds of personal liberty.
Govind v. State of M.P. (1975): A 3-judge bench recognized a limited, penumbral right to privacy under Articles 19(1)(d) and 21, subject to compelling state interest.

The 9-Judge Benchmark in Puttaswamy (2017): Expressly overruled M.P. Sharma and the majority in Kharak Singh, declaring privacy to be a natural, inalienable fundamental right located primarily in Article 21, while radiating through the entire freedoms cluster in Part III.

valueAddition.title: The Puttaswamy Four-Fold Proportionality Test
bullets: Legality: Any state encroachment on privacy must be sanctioned by a valid, existing statutory law, not mere executive orders or circulars.
Legitimate State Aim: The encroaching law must serve a clearly identifiable legitimate governmental objective (e.g., national security, crime prevention, public health).
Suitability (Rational Nexus): The statutory measure adopted must be rationally connected to achieving that designated public objective.

Necessity & Least Restrictive Measure: The measure must be strictly necessary; the State must demonstrate that no less intrusive alternative could achieve the goal, and the degree of infringement must not be disproportionate to the benefit gained.

3. This Committee cannot take up any matter which is sub-judice.

keywords.shortNote: First constituted in the Rajya Sabha in 1997; in the Lok Sabha, an ad-hoc committee was constituted in 2000 before becoming a permanent Standing Committee in 2015.
keywords.concept: Ethics Committee Genesis: First constituted in the Rajya Sabha in 1997; in the Lok Sabha, an ad-hoc committee was constituted in 2000 before becoming a permanent Standing Committee in 2015.

keywords.shortNote: Any person—not just an MP—can file a complaint against an MP's unethical conduct, provided it is routed through an MP or supported by an affidavit.
keywords.concept: Complaint Mechanism (Rule 316B): Any person—not just an MP—can file a complaint against an MP's unethical conduct, provided it is routed through an MP or supported by an affidavit.

valueAddition.title: 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023: Key Articles
bullets: Article 330A: Inserts reservation of one-third of total seats for women in the Lok Sabha, including a one-third sub-quota for SC and ST women.
Article 332A: Mandates one-third reservation for women in all State Legislative Assemblies, including the sub-quota for SC and ST women.
Article 239AA(2)(b): Amends the special provisions for Delhi to extend one-third reservation for women in the Legislative Assembly of NCT of Delhi.

No Upper House Reservation: The Act applies exclusively to the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies, and the Delhi Legislative Assembly; it does not provide reservation in the Rajya Sabha or State Legislative Councils.

Article 334A(1) expressly stipulates a sunset clause stating that the reservation shall cease to have effect on the expiration of a period of fifteen years from such commencement, unless extended by Parliament by law.

Article 330A(2) and Article 332A(2) explicitly provide that one-third of the seats reserved under Article 330 (for SCs and STs) in the Lok Sabha and Article 332 in State Assemblies shall be reserved for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

subject: Indian Polity
stem: A Writ of Prohibition is an order issued by the Supreme Court or High Courts to :

options.text: a government officer prohibiting him from taking a particular action.
options.label: a

options.text: the Parliament/Legislative Assembly to pass a law on Prohibition.
options.label: b

options.text: the lower court prohibiting continuation of proceedings in a case.
options.label: c

options.text: the Government prohibiting it from following an unconstitutional policy.
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: A prerogative writ issued by a superior court to a subordinate court or tribunal commanding it to cease proceedings exceeding its jurisdiction.
keywords.concept: Writ of Prohibition: A prerogative writ issued by a superior court to a subordinate court or tribunal commanding it to cease proceedings exceeding its jurisdiction.

keywords.shortNote: An administrative authority or tribunal having legal powers to investigate and adjudicate disputes similarly to a regular court of law.
keywords.concept: Quasi-judicial Body: An administrative authority or tribunal having legal powers to investigate and adjudicate disputes similarly to a regular court of law.

keywords.shortNote: The threshold ground for Prohibition where a court acts beyond the limits demarcated by statute, violates natural justice, or acts under an unconstitutional law.
keywords.concept: Excess of Jurisdiction: The threshold ground for Prohibition where a court acts beyond the limits demarcated by statute, violates natural justice, or acts under an unconstitutional law.

keywords.shortNote: Mandamus commands performance of a public duty by an officer/body; Prohibition commands an inferior court to refrain from acting beyond its legal authority.
keywords.concept: Mandamus vs. Prohibition: Mandamus commands performance of a public duty by an officer/body; Prohibition commands an inferior court to refrain from acting beyond its legal authority.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because restraining or directing executive officers belongs to negative injunctions or Mandamus; Prohibition does not lie against purely administrative officers.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because the judiciary cannot issue writs to Parliament or State Legislatures commanding them to enact a specific statute.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (c) is correct. Prohibition is issued exclusively by a higher court to an inferior court or tribunal to prevent it from usurping or exceeding its jurisdiction in an ongoing case.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because executive policies are challenged through Quo Warranto, Mandamus, or direct declarations of unconstitutionality under Certiorari, not via the judicial Writ of Prohibition.

valueAddition.title: Anatomy of the Writ of Prohibition & Operational Boundaries
bullets: Target Bodies (Judicial & Quasi-Judicial Only): Prohibition lies solely against subordinate judicial courts and statutory tribunals exercising adjudicatory powers; it is not available against administrative authorities, legislative bodies, or private individuals.

Temporal Timing ('Prevention is Better than Cure'): Prohibition is preventive—it must be sought while the matter is still pending before the lower court. Once the subordinate tribunal renders a final order, the proper remedy shifts from Prohibition to Certiorari.

Hari Vishnu Kamath (1955) Distinction: The Supreme Court held that both Prohibition and Certiorari serve the common purpose of restraining lower courts from acting without jurisdiction; Prohibition acts before final decree, while Certiorari corrects completed excess.

valueAddition.title: Target Classification & Layman Word-Trap
bullets: Literal Meaning Trap: In ordinary English, 'prohibition' means stopping someone from doing something; UPSC exploits this by offering distractors like stopping a government officer (Option a) or stopping unconstitutional policies (Option d).
Alcohol Prohibition Distractor: Option (b) playfully introduces statutory alcohol/liquor prohibition under Article 47 to test whether candidates confuse administrative policy with prerogative writs.

The 'Administrative Agency' Boundary: If a body does not have a statutory duty to act judicially (i.e., pure executive/administrative action), neither Prohibition nor Certiorari can be issued against it.

inNews.relevance: High Courts and the Supreme Court regularly intervene via Prohibition to prevent specialized regulatory tribunals from adjudicating disputes outside their statutory mandates, demonstrating the live application of prerogative writs.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. It is the Governor of the State who recognizes and declares any community of that State as a Scheduled Tribe.
2. A community declared as a Scheduled Tribe in a State need not be so in another State.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: Constitutional procedure empowering the President to specify Scheduled Tribes for a State/UT (after consultation with the Governor), with subsequent additions or exclusions made exclusively by an Act of Parliament.
keywords.concept: Article 342 (Scheduled Tribes): Constitutional procedure empowering the President to specify Scheduled Tribes for a State/UT (after consultation with the Governor), with subsequent additions or exclusions made exclusively by an Act of Parliament.

keywords.shortNote: The constitutional doctrine that Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe status is state-specific and does not automatically migrate across state boundaries.
keywords.concept: State-Specific Enumeration Principle: The constitutional doctrine that Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe status is state-specific and does not automatically migrate across state boundaries.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: The Governor merely offers consultation; the power to declare belongs exclusively to the President, and modifications belong to Parliament.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Only statement 2 accurately reflects the state-specific nature of ST scheduling under Article 342.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 erroneously vests the declaring power in the Governor.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 2 is a well-settled constitutional and judicial principle.

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Machinery of Notification & Modification (Article 342)
bullets: Presidential Notification (Art. 342(1)): The President specifies the tribes or tribal communities deemed to be Scheduled Tribes with respect to a State, after consultation with the Governor (consultation is not binding concurrence).

Parliamentary Monopoly (Art. 342(2)): Once the initial Presidential list is issued, neither the President nor any State Government or Governor can modify it. Any inclusion or exclusion can be enacted only by Parliament by law.

Definition in Art. 366(25): Defines Scheduled Tribes as 'such tribes or tribal communities or parts of or groups within such tribes or tribal communities as are deemed under article 342 to be Scheduled Tribes for the purposes of this Constitution'.

valueAddition.title: State-Specific Doctrine & Inter-State Migration
bullets: Marri Chandra Shekhar Rao v. Dean, Seth G.S. Medical College (1990): A Constitution Bench held that an ST member migrating from their state of origin to another state does not automatically carry reservation benefits in the destination state.

Action Committee v. Union of India (1994): Reaffirmed that a person belonging to an SC/ST in State 'A' cannot claim the rights and privileges admissible to SC/STs in State 'B' unless specifically notified in State 'B'.

Lokur Committee Criteria (1965): Standard administrative benchmark used for identifying ST status: (1) indications of primitive traits, (2) distinctive culture, (3) geographical isolation, (4) shyness of contact with the community at large, and (5) backwardness.

inNews.source: The Hindu / PIB
inNews.headline: Parliament enacts Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order Amendment Bill to modify tribal list in Union Territories and States
inNews.relevance: Affirms the operation of Article 342(2), showing that only an Act of Parliament can modify the Scheduled Tribes order of a state.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Under Article 342(1), it is the President of India—not the Governor—who specifies the communities deemed to be Scheduled Tribes in relation to that State, by public notification after consultation with the Governor. Furthermore, any inclusion or exclusion thereafter can only be made by Parliament by law under Article 342(2).

Article 342(1) uses the phrase 'in relation to that State or Union territory'. As held by the Supreme Court in Marri Chandra Shekhar Rao (1990) and Action Committee (1994), ST status is geographically localized to the social and economic conditions of that specific State, so a community declared as an ST in one State need not be recognised as such in another State.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
With reference to Union Budget, consider the following statements :
1. The Union Finance Minister on behalf of the Prime Minister lays the Annual Financial Statement before both the Houses of Parliament.
2. At the Union level, no demand for a grant can be made except on the recommendation of the President of India.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: Mandates that the President shall in respect of every financial year cause to be laid before both the Houses of Parliament the statement of estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India.
keywords.concept: Annual Financial Statement (Article 112(1)): Mandates that the President shall in respect of every financial year cause to be laid before both the Houses of Parliament the statement of estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India.

keywords.shortNote: Constitutional safeguard providing that no demand for a grant shall be made except on the recommendation of the President.
keywords.concept: Demands for Grants (Article 113(3)): Constitutional safeguard providing that no demand for a grant shall be made except on the recommendation of the President.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Identifies Statement 2 as the sole correct statement while eliminating Statement 1.

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Provisions for the Union Budget
bullets: Article 112(1): The word 'Budget' is absent in the Constitution; it is officially designated as the 'Annual Financial Statement'. The constitutional duty to cause it to be laid before Parliament rests squarely with the President.
Article 113(1): Expenditures charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India can be discussed in either House of Parliament but are not submitted to the vote of Parliament.
Article 113(2): Estimates relating to other expenditure are submitted in the form of demands for grants exclusively to the Lok Sabha, which has the power to assent, refuse, or reduce any demand.
Article 113(3): Enforces executive financial initiative; no private member can move a demand for grant without the President's prior recommendation.
Article 114: Mandates an Appropriation Bill to authorize payments and withdrawals out of the Consolidated Fund of India for voted grants and charged expenditure.

valueAddition.title: President's Role in Financial Enactments
bullets: Laying the Budget: Article 112(1) (caused to be laid by the President).
Demands for Grants: Article 113(3) (made on presidential recommendation).
Money Bills & Financial Bills (I): Article 117(1) (cannot be introduced without presidential recommendation).
Expenditure Incurring Bills (Financial Bill II): Article 117(3) (cannot be passed by either House without presidential recommendation).

inNews.relevance: Directly highlights the constitutional necessity of presidential sanction across demands for grants and financial appropriations.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
With reference to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, consider the following statements :
While any resolution for the removal of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha is under consideration :
1. He/She shall not preside.
2. He/She shall not have the right to speak.
3. He/She shall not be entitled to vote on the resolution in the first instance.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: Mandates that at any sitting of the Lok Sabha, while any resolution for the removal of the Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Speaker shall not preside, even if present.
keywords.concept: Article 96(1): Mandates that at any sitting of the Lok Sabha, while any resolution for the removal of the Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Speaker shall not preside, even if present.

keywords.shortNote: Confers on the Speaker the explicit right to speak and take part in proceedings during his removal resolution, with the right to vote in the first instance but no casting vote in the case of equality of votes.
keywords.concept: Article 96(2): Confers on the Speaker the explicit right to speak and take part in proceedings during his removal resolution, with the right to vote in the first instance but no casting vote in the case of equality of votes.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Isolates Statement 1 as the sole correct statement.

valueAddition.title: Article 96 vs. Article 100: Reversal of Voting Rights
bullets: Ordinary Parliamentary Sitting (Article 100(1)): The Speaker presides, cannot vote in the first instance, but exercises a casting vote in case of an equality of votes.
Removal Resolution Sitting (Article 96(2)): The Speaker does not preside, votes in the first instance like an ordinary member, but has no casting vote if the votes are tied.
Right of Audience: The Speaker retains the right to defend themselves, address the House, and participate fully in the debate (Article 96(2)).
Presiding Officer: The Deputy Speaker, or if absent, a person determined by the Rules of Procedure of the House, presides (Article 96(1)).

valueAddition.title: Removal Mechanics under Article 94(c)
bullets: Notice Threshold: Requires at least 14 days' advance notice before the resolution can be moved.
Majority Benchmark: Must be passed by a majority of all the then members of the House (effective majority).
Admissibility Support: Under Lok Sabha Rule 201, at least 50 members must rise in their places to grant leave of the House to move the removal motion.

inNews.headline: Supreme Court examines presiding protocols and adjudicatory limits of legislative officers facing removal notices
inNews.relevance: Directly reinforces the strict constitutional bar under Article 96 and Article 181 preventing presiding officers under removal from occupying the chair.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Article 96(1) provides that at any sitting of the House of the People, while any resolution for the removal of the Speaker from office is under consideration, the Speaker shall not preside.
Article 96(2) explicitly grants the Speaker the right to speak in, and otherwise take part in the proceedings of, the House of the People while any resolution for his removal is under consideration.

Under Article 96(2), the Speaker is entitled to vote in the first instance on such resolution or any other matter during such proceedings, but is barred from exercising a casting vote in the case of equality of votes.

The catch is simple: the Speaker votes in the first instance like an ordinary member, but has no casting vote if there is a tie.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
With reference to the Indian Parliament, consider the following statements :
1. A bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on its dissolution.
2. A bill passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
3. A bill in regard to which the President of India notified his/her intention to summon the Houses to a joint sitting lapses on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: A Bill pending in the Lok Sabha, or passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha, lapses upon the dissolution of the House of the People.
keywords.concept: Lapsing of Bills (Article 107(5)): A Bill pending in the Lok Sabha, or passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha, lapses upon the dissolution of the House of the People.

keywords.shortNote: If the President notifies an intention to summon a joint sitting under Article 108 before the dissolution of the Lok Sabha, the Bill does not lapse despite the dissolution.
keywords.concept: Joint Sitting Notification Shield (Article 108(5)): If the President notifies an intention to summon a joint sitting under Article 108 before the dissolution of the Lok Sabha, the Bill does not lapse despite the dissolution.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Combines verified Statements 1 and 2 while correctly rejecting Statement 3.

valueAddition.title: Comprehensive Rules on Lapsing of Bills on Dissolution
bullets: Lapses: Bill pending in the Lok Sabha (whether originated in LS or transmitted by RS) (Art. 107(5)).
Lapses: Bill passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha (Art. 107(5)).
Does NOT Lapse: Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha which has not been passed by the Lok Sabha (Art. 107(4)).
Does NOT Lapse: Bill passed by both Houses and pending presidential assent (Purushothaman Nambudiri v. State of Kerala, 1962).
Does NOT Lapse: Bill returned by the President for reconsideration of the Houses.
Does NOT Lapse: Bill where the President has already notified intention to summon a joint sitting (Art. 108(5)).

valueAddition.title: Prorogation vs. Dissolution Impact
bullets: Prorogation (Article 107(3)): A Bill pending in Parliament does not lapse by reason of the prorogation of the Houses.
Dissolution (Article 107(5)): Terminates the very life of the Lok Sabha; all business pending before the House or its committees lapses, subject to express constitutional exceptions.

inNews.relevance: Directly illustrates the real-world operational application of Article 107(5) upon general elections and house dissolution.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
With reference to the Parliament of India, consider the following statements :
1. Prorogation of a House by the President of India does not require the advice of the Council of Ministers.
2. Prorogation of a House is generally done after the House is adjourned sine die but there is no bar to the President of India prorogating the House which is in session.
3. Dissolution of the Lok Sabha is done by the President of India who, save in exceptional circumstances, does so on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?

keywords.shortNote: The termination of a session of Parliament by an order issued by the President, acting on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers under Article 74(1).
keywords.concept: Prorogation (Article 85(2)(a)): The termination of a session of Parliament by an order issued by the President, acting on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers under Article 74(1).

keywords.shortNote: While adjournment sine die terminates a sitting indefinitely by the presiding officer, the President usually prorogues the House a few days later, though no constitutional provision prevents proroguing while the House is in active session.
keywords.concept: Adjournment Sine Die: While adjournment sine die terminates a sitting indefinitely by the presiding officer, the President usually prorogues the House a few days later, though no constitutional provision prevents proroguing while the House is in active session.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Combines verified Statements 2 and 3 while eliminating Statement 1.

valueAddition.title: Adjournment vs. Prorogation vs. Dissolution
bullets: Adjournment / Adjournment Sine Die: Terminates a sitting, not a session. Done solely by the Presiding Officer (Speaker/Chairman). Does not affect pending bills or business.
Prorogation: Terminates a session of the House. Done by the President under Article 85(2)(a) on ministerial advice. Does not lapse pending bills under Article 107(3).
Dissolution: Ends the very life of the Lok Sabha under Article 85(2)(b). Done by the President on ministerial advice. Causes pending bills to lapse subject to Article 107(4), 107(5), and 108(5).

valueAddition.title: Presidential Discretion in Dissolution
bullets: Majority Ministry: Advice to dissolve the Lok Sabha is strictly binding on the President.
Defeated / Minority Ministry: If the ministry loses a vote of confidence and advises dissolution, the President is not bound to accept it if an alternative viable government can be formed.

inNews.relevance: Directly illustrates the standard constitutional progression from adjournment sine die to formal presidential prorogation under Article 85.

hook.headline: Can the President prorogue Parliament while an active session is running?
hook.teaser: UPSC tested Article 85 in 2024. Here is where most aspirants slip on prorogation.

activePhrases: Prorogation of a House by the President of India does not require the advice of the Council of Ministers

keywords.calloutNote: Recall that while adjournment sine die normally comes first, the President is never legally barred from acting mid-session.

dimmedPhrases: Prorogation of a House by the President of India does not require the advice of the Council of Ministers

verdicts.source: Look at Article 74—the President exercises powers under Article 85 only on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.

The President dissolves Lok Sabha on cabinet advice, with rare exceptions only if a ministry has lost its majority.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
Statement-I: India accounts for 3.2% of global export of goods.
Statement-II: Many local companies and some foreign companies operating in India have taken of India's Production-linked advantage Incentive' scheme.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I.
options.label: a

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-I is not the correct explanation for Statement-I.
options.label: b

options.text: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is
options.label: c

keywords.shortNote: A country's total physical goods exports divided by total world merchandise exports as tracked by the World Trade Organization (WTO); India's share in global goods exports stands at roughly 1.8% (well below 3.2%, which approximates India's share in global services exports rather than goods).
keywords.concept: Global Merchandise Export Share: A country's total physical goods exports divided by total world merchandise exports as tracked by the World Trade Organization (WTO); India's share in global goods exports stands at roughly 1.8% (well below 3.2%, which approximates India's share in global services exports rather than goods).

keywords.shortNote: A flagship Government of India fiscal incentive program offering eligible domestic and foreign manufacturers operating in India cash incentives (typically 4% to 6% on incremental sales of goods manufactured in India over a base year) across 14 key strategic sectors to boost domestic manufacturing and exports.
keywords.concept: Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme: A flagship Government of India fiscal incentive program offering eligible domestic and foreign manufacturers operating in India cash incentives (typically 4% to 6% on incremental sales of goods manufactured in India over a base year) across 14 key strategic sectors to boost domestic manufacturing and exports.

keywords.shortNote: The distinction in WTO trade statistics between physical goods exports (where India's global share is 1.8%) and cross-border commercial services exports (where India's global share is 4.3%–4.5%).
keywords.concept: Merchandise vs. Services Export Share: The distinction in WTO trade statistics between physical goods exports (where India's global share is 1.8%) and cross-border commercial services exports (where India's global share is 4.3%–4.5%).

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I.
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly accepts the inflated 3.2% figure for India's share in world merchandise exports.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I.
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to catch that India's global goods export share is ~1.8%, nearly half of the stated 3.2%.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.text: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect.
optionBreakdown.explanation: Reverses both facts—accepting the false 3.2% goods export share while denying well-documented participation by domestic and foreign firms in the PLI scheme.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.text: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct.
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accurately rejects the 3.2% global goods export claim (~1.8% in reality) while confirming broad uptake of India's PLI scheme by both domestic and foreign firms.

valueAddition.title: India's Global Trade Share Benchmarks (Goods vs. Services)
bullets: Merchandise (Goods) Exports: India accounts for roughly 1.8% of global goods exports (and around 2.5%–2.7% of global goods imports), ranking among the top 20 global merchandise exporters.
Commercial Services Exports: India accounts for over 4.3% of global commercial services exports—more than double its merchandise export share—ranking among the top 7 global services exporters.
Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) 2023 Target: Aims to scale India's combined goods and services exports to USD 2 trillion by 2030.

valueAddition.title: How India's Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme Works
bullets: Launched in 2020 (starting with mobile phones, APIs/bulk drugs, and medical devices) and expanded to 14 key sectors with an outlay of ~Rs. 1.97 lakh crore, the PLI scheme rewards companies on incremental sales over a base year rather than upfront capital subsidies.
It is open to both Indian-owned companies and foreign companies incorporated/operating in India—driving major export surges in smartphones, electronics, pharmaceuticals, and solar PV modules.

inNews.source: Ministry of Commerce & Industry / PIB
inNews.headline: Cumulative Production Under 14 PLI Schemes Crosses Rs. 16 Lakh Crore with Electronics and Pharma Leading Export Gains
inNews.relevance: October 2026 DPIIT review data showed domestic and foreign PLI beneficiaries driving record smartphone and pharmaceutical exports even as India's overall share in global goods exports hovered near 1.8%.

statementBreakdown.reference: WTO World Trade Statistical Review & Economic Survey of India
statementBreakdown.explanation: India's share in global merchandise (goods) exports is around 1.8%—not 3.2% (a figure closer to India's share in global services exports at the time).

statementBreakdown.reference: Ministry of Commerce & Industry / DPIIT — PLI Scheme Progress Reports
statementBreakdown.explanation: Both domestic Indian enterprises and multinational foreign companies operating in India (across mobile manufacturing, electronics, pharmaceuticals, automobiles, and telecom equipment) have actively enrolled in and received incentives under India's 14-sector Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme.

hook.teaser: Notice how UPSC swaps India's higher services export share onto physical goods in Statement-I.

keywords.calloutNote: India's share in global goods exports is roughly 1.8%—the 3.2% figure was close to India's share in services exports, not physical merchandise.
activePhrases: 3.2% of global export of goods

keywords.calloutNote: India's 14-sector PLI scheme is open to both Indian companies and foreign manufacturers operating in India, making Statement-II straightforwardly true.

Both domestic firms and foreign companies operating in India have participated in and benefited from the Production-Linked Incentive scheme.

answer.label: D
answer.text: India's global goods export share is ~1.8% rather than 3.2%, while PLI participation is genuine—so Statement-I is wrong and Statement-II is right.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following:
1. Demographic performance
2. Forest and ecology
3. Governance reforms
4. Stable government
5. Tax and fiscal efforts For the horizontal tax devolution, the Fifteenth Finance Commission used
how many of the above as criteria other than population area and income distance?

keywords.shortNote: The distribution of the States' collective 41% share of the central divisible tax pool among individual States using a weighted formula balancing equity, fiscal need, demographic outcomes, ecology, and tax effort.
keywords.concept: Horizontal Tax Devolution: The distribution of the States' collective 41% share of the central divisible tax pool among individual States using a weighted formula balancing equity, fiscal need, demographic outcomes, ecology, and tax effort.

keywords.shortNote: A horizontal devolution parameter carrying 12.5% weight in the 15th Finance Commission formula, computed using the reciprocal of a State's Total Fertility Rate (TFR) scaled by 1971 population to reward states that stabilized population growth.
keywords.concept: Demographic Performance Criterion: A horizontal devolution parameter carrying 12.5% weight in the 15th Finance Commission formula, computed using the reciprocal of a State's Total Fertility Rate (TFR) scaled by 1971 population to reward states that stabilized population growth.

keywords.shortNote: The gap between a State's per capita Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) and that of the highest-income benchmark State, carrying the largest weight (45%) in the 15th Finance Commission's horizontal formula.
keywords.concept: Income Distance: The gap between a State's per capita Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) and that of the highest-income benchmark State, carrying the largest weight (45%) in the 15th Finance Commission's horizontal formula.

keywords.shortNote: A horizontal devolution criterion assigned 2.5% weight by the 15th Finance Commission, measured as the ratio of a State's average per capita own-tax revenue to its per capita GSDP.
keywords.concept: Tax and Fiscal Efforts: A horizontal devolution criterion assigned 2.5% weight by the 15th Finance Commission, measured as the ratio of a State's average per capita own-tax revenue to its per capita GSDP.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Misses one of the three valid non-core devolution criteria (Demographic performance, Forest and ecology, and Tax and fiscal efforts).

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Exactly three items—Demographic performance (12.5%), Forest and ecology (10%), and Tax and fiscal efforts (2.5%)—complete the 15th FC's six-parameter formula alongside Income distance (45%), Population (15%), and Area (15%).

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly includes either Governance reforms or Stable government inside the tax devolution formula.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to separate objective quantitative devolution criteria from subjective political or administrative terms.

valueAddition.title: Complete 15th Finance Commission Formula (Total = 100%)
bullets: Equity & Need Criteria (75% combined): Income Distance (45%), Population based on 2011 Census (15%), and Geographical Area (15%).
Performance & Ecology Criteria (25% combined): Demographic Performance (12.5%), Forest and Ecology (10%), and Tax and Fiscal Efforts (2.5%).
Notice how the question stem already names the three core criteria (Population, Area, Income Distance = 75%), leaving the exact three performance/ecology criteria (25%) for you to pick.

valueAddition.title: How 14th FC and 15th FC Weights Shifted
bullets: The 14th FC used five criteria: Income Distance (50%), Population 1971 (17.5%), Demographic Change 2011 (10%), Area (15%), and Forest Cover (7.5%).

The 15th FC dropped 1971 population entirely as directed by its Terms of Reference, compensated southern States via the 12.5% Demographic Performance weight, raised Forest & Ecology to 10%, and restored Tax Effort at 2.5%.

inNews.source: 16th Finance Commission / The Hindu
inNews.headline: States Debate Weightage of Income Distance and Demographic Performance Before 16th Finance Commission
inNews.relevance: Industrialized States urged the 16th Finance Commission in October 2026 to trim the 45% Income Distance weight and raise Demographic Performance and Tax Effort weights in the upcoming 2026–31 devolution formula.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Demographic performance was introduced with a 12.5% weight to balance the mandatory switch to 2011 Census population data and reward States that lowered their Total Fertility Rates.
Forest and ecology received a 10% weight (raised from 7.5% under the 14th FC), based on each State's share in the country's dense and very dense forest cover.
Governance reforms was not a parameter in the horizontal tax devolution formula; governance and administrative reforms were addressed separately through conditional grants-in-aid.
Stable government is not a Finance Commission devolution metric—weighting political stability would violate constitutional neutrality in federal fiscal transfers.
Tax and fiscal efforts was reintroduced with a 2.5% weight to reward States demonstrating higher own-tax revenue collection efficiency relative to their economic size.

visualSuggestion.title: 15th Finance Commission Horizontal Devolution Weights (2021–26)

hook.headline: Can you name all six criteria in the 15th Finance Commission's tax formula?
hook.teaser: Notice how the stem already gives you three criteria—leaving you to spot the exact remaining three.

keywords.calloutNote: Carrying 12.5% weight, this criterion rewarded States that controlled population growth after the Commission shifted to 2011 Census figures.
activePhrases: Demographic performance

keywords.calloutNote: Reintroduced at 2.5% weight alongside Forest and ecology (10%), this rounds out the six-parameter devolution formula.
activePhrases: Tax and fiscal efforts
dimmedPhrases: Demographic performance

verdicts.source: Demographic performance carries 12.5% weight in the 15th FC horizontal formula to reward States with lower fertility rates.
Forest and ecology carries 10% weight based on each State's share of dense forest cover.
Governance reforms was never included as a horizontal tax devolution parameter.
Stable government is a subjective political decoy—Finance Commissions only use objective economic and ecological indicators.
Tax and fiscal efforts was reintroduced at 2.5% weight to reward own-tax collection efficiency.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Demographic performance, Forest and ecology, and Tax and fiscal efforts complete the six criteria—so only three is right.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Fiscal Federalism notes

items.title: 75% Equity vs. 25% Effort
items.desc: Income Distance (45%), Population (15%), and Area (15%) form 75%, while Demographic, Forest, and Tax Effort form 25%.

items.title: 2011 Data Mandate
items.desc: The 15th FC used 2011 Census population exclusively, using Demographic Performance to protect States that curbed fertility early.

items.title: Objective Data Only
items.desc: Horizontal devolution formulas never include subjective political terms like 'stable government' or 'governance reforms'.

valueAddition.note: Whenever a Finance Commission list mixes hard statistical metrics with vague political phrases like 'stable government', eliminate the subjective phrases immediately.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements in relation to Janani Suraksha Yojana:
1. It is a safe motherhood intervention of the State Health Departments.
2. Its objective is to reduce maternal and neonatal mortality among poor pregnant women.
3. It aims to promote institutional delivery among poor pregnant women.
4. Its objective includes providing public health facilities to sick infants up to one year of age.
How many of the statements given above are correct?

keywords.shortNote: A 100% Centrally Sponsored safe motherhood intervention launched in April 2005 under the National Rural Health Mission (now NHM) by modifying the National Maternity Benefit Scheme to reduce maternal and neonatal mortality by promoting institutional delivery among poor pregnant women through conditional cash assistance.
keywords.concept: Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY): A 100% Centrally Sponsored safe motherhood intervention launched in April 2005 under the National Rural Health Mission (now NHM) by modifying the National Maternity Benefit Scheme to reduce maternal and neonatal mortality by promoting institutional delivery among poor pregnant women through conditional cash assistance.

keywords.shortNote: A separate entitlement scheme launched in June 2011 guaranteeing completely free and cashless institutional delivery, C-sections, drugs, diagnostics, diet, blood, and free transport for pregnant women and sick infants up to one year of age in public health institutions.
keywords.concept: Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK): A separate entitlement scheme launched in June 2011 guaranteeing completely free and cashless institutional delivery, C-sections, drugs, diagnostics, diet, blood, and free transport for pregnant women and sick infants up to one year of age in public health institutions.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because both Statement 2 (reducing maternal and neonatal mortality) and Statement 3 (promoting institutional delivery) are verbatim official objectives of JSY.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statements 2 and 3 accurately define JSY's core objective and conditional-cash mechanism, whereas Statement 1 misstates its Central sponsorship and Statement 4 borrows a provision from JSSK.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because JSY is neither a State Health Department scheme nor a sick-infant treatment program.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because Statement 4 lifts the sick-infant entitlement directly from JSSK.

valueAddition.title: JSY (2005) vs. JSSK (2011): Why Aspirants Mix Them Up
bullets: Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY, 2005): A 100% Centrally Sponsored demand-side conditional cash transfer scheme under NHM that pays cash directly to mothers and ASHAs to incentivize institutional delivery.

Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK, 2011): A supply-side zero-expense entitlement scheme eliminating out-of-pocket costs during delivery and extending free treatment, drugs, diagnostics, and transport to sick infants up to 1 year of age.

valueAddition.title: Differentiated Cash Assistance Across LPS and HPS Under JSY
bullets: Low Performing States (LPS — UP, Uttarakhand, Bihar, Jharkhand, MP, Chhattisgarh, Assam, Rajasthan, Odisha, and J&K): Higher cash assistance (Rs. 1,400 rural / Rs. 1,000 urban) extended to all pregnant women delivering in government or accredited private health facilities.
High Performing States (HPS): Cash assistance (Rs. 700 rural / Rs. 600 urban) restricted to BPL, Scheduled Caste (SC), and Scheduled Tribe (ST) pregnant women aged 19 years and above.

inNews.source: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) / Sample Registration System (SRS)
inNews.headline: Health Ministry National Health Mission review links sustained decline in India's Maternal Mortality Ratio to JSY institutional delivery incentives and JSSK zero-expense care
inNews.relevance: September 2026 NHM implementation reviews reported over 1 crore annual JSY beneficiaries alongside expanded JSSK referral transport, driving institutional deliveries above 89% nationwide.

statementBreakdown.reference: MoHFW National Health Mission · 100% Centrally Sponsored Scheme
statementBreakdown.explanation: Janani Suraksha Yojana is a 100% Centrally Sponsored safe motherhood intervention under the National Health Mission (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare), not an independent scheme of State Health Departments.

statementBreakdown.reference: JSY Official Objective · Maternal & Neonatal Mortality Reduction
statementBreakdown.explanation: The core stated objective of JSY is reducing maternal and neonatal mortality by encouraging poor pregnant women to opt for supervised childbirth at health facilities.

statementBreakdown.reference: JSY Core Mechanism · Conditional Cash Transfer & ASHA Mobilization
statementBreakdown.explanation: JSY promotes institutional delivery among poor pregnant women by providing conditional cash transfers to mothers alongside performance-linked incentives to Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs).

statementBreakdown.reference: Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK, 2011) · Sick Infant Coverage
statementBreakdown.explanation: Providing free public health facilities, diagnostics, drugs, and transport to sick infants up to one year of age is the mandate of Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK), not Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY).

visualSuggestion.title: Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) vs. Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK)

rows: Conditional cash transfer to mother & ASHA worker
Free & cashless healthcare entitlements (no direct cash handout)
100% Centrally Sponsored Scheme under National Health Mission
National Health Mission entitlement initiative across public facilities
Covers safe delivery & immediate neonatal survival only
Covers sick newborns & infants up to 1 year of age

hook.headline: How many of these four statements actually describe Janani Suraksha Yojana?
hook.teaser: Watch out for Statement 1 and Statement 4—one swaps the Central sponsor, and the other belongs to JSSK.

keywords.calloutNote: JSY is a 100% Centrally Sponsored Scheme under the National Health Mission—not an initiative of State Health Departments.
activePhrases: State Health Departments

keywords.term: sick infants up to one year of age
keywords.calloutNote: Free treatment for sick infants up to one year of age belongs to Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK), not JSY.
activePhrases: sick infants up to one year of age
dimmedPhrases: State Health Departments

verdicts.source: JSY is a 100% Centrally Sponsored safe motherhood intervention under the National Health Mission, not a State Health Department scheme.
JSY's primary objective is reducing maternal and neonatal mortality among poor pregnant women.
JSY promotes institutional delivery among poor pregnant women through conditional cash transfers and ASHA support.
Free healthcare and transport for sick infants up to one year of age is provided under Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK).

answer.label: B
answer.text: Only two statements (2 and 3) are correct—JSY is centrally sponsored and promotes institutional delivery, while sick-infant care belongs to JSSK.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Maternal Health Schemes notes

items.title: Cash For Delivery
items.desc: 100% Centrally Sponsored scheme paying conditional cash to mothers and ASHAs for institutional births.

items.title: Zero-Expense + Infant Care
items.desc: Guarantees cashless delivery, free diet, free transport, and free care for sick infants up to 1 year.

items.title: Universal vs Targeted
items.desc: In 10 Low Performing States, all women in public facilities qualify; in High Performing States, BPL/SC/ST women qualify.

valueAddition.note: Examiners love blending look-alike scheme names—keep Janani Suraksha Yojana (cash incentive) separate from Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (cashless care + 1-year infant cover).

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
Statement-I: Switzerland is one of the leading exporters of gold in terms of value.
Statement-II: Switzerland has the second largest gold reserves in the world.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I.
options.label: a

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I.
options.label: b

options.text: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect.
options.label: c

options.text: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct.
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: A commercial bullion processing centre—exemplified by Switzerland—that imports unrefined doré bars and scrap gold from mining nations, refines them into investment-grade bars, and re-exports them globally without possessing domestic gold mines.
keywords.concept: Gold Refining Hub (Entrepot Trade): A commercial bullion processing centre—exemplified by Switzerland—that imports unrefined doré bars and scrap gold from mining nations, refines them into investment-grade bars, and re-exports them globally without possessing domestic gold mines.

keywords.shortNote: Sovereign monetary bullion held by a country's central bank as part of its foreign exchange reserves to back currency stability and diversify reserve assets, led globally by the United States followed by Germany.
keywords.concept: Official Gold Reserves: Sovereign monetary bullion held by a country's central bank as part of its foreign exchange reserves to back currency stability and diversify reserve assets, led globally by the United States followed by Germany.

keywords.shortNote: The difference between a country's physical goods exports and imports within the Current Account of the Balance of Payments; in Switzerland, large raw gold imports nearly offset refined gold exports in net trade terms.
keywords.concept: Merchandise Trade Balance: The difference between a country's physical goods exports and imports within the Current Account of the Balance of Payments; in Switzerland, large raw gold imports nearly offset refined gold exports in net trade terms.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I.
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly attributes Switzerland's commercial bullion exports to sovereign central bank reserves and misstates global reserve rankings.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I.
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to catch that Germany, not Switzerland, holds the world's second-largest official gold reserves.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.text: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect.
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accurately distinguishes Switzerland's dominance in commercial gold refining and re-exports from its seventh-place standing in central bank gold reserves.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.text: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct.
optionBreakdown.explanation: Reverses both facts—denying Switzerland's top gold-export status while falsely placing it second in sovereign reserves.

valueAddition.title: Why Switzerland Dominates Gold Exports Without Any Gold Mines
bullets: Switzerland has zero commercial gold mines and holds only the 7th-largest central bank gold reserve (~1,040 tonnes), yet it dominates global gold exports by value because four of the world's largest gold refineries (Valcambi, PAMP, Argor-Heraeus, and Metalor) operate there.

Switzerland imports unrefined doré gold from Africa, Latin America, and Australia, refines it to 99.99% purity, and exports finished bullion bars to major consumer hubs like India, China, the UK, and the UAE—making gold both a top import and top export in Swiss trade accounts.

valueAddition.title: Top Sovereign Gold Reserve Holders (World Gold Council Benchmark)
bullets: 1. United States (~8,133 tonnes) | 2. Germany (~3,352 tonnes) | 3. Italy (~2,452 tonnes) | 4. France (~2,437 tonnes) | 5. Russia (~2,333 tonnes) | 6. China (~2,264+ tonnes) | 7. Switzerland (~1,040 tonnes), with India ranking among the top 8–9 global sovereign holders.

inNews.source: World Gold Council / Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
inNews.headline: Global Central Bank Gold Purchases Stay Elevated in 2026 as RBI Expands Domestic Vaulting Share
inNews.relevance: World Gold Council reserve updates in October 2026 showed the United States and Germany maintaining the top two sovereign gold reserve slots while India continued steady reserve accumulation and domestic vault repatriation.

statementBreakdown.reference: UN Comtrade / Swiss Federal Customs Gold Trade Data
statementBreakdown.explanation: Switzerland consistently ranks as the world's largest or second-largest exporter of gold by value (accounting for roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of global gold exports) because its major refineries process roughly 70% of the world's mined gold for re-export.

statementBreakdown.reference: World Gold Council — Official Central Bank Gold Reserves Rankings
statementBreakdown.explanation: Switzerland ranks seventh in official sovereign gold reserves (around 1,040 tonnes held by the Swiss National Bank)—the top three holders are the United States (~8,133 tonnes), Germany (~3,352 tonnes), and Italy (~2,452 tonnes).

hook.headline: Switzerland has no gold mines—so how is it a top global gold exporter?
hook.teaser: Notice how UPSC separates commercial bullion refining from central bank gold reserves.

keywords.term: leading exporters of gold in terms of value
keywords.calloutTerm: “leading exporters of gold in terms of value”
keywords.calloutNote: Switzerland imports raw gold from mining countries, refines nearly 70% of the world's bullion, and re-exports it—making it a top global gold exporter.
activePhrases: leading exporters of gold in terms of value

keywords.term: second largest gold reserves in the world
keywords.calloutTerm: “second largest gold reserves in the world”
keywords.calloutNote: Germany holds the second-largest central bank gold reserves after the United States—Switzerland sits down at seventh place.
activePhrases: second largest gold reserves in the world
dimmedPhrases: leading exporters of gold in terms of value

verdicts.source: Swiss refineries process roughly 70% of global gold, making Switzerland one of the world's largest exporters of gold by value.
The United States is first and Germany is second in official gold reserves—Switzerland ranks seventh with around 1,040 tonnes.

answer.label: C
answer.text: Switzerland is a top commercial gold exporter through refining, not because of sovereign reserves—so Statement-I is right and Statement-II is wrong.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your External Sector & Reserves notes

items.title: Sovereign Reserve Leaders
items.desc: USA (~8,133t), Germany (~3,352t), and Italy (~2,452t) hold the top three central bank gold reserves; Switzerland is 7th.

items.title: Entrepot Refining Model
items.desc: Switzerland imports unrefined doré bars and exports 99.99% refined bullion to India, China, and London without mining gold.

items.title: India-Switzerland Trade Deficit
items.desc: Refined gold imports account for the overwhelming share of India's bilateral trade deficit with Switzerland.

valueAddition.note: In Statement-I / Statement-II questions, watch for a true trade headline paired with a false ranking explanation—commercial exports come from refining flows, not central bank vaults.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the investments in the following assets:
1. Brand recognition
2. Inventory
3. Intellectual property
4. Mailing list of clients
How many of the above are considered intangible investments?

keywords.shortNote: Identifiable, non-monetary economic resources without physical substance that yield future economic benefits (e.g., patents, software, brand equity, customer lists, and proprietary databases).
keywords.concept: Intangible Assets / Investments: Identifiable, non-monetary economic resources without physical substance that yield future economic benefits (e.g., patents, software, brand equity, customer lists, and proprietary databases).

keywords.shortNote: Physical assets that can be seen and touched, such as machinery, land, physical buildings, equipment, and inventories of goods.
keywords.concept: Tangible Assets / Investments: Physical assets that can be seen and touched, such as machinery, land, physical buildings, equipment, and inventories of goods.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Brand recognition, intellectual property, and mailing lists of clients are all intangible.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Omits either customer lists or brand recognition.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Three assets (Brand recognition, Intellectual property, and Mailing list of clients) are intangible investments, while Inventory is a tangible asset.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Inventory is a physical, tangible asset.

valueAddition.title: Knowledge-Based Capital (KBC) & Intangible Taxonomy
bullets: Computerized Information: Software, computer code, machine-readable data architecture, and databases.
Innovative Property: R&D outputs, patents, copyrights, trademarks, designs, and mineral exploration blueprints (capitalized as Intellectual Property Products under SNA 2008).

Economic Competencies: Brand equity, advertising capital, firm-specific human capital (specialized employee training), and organizational design/processes (e.g., client mailing lists, vendor relationships).

valueAddition.title: Accounting vs. National Accounting Treatment
bullets: Accounting Standard Defines an intangible asset as an identifiable non-monetary asset without physical substance. Explicitly notes that customer lists, publishing titles, and licenses meet this criterion.

SNA 2008 Shift: Replaced 'intangible fixed assets' with the broader classification 'Intellectual Property Products' (IPP), recognizing software, R&D, and artistic originals as gross fixed capital formation rather than intermediate consumption.
Balance Sheet Distinction: Tangible assets are depreciated over time; intangible assets are amortized (or tested annually for impairment in the case of goodwill).

inNews.source: WIPO / Ministry of Commerce and Industry
inNews.headline: India registers record trademark and patent filings, driving corporate intangible asset valuation to 38% of enterprise value
inNews.relevance: Reflects the transition of the modern economy where intangible investments (IP, software, brand equity, customer data) outpace physical machinery in capital formation.

statementBreakdown.reference: Ind AS 38 & OECD Knowledge-Based Capital Framework
statementBreakdown.explanation: Brand recognition (brand equity/goodwill) lacks physical substance but embodies high commercial value and pricing power, representing an intangible investment.
Inventory consists of physical raw materials, work-in-progress, and finished goods held in warehouses for sale or processing, making it a tangible asset.

statementBreakdown.reference: System of National Accounts (SNA 2008) · Intellectual Property Products
statementBreakdown.explanation: Intellectual property (patents, copyrights, trademarks, industrial designs, trade secrets) represents legal ownership over created knowledge and lacks physical substance, classifying it as an intangible asset.

A mailing list of clients (customer database/customer relationships) is an informational, non-physical proprietary data asset that drives future sales, classified under accounting and economic standards as an intangible asset.

rows: Ind AS 2 / SNA 2008 Changes in Inventories

hook.headline: Is a customer mailing list considered an intangible asset?
hook.teaser: Here is the exact asset classification trap UPSC tested in Prelims 2023.

keywords.calloutNote: Inventory consists of physical raw materials and finished products—it is strictly tangible.
activePhrases: 2. Inventory

keywords.calloutNote: A proprietary customer list is a non-physical data asset that drives future sales—an intangible asset.
activePhrases: 4. Mailing list of clients
dimmedPhrases: 2. Inventory

verdicts.source: Brand recognition represents market goodwill and pricing power without physical substance.
Inventory consists of tangible physical raw materials and finished goods.
Intellectual property is a non-physical legal right protecting knowledge and innovation.
Customer mailing lists are non-physical information assets under Ind AS 38.

answer.label: C
answer.text: Only three assets (1, 3, and 4) are intangible investments, making (c) the correct answer.
