subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
Statement-I: Interest income from the deposits in Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) distributed to their investors is exempted from tax, but the dividend is taxable.
Statement-II: InvITs are recognized as borrowers under the 'Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002'.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
options.label: a

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
options.label: b

options.text: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
options.label: c

options.text: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: A SEBI-regulated pooled investment vehicle structured like a mutual fund that owns and operates revenue-generating infrastructure assets (highways, power transmission lines, pipelines) and distributes regular cash flows to unit holders.
keywords.concept: Infrastructure Investment Trust (InvIT): A SEBI-regulated pooled investment vehicle structured like a mutual fund that owns and operates revenue-generating infrastructure assets (highways, power transmission lines, pipelines) and distributes regular cash flows to unit holders.

keywords.shortNote: The tax regime under the Income-tax Act, 1961 whereby interest and dividend income received by an InvIT from its Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) is exempt at the trust level and taxed directly in the hands of unit holders (with dividends exempt in investors' hands if the SPV has not opted for the lower Section 115BAA corporate tax rate).
keywords.concept: Pass-Through Taxation (Section 115UA): The tax regime under the Income-tax Act, 1961 whereby interest and dividend income received by an InvIT from its Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) is exempt at the trust level and taxed directly in the hands of unit holders (with dividends exempt in investors' hands if the SPV has not opted for the lower Section 115BAA corporate tax rate).

keywords.shortNote: The Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 enabling banks and financial institutions to auction collateralized assets of defaulting borrowers without court intervention; amended in 2021 to formally include pooled investment vehicles like InvITs and REITs as 'borrowers'.
keywords.concept: SARFAESI Act, 2002: The Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 enabling banks and financial institutions to auction collateralized assets of defaulting borrowers without court intervention; amended in 2021 to formally include pooled investment vehicles like InvITs and REITs as 'borrowers'.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly accepts that interest distributed by InvITs is tax-exempt while dividends are universally taxable.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to catch the reversed interest-vs-dividend taxation rule under Section 10(23FD).

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.text: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
optionBreakdown.explanation: Inverts both statements—missing the 2021 SARFAESI amendment and misreading InvIT pass-through tax rules.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.text: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accurately identifies that interest distributed by InvITs is taxable in investors' hands (not exempt) while confirming InvITs' statutory recognition as borrowers under the SARFAESI Act.

valueAddition.title: Exact Tax Mechanics of InvIT Distributions (Section 115UA & Section 10(23FD))
bullets: Interest Component: Interest paid by an SPV to the InvIT is exempt at the InvIT level under Section 10(23FC), but becomes taxable in the hands of unit holders upon distribution (subject to TDS).

Dividend Component: Dividend received from an SPV and distributed to unit holders is exempt from tax in the investors' hands under Section 10(23FD), unless the SPV has opted for the lower 22% corporate tax rate under Section 115BAA.

Capital Repayment (Amortization of Debt): Budget 2023 plugged a tax arbitrage loophole by making distributions structured as 'repayment of debt' taxable in unit holders' hands to the extent they exceed the issue price of the units.

valueAddition.title: Why Recognizing InvITs as 'Borrowers' Under SARFAESI Mattered
bullets: Because InvITs are registered as trusts under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 rather than companies, banks previously lacked clear statutory enforcement remedies under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 if an InvIT defaulted on debt.

Amending Section 2(1)(f) of the SARFAESI Act via the Finance Act, 2021 granted lenders legal certainty and recovery teeth, unlocking lower-cost institutional debt financing for infrastructure monetization.

inNews.source: SEBI / Economic Times
inNews.headline: SEBI Reviews Minimum Public Unitholding and Debt-Leverage Norms for Infrastructure Investment Trusts
inNews.relevance: SEBI's November 2026 consultation paper on InvIT governance proposed streamlining debt-raising disclosures and retail participation thresholds as highway and power-grid InvITs expanded institutional fundraising.

statementBreakdown.explanation: The tax treatment is reversed: under Section 10(23FD), interest income received by an InvIT from its SPVs and distributed to unit holders is taxable in the hands of the investors (at their applicable slab rate), whereas dividend income distributed by the InvIT is exempt in the hands of investors (provided the underlying SPV has not opted for the concessional tax regime under Section 115BAA).

statementBreakdown.reference: Finance Act, 2021 Amendment to SARFAESI Act, 2002 (Section 2(1)(f))
statementBreakdown.explanation: Through the Finance Act, 2021, the definition of 'borrower' under Section 2(1)(f) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 was amended to explicitly include pooled investment vehicles such as InvITs and REITs, enabling banks and debt financiers to lend directly to InvITs with enforceable security rights.

visualSuggestion.title: InvIT Cash-Flow Distributions & Legal Status in India

rows: Exempt in investors' hands (if SPV is outside Sec. 115BAA)
Recognized as 'borrower' since Finance Act, 2021 amendment

hook.headline: Is interest from InvITs tax-free for investors while dividends are taxed?
hook.teaser: Notice how UPSC flips interest and dividend tax rules in Statement-I while testing a 2021 banking law amendment in Statement-II.

keywords.term: Interest income from the deposits in Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) distributed to their investors is exempted from tax
keywords.calloutNote: UPSC flipped the rule—interest distributed by an InvIT is taxable in the investor's hands, whereas dividends are exempt (unless the SPV opted for Section 115BAA).
activePhrases: Interest income from the deposits in Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) distributed to their investors is exempted from tax

keywords.term: recognized as borrowers under the 'Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002'
keywords.calloutTerm: “recognized as borrowers under the SARFAESI Act, 2002”
keywords.calloutNote: Finance Act, 2021 amended SARFAESI Section 2(1)(f) to formally classify InvITs and REITs as borrowers so banks can lend to them safely.
activePhrases: recognized as borrowers under the 'Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002'
dimmedPhrases: Interest income from the deposits in Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) distributed to their investors is exempted from tax

verdicts.source: Under Section 10(23FD) of the Income-tax Act, interest distributed by InvITs is taxable in investors' hands, while dividends are exempt (unless the SPV chose Section 115BAA).
The Finance Act, 2021 amended the SARFAESI Act, 2002 to explicitly recognize pooled investment vehicles like InvITs as borrowers.

answer.label: D
answer.text: Statement-I gets InvIT tax treatment backwards while Statement-II accurately states the 2021 SARFAESI rule—so Option D is right.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Capital Markets & Taxation notes

items.title: Pass-Through Entity Rule
items.desc: InvITs enjoy pass-through status—interest is taxed in the investor's slab, while dividends remain tax-exempt if the SPV pays regular corporate tax.

items.title: Why SARFAESI Included InvITs
items.desc: Because InvITs are trusts rather than companies, amending SARFAESI gave banks direct collateral recovery rights when lending to InvITs.

items.title: Debt Repayment Plugged
items.desc: Budget 2023 made debt-amortization payouts by InvITs/REITs taxable once cumulative payouts cross the unit's issue price.

valueAddition.note: In Statement-I / Statement-II questions on recent financial instruments, check if UPSC swapped two halves of a tax rule—interest vs. dividend is a classic swap.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
Statement-I: In the post-pandemic recent past, many Central Banks worldwide had carried out interest rate hike.
Statement-II: Central Banks generally assume that they have the ability to counteract the rising consumer prices via monetary policy means.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
options.label: a

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statements-II is are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-II
options.label: b

options.text: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
options.label: c

options.text: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: A coordinated or parallel cycle of policy rate hikes by central banks globally to cool aggregate demand and anchor elevated inflation expectations.
keywords.concept: Synchronised Monetary Tightening: A coordinated or parallel cycle of policy rate hikes by central banks globally to cool aggregate demand and anchor elevated inflation expectations.

keywords.shortNote: The theoretical premise that raising policy benchmark rates increases borrowing costs, slows credit expansion, and dampens aggregate expenditure, thereby curbing consumer price inflation.
keywords.concept: Monetary Transmission Mechanism: The theoretical premise that raising policy benchmark rates increases borrowing costs, slows credit expansion, and dampens aggregate expenditure, thereby curbing consumer price inflation.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement-II provides the precise doctrinal rationale for Statement-I: central banks enacted global rate hikes specifically because they operate on the belief that monetary tightening can control and tame rising consumer prices.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks the direct, unbroken link between the monetary mechanism (the belief that rate hikes tame price rise) and the observed action (raising interest rates).

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Falsely treats the core theoretical premise of central banking as incorrect.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: Statement-I is an established historical fact
optionBreakdown.explanation: Denies the well-documented post-2021 global monetary tightening cycle.

valueAddition.title: Post-Pandemic Global Inflation Shock & Policy Reaction
bullets: Twin Pressures: Post-pandemic stimulus packages unleashed pent-up consumer demand, while global semiconductor shortages, shipping disruptions, and the 2022 war in Ukraine created historic supply-side commodity price shocks.
Federal Reserve Pivot: The US Fed executed a rapid series of 75 bps and 50 bps rate hikes, moving from near-zero to above 5% within eighteen months to avert wage-price spirals.
RBI Reaction: The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) raised the policy repo rate by a cumulative 250 bps (from 4.00% to 6.50%) between May 2022 and February 2023.

valueAddition.title: Channels of Monetary Policy Transmission
bullets: Interest Rate Channel: Higher policy rates increase marginal cost of lending (MCLR/EBLR), increasing EMIs, reducing disposable income, and discouraging discretionary consumption and corporate capital expenditure.
Expectations Channel: Demonstrating credible commitment to price stability anchors inflation expectations, preventing businesses and unions from setting higher prices and wages.
Exchange Rate Channel: Raising domestic rates narrows interest rate differentials, mitigating capital outflows, defending the currency, and lowering imported inflation.

valueAddition.title: The Debate: Supply-Side Shocks vs. Monetary Limits
bullets: Core Limitation: Monetary policy directly impacts only the aggregate demand curve. It cannot repair broken trade corridors, harvest more foodgrains, or pump more crude oil.
Sacrifice Ratio: To suppress supply-driven inflation, monetary policy must compress aggregate demand sufficiently hard to match damaged supply, risking growth contraction or recession.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India / Bank for International Settlements
inNews.headline: BIS Report Evaluates Soft-Landing Milestones as Global Central Banks Navigate Disinflation and Easing Cycles
inNews.relevance: Directly evaluates the full cycle of the post-pandemic rate-hiking campaign, examining how monetary tools successfully restrained consumer price inflation while managing growth trade-offs.

statementBreakdown.explanation: In response to historic inflation following pandemic recovery, supply-chain bottlenecks, and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, major central banks—including the US Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, Bank of England, and the RBI—embarked on aggressive, synchronised interest rate hiking cycles.

statementBreakdown.reference: Classical Monetary Doctrine & Central Bank Mandates
statementBreakdown.explanation: Modern central banking doctrine rests on the core operational premise that central banks possess the ability to control and counteract inflation by manipulating the policy rate (tightening monetary policy to compress demand and realign inflation with target levels).

visualSuggestion.title: How Monetary Policy Counteracts Rising Consumer Prices

rows: Cost of funds for commercial banks rises
Banks pass on higher lending rates to retail & corporate borrowers
Loans become expensive; savings incentives rise
Consumer spending and capital expenditure slow down
Firms reduce price markup; wage renegotiation pressures subside
Inflation returns towards the target band (e.g., 4% ± 2%)

hook.headline: Why did every central bank hike rates after COVID?
hook.teaser: Two statements, one clear cause-and-effect—here is how the reasoning works.

keywords.calloutNote: Statement-I states the historical fact: global central banks engaged in synchronised rate hikes.
activePhrases: many Central Banks worldwide had carried out interest rate hike

keywords.term: ability to counteract the rising consumer prices
keywords.calloutNote: Statement-II gives the textbook reason: they hike rates because they believe tightening monetary policy tames inflation.
activePhrases: ability to counteract the rising consumer prices via monetary policy means
dimmedPhrases: many Central Banks worldwide had carried out interest rate hike

verdicts.source: Central banks worldwide, including the Fed and RBI, rapidly hiked rates to battle four-decade-high inflation.
Central banks operate on the principle that raising interest rates compresses demand and curbs consumer price rise.

answer.label: A
answer.text: Both statements are correct and Statement-II is the direct explanation for Statement-I.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Monetary Policy notes

items.title: RBI Tightening
items.desc: The RBI raised repo from 4.00% to 6.50% between May 2022 and February 2023 to tame inflation.

items.title: Policy Limits
items.desc: Monetary policy compresses aggregate demand, but cannot resolve physical supply chain disruptions.

items.title: Core Transmission
items.desc: Credible rate hikes anchor long-term inflation expectations, preventing self-fulfilling price spirals.

valueAddition.note: When evaluating Statement-II as an explanation, ask: 'Did central banks perform Action I specifically because they believe Principle II?' Here, the causal link is direct and complete.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements in the context of interventions being undertaken under Anaemia Mukt Bharat Strategy:
1. It provides prophylactic calcium supplementation for pre-school children, adolescents and pregnant women.
2. It runs a campaign for delayed cord clamping at the time of child- birth.
3. It provides for periodic deworming to children and adolescents.
4. It addresses non-nutritional causes of anaemia in endemic pockets with special focus on malaria, hemoglobinopathies and fluorosis.
How many of the statements given above are correct?

keywords.shortNote: A flagship Ministry of Health and Family Welfare initiative launched in 2018 under POSHAN Abhiyaan following a 6x6x6 architecture (6 target beneficiary groups, 6 key interventions, and 6 institutional mechanisms) to reduce anaemia prevalence across India.
keywords.concept: Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) Strategy: A flagship Ministry of Health and Family Welfare initiative launched in 2018 under POSHAN Abhiyaan following a 6x6x6 architecture (6 target beneficiary groups, 6 key interventions, and 6 institutional mechanisms) to reduce anaemia prevalence across India.

keywords.term: Prophylactic Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) Supplementation
keywords.shortNote: Preventive administration of age-specific Iron and Folic Acid tablets or syrup (not calcium) across six target age groups—children, adolescents, women of reproductive age, pregnant women, and lactating mothers—under AMB.
keywords.concept: Prophylactic Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) Supplementation: Preventive administration of age-specific Iron and Folic Acid tablets or syrup (not calcium) across six target age groups—children, adolescents, women of reproductive age, pregnant women, and lactating mothers—under AMB.

keywords.shortNote: Waiting 1 to 3 minutes after birth before clamping and cutting the umbilical cord so placental blood transfers into the newborn, boosting neonatal iron stores and preventing infant iron-deficiency anaemia.
keywords.concept: Delayed Umbilical Cord Clamping: Waiting 1 to 3 minutes after birth before clamping and cutting the umbilical cord so placental blood transfers into the newborn, boosting neonatal iron stores and preventing infant iron-deficiency anaemia.

keywords.shortNote: Inherited genetic disorders affecting the structure or synthesis of haemoglobin molecules—primarily Sickle Cell Disease and Thalassemia—targeted as non-nutritional causes of anaemia under AMB.
keywords.concept: Hemoglobinopathies: Inherited genetic disorders affecting the structure or synthesis of haemoglobin molecules—primarily Sickle Cell Disease and Thalassemia—targeted as non-nutritional causes of anaemia under AMB.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because Statements 2, 3, and 4 are all official pillars of the 6x6x6 AMB framework.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because three of the four listed interventions belong directly to Anaemia Mukt Bharat.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Delayed cord clamping, periodic deworming, and addressing malaria, hemoglobinopathies, and fluorosis are verbatim AMB interventions, whereas Statement 1 swaps Iron and Folic Acid with calcium.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: Statement 1 false (Calcium vs. Iron & Folic Acid)
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because AMB provides prophylactic Iron and Folic Acid supplementation, not calcium.

valueAddition.title: The 6x6x6 Architecture of Anaemia Mukt Bharat
bullets: Six Beneficiary Groups: Children (6–59 months), Children (5–9 years), Adolescents (10–19 years), Women of Reproductive Age (20–49 years), Pregnant Women, and Lactating Mothers.

Six Core Interventions: (1) Prophylactic Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) supplementation, (2) Periodic deworming, (3) Year-round Behaviour Change Communication (including delayed cord clamping and iron-rich diets), (4) Digital haemoglobinometer testing and point-of-care treatment, (5) Mandatory provision of Iron and Folic Acid fortified foods in public health programmes, and (6) Addressing non-nutritional anaemia (malaria, hemoglobinopathies, fluorosis).

valueAddition.title: Why Calcium Is Not the AMB Supplement
bullets: Iron-Calcium Antagonism: Dietary and supplemental calcium competes with iron in the gut and inhibits non-heme iron absorption—which is why maternal health protocols schedule IFA and calcium tablets at separate meals rather than treating calcium as an anti-anaemia supplement.

inNews.source: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) / National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission
inNews.headline: Health Ministry integrates Anaemia Mukt Bharat digital haemoglobin screening with National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission across tribal districts
inNews.relevance: October 2026 Health Ministry updates linked AMB's sixth intervention on hemoglobinopathies with over 5 crore sickle cell screenings across endemic tribal belts alongside expanded IFA supplementation.

statementBreakdown.reference: AMB Intervention #1 · Prophylactic Iron and Folic Acid (Not Calcium)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Anaemia Mukt Bharat provides prophylactic Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) supplementation—not calcium supplementation, which actually inhibits iron absorption if taken simultaneously.

statementBreakdown.reference: AMB Intervention #3 · Behaviour Change Communication (Delayed Cord Clamping)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Intensified year-round Behaviour Change Communication under AMB explicitly includes a national campaign promoting delayed umbilical cord clamping (for at least 1–3 minutes) at childbirth.

statementBreakdown.reference: AMB Intervention #2 · National Deworming Day (Biannual Albendazole)
statementBreakdown.explanation: AMB mandates periodic biannual deworming (using Albendazole tablets) for children and adolescents aged 1–19 years (plus pregnant women in the second trimester) to prevent intestinal worm-induced blood loss.

statementBreakdown.reference: AMB Intervention #6 · Non-Nutritional Causes of Anaemia
statementBreakdown.explanation: The sixth intervention of AMB specifically targets non-nutritional causes of anaemia in endemic pockets with focused screening and management of malaria, hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell/thalassemia), and fluorosis.

visualSuggestion.title: Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) 6x6x6 Framework Summary

rows: Children (6–59m & 5–9y), Adolescents (10–19y), Women of Reproductive Age (20–49y), Pregnant & Lactating Women

1. Prophylactic IFA supplementation | 2. Deworming | 3. BCC (Delayed cord clamping) | 4. Digital testing & treatment | 5. Fortified foods | 6. Non-nutritional causes (Malaria, Hemoglobinopathies, Fluorosis)

hook.headline: How many of these four interventions belong to Anaemia Mukt Bharat?
hook.teaser: Notice Statement 1—anaemia is iron deficiency, yet the statement slips in calcium supplementation.

keywords.calloutNote: Anaemia Mukt Bharat provides prophylactic Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) supplementation—not calcium, which actually blocks iron absorption.
activePhrases: prophylactic calcium supplementation

keywords.calloutNote: The sixth intervention of AMB targets non-nutritional anaemia in endemic pockets caused by malaria, sickle cell/thalassemia, and fluorosis.
activePhrases: malaria, hemoglobinopathies and fluorosis
dimmedPhrases: prophylactic calcium supplementation

verdicts.source: Anaemia Mukt Bharat provides prophylactic Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) supplementation—not calcium supplementation.
AMB runs a year-round behaviour change campaign promoting delayed cord clamping at birth to build infant iron stores.
Periodic biannual deworming with Albendazole is provided to children and adolescents under Anaemia Mukt Bharat.
AMB explicitly targets non-nutritional anaemia caused by malaria, hemoglobinopathies, and fluorosis in endemic districts.

answer.label: C
answer.text: Only three statements (2, 3, and 4) are correct—AMB supplies Iron and Folic Acid rather than calcium.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Health & Nutrition Schemes notes

items.title: AMB Core Formula
items.desc: Covers 6 beneficiary groups, 6 interventions, and 6 institutional mechanisms under POSHAN Abhiyaan.

items.title: Delayed Cord Clamping
items.desc: Delaying umbilical cord clamping by 1–3 minutes transfers placental blood, boosting newborn iron reserves.

items.title: Three Endemic Triggers
items.desc: Remember the exact trio in Intervention 6: Malaria, Hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell/thalassemia), and Fluorosis.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements about G-20:
1. The G-20 group was originally established as a platform for the Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors to discuss the international economic and financial issues.
2. Digital public infrastructure is one of India's G-20 priorities.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: A premier forum for international economic cooperation representing around 85% of global GDP, over 75% of global trade, and two-thirds of the world's population—comprising 19 sovereign nations, the European Union, and the African Union (admitted in 2023).
keywords.concept: Group of Twenty (G20): A premier forum for international economic cooperation representing around 85% of global GDP, over 75% of global trade, and two-thirds of the world's population—comprising 19 sovereign nations, the European Union, and the African Union (admitted in 2023).

keywords.shortNote: The foundational G20 workstream established in September 1999 in the aftermath of the 1997–98 Asian Financial Crisis, bringing together Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors to coordinate macroeconomic and financial stability policies.
keywords.concept: G20 Finance Track: The foundational G20 workstream established in September 1999 in the aftermath of the 1997–98 Asian Financial Crisis, bringing together Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors to coordinate macroeconomic and financial stability policies.

keywords.shortNote: Interoperable, open-source population-scale digital building blocks—exemplified by India Stack (Aadhaar digital identity, UPI fast payments, and DigiLocker/Account Aggregator data exchange)—championed as a core priority during India's 2023 G20 Presidency.
keywords.concept: Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI): Interoperable, open-source population-scale digital building blocks—exemplified by India Stack (Aadhaar digital identity, UPI fast payments, and DigiLocker/Account Aggregator data exchange)—championed as a core priority during India's 2023 G20 Presidency.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks that Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) was one of the signature policy priorities championed by India during its 2023 G20 Presidency.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Misses the G20's original 1999 institutional birth as a Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors forum.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accurately pairs the G20's 1999 central-bank/finance-ministry origin with India's 2023 Digital Public Infrastructure agenda.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Rejects two well-established institutional facts about the G20's origin and India's presidency deliverables.

valueAddition.title: Two Crisis Milestones That Shaped the G20 Architecture
bullets: 1999 (Asian Financial Crisis): Established as a forum for Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors (first meeting in Berlin, December 1999) to bring systemically important emerging economies into global financial dialogue.

2008 (Global Financial Crisis): Elevated to the Heads of State/Government Leaders' Summit level (first Leaders' Summit in Washington D.C., November 2008), splitting G20 work into the Finance Track and the Sherpa Track.

valueAddition.title: Structural Facts About G20 Governance & Membership
bullets: No Permanent Secretariat: The G20 has no permanent headquarters or staff; its agenda is steered by the 'Troika'—comprising the past, current, and incoming G20 Presidencies.
21 Full Members: Following the African Union's admission at the 2023 New Delhi Summit, the G20 comprises 19 countries plus the European Union and the African Union.

inNews.source: Ministry of Finance / G20 Presidency

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements with reference to India:
1. According to the Micro, Small and Development Enterprises (MSMED) Act, 2006, the 'medium enterprises are those with investment in plants and machinery between Rs. 15 crore and 25 crore.
2. All bank loans to the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises qualify under the priority sector.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: Under the original MSMED Act, 2006, medium manufacturing enterprises were defined as investment between ₹5 crore and ₹10 crore; under the revised 2020 composite criteria, investment is up to ₹50 crore with turnover up to ₹250 crore. ₹15 crore to ₹25 crore is factually incorrect under both.
keywords.concept: Medium Enterprises Definition: Under the original MSMED Act, 2006, medium manufacturing enterprises were defined as investment between ₹5 crore and ₹10 crore; under the revised 2020 composite criteria, investment is up to ₹50 crore with turnover up to ₹250 crore. ₹15 crore to ₹25 crore is factually incorrect under both.

keywords.shortNote: Under the RBI Master Directions on PSL, all eligible bank loans to entities qualifying as Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (as per definition and valid Udyam Registration) are classified under Priority Sector Lending without arbitrary loan-size ceilings.
keywords.concept: Priority Sector Lending (PSL) for MSMEs: Under the RBI Master Directions on PSL, all eligible bank loans to entities qualifying as Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (as per definition and valid Udyam Registration) are classified under Priority Sector Lending without arbitrary loan-size ceilings.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 provides fabricated numerical thresholds that match neither the original 2006 Act nor the 2020 revision.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: RBI Master Directions on Priority Sector Lending
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect while Statement 2 correctly reflects the regulatory framework governing priority sector lending to the MSME sector.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to identify the false financial range in Statement 1.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks that bank credit to all qualifying MSME entities is classified under the PSL framework.

valueAddition.title: Evolution of MSME Classification Criteria
bullets: Original MSMED Act, 2006 Criteria: Separated manufacturing (investment in plant and machinery) from services (investment in equipment). Manufacturing: Micro (≤ ₹25 lakh), Small (> ₹25 lakh to ₹5 crore), Medium (> ₹5 crore to ₹10 crore). Services: Micro (≤ ₹10 lakh), Small (> ₹10 lakh to ₹2 crore), Medium (> ₹2 crore to ₹5 crore).
Revised Composite Criteria (Effective 1 July 2020): Eliminated the distinction between manufacturing and service enterprises, establishing a composite criteria of Investment and Turnover.
Revised Thresholds (2020): Micro (Investment ≤ ₹1 crore & Turnover ≤ ₹5 crore); Small (Investment ≤ ₹10 crore & Turnover ≤ ₹50 crore); Medium (Investment ≤ ₹50 crore & Turnover ≤ ₹250 crore).
Export Turnover Exclusion: Exports of goods or services are statutorily excluded when calculating the turnover threshold for MSME classification.

valueAddition.title: Priority Sector Lending (PSL) Mandates for MSMEs
bullets: Universal Coverage: Bank credit to all registered MSMEs (holding Udyam Registration) is eligible for priority sector status.

Sub-target for Micro Enterprises: Within the total PSL target of 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) for domestic commercial banks, a dedicated sub-target of 7.5% is earmarked specifically for Micro enterprises.
Non-Corporate Farmer & Retail Trade: In 2021, the Ministry of MSME and RBI included Retail and Wholesale trade under MSMEs, allowing them PSL benefits for priority sector credit purposes.

statementBreakdown.reference: Section 7 of MSMED Act, 2006 & Gazetted Revision (June 2020)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Under the original MSMED Act 2006, a medium enterprise in manufacturing was defined as investment in plant and machinery between ₹5 crore and ₹10 crore (and between ₹2 crore and ₹5 crore in services). Under the revised composite criteria effective July 1, 2020, a medium enterprise is defined as investment in plant and machinery not exceeding ₹50 crore and turnover not exceeding ₹250 crore. The range '₹15 crore to ₹25 crore' does not correspond to any statutory threshold in Indian law.

statementBreakdown.reference: RBI Master Directions – Priority Sector Lending (PSL), Section on MSME Sector
statementBreakdown.explanation: As per RBI Master Directions on PSL, bank loans to Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises qualify under Priority Sector Lending. For MSMEs, all eligible credit extended by scheduled commercial banks for both manufacturing and service sectors qualifies under the PSL umbrella (with sub-targets explicitly carved out for Micro enterprises).

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
Statement-I: Recently, the United States of America (USA) and the European Union (EU) have launched the Trade and Technology Council".
Statement-II: The USA and the EU claim that through this they are trying to bring technological progress and physical productivity under their control.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
options.label: a

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
options.label: b

options.text: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
options.label: c

options.text: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: A transatlantic diplomatic and economic forum launched by the United States and the European Union in June 2021 (with its inaugural ministerial meeting in Pittsburgh in September 2021) to coordinate approaches to global trade, semiconductor supply chains, artificial intelligence governance, export controls, and technical standards.
keywords.concept: US-EU Trade and Technology Council (TTC): A transatlantic diplomatic and economic forum launched by the United States and the European Union in June 2021 (with its inaugural ministerial meeting in Pittsburgh in September 2021) to coordinate approaches to global trade, semiconductor supply chains, artificial intelligence governance, export controls, and technical standards.

keywords.shortNote: A bilateral strategic coordination mechanism launched by India and the European Union in February 2023—making India only the second partner after the United States with whom the EU established a dedicated Trade and Technology Council.
keywords.concept: India-EU Trade and Technology Council: A bilateral strategic coordination mechanism launched by India and the European Union in February 2023—making India only the second partner after the United States with whom the EU established a dedicated Trade and Technology Council.

keywords.shortNote: Regulatory mechanisms coordinated through the TTC to safeguard sensitive dual-use technologies, monitor inbound foreign direct investment in critical infrastructure, and prevent non-market supply chain dependencies.
keywords.concept: Export Controls & Investment Screening: Regulatory mechanisms coordinated through the TTC to safeguard sensitive dual-use technologies, monitor inbound foreign direct investment in critical infrastructure, and prevent non-market supply chain dependencies.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly accepts a distorted, authoritarian-sounding phrasing ('bring technological progress and physical productivity under their control') that never appeared in any US-EU TTC declaration.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to spot that Statement-II is a fabricated distortion of the TTC's cooperative trade-and-standards mandate.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.text: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accurately confirms the launch of the US-EU Trade and Technology Council while rejecting the fabricated claim about controlling technological progress and physical productivity.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.text: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
optionBreakdown.explanation: Reverses both facts—denying the real US-EU TTC launch while endorsing an invented claim.

valueAddition.title: The India-EU Trade and Technology Council Link
bullets: The EU established its very first Trade and Technology Council with the United States in 2021, and in February 2023 launched its second-ever TTC with India—operating through three working groups: (1) Strategic Technologies, Digital Governance and Digital Connectivity; (2) Green and Clean Energy Technologies; and (3) Trade, Investment and Resilient Value Chains.

Notice the examiner's pattern in Statement-II: whenever a statement attributes an implausible, heavy-handed motive ('bring technological progress and physical productivity under their control') to a multilateral or bilateral forum, it is a classic fabricated distractor.

subject: Economy
stem: Which one of the following activities of the Reserve Bank of India is considered to be part of 'sterilization'?

options.text: Oversight of settlement and payment systems
options.label: b

options.text: Debt and cash management for the Central and State Governments
options.label: c

options.text: Regulating the functions of Non-banking Financial Institutions
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: A monetary policy operation through which a central bank neutralizes the impact of foreign exchange interventions (inflows or outflows) on the domestic money supply and reserve money (M0).
keywords.concept: Sterilization: A monetary policy operation through which a central bank neutralizes the impact of foreign exchange interventions (inflows or outflows) on the domestic money supply and reserve money (M0).

keywords.shortNote: Outright sales or purchases of government securities by the central bank in the secondary market to mop up or inject durable domestic liquidity.
keywords.concept: Open Market Operations (OMOs): Outright sales or purchases of government securities by the central bank in the secondary market to mop up or inject durable domestic liquidity.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.reference: NCERT Class 12 Macroeconomics & RBI Operating Procedure of Monetary Policy
optionBreakdown.explanation: When heavy foreign currency inflows enter India, RBI purchases foreign exchange to prevent excessive rupee appreciation, which inadvertently injects rupee liquidity into the banking system. To neutralize ('sterilize') this expansionary effect on domestic money supply and prevent inflation, the RBI conducts Open Market Operations (OMOs) by selling government securities to absorb the excess liquidity.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Payment system oversight is an institutional regulatory function aimed at financial stability and system resilience, having no direct connection to neutralizing foreign currency liquidity impacts.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: Public Debt Act, 1944 / Government Securities Act, 2006
optionBreakdown.explanation: Managing borrowing, Ways and Means Advances (WMA), and sovereign bond auctions is part of RBI's statutory role as the debt and cash manager to the government, not monetary sterilization.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Regulating and supervising NBFCs constitutes prudential sector oversight to protect depositors and prevent systemic financial contagion.

valueAddition.title: Mechanics of the Sterilization Process
bullets: The Inflow Trigger: When foreign capital (FPI/FDI) surges into India, market demand for Indian Rupees increases, causing the rupee to appreciate against the US Dollar.

Central Bank Intervention: To maintain export competitiveness and prevent exchange rate volatility, the RBI intervenes in the forex market by purchasing US Dollars and releasing an equivalent amount of Indian Rupees.
The Liquidity Dilemma: This intervention directly expands the monetary base (Reserve Money, M0) and domestic high-powered money, risking demand-pull inflation and credit bubbles.

The Sterilization Countermeasure: To restore monetary neutrality, the RBI sells an equivalent amount of government bonds (dated G-Secs or Treasury Bills) via Open Market Operations (OMOs), sucking back the injected rupees from commercial banks.

valueAddition.title: Key Policy Instruments for Sterilization in India
bullets: Outright OMO Sales: Traditional outright secondary market sale of Government Securities from the RBI's domestic investment portfolio.

Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS): Introduced in April 2004 when the RBI's stock of G-Secs was exhausted due to massive capital inflows; the government issues special dated Treasury bills/bonds solely for liquidity absorption, with proceeds impounded in a separate, non-spendable cash account with the RBI.
Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) Adjustments: Raising CRR immobilizes bank reserves, though it acts as a blunt, non-market instrument compared to market-based OMOs.
Standing Deposit Facility (SDF): Introduced in 2022 to absorb overnight uncollateralized excess liquidity from banks without needing to provide G-Secs as collateral.

valueAddition.title: The Impossible Trinity (Mundell-Fleming Trilemma)
bullets: Core Axiom: An open economy cannot simultaneously sustain all three: 1) A fixed/managed exchange rate, 2) Free capital mobility, and 3) An independent monetary policy.

India's Managed Choice: India maintains managed capital mobility and an independent monetary policy focused on domestic inflation targeting, meaning foreign exchange intervention must be actively sterilized to avoid losing domestic monetary autonomy.

inNews.relevance: Directly illustrates the real-world operational execution of sterilization, where forex reserve accumulation is counterbalanced with domestic liquidity absorption tools to safeguard price stability.

hook.teaser: It has nothing to do with hygiene—it's how the RBI absorbs billions in excess cash.

answer.text: Conducting Open Market Operations (OMOs) to absorb surplus rupees generated by forex intervention is the textbook definition of sterilization.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Self-Help Group (SHG) programme was originally initiated by the State Bank of India by providing microcredit to the financially deprived.
2. In an SHG, all members of a group take responsibility for a loan that an individual member takes.
3. The Regional Rural Banks and Scheduled Commercial Banks support SHGs.
How many of the above statements are correct?

keywords.shortNote: A landmark microfinance programme conceptualised and launched as a pilot project by NABARD in 1992 following consultation with the RBI to link informal grassroots credit groups with the formal banking sector.
keywords.concept: SHG-Bank Linkage Programme (SHG-BLP): A landmark microfinance programme conceptualised and launched as a pilot project by NABARD in 1992 following consultation with the RBI to link informal grassroots credit groups with the formal banking sector.

keywords.shortNote: The core collateral-substitute mechanism where the entire self-help group assumes collective social responsibility and mutual liability for loan repayments sanctioned to individual members.
keywords.concept: Peer Pressure & Mutual Guarantee: The core collateral-substitute mechanism where the entire self-help group assumes collective social responsibility and mutual liability for loan repayments sanctioned to individual members.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to acknowledge that both Statement 2 (joint liability) and Statement 3 (institutional banking support) are correct.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Exactly two statements (Statements 2 and 3) are factually and procedurally correct; Statement 1 misattributes the origin of the programme to SBI instead of NABARD.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly treats State Bank of India as the originator of the national SHG-Bank Linkage Programme.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Incorrectly asserts that all three statements are false.

valueAddition.title: Genesis of the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme (SHG-BLP)
bullets: Pilot Launch (1992): NABARD launched the pilot project linking 500 SHGs with commercial and cooperative banks after research driven by S.K. Kalia and extensive consultations with the RBI and NGOs (notably MYRADA in Karnataka).

RBI Endorsement: In 1996, the RBI mainstreamed the scheme, advising scheduled commercial banks to treat lending to SHGs as an integral component of their normal business and priority sector portfolios.

Collateral-Free Lending: Banks lend directly to the group without demanding collateral security, relying on the group's internal corpus, regular thrift savings habit, and collective social enforcement.

valueAddition.title: Delivery Models of Microfinance in India
bullets: Model I (SHGs formed and financed directly by Banks): Banks promote, nurture, and finance the self-help groups directly.
Model II (SHGs formed by NGOs / Agencies but financed by Banks): Formal financial institutions provide credit directly to groups promoted and nurtured by developmental facilitators.
Model III (NGOs as Financial Intermediaries / MFI Model): Banks lend wholesale funds to Microfinance Institutions (MFIs) or non-profits, which in turn on-lend microloans to end borrowers.

valueAddition.title: Integration with National Livelihood Missions
bullets: DAY-NRLM (Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Rural Livelihoods Mission): Implemented by the Ministry of Rural Development, organising rural poor women into universal SHG federations (Village Organisations and Cluster Level Federations).

Interest Subvention Scheme: Enables women SHGs to access credit up to ₹3 lakh at a concessional interest rate of 7% per annum, with an additional 3% subvention for prompt repayment (effective net interest rate of 4%).
Credit Guarantee Scheme: Under the Credit Guarantee Fund for Micro Units (CGFMU), collateral-free loans extended to SHGs enjoy structured credit guarantee coverage.

inNews.source: NABARD / The Hindu
inNews.headline: NABARD Status of Microfinance in India Highlights SHG-Bank Linkage Loan Portfolio Surpassing Historic Formal Credit Milestones
inNews.relevance: Directly highlights the role of NABARD as the apex monitoring and refinancing authority of the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme, tracking NPA metrics and bank credit disbursement across RRBs and commercial banks.

statementBreakdown.reference: NABARD Annual Report 1991–92 & S.K. Kalia Working Group (1989)
statementBreakdown.explanation: The SHG-Bank Linkage Programme was conceptualised and piloted by the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) in 1992, with policy support and endorsement from the Reserve Bank of India, not by the State Bank of India.

statementBreakdown.reference: RBI Master Directions – Microcredit & NABARD Operational Guidelines
statementBreakdown.explanation: SHGs operate on the doctrine of mutual trust and joint liability. The group collectively appraises individual loan needs and all members assume collective responsibility for recovery and repayment, replacing physical asset collateral with social collateral.

statementBreakdown.reference: RBI Master Directions – Priority Sector Lending & Commercial Banking Delivery
statementBreakdown.explanation: Both Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) and Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs), alongside Cooperative Banks, actively support, open savings accounts for, and extend credit linkage to SHGs under priority sector lending guidelines.

visualSuggestion.title: SHG-BLP Model vs. Joint Liability Group (JLG) Model

rows: Compulsory internal thrift savings precedes credit
Pure credit delivery; no mandatory pre-savings corpus
Collective social responsibility and group guarantee
Mutual joint guarantee for individual crop/activity loans

hook.headline: Did SBI really start the Self-Help Group movement?
hook.teaser: One institutional swap in statement 1 changes the entire answer count.

keywords.term: originally initiated by the State Bank of India
keywords.calloutNote: Look for the founding agency: NABARD launched the SHG pilot in 1992, not SBI.
activePhrases: originally initiated by the State Bank of India by providing microcredit to the financially deprived

keywords.term: all members of a group take responsibility
keywords.calloutNote: Peer pressure replaces physical collateral—every member guarantees individual borrowing.
activePhrases: all members of a group take responsibility for a loan that an individual member takes
dimmedPhrases: originally initiated by the State Bank of India by providing microcredit to the financially deprived
contextPhrases: Regional Rural Banks and Scheduled Commercial Banks

verdicts.source: The national SHG-Bank Linkage Programme was conceptualised and piloted by NABARD in 1992 following the S.K. Kalia committee.
SHGs function on mutual peer monitoring; the entire group assumes collective responsibility for an individual's loan repayment.
Both Scheduled Commercial Banks and Regional Rural Banks actively open accounts and lend directly to SHGs under PSL norms.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Only two statements (2 and 3) are correct; statement 1 is false because NABARD pioneered the SHG programme.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
The Stability and Growth Pact of the European Union is a treaty that
1. limits the levels of the budgetary deficit of the countries of the European Union
2. makes the countries of the European Union to share their infrastructure facilities
3. enables the countries of the European Union to share their technologies
How many of the above statements are correct?

keywords.shortNote: A set of legally binding fiscal rules adopted by European Union member states in 1997 to coordinate national fiscal policies, enforce budgetary discipline, and safeguard the stability of the Economic and Monetary Union.
keywords.concept: Stability and Growth Pact (SGP): A set of legally binding fiscal rules adopted by European Union member states in 1997 to coordinate national fiscal policies, enforce budgetary discipline, and safeguard the stability of the Economic and Monetary Union.

keywords.shortNote: The benchmark economic and fiscal conditions—specifically capping annual fiscal deficits at 3% of GDP and public debt at 60% of GDP—that EU member states must meet to adopt and sustain the Euro.
keywords.concept: Maastricht Convergence Criteria: The benchmark economic and fiscal conditions—specifically capping annual fiscal deficits at 3% of GDP and public debt at 60% of GDP—that EU member states must meet to adopt and sustain the Euro.

keywords.shortNote: The corrective enforcement arm of the Stability and Growth Pact under which the European Commission monitors fiscal breaches and can impose financial sanctions on non-compliant Eurozone members.
keywords.concept: Excessive Deficit Procedure (EDP): The corrective enforcement arm of the Stability and Growth Pact under which the European Commission monitors fiscal breaches and can impose financial sanctions on non-compliant Eurozone members.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Only the first statement accurately describes the SGP's core fiscal discipline mandate.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly attributes infrastructure or technology sharing mandates to a pure fiscal rules framework.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to isolate the SGP's narrow macroeconomic focus on deficits and public debt.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks the pact's foundational 3% fiscal deficit ceiling.

valueAddition.title: Why a Monetary Union Needs Fiscal Rules
bullets: In the Eurozone, monetary policy is centralized under the European Central Bank (ECB), while taxation and spending remain decentralized with national governments.
Without binding fiscal caps, a single member running chronic deficits can drive up borrowing costs and inflation across the entire currency bloc—creating a classic free-rider moral hazard.
The SGP enforces two quantitative anchors: annual budget deficit below 3% of GDP and gross government debt below 60% of GDP (or declining toward it at a satisfactory pace).

valueAddition.title: Preventive Arm vs. Corrective Arm
bullets: Preventive Arm: Requires EU states to submit annual Stability or Convergence Programmes outlining medium-term budgetary objectives to prevent deficits from breaching thresholds.

Corrective Arm (Excessive Deficit Procedure): Triggers binding recommendations and potential fines of up to 0.2% of GDP for Eurozone members that breach the 3% deficit rule without exceptional justification.

General Escape Clause: Activated during severe symmetric shocks (such as the 2020 pandemic and 2022 energy crisis) to temporarily suspend fiscal limits, followed by reformed country-specific debt-reduction paths.

inNews.source: European Commission / Reuters
inNews.headline: EU Council Reviews Medium-Term Fiscal Plans Under Reformed Stability and Growth Pact
inNews.relevance: Following the reinstatement of EU fiscal rules and the 2024 governance overhaul, Brussels assessed member states' four-to-seven-year net expenditure trajectories in July 2026 under Excessive Deficit Procedures.

statementBreakdown.explanation: The Stability and Growth Pact operationalizes the Maastricht fiscal benchmarks by capping a member state's annual general government budget deficit at 3% of GDP and gross public debt at 60% of GDP.

The SGP is strictly a macroeconomic and fiscal surveillance pact governing deficits and debt; cross-border infrastructure financing falls under separate EU programs like the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) or Cohesion Policy.
Technology sharing and R&D cooperation are governed by frameworks like Horizon Europe, not by the Stability and Growth Pact.

hook.teaser: Notice how UPSC pairs one exact macroeconomic treaty rule with two plausible-sounding fillers.

keywords.calloutNote: Link this treaty immediately to the Eurozone's 3% budget deficit and 60% public debt rules.
activePhrases: Stability and Growth Pact

keywords.calloutNote: Recall that a common currency like the Euro cannot survive if member states run unchecked national deficits.
activePhrases: budgetary deficit
dimmedPhrases: Stability and Growth Pact

verdicts.source: The Stability and Growth Pact enforces the Maastricht rule capping EU member budget deficits at 3% of GDP and public debt at 60% of GDP.
Infrastructure sharing is handled through separate EU funds like the Connecting Europe Facility, not the Stability and Growth Pact.
Technology and R&D collaboration fall under Horizon Europe, whereas the SGP deals strictly with fiscal surveillance.

answer.label: A
answer.text: Only the first statement on budgetary deficit limits is true—so only one is the right answer.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
Statement-I: India's public sector health care system largely focuses on curative care with limited preventive, promotive and rehabilitative care.
Statement-II: Under India's decentralized approach to health care delivery, the States are primarily responsible for organizing health services.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-I are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
options.label: a

options.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
options.label: b

options.text: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
options.label: c

options.text: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
options.label: d

keywords.term: Curative vs. Preventive and Promotive Health Care
keywords.shortNote: Curative care treats existing illnesses and acute conditions through hospital diagnosis and medication, whereas preventive and promotive care stops disease onset and builds population wellness through immunization, screening, sanitation, and primary nutrition.
keywords.concept: Curative vs. Preventive and Promotive Health Care: Curative care treats existing illnesses and acute conditions through hospital diagnosis and medication, whereas preventive and promotive care stops disease onset and builds population wellness through immunization, screening, sanitation, and primary nutrition.

keywords.shortNote: The constitutional entry assigning 'Public health and sanitation; hospitals and dispensaries' to the State List, making State Governments primarily responsible for organizing and delivering health services across India.
keywords.concept: Seventh Schedule — State List Entry 6: The constitutional entry assigning 'Public health and sanitation; hospitals and dispensaries' to the State List, making State Governments primarily responsible for organizing and delivering health services across India.

keywords.shortNote: The core reform strategy under the National Health Policy, 2017 and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (Health and Wellness Centres) aimed at shifting India's public health system from episodic curative care toward continuum-of-care preventive, promotive, curative, and rehabilitative services.
keywords.concept: Comprehensive Primary Health Care (CPHC): The core reform strategy under the National Health Policy, 2017 and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (Health and Wellness Centres) aimed at shifting India's public health system from episodic curative care toward continuum-of-care preventive, promotive, curative, and rehabilitative services.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.reference: No Causal Link Between Decentralization and Curative Skew
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because State-level organization of health services (Statement-II) is not the reason public health systems focus disproportionately on curative care (Statement-I).

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: Both Statements True; Statement-II Does Not Explain Statement-I
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements are factually grounded in the National Health Policy 2017 and the Seventh Schedule, but they address two distinct structural dimensions—care-continuum imbalance versus federal division of responsibility.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because public health and hospitals are constitutionally assigned to the State List, making States primarily responsible for service delivery.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because India's historical over-reliance on curative hospital care over preventive and rehabilitative care is an established policy diagnosis in the National Health Policy, 2017.

valueAddition.title: Why Statement-I Exists & How National Health Policy 2017 Addresses It
bullets: Root Causes of Curative Bias: Chronic low public health expenditure (~1.8–2.1% of GDP versus the NHP 2017 target of 2.5% of GDP) and hospital-heavy budgeting historically crowded out preventive screening, rehabilitation, and palliative care.

Shift to Continuum of Care: Under Ayushman Bharat – Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (formerly Health and Wellness Centres), over 1.7 lakh Sub-Health Centres and PHCs were upgraded to deliver Comprehensive Primary Health Care covering non-communicable disease screening, mental health, elderly care, and rehabilitation.

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Division of Health Subjects Across Seventh Schedule Lists
bullets: State List (List II, Entry 6): Public health and sanitation; hospitals and dispensaries—giving States primary operational responsibility for health delivery.

Concurrent List (List III): Population control and family planning (Entry 20A), drugs and poisons (Entry 19), medical education and profession (Entry 26), and prevention of extension of infectious/contagious diseases from one State to another (Entry 29).

inNews.source: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) / National Health Accounts
inNews.headline: National Health Accounts and Ayushman Arogya Mandir review highlight rising primary preventive share and declining out-of-pocket health expenditure
inNews.relevance: October 2026 Health Ministry data showed expanded non-communicable disease screening across over 1.75 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs alongside sustained State-led public health expenditure reducing household out-of-pocket spending.

statementBreakdown.reference: National Health Policy, 2017 · Selective Primary & Curative Skew
statementBreakdown.explanation: Historically, India's public health infrastructure operated through selective, episodic curative services and narrow vertical disease programmes with limited preventive, promotive, and rehabilitative coverage—the exact structural gap National Health Policy 2017 sought to correct.

statementBreakdown.reference: Constitution of India Seventh Schedule · State List Entry 6 (Not Explanatory of Statement-I)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Health is a State subject under Entry 6 of the State List, so States bear primary responsibility for organizing health services; however, federal decentralization does not cause the curative skew described in Statement-I, which stems instead from chronic underfunding and hospital-centric resource allocation.

States fund ~60–65% of total public health spending and run primary/secondary facilities

hook.headline: Both health care statements are true—but does Statement-II explain Statement-I?
hook.teaser: Test the 'because' link between State-led health delivery and India's curative care bias.

keywords.calloutNote: National Health Policy 2017 flags that India's public health system historically prioritized hospital curative treatment over preventive and rehabilitative care.
activePhrases: curative care with limited preventive, promotive and rehabilitative care

keywords.term: States are primarily responsible for organizing health services
keywords.calloutNote: Public health and hospitals sit in Entry 6 of the State List—true on its own, but federal decentralization is not what causes curative bias.
activePhrases: States are primarily responsible for organizing health services
dimmedPhrases: curative care with limited preventive, promotive and rehabilitative care

verdicts.source: India's public health system historically focused heavily on episodic curative care while under-investing in preventive and rehabilitative services.
Health is a State subject under Entry 6 of the State List, but decentralization does not explain why care skewed toward curative hospitals.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but State-level responsibility for health delivery does not explain the curative bias.

items.desc: Public health and hospitals are in the State List, while drugs, family planning, medical education, and inter-state contagion are Concurrent.

items.desc: National Health Policy 2017 targets raising public health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP with two-thirds earmarked for primary care.

valueAddition.note: In Statement-I / Statement-II questions, read 'Statement-I BECAUSE Statement-II' aloud—if the causal link breaks, pick Option (b).

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following markets:
1. Government Bond Market
2. Call Money Market
3. Treasury Bill Market
4. Stock Market
How many of the above are included in capital markets?

keywords.shortNote: The segment of the financial system where long-term debt and equity securities with original maturities exceeding one year are issued and traded to channel savings into productive capital.
keywords.concept: Capital Market: The segment of the financial system where long-term debt and equity securities with original maturities exceeding one year are issued and traded to channel savings into productive capital.

keywords.shortNote: The wholesale financial market for short-term borrowing and lending of highly liquid debt instruments with maturities of up to one year.
keywords.concept: Money Market: The wholesale financial market for short-term borrowing and lending of highly liquid debt instruments with maturities of up to one year.

keywords.shortNote: Long-term tradable sovereign debt obligations issued by the Central or State Governments with fixed or floating coupon rates and maturities ranging from 5 to 40 years.
keywords.concept: Dated Government Securities (G-Secs): Long-term tradable sovereign debt obligations issued by the Central or State Governments with fixed or floating coupon rates and maturities ranging from 5 to 40 years.

keywords.shortNote: An inter-bank money market segment where funds are borrowed and lent overnight (for 1 day) without collateral to manage daily Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) requirements.
keywords.concept: Call Money Market: An inter-bank money market segment where funds are borrowed and lent overnight (for 1 day) without collateral to manage daily Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) requirements.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Misses the fact that both long-term sovereign debt (Government Bonds) and equity (Stock Market) belong to the capital market.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Only two markets—Government Bond Market and Stock Market—deal in long-term instruments exceeding one year.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly pulls either Treasury Bills or Call Money into the capital market despite their sub-one-year tenors.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to separate short-term liquidity markets (Call Money, T-Bills) from long-term capital formation markets.

valueAddition.title: The One-Year Maturity Dividing Line
bullets: Financial markets split along a strict 365-day boundary: instruments maturing within 1 year trade in the Money Market, while instruments exceeding 1 year (or perpetual equity) trade in the Capital Market.

Sovereign borrowing spans both worlds—the Government of India issues short-term Treasury Bills (91, 182, 364 days) in the money market and long-term Dated G-Secs (up to 40 years) in the capital market.
Money markets exist primarily for working capital and overnight bank liquidity management, whereas capital markets finance long-gestation infrastructure and corporate expansion.

valueAddition.title: Regulatory Split: RBI vs. SEBI
bullets: The Reserve Bank of India regulates the entire Money Market (Call/Notice/Term Money, T-Bills, Commercial Paper, Certificates of Deposit) as well as the Government Securities (G-Sec) market.
SEBI regulates the corporate equity market, corporate bond market, mutual funds, and exchange-traded derivatives.
Both regulators jointly coordinate settlement infrastructure through platforms like NDS-OM (for G-Secs) and stock exchanges (NSE/BSE) to expand retail participation.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
inNews.headline: RBI Relaxes FPI Investment Limits in Central and State Government Securities
inNews.relevance: RBI removed concentration and short-term limits for Foreign Portfolio Investors in June 2026 and added 15-, 30-, and 40-year G-Secs to the Fully Accessible Route to deepen long-term capital inflows.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Government bonds (dated G-Secs and State Development Loans) carry original maturities exceeding one year (typically 5 to 40 years), placing the Government Bond Market squarely inside the long-term capital market.
The Call Money Market deals exclusively in overnight (1-day) inter-bank funds and notice money (2 to 14 days), making it the core liquidity segment of the short-term money market.
Treasury Bills (T-Bills) are zero-coupon sovereign instruments issued strictly in 91-day, 182-day, and 364-day tenors—all under one year—which classifies the T-Bill market under the money market.
The Stock Market facilitates the issuance and secondary trading of perpetual equity shares and long-term corporate securities, serving as the primary pillar of the capital market.

visualSuggestion.title: Money Market vs. Capital Market Matrix

rows: Up to 1 year (1 day to 364 days)
Call Money, T-Bills, Commercial Paper, CDs
Dated G-Secs, Corporate Bonds, Equity Shares

hook.headline: Does the Government Bond Market count as a capital market?
hook.teaser: Notice how UPSC tests one simple 365-day rule across four everyday financial markets.

keywords.calloutNote: Look at the tenure: dated government bonds run from 5 to 40 years, putting them squarely in the long-term capital market.
activePhrases: Government Bond Market

keywords.calloutNote: Do not confuse T-Bills with bonds—T-Bills mature in 91, 182, or 364 days, which keeps them inside the money market.
activePhrases: Treasury Bill Market
dimmedPhrases: Government Bond Market

verdicts.source: Dated government bonds carry maturities exceeding one year, making the Government Bond Market a core pillar of the capital market.
Call money is 1-day inter-bank borrowing for overnight liquidity, so it belongs strictly to the money market.
Treasury Bills mature in 91, 182, or 364 days—under one year—placing them in the short-term money market.
The stock market trades perpetual equity shares and long-term securities, which is the textbook definition of a capital market.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Only the Government Bond Market and the Stock Market exceed the one-year maturity line—so only two is correct.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Financial Markets notes

items.title: The 365-Day Dividing Line
items.desc: Up to 1 year equals Money Market; above 1 year (or perpetual equity) equals Capital Market.

items.title: G-Secs vs. T-Bills
items.desc: Both are sovereign debt, but T-Bills (under 1 year) sit in the money market while Dated G-Secs (5–40 years) sit in the capital market.

items.title: RBI vs. SEBI
items.desc: RBI regulates the money market and G-Secs; SEBI regulates the stock market and corporate bonds.

valueAddition.note: Examiners pair Treasury Bills with Government Bonds to see if you separate sovereign instruments by maturity rather than by issuer.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to Central Bank digital currencies, consider the following statements:
1. It is possible to make payments in a digital currency without using US dollar or SWIFT system.
2. A digital currency can be distributed with condition programmed into it such as a time- frame for spending it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct:

keywords.shortNote: Legal tender issued by a central bank in digital form (such as India's e-Rupee), representing a direct sovereign liability on the central bank's balance sheet and exchangeable one-to-one with physical fiat currency.
keywords.concept: Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC): Legal tender issued by a central bank in digital form (such as India's e-Rupee), representing a direct sovereign liability on the central bank's balance sheet and exchangeable one-to-one with physical fiat currency.

keywords.shortNote: The Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication—a global financial messaging network used by correspondent banks to transmit cross-border payment instructions, which bilateral or multi-CBDC bridges can bypass for direct instant settlement.
keywords.concept: SWIFT Messaging System: The Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication—a global financial messaging network used by correspondent banks to transmit cross-border payment instructions, which bilateral or multi-CBDC bridges can bypass for direct instant settlement.

keywords.shortNote: Digital currency embedded with smart-contract rules or conditional logic—such as expiry deadlines, merchant-category restrictions, or beneficiary-specific usage—prior to distribution.
keywords.concept: Programmable Money (Purpose-Bound Money): Digital currency embedded with smart-contract rules or conditional logic—such as expiry deadlines, merchant-category restrictions, or beneficiary-specific usage—prior to distribution.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks programmability—one of the defining technical capabilities highlighted in the RBI's 2022 CBDC Concept Note for targeted Direct Benefit Transfers.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Misses that multi-CBDC bridges are explicitly designed to settle cross-border trade directly in domestic currencies without routing through the US dollar or SWIFT.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accurately captures both core policy rationales for CBDCs: bypassing legacy correspondent banking/SWIFT networks in cross-border payments and enabling programmable, time-bound money.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Rejects two foundational design features of Central Bank Digital Currencies documented by the RBI and BIS.

valueAddition.title: Why Central Banks Build Programmable & Cross-Border CBDCs
bullets: Cross-Border Settlement Without Intermediaries: Traditional international transfers rely on multi-bank correspondent chains, SWIFT messaging, and US dollar clearing—adding fees and multi-day delays. Interlinked CBDC platforms settle bilaterally in real time.

Purpose-Bound & Time-Bound Welfare Delivery: Programming an expiry date or sector lock into CBDC tokens ensures that fiscal stimulus or agricultural/fertilizer subsidies are spent quickly and strictly on intended goods without leakage.

valueAddition.title: Retail CBDC (CBDC-R) vs. Wholesale CBDC (CBDC-W) in India
bullets: Retail e-Rupee (CBDC-R) is available to households and merchants for everyday person-to-person and person-to-merchant payments (including offline capability), while Wholesale e-Rupee (CBDC-W) is restricted to banks and financial institutions for interbank call-money and government-securities settlement.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) / Bank for International Settlements (BIS)
inNews.headline: RBI Expands Programmable e-Rupee Pilots for Targeted Agricultural Subsidies and Cross-Border Bilateral Settlement Corridors
inNews.relevance: October 2026 RBI digital-currency updates highlighted purpose-bound e-Rupee disbursements with built-in validity windows alongside bilateral CBDC settlement trials operating outside legacy correspondent banking rails.

statementBreakdown.reference: BIS Project mBridge & RBI Concept Note on CBDC (Cross-Border Payments)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Bilateral or multi-CBDC settlement corridors (such as BIS Project mBridge and RBI's cross-border e-Rupee linkages) enable direct peer-to-peer cross-border settlement in local digital currencies, bypassing correspondent banking chains, US dollar intermediation, and the SWIFT messaging network.

statementBreakdown.reference: RBI Concept Note on CBDC (2022) — Programmability & Targeted Subsidies
statementBreakdown.explanation: Because CBDCs operate on programmable digital ledgers, central banks or governments can embed conditional rules—such as an expiration time-frame for spending, geographic boundaries, or end-use restrictions for welfare transfers and stimulus payouts.

visualSuggestion.title: Core Design Capabilities of Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs)

rows: Relies on correspondent banks, US dollar clearing & SWIFT messaging
Direct bilateral/multi-CBDC settlement without USD or SWIFT (Statement 1)
Physical cash cannot restrict when or where it is spent

hook.headline: Can a Central Bank Digital Currency bypass SWIFT and expire if you don't spend it in time?
hook.teaser: Notice how both statements describe real features tested in the RBI's own e-Rupee pilots.

keywords.term: without using US dollar or SWIFT system
keywords.calloutTerm: “without using US dollar or SWIFT system”
keywords.calloutNote: Multi-CBDC bridges let two countries settle cross-border payments directly in their own digital currencies, skipping correspondent banks, US dollars, and SWIFT.
activePhrases: without using US dollar or SWIFT system

keywords.term: condition programmed into it such as a time- frame for spending it
keywords.calloutTerm: “condition programmed into it such as a time- frame for spending it”
keywords.calloutNote: Programmable CBDCs allow governments to attach expiry dates or specific usage rules—ideal for targeted subsidies or stimulus payouts.
activePhrases: condition programmed into it such as a time- frame for spending it
dimmedPhrases: without using US dollar or SWIFT system

verdicts.source: Interlinked CBDC platforms enable direct cross-border settlement in local digital currencies without relying on the US dollar or SWIFT.
CBDCs can carry programmed smart-contract conditions such as spending deadlines or purpose-specific restrictions.

answer.label: C
answer.text: CBDCs can settle cross-border payments outside SWIFT and carry programmable spending deadlines—so Both 1 and 2 is right.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Digital Currency & Payment Systems notes

items.desc: CBDC-R serves households and merchants; CBDC-W serves banks for interbank and G-Sec settlement.

items.desc: Unlike UPI (which moves commercial bank deposits), e-Rupee is sovereign legal tender directly on the RBI's balance sheet.

items.title: Multi-CBDC Cross-Border Rails
items.desc: BIS-led multi-CBDC projects demonstrate real-time cross-border FX settlement without correspondent bank chains.
