rows: Creates or upgrades multi-year productive assets
Acquiring new technology, machinery, plants, patents
Recurring day-to-day operational cost within 1 year
Salaries, raw materials, utility bills, interest paid on loans
Raises capital via liabilities or ownership (NOT expenditure)
Debt financing (issuing bonds/loans) & Equity financing (issuing shares)

hook.headline: Is raising money through debt or equity an 'expenditure'?
hook.teaser: Notice the classic category error UPSC hides inside Statement 2—confusing how you raise money with how you spend it.

keywords.calloutNote: Buying new technology builds multi-year productive capacity—whether hardware or software, that is textbook capital expenditure.
activePhrases: Acquiring new technology

keywords.term: Debt financing is considered capital expenditure, while equity financing is considered revenue expenditure
keywords.calloutNote: Here is the catch: debt and equity financing are ways of raising capital, not expenditures at all.
activePhrases: Debt financing is considered capital expenditure, while equity financing is considered revenue expenditure
dimmedPhrases: Acquiring new technology
contextPhrases: expenditure made by an organisation or a company

verdicts.source: Acquiring new technology creates a lasting productive asset that generates returns over several years, making it capital expenditure.
Debt financing and equity financing are ways a company raises funds—they are capital inflows, not capital or revenue expenditures.

answer.label: A
answer.text: Buying new technology is capital expenditure, while debt and equity financing are inflows rather than spending—so 1 only is right.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Economy & Accounting notes

items.title: Raising vs. Spending Funds
items.desc: Debt and equity financing are sources of funds (inflows); CapEx and OpEx are uses of funds (outflows).

items.title: Intangible CapEx Counts
items.desc: Capital expenditure includes both physical machinery and intangible assets like software, patents, and new technology.

items.title: Interest Is Revenue Outlay
items.desc: Borrowing money is a debt inflow, repaying principal reduces a liability, and paying annual interest is revenue expenditure.

valueAddition.note: Examiners love pairing two authentic finance terms—debt financing and equity financing—inside a false classification to test if you confuse sources of capital with expenditure.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to foreign-owned e-commerce firms operating in India, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. They can sell their own goods in addition to offering their platforms as market-
2. The degree to which they can own big sellers on their platforms is limited.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:

keywords.shortNote: An e-commerce model where an entity provides an information technology platform on a digital network strictly as a facilitator between independent buyers and sellers, eligible for 100% FDI under the automatic route.
keywords.concept: Marketplace-Based Model of E-Commerce: An e-commerce model where an entity provides an information technology platform on a digital network strictly as a facilitator between independent buyers and sellers, eligible for 100% FDI under the automatic route.

keywords.shortNote: An e-commerce activity where the inventory of goods and services is owned directly by the e-commerce entity and sold to consumers—barred for FDI in domestic retail under India's FDI Policy.
keywords.concept: Inventory-Based Model of E-Commerce: An e-commerce activity where the inventory of goods and services is owned directly by the e-commerce entity and sold to consumers—barred for FDI in domestic retail under India's FDI Policy.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because FDI is prohibited in domestic inventory-based B2C e-commerce.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Foreign-funded marketplaces cannot sell their own inventory domestically, and strict equity-participation and 25% sourcing-control caps restrict them from owning or controlling major sellers on their platforms.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because a foreign-owned marketplace cannot operate a hybrid domestic inventory-plus-marketplace retail model.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because DPIIT explicitly restricts equity ownership and inventory control over platform vendors.

valueAddition.title: Core Guardrails Under DPIIT's E-Commerce FDI Rules
bullets: Marketplace vs. Inventory Split: 100% FDI under the automatic route is allowed in B2B e-commerce and the B2C marketplace model, whereas FDI is barred in domestic B2C inventory-based e-commerce to prevent backdoor entry into multi-brand retail.

Press Note 2 (2018) Anti-Circumvention Rules: Any seller in which the marketplace or its group company holds equity—or from which the vendor buys over 25% of its inventory—cannot sell on that platform; marketplaces are also barred from enforcing exclusivity clauses or influencing retail sale prices.

valueAddition.title: Recent Policy Relaxation: Export-Only Inventory Exception
bullets: Via Press Note No. 3 (2026 Series) notified in July 2026, DPIIT amended Para 5.2.15.2 of the Consolidated FDI Policy to permit FDI in an inventory-based e-commerce model exclusively for exporting goods manufactured or produced in India.
Domestic B2C retail restrictions remain completely unchanged: foreign-owned e-commerce firms still cannot sell their own inventory directly to Indian consumers.

inNews.source: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) / DGFT
inNews.headline: DPIIT Press Note 3 (2026 Series) and DGFT framework permit FDI in inventory-based e-commerce exclusively for Indian exports
inNews.relevance: DPIIT's July 2026 Press Note and DGFT's August 2026 operational framework carved out a narrow export-only exception allowing FDI e-commerce firms to hold Indian-made inventory for overseas shipments while keeping domestic retail rules strictly marketplace-only.

statementBreakdown.reference: DPIIT Consolidated FDI Policy · Para 5.2.15.2 (Inventory Prohibition)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Foreign-owned e-commerce entities operating in India's domestic retail market are permitted 100% FDI only under the marketplace model; they are prohibited from holding inventory and selling their own goods directly to domestic consumers.

statementBreakdown.reference: Press Note 2 (2018 Series) · Equity & Control Restrictions on Vendors
statementBreakdown.explanation: Under DPIIT's Press Note 2 of 2018, an entity having equity participation by an e-commerce marketplace entity or its group companies—or having control over its inventory by the marketplace entity—is not permitted to sell its products on the platform run by that marketplace.

E-commerce entity holds export-only Indian inventory
Barred from selling if marketplace holds equity or supplies >25% inventory

hook.headline: Can foreign-owned e-commerce giants sell their own goods directly in India?
hook.teaser: No—India's FDI rules draw a strict firewall between running a marketplace and owning retail inventory.

keywords.calloutNote: DPIIT bans FDI in domestic inventory-based e-commerce—foreign-funded platforms can only act as neutral marketplaces.
activePhrases: sell their own goods

keywords.term: own big sellers on their platforms is limited
keywords.calloutNote: Press Note 2 of 2018 bars any seller from listing on a marketplace if the platform holds equity in it or supplies over 25% of its stock.
activePhrases: own big sellers on their platforms is limited
dimmedPhrases: sell their own goods

verdicts.source: Foreign-owned e-commerce firms get 100% FDI only as neutral marketplaces; selling their own inventory domestically is prohibited.
DPIIT rules bar vendors from selling on a marketplace if the platform owns equity in them or controls over 25% of their purchases.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Only Statement 2 is correct—foreign e-commerce marketplaces cannot sell their own goods domestically, and their ownership of platform sellers is strictly restricted.

subject: Economy
stem:
Which of the following activities constitute real sector in the economy?
1. Farmers harvesting their crops
2. Textile mills converting raw cotton into fabrics
3. A commercial bank lending money to a trading company
4. A corporate body issuing Rupee Denominated Bonds overseas
Select the correct answer using the code given below:

keywords.shortNote: The segment of an economy directly engaged in producing tangible goods and non-financial services—encompassing agriculture, mining, manufacturing, construction, and physical trade—that directly contributes to Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
keywords.concept: Real Sector: The segment of an economy directly engaged in producing tangible goods and non-financial services—encompassing agriculture, mining, manufacturing, construction, and physical trade—that directly contributes to Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

keywords.shortNote: The network of banks, capital markets, non-banking financial companies, and debt/equity instruments that mobilizes savings, allocates credit, and manages financial claims rather than directly producing physical goods or non-financial services.
keywords.concept: Financial Sector: The network of banks, capital markets, non-banking financial companies, and debt/equity instruments that mobilizes savings, allocates credit, and manages financial claims rather than directly producing physical goods or non-financial services.

keywords.shortNote: Debt securities issued outside India in foreign capital markets but denominated in Indian Rupees rather than local foreign currency, shifting currency exchange risk onto overseas investors.
keywords.concept: Rupee Denominated Bonds (Masala Bonds): Debt securities issued outside India in foreign capital markets but denominated in Indian Rupees rather than local foreign currency, shifting currency exchange risk onto overseas investors.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Cleanly separates physical production activities (agriculture and textile manufacturing) in the real sector from credit intermediation and bond issuance in the financial sector.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Mixes banking credit and bond financing into the real sector while omitting crop harvesting.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly treats bank lending and bond issuance as real-sector production while leaving out textile manufacturing.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to distinguish between producing real goods and raising or lending financial capital.

valueAddition.title: The Four Macroeconomic Accounts Framework (Real vs. Financial Split)
bullets: Standard macroeconomic analysis divides an economy into four interconnected sectors: (1) Real Sector (production of goods and non-financial services—agriculture, industry, construction, transport), (2) Financial/Monetary Sector (banks, NBFCs, bond/equity markets, money supply), (3) Fiscal Sector (government taxation, expenditure, borrowing), and (4) External Sector (Balance of Payments, trade, exchange rate).
While the financial sector channels savings to fund factories and farms, issuing bonds or disbursing loans represents financial claim creation—not real-sector production itself.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) / Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI)
inNews.headline: RBI Monetary Policy Report Highlights Strong Real-Sector Manufacturing and Agricultural Momentum Supporting FY27 GDP Growth
inNews.relevance: October 2026 RBI policy assessments contrasted resilient real-sector output in agriculture and textiles with steady bank credit and corporate bond mobilization in the financial sector.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Farmers harvesting agricultural crops directly produce physical farm output, forming the primary pillar of the real sector.
Textile mills converting raw cotton into woven fabrics add tangible physical value through industrial manufacturing, placing the activity squarely in the real sector.
Commercial bank lending is financial intermediation (creating a credit claim and moving funds), which belongs to the financial sector rather than direct real-sector goods production.
Issuing Rupee Denominated Bonds (Masala Bonds) overseas is a capital-market debt financing transaction, placing it in the financial/external sector rather than the real sector.

visualSuggestion.title: Real Sector vs. Financial Sector Classification in UPSC CSE Pre 2022 Q#4

rows: Primary production of physical agricultural output
Textile mills converting cotton into fabrics
Secondary industrial manufacturing of physical goods
Commercial bank lending to a trading company
Corporate body issuing Rupee Denominated Bonds overseas

hook.headline: Does issuing Masala Bonds overseas count as a 'real sector' activity?
hook.teaser: Notice how separating physical production from money and credit markets splits these four items right down the middle.

keywords.calloutNote: The real sector covers activities that directly produce physical goods and non-financial services—like farming crops and weaving textiles.
activePhrases: real sector in the economy

keywords.calloutNote: Bank loans and overseas Rupee Denominated Bonds move money and create financial claims—putting both in the financial sector, not the real sector.
activePhrases: commercial bank lending money
dimmedPhrases: real sector in the economy

verdicts.source: Farmers harvesting crops directly produce tangible agricultural goods in the real sector.
Textile mills turning raw cotton into fabrics carry out physical manufacturing in the real sector.
Commercial bank lending is a financial-sector credit operation rather than physical production.
Issuing Rupee Denominated Bonds (Masala Bonds) overseas is a financial capital-raising transaction, not a real-sector activity.

answer.label: A
answer.text: Farming and textile manufacturing produce physical goods in the real sector while bank loans and bonds belong to the financial sector—so 1 and 2 only is right.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Macroeconomics & Financial Markets notes

items.title: Macroeconomic Sector Map
items.desc: Macroeconomics splits into Real (goods/services), Financial (banks/markets), Fiscal (government budget), and External (BoP).

items.title: Rupee Denominated Bonds
items.desc: Masala Bonds are issued abroad in Indian Rupees, meaning foreign investors—not the Indian issuer—bear currency depreciation risk.

items.title: Production vs. Financing Test
items.desc: Ask if the activity creates tangible output or moves financial claims—only the former sits in the real sector.

valueAddition.note: Always keep the boundary crisp: producing goods and physical services = Real Sector; lending money or issuing securities = Financial Sector.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to the Indian economy, consider the following statements:
1. A share of the household financial savings goes towards government borrowings.
2. Dated securities issued at market-related rates in auctions form a large component of internal debt.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: The net financial assets held by households—including bank deposits, life insurance funds, provident and pension funds, small savings, and direct securities—that serve as the primary surplus pool funding public and private investment.
keywords.concept: Household Financial Savings: The net financial assets held by households—including bank deposits, life insurance funds, provident and pension funds, small savings, and direct securities—that serve as the primary surplus pool funding public and private investment.

keywords.shortNote: The portion of total sovereign public debt raised within India and denominated in Indian Rupees, comprising marketable dated G-Secs, Treasury Bills, and non-marketable special securities.
keywords.concept: Internal Debt: The portion of total sovereign public debt raised within India and denominated in Indian Rupees, comprising marketable dated G-Secs, Treasury Bills, and non-marketable special securities.

keywords.shortNote: Long-term sovereign bonds with fixed or floating coupon rates and specified maturity dates ranging from 5 to 40 years, issued primarily through competitive yield- or price-based auctions conducted by the RBI.
keywords.concept: Dated Government Securities (Dated G-Secs): Long-term sovereign bonds with fixed or floating coupon rates and specified maturity dates ranging from 5 to 40 years, issued primarily through competitive yield- or price-based auctions conducted by the RBI.

keywords.shortNote: The minimum percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that commercial banks must maintain in liquid assets such as cash, gold, or unencumbered government securities.
keywords.concept: Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR): The minimum percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that commercial banks must maintain in liquid assets such as cash, gold, or unencumbered government securities.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Misses the structural dominance of auctioned dated G-Secs within India's internal public debt.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks how household deposits, insurance premiums, and small savings channel directly and indirectly into government debt.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements accurately capture how India finances its fiscal deficit from domestic household savings via market-auctioned dated securities.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Contradicts basic RBI flow-of-funds and Union Budget debt composition data.

valueAddition.title: How Household Savings Reach the Government
bullets: Indirect Institutional Channel: When households park savings in bank deposits, LIC policies, or EPFO/pension funds, those institutions deploy a large mandatory and prudential share into Government Securities (driven by SLR rules for banks and investment norms for insurers).

Direct Retail Channel: Households lend directly to the Centre through National Small Savings Fund (NSSF) instruments (PPF, Sukanya Samriddhi, NSC) and by bidding in G-Sec auctions via the RBI Retail Direct portal.
Macroeconomic Role: Because India's corporate and government sectors are net borrowers, household financial surplus is the primary domestic cushion preventing excessive reliance on external debt.

valueAddition.title: Anatomy of India's Internal Debt
bullets: Marketable Dated G-Secs form the lion's share (over three-fourths) of the Union Government's internal debt, shifting India away from pre-1991 administered interest rates to market-discovered auction yields.

The remaining internal debt consists of short-term Treasury Bills, Cash Management Bills, Securities issued against Small Savings (NSSF), and non-marketable special securities issued to international financial institutions.
Over 95% of India's total public debt is denominated in domestic currency (internal debt), insulating the sovereign balance sheet from exchange-rate shocks.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
inNews.headline: RBI Bulletin Highlights Shift in Household Financial Assets Toward Equities and Small Savings
inNews.relevance: RBI's September 2026 flow-of-funds analysis noted that while households increasingly diversify into mutual funds, bank deposits, insurance, and small savings still channel substantial domestic liquidity into Central G-Sec auctions.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Households are the net surplus sector of the Indian economy; their financial savings flow into government borrowings both directly (via Small Savings Schemes like PPF/NSC and RBI Retail Direct) and indirectly (through commercial banks under SLR, LIC, and EPFO buying G-Secs).

statementBreakdown.reference: Union Budget Receipt Budget — Public Debt
statementBreakdown.explanation: Marketable dated securities auctioned by the RBI at market-determined yields constitute the single largest component—consistently accounting for roughly 75% to 80%—of the Central Government's internal debt.

visualSuggestion.title: Channels Linking Household Savings to Government Borrowings

rows: Banks invest deposits in G-Secs to meet Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) norms
Long-term premiums and provident contributions are mandated to hold sovereign bonds
Pooled into National Small Savings Fund (NSSF) to finance Centre and State deficits
Individuals bid directly in primary RBI auctions for Dated G-Secs and T-Bills

hook.headline: Does your bank deposit or PPF actually fund government borrowing?
hook.teaser: Notice how UPSC connects everyday household savings to the Union Budget's internal debt structure.

keywords.calloutNote: Think of households as the economy's net savers—their bank deposits, LIC policies, and PPF money flow straight into government bonds.
activePhrases: household financial savings

keywords.calloutNote: Recall that long-term G-Secs auctioned by the RBI at market yields make up roughly 75–80% of India's internal debt.
activePhrases: Dated securities
dimmedPhrases: household financial savings

verdicts.source: Household savings flow into government debt both directly via Small Savings (PPF, NSC) and indirectly when banks, LIC, and EPFO buy G-Secs.
Marketable dated securities issued through RBI auctions at market-determined rates form the single largest block of India's internal debt.

answer.label: C
answer.text: Both statements reflect core macroeconomic realities of how India finances its deficit—making Both 1 and 2 the right choice.

valueAddition.note: In macroeconomy statements phrased broadly like 'a share of' or 'a large component of', UPSC is testing foundational structural truths rather than hidden numerical traps.

subject: Economy
stem: "Rapid Financing Instrument and "Rapid Credit Facility" are related to the provisions of lending by which one of the following?

options.text: United Nations Environment Programme Finance Initiative
options.label: c

keywords.shortNote: An emergency lending window of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) that provides rapid, upfront financial assistance with limited conditionality to any IMF member country facing an urgent Balance of Payments need caused by commodity price shocks, natural disasters, conflict, or emergencies.
keywords.concept: Rapid Financing Instrument (RFI): An emergency lending window of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) that provides rapid, upfront financial assistance with limited conditionality to any IMF member country facing an urgent Balance of Payments need caused by commodity price shocks, natural disasters, conflict, or emergencies.

keywords.shortNote: A concessional emergency lending facility under the IMF's Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust (PRGT) providing rapid zero-interest financial support with limited conditionality specifically to low-income countries facing urgent Balance of Payments pressures.
keywords.concept: Rapid Credit Facility (RCF): A concessional emergency lending facility under the IMF's Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust (PRGT) providing rapid zero-interest financial support with limited conditionality specifically to low-income countries facing urgent Balance of Payments pressures.

keywords.shortNote: Short-to-medium-term external liquidity assistance extended by the IMF to help member nations stabilize foreign exchange reserves and import payments without resorting to destructive trade or currency restrictions.
keywords.concept: Balance of Payments (BoP) Support: Short-to-medium-term external liquidity assistance extended by the IMF to help member nations stabilize foreign exchange reserves and import payments without resorting to destructive trade or currency restrictions.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: ADB provides long-term project loans, policy-based development financing, and technical assistance for Asia-Pacific infrastructure and social sectors—not IMF Balance of Payments emergency windows like RFI and RCF.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both the Rapid Financing Instrument (open to all IMF members) and the Rapid Credit Facility (concessional zero-interest support for low-income countries) are flagship emergency Balance of Payments lending windows operated by the International Monetary Fund.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.text: United Nations Environment Programme Finance Initiative
optionBreakdown.explanation: UNEP FI is a global partnership between the UN Environment Programme and private-sector banks, insurers, and investors to align finance with sustainability goals—not a sovereign Balance of Payments lender.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: Long-Term Development Finance vs. IMF BoP Lending
optionBreakdown.explanation: The World Bank (IBRD and IDA) finances long-term development projects and structural reforms rather than rapid emergency Balance of Payments liquidity windows.

valueAddition.title: How RFI and RCF Differ Inside the IMF Emergency Toolkit
bullets: Rapid Financing Instrument (RFI): Available to all IMF member countries (including middle-income economies) through the General Resources Account (GRA); disbursed quickly as an outright purchase without a full multi-year upper-credit-tranche program.

Rapid Credit Facility (RCF): Restricted exclusively to eligible Low-Income Countries (LICs) through the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust (PRGT), carrying a zero percent interest rate and a 5.5-year grace period with 10-year final maturity.

valueAddition.title: Other Signature IMF Lending Facilities Tested in UPSC
bullets: Extended Fund Facility (EFF): Medium-term structural Balance of Payments assistance (3–4 years) for economies facing deep-seated structural macroeconomic imbalances.

Stand-By Arrangement (SBA) & Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF): SBA addresses short-term cyclical BoP crises, while RSF provides long-term affordable financing to build resilience against climate change and pandemic preparedness.

inNews.source: International Monetary Fund (IMF) / Reuters
inNews.headline: IMF Executive Board Reviews Emergency Financing Access Limits Under Rapid Financing Instrument and Rapid Credit Facility
inNews.relevance: October 2026 IMF lending-policy reviews assessed emergency access ceilings under the RFI and zero-interest RCF to help climate- and shock-hit emerging and low-income economies bridge urgent Balance of Payments gaps.

visualSuggestion.title: IMF Rapid Financing Instrument (RFI) vs. Rapid Credit Facility (RCF)

rows: Standard GRA rates, upfront disbursement, limited conditionality

hook.headline: Which global institution lends through the 'Rapid Financing Instrument' and 'Rapid Credit Facility'?
hook.teaser: Notice how both windows exist for one exact purpose—emergency Balance of Payments support without waiting for a multi-year reform program.

keywords.calloutNote: The IMF uses RFI to rush emergency Balance of Payments funds to any member country hit by sudden shocks like natural disasters or commodity spikes.
activePhrases: Rapid Financing Instrument

keywords.calloutNote: RCF is the IMF's zero-interest concessional counterpart to RFI, reserved strictly for low-income countries facing urgent external liquidity shortfalls.
activePhrases: Rapid Credit Facility
dimmedPhrases: Rapid Financing Instrument

verdicts.source: The Asian Development Bank provides long-term infrastructure and development financing, not IMF emergency Balance of Payments windows.
Both the Rapid Financing Instrument (for all members) and the Rapid Credit Facility (for low-income countries) are emergency lending facilities of the IMF.
UNEP FI is a UN-private finance sustainability partnership, not a sovereign crisis lender.
The World Bank lends through IBRD and IDA for long-term development projects rather than emergency BoP support.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Both the Rapid Financing Instrument and the zero-interest Rapid Credit Facility are emergency Balance of Payments windows of the IMF—so Option B is right.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your IMF & International Organisations notes

items.desc: RFI serves all IMF members at standard terms; RCF serves low-income countries at 0% interest under the PRGT.

items.title: Core Program Windows
items.desc: Stand-By Arrangement (SBA) handles short-term BoP crises, while Extended Fund Facility (EFF) tackles structural multi-year imbalances.

items.title: Climate & Pandemic Buffer
items.desc: The IMF's Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF) provides long-term financing for climate and pandemic preparedness.

valueAddition.note: Always anchor the Bretton Woods split: World Bank (IBRD/IDA) funds long-term development projects, whereas the IMF provides short-to-medium-term Balance of Payments liquidity.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to casual workers employed in India, consider the following statements:
1. All casual workers are entitled for Employees Provident Fund Coverage.
2. All casual workers are entitled for regular working hours and overtime payment.
3. The government can by a notification specify that an establishment or industry shall pay wages only through its bank account.
Which of the above statement are correct?

keywords.shortNote: A worker engaged on an ad-hoc or temporary basis for sporadic or non-permanent work, who nonetheless enjoys statutory labor protections under judicial precedents and welfare legislation.
keywords.concept: Casual Worker: A worker engaged on an ad-hoc or temporary basis for sporadic or non-permanent work, who nonetheless enjoys statutory labor protections under judicial precedents and welfare legislation.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Omits statement 3, which is an explicit statutory clause inserted by the 2017 amendment to eliminate cash wage pilferage.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Falls for the classic extreme-word trap ('All casual workers') and erroneously assumes EPF excludes casual labor.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ignores the universal applicability of regular working hours and overtime rules under minimum wage frameworks.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: All three statements are correct: the Supreme Court confirmed EPF eligibility for casual labor, minimum wage rules mandate overtime/hours, and Section 6 allows mandatory bank wage notifications.

valueAddition.title: Judicial Jurisprudence on Casual & Contract Workers
bullets: Pawan Hans Case (2020): Supreme Court reiterated that social welfare legislation like the EPF Act must be given broad beneficial interpretation; casual or ad-hoc workers rendering continuous service cannot be excluded from provident fund schemes.

State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh (2016): Supreme Court ruled that temporary, casual, and daily-wage employees performing duties identical to regular employees are entitled to the same minimum wages under the doctrine of 'Equal Pay for Equal Work'.

Definition of Employee under EPF: Covers full-time, part-time, temporary, contract, and casual workers, provided the establishment is covered under the Act (≥ 20 employees) and basic statutory wage ceilings apply.

valueAddition.title: Digital Wage Mandate & Financial Inclusion
bullets: Payment of Wages (Amendment) Act, 2017: Replaced the mandatory cash-payment clause, allowing wage payments through bank accounts without requiring written consent from workers.

Section 6(2) Powers: Empowers both Central and State Governments to designate specific sectors (e.g., plantations, construction, factories) where cash payment is banned and bank transfers are mandatory.
Code on Wages, 2019: Retains this architecture, encouraging digital public infrastructure (DPI) and direct bank account transfers to eliminate intermediary commission skimming.

valueAddition.title: Statutory Standards under Minimum Wages Rules
bullets: Working Hours: An adult worker's normal working day cannot exceed 9 hours inclusive of rest intervals (and no continuous work exceeding 5 hours without a half-hour break).
Overtime Multiplier: Any work rendered beyond the designated hours entitles the worker to overtime pay at not less than twice the normal rate of wages.
Weekly Holiday: Every employee (including casual labor engaged on daily terms) who works continuously for six days is statutorily entitled to a paid day of rest.

inNews.source: Ministry of Labour and Employment / The Hindu
inNews.headline: Union Labour Ministry Recommends Universal Bank Transfer of Wages and Social Security Portability under Unified Labour Codes
inNews.relevance: Directly links to statutory wage disbursement via banking channels (Statement 3) and universal social security net expansion across casual and unorganized workers.

statementBreakdown.reference: Supreme Court of India in Pawan Hans Ltd. v. Aviation Karmachari Sanghatana (2020) & Section 2(f) of EPF Act, 1952
statementBreakdown.explanation: The Supreme Court ruled that contractual and casual employees are entitled to social security benefits under the EPF Act on par with regular employees. Section 2(f) defines an 'employee' widely to include any person employed for wages in any kind of work, manual or otherwise, directly or indirectly, without excluding casual workers.

statementBreakdown.reference: Rule 24 & Rule 25 of Minimum Wages (Central) Rules, 1950
statementBreakdown.explanation: Under the Minimum Wages (Central) Rules, provisions concerning fixing daily working hours (normally 9 hours per day for an adult worker), rest intervals, weekly day of rest, and overtime wages (payable at double the ordinary wage rate) apply universally to any person employed in a scheduled employment, including casual workers.

statementBreakdown.reference: Section 6 of Payment of Wages Act, 1936 (as amended by Payment of Wages (Amendment) Act, 2017)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Section 6(2) provides that the appropriate government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify the industrial or other establishment where an employer shall pay every employed person the wages only by cheque or by crediting the wages directly in their bank account.

hook.headline: Are ALL casual workers entitled to Provident Fund?
hook.teaser: Don't eliminate statement 1 just because it uses the word 'All'—here is the Supreme Court ruling.

keywords.calloutNote: This looks like an extreme qualifier trap, but the Supreme Court explicitly upheld EPF coverage for casual workers.
activePhrases: All casual workers are entitled for Employees Provident Fund Coverage

keywords.term: pay wages only through its bank account
keywords.calloutNote: Section 6 of the Payment of Wages Act empowers governments to notify industries to pay only via bank transfer.
activePhrases: specify that an establishment or industry shall pay wages only through its bank account
dimmedPhrases: All casual workers are entitled for Employees Provident Fund Coverage
contextPhrases: regular working hours and overtime payment

verdicts.source: The Supreme Court confirmed that casual and contractual workers are entitled to EPF benefits under Section 2(f).
Working hours caps (9 hours) and double-rate overtime wages protect all workers in scheduled employment, including casual laborers.
Governments can issue notifications requiring establishments to pay wages exclusively via cheque or direct bank credit.

answer.label: D
answer.text: All three statements are correct under Indian labour statutes and Supreme Court judgments.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Labour Laws & Banking notes

items.title: EPF Coverage
items.desc: Supreme Court held social welfare laws must be interpreted beneficially to cover casual staff.

items.title: Wage Multiplier
items.desc: Overtime under Minimum Wages Rules must be paid at double the ordinary wage rate.

items.title: Digital Wages
items.desc: Payment of Wages Act allows governments to mandate 100% cashless bank salary disbursal.

valueAddition.note: Aspirants instinctively eliminate statements containing 'All', but when statutory definitions and constitutional courts extend universal rights to vulnerable classes, 'All' can be legally correct.

subject: Economy
stem: In India, which one of the following Compiles information on industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments and lay-offs in factories employing workers?

options.text: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
options.label: b

keywords.shortNote: An attached office under the Ministry of Labour and Employment (headquartered in Chandigarh/Shimla) responsible for collecting, compiling, analyzing, and disseminating official statistics on wages, earnings, productivity, absenteeism, labour turnover, industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments, and lay-offs.
keywords.concept: Labour Bureau: An attached office under the Ministry of Labour and Employment (headquartered in Chandigarh/Shimla) responsible for collecting, compiling, analyzing, and disseminating official statistics on wages, earnings, productivity, absenteeism, labour turnover, industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments, and lay-offs.

keywords.shortNote: The termination by an employer of the service of a worker for any reason whatsoever (such as surplus staff or restructuring) other than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, voluntary retirement, or superannuation.
keywords.concept: Retrenchment: The termination by an employer of the service of a worker for any reason whatsoever (such as surplus staff or restructuring) other than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, voluntary retirement, or superannuation.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: The Central Statistics Office (merged into NSO under MoSPI in 2019) compiles macroeconomic aggregates like National Accounts (GDP), Index of Industrial Production (IIP), and Consumer Price Index (CPI), not factory-level industrial dispute records.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: DPIIT formulates industrial and FDI policy, tracks Eight Core Industries data, and promotes ease of doing business, rather than compiling statutory labour dispute and retrenchment statistics.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: Ministry of Labour & Employment · Labour Bureau Mandate
optionBreakdown.explanation: The Labour Bureau compiles voluntary and statutory returns submitted by State Labour Departments and Regional Labour Commissioners to publish the annual report on 'Statistics on Industrial Disputes, Closures, Retrenchments and Lay-offs in India'.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: NTMIS was operated under AICTE (Ministry of Education) to forecast supply and demand of engineering and technical graduates, unrelated to factory strikes, lockouts, or retrenchments.

valueAddition.title: Core Statistical Outputs of the Labour Bureau
bullets: Price Indices for Workers: Compiles Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW, used to calculate Dearness Allowance for central/state government employees), CPI for Agricultural Labourers (CPI-AL), and CPI for Rural Labourers (CPI-RL).

Employment & Industrial Relations Surveys: Conducts the Quarterly Employment Survey (QES), All-India Quarterly Establishment-based Employment Survey (AQEES), and compiles annual reports on Trade Unions, Industrial Disputes (strikes & lockouts), Closures, Retrenchments, and Lay-offs.

valueAddition.title: Lay-off vs. Retrenchment vs. Lockout
bullets: Lay-off: Temporary inability of an employer to provide work due to external/operational bottlenecks (power/raw material shortage or machinery breakdown); employer-employee relationship continues.

Retrenchment vs. Lockout: Retrenchment permanently terminates surplus workers for economic/operational reasons, whereas a Lockout is the temporary closing of a workplace or suspension of work by an employer during an industrial dispute (the employer counterpart to a workers' Strike).

inNews.source: Ministry of Labour and Employment / Labour Bureau
inNews.headline: Labour Bureau releases updated Annual Report on Industrial Disputes, Closures, Retrenchments and Lay-offs alongside revised CPI-IW series
inNews.relevance: Labour Bureau statistical releases in 2026 tracked man-days lost to strikes and lockouts across manufacturing states alongside updated CPI-IW numbers governing Dearness Allowance revisions.

National Accounts (GDP), CPI (Rural/Urban/Combined), Index of Industrial Production (IIP), PLFS

hook.headline: Which agency tracks factory strikes, closures, retrenchments, and lay-offs in India?
hook.teaser: Look straight at the terminology—industrial disputes and lay-offs fall under one attached office of the Labour Ministry.

keywords.term: industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments and lay-offs
keywords.calloutNote: These exact four terms appear in the title of the annual statistical report published by the Labour Bureau.
activePhrases: industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments and lay-offs

keywords.calloutNote: Do not confuse NSO's macro GDP/IIP data with the Labour Bureau's factory-level industrial relations and CPI-IW records.
activePhrases: compiles information
dimmedPhrases: industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments and lay-offs

verdicts.source: CSO (now merged into NSO under MoSPI) compiles GDP, IIP, and headline CPI—not factory dispute and retrenchment returns.
DPIIT tracks FDI inflows and the Eight Core Industries index, not workplace lay-offs or strikes.
The Labour Bureau collects returns from state labour departments to publish annual statistics on industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments, and lay-offs.
NTMIS tracks engineering and technical education manpower supply, unrelated to factory industrial disputes.

answer.label: C
answer.text: The Labour Bureau compiles national data on industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments, and lay-offs in factories.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Labour & Statistical Agencies notes

items.desc: Labour Bureau compiles CPI for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW), which decides Dearness Allowance revisions.

items.title: Temporary vs Permanent
items.desc: Lay-off is temporary suspension due to power or raw-material shortage; retrenchment is permanent termination of surplus staff.

items.title: Merged Into NSO
items.desc: In 2019, CSO and NSSO were merged into the National Statistical Office (NSO) under MoSPI.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to the Indian economy, consider the following statements:
1. An increase in Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) indicates the appreciation of rupee.
2. An increase in the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) indicates an improvement in trade competitiveness.
3. An increasing trend in domestic inflation relative to inflation in other countries is likely to cause an increasing divergence between NEER and REER.
Which of the above statements are correct?

keywords.shortNote: An unadjusted, trade-weighted geometric average of bilateral exchange rates of the domestic currency against a designated basket of foreign currencies.
keywords.concept: Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER): An unadjusted, trade-weighted geometric average of bilateral exchange rates of the domestic currency against a designated basket of foreign currencies.

keywords.shortNote: The NEER adjusted for the relative price or inflation differential between the home country and its key trading partners.
keywords.concept: Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER): The NEER adjusted for the relative price or inflation differential between the home country and its key trading partners.

keywords.shortNote: The relative price attractiveness of a country's exported goods and services on the global market compared to foreign alternatives.
keywords.concept: Trade Competitiveness: The relative price attractiveness of a country's exported goods and services on the global market compared to foreign alternatives.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 2 states that higher REER improves competitiveness, whereas it actually makes exports pricier and less competitive.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: Statement 1 is valid, Statement 2 is invalid
optionBreakdown.explanation: Omits Statement 1 and incorrectly includes Statement 2.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Correctly pairs the appreciation indicated by rising NEER with the inflation-driven divergence between nominal and real effective exchange rates.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because Statement 2 misidentifies an increase in REER as an improvement in external competitiveness.

valueAddition.title: RBI's NEER and REER Basket Framework
bullets: The Reserve Bank of India tracks trade-weighted effective exchange rates across two standard baskets: the 40-currency basket (comprehensive) and the 6-currency basket (key advanced trading partners).

Weights are assigned using a geometric average based on bilateral trade shares (exports plus imports) alongside third-country competition dynamics, with base years periodically updated (currently base year 2015-16).

valueAddition.title: Competitiveness Dynamics: Appreciation vs. Depreciation
bullets: Rising REER (Overvaluation): Domestic export prices rise relative to international competitors; exports become costlier abroad, imports become cheaper domestically, deteriorating the trade balance.
Falling REER (Depreciation / Competitive Real Valuation): Restores external price competitiveness by making exports cheaper in foreign currency terms, boosting export volumes.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India / The Indian Express
inNews.headline: RBI monthly bulletin highlights widening spread between 40-currency NEER and REER amid stubborn domestic food inflation differentials
inNews.relevance: Direct real-world manifestation of Statement 3, where elevated domestic headline CPI relative to global trading partners pushes REER higher than nominal indices.

statementBreakdown.explanation: NEER is a trade-weighted geometric average of bilateral exchange rates. In the RBI's indexation, an upward movement in the NEER index directly signifies that the domestic currency (the Indian rupee) is appreciating against the basket of currencies.

An increase in REER implies that domestic goods have become relatively more expensive than foreign goods (in common currency terms), which leads to a deterioration—not an improvement—in trade competitiveness.

Since REER is essentially NEER adjusted for relative price indices (REER = NEER × [Domestic Price Index / Foreign Price Index]), persistent higher inflation at home relative to trading partners expands the price differential, driving an increasing wedge or divergence between NEER and REER.

visualSuggestion.title: NEER vs. REER Comparison Matrix

rows: Adjusted for domestic vs. foreign price differentials
No direct signal of real purchasing power
Rising REER implies loss of price competitiveness
Inflation gap between home and partner economies

hook.headline: Does a stronger rupee always mean better trade competitiveness?
hook.teaser: Here is the textbook trap UPSC set in 2022 on NEER versus REER.

keywords.calloutNote: An appreciated REER makes domestic exports more expensive abroad, eroding export competitiveness.
activePhrases: improvement in trade competitiveness

keywords.calloutNote: The only bridge between nominal and real indices is the relative inflation differential.
activePhrases: divergence between NEER and REER
dimmedPhrases: improvement in trade competitiveness
contextPhrases: domestic inflation relative to inflation in other countries

verdicts.source: An upward movement in the RBI's trade-weighted NEER index directly signifies nominal rupee appreciation against the currency basket.
An increase in REER means domestic goods are relatively costlier than foreign goods, which reduces trade competitiveness.
Since REER equals NEER scaled by relative price levels, higher domestic inflation forces NEER and REER to diverge.

answer.label: C
answer.text: Statements 1 and 3 are correct; a higher REER erodes export competitiveness, making Statement 2 incorrect.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your External Sector notes

items.title: 40-Currency Basket
items.desc: RBI computes trade-weighted indices across 40-currency and 6-currency baskets using geometric averages with 2015-16 base.

items.title: The REER Formula
items.desc: REER = NEER × (P_domestic / P_foreign); domestic inflation higher than foreign inflation drives REER above NEER.

items.title: Overvaluation Risk
items.desc: A rising REER signals that currency appreciation or local price increases are hurting the price appeal of exports.

valueAddition.note: Examiners repeatedly test the counter-intuitive direction in REER: higher index values signify loss of export competitiveness, not a gain.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, consider the following statements:
1. Private and public hospitals must adopt it.
2. As it aims to achieve universal health coverage, every citizen of India should be part of it ultimately.
3. It has seamless portability across the country.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: A flagship Digital Public Infrastructure initiative launched nationally in September 2021 and implemented by the National Health Authority (NHA) to create an open, interoperable, consent-based digital health ecosystem connecting patients, doctors, and health facilities across India.
keywords.concept: Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM): A flagship Digital Public Infrastructure initiative launched nationally in September 2021 and implemented by the National Health Authority (NHA) to create an open, interoperable, consent-based digital health ecosystem connecting patients, doctors, and health facilities across India.

keywords.shortNote: A voluntary, randomly generated 14-digit unique health identification number enabling citizens to link, access, and share longitudinal medical records digitally across participating healthcare providers with explicit patient consent.
keywords.concept: Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA): A voluntary, randomly generated 14-digit unique health identification number enabling citizens to link, access, and share longitudinal medical records digitally across participating healthcare providers with explicit patient consent.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because adoption is voluntary for both healthcare facilities and citizens.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: ABDM operates on voluntary opt-in for hospitals and citizens while providing seamless nationwide portability of digital health records across interoperable platforms.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because private and public hospitals are not legally compelled to join ABDM.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because both mandatory facility adoption and compulsory universal citizen participation contradict ABDM's voluntary consent framework.

valueAddition.title: Four Core Building Blocks of the ABDM Ecosystem
bullets: Core Registries & Accounts: (1) Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA — 14-digit unique health ID), (2) Healthcare Professionals Registry (HPR — doctors/nurses across Allopathy and AYUSH), (3) Health Facility Registry (HFR — hospitals, clinics, labs, pharmacies), and (4) Unified Health Interface (UHI — open protocol enabling interoperable teleconsultation and lab booking across apps).

Federated Data Storage (Zero Central Repository): Medical records remain decentralized at the point of creation (the respective hospital or lab) rather than being pooled into a central government database, and move only via encrypted, time-bound patient consent.

valueAddition.title: ABDM vs. AB-PMJAY: Two Distinct Arms of Ayushman Bharat
bullets: AB-PMJAY (Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana, 2018): Publicly funded health assurance scheme providing Rs. 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalization to bottom-40% vulnerable families (plus all senior citizens aged 70+ regardless of income).
ABDM (Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, 2021): Universal, voluntary digital health infrastructure backbone open to every resident of India—not an insurance scheme.

inNews.source: National Health Authority (NHA) / Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
inNews.headline: Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission crosses 70 crore ABHA accounts and 45 crore linked health records as Scan-and-Share OPD queues expand nationwide
inNews.relevance: October 2026 National Health Authority data showed over 70 crore voluntary ABHA IDs and 3.5 lakh registered health facilities utilizing ABDM's interoperable Scan-and-Share and portable health-record exchange across states.

statementBreakdown.reference: NHA ABDM Strategy Overview · Voluntary Participation for Health Facilities
statementBreakdown.explanation: Participation in the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission is completely voluntary for both public and private hospitals, clinics, and diagnostic laboratories—there is no statutory mandate forcing facilities to adopt it.

statementBreakdown.reference: ABDM Health Data Management Policy · Voluntary Citizen Opt-In
statementBreakdown.explanation: Enrollment in ABDM and creation of an ABHA ID is strictly voluntary and consent-driven for citizens; individuals can still receive healthcare services without an ABHA number, so universal mandatory citizen enrollment is not required.

statementBreakdown.reference: ABDM Federated Architecture · Nationwide Interoperability & Portability
statementBreakdown.explanation: Built on open APIs and national interoperability standards, ABDM allows a patient's longitudinal health records linked to their ABHA ID to be accessed seamlessly across participating hospitals, states, and telehealth providers nationwide upon patient consent.

visualSuggestion.title: Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) vs. Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY

rows: Interoperable digital health infrastructure & portable health records
Cashless secondary & tertiary hospitalization cover up to Rs. 5 lakh/year
Strictly voluntary opt-in for both citizens and hospitals
Targeted entitlement for SECC-eligible families & senior citizens aged 70+

hook.headline: Are Indian hospitals and citizens required to join the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission?
hook.teaser: Look at the compulsory words 'must' and 'should'—ABDM is strictly voluntary from top to bottom.

keywords.calloutNote: Participation in ABDM is completely voluntary for both public and private hospitals—there is no legal mandate.
activePhrases: must adopt it

keywords.calloutNote: Built on open interoperable APIs, ABDM lets citizens carry and share verified medical records across hospitals nationwide.
activePhrases: seamless portability across the country
dimmedPhrases: must adopt it

verdicts.source: Joining ABDM is optional for both public and private hospitals; no rule compels facilities to adopt it.
Creating an ABHA health ID is strictly voluntary for citizens, and healthcare cannot be denied without one.
ABDM's interoperable framework allows seamless nationwide portability of patient health records across participating providers.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Only Statement 3 is correct—ABDM provides seamless nationwide portability of health records while remaining completely voluntary for hospitals and citizens.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Digital Health & Schemes notes
