subject: Indian Polity
stem:
With reference to India, consider the following statements:
1. Judicial custody means an accused is in the custody of the concerned magistrate and such accused is locked up in police station, not in jail.
2. During judicial custody, the police officer in charge of the case is not allowed to interrogate the suspect without the approval of the court.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: Custody of an accused under the direct authority and surveillance of the Magistrate, where the accused is lodged in a central or district jail under prison authorities, not in a police lockup.
keywords.concept: Judicial Custody: Custody of an accused under the direct authority and surveillance of the Magistrate, where the accused is lodged in a central or district jail under prison authorities, not in a police lockup.

keywords.shortNote: Physical confinement of the accused in a police station lockup under the direct charge of investigating police officers for ongoing interrogation and recoveries.
keywords.concept: Police Custody: Physical confinement of the accused in a police station lockup under the direct charge of investigating police officers for ongoing interrogation and recoveries.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 inverts the fundamental institutional difference between jail and a police station lockup.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: Section 167 CrPC & established criminal procedure jurisprudence
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 is false because judicial custody entails lodging in jail, while Statement 2 correctly reflects the requirement of judicial sanction for police interrogation during judicial custody.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Includes Statement 1, which confuses police station lockups with judicial custody.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 2 is fully accurate and legally established.

valueAddition.title: Police Custody vs. Judicial Custody: Core Distinctions
bullets: Physical Location: In Police Custody (PC), the accused is housed in a police lock-up under police personnel. In Judicial Custody (JC), the accused is lodged in jail under prison administrators and wardens.

Interrogation Freedom: In PC, the investigating agency conducts continuous questioning and physical recoveries under Section 27 of the Evidence Act. In JC, police have no direct access; interrogation requires an application showing sufficient grounds and prior leave from the Magistrate.
Medical Examination Safeguard: Under Section 54 of CrPC, mandatory independent medical checkups are required every 48 hours during detention to deter custodial torture.

Statutory Ceiling: Under Section 167 CrPC, police custody can generally be authorized only during the first 15 days of remand, whereas judicial custody can extend up to 60 or 90 days depending on the gravity of the offence.

valueAddition.title: Remand Mechanics & Default Bail (Section 167)
bullets: Initial 24-Hour Rule: Article 22(2) and Section 57 CrPC mandate producing an arrested person before the nearest Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest (excluding journey time).
Remand Order: If investigation cannot be completed within 24 hours, the Magistrate determines whether remand should be to police custody or judicial custody.

Default Bail (Statutory Bail): If the charge sheet (police report) is not filed within 90 days (for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or minimum 10 years imprisonment) or 60 days (for any other offence), the accused acquires an indefeasible right to default bail under Section 167(2).

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Safeguards Surrounding Custody
bullets: Article 20(3): Protection against self-incrimination ensures no accused can be compelled to be a witness against himself during custody.
Article 21: Right to life and personal liberty prohibits custodial torture and guarantees access to legal counsel (D.K. Basu guidelines, 1997).
Article 22(1): Right to be informed of grounds of arrest and right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice.

inNews.source: Supreme Court of India / The Hindu
inNews.headline: Supreme Court clarifies police interrogation rules for accused lodged in judicial custody under new criminal codes
inNews.relevance: Directly links to the procedural jurisprudence governing police access, interrogation permissions, and remand transitions between police and judicial custody under Section 187 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).

statementBreakdown.explanation: Judicial custody means the accused is in the custody of the concerned Magistrate, but the person is lodged in jail (prison under state jail authorities), NOT locked up in a police station lockup. Being locked up in a police station lockup constitutes 'police custody'.

statementBreakdown.reference: Section 167, CrPC & State (Delhi Admn.) v. Dharam Pal (1982)
statementBreakdown.explanation: During judicial custody, investigating police officers have no unfettered access to the accused. To interrogate, question, or conduct test identification or voice samples while the accused is in judicial custody (jail), the investigating officer must obtain prior permission and an express order from the concerned Magistrate.

visualSuggestion.title: Police Custody vs Judicial Custody Comparison

rows: Direct and routine during custody period
Strictly prohibited without prior court permission
Facilitate interrogation, recovery of evidence, reconstruction
Prevent tampering of evidence, secure presence for trial
Can continue up to 60 or 90 days before default bail accrues

hook.headline: Is judicial custody spent inside a police station?
hook.teaser: Statement 1 sounds convincing—and trips up thousands of aspirants every single year.

keywords.term: locked up in police station, not in jail
keywords.calloutNote: A direct factual inversion: judicial custody means jail, while police custody means police station lockup.
activePhrases: locked up in police station, not in jail.

keywords.term: not allowed to interrogate without approval
keywords.calloutNote: Once an accused is in judicial custody, police must seek formal court permission to interrogate.
activePhrases: not allowed to interrogate the suspect without the approval of the court
dimmedPhrases: locked up in police station, not in jail.

verdicts.source: In judicial custody, the accused is lodged in jail under prison authorities, not in a police lockup.
Police cannot interrogate an accused in judicial custody without an express order from the court.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Statement 1 is incorrect because judicial custody means detention in jail; Statement 2 is correct because police need court permission to interrogate.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Criminal Procedure notes

items.desc: Police custody is in a police station; judicial custody is in jail under the court.

items.title: 24-Hour rule
items.desc: Mandates production of an arrested individual before a magistrate within 24 hours.

items.title: Default bail
items.desc: Accused is entitled to bail if the charge sheet is not filed within 60 or 90 days.

subject: Indian Polity
stem: What was the exact constitutional status of India on 26" January, 1950

options.text: A Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: Complete internal supremacy and total external independence; India is neither a dominion nor a dependency of any external power.
keywords.concept: Sovereign: Complete internal supremacy and total external independence; India is neither a dominion nor a dependency of any external power.

keywords.shortNote: Democratic socialism (blended Gandhian-Marxist model leaning towards Gandhism) aiming to end poverty, ignorance, and inequality through a mixed economy.
keywords.concept: Socialist: Democratic socialism (blended Gandhian-Marxist model leaning towards Gandhism) aiming to end poverty, ignorance, and inequality through a mixed economy.

keywords.shortNote: Positive secularism where all religions have equal status and support from the state, distinct from Western negative wall-of-separation secularism.
keywords.concept: Secular: Positive secularism where all religions have equal status and support from the state, distinct from Western negative wall-of-separation secularism.

keywords.shortNote: Popular sovereignty exercised via representative parliamentary democracy with universal adult franchise, rule of law, and periodic free elections.
keywords.concept: Democratic: Popular sovereignty exercised via representative parliamentary democracy with universal adult franchise, rule of law, and periodic free elections.

keywords.shortNote: The head of state (President) is directly or indirectly elected for a fixed term, meaning political sovereignty rests in the people and there is no hereditary privilege.
keywords.concept: Republic: The head of state (President) is directly or indirectly elected for a fixed term, meaning political sovereignty rests in the people and there is no hereditary privilege.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because it drops the defining qualifier 'Sovereign'; India was never designated merely as a 'Democratic Republic'.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (b) is correct. The original Preamble that took effect on 26 January 1950 solemnly constituted India into a 'Sovereign Democratic Republic'.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because 'Secular' was not present in the 1950 text; it was explicitly inserted in 1976.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because this reflects India's post-1976 constitutional status after the 42nd Amendment added 'Socialist' and 'Secular'.

valueAddition.title: Constituent Assembly Debates & Judicial Doctrines
bullets: Ambedkar's Stand on 'Secular & Socialist': In November 1948, Prof. K.T. Shah moved an amendment to explicitly include 'Secular, Socialist' in the Preamble. Dr. Ambedkar rejected it, arguing the Constitution should lay down state machinery without binding future generations to specific economic dogmas.

Democratic Socialism via D.S. Nakara (1983): The Supreme Court ruled that Indian socialism is a blend of Marxism and Gandhism leaning heavily towards Gandhian socialism—aimed at eliminating economic vulnerability through a mixed economy, not complete nationalization.

Secularism as Basic Structure via S.R. Bommai (1994): A 9-judge Constitution Bench settled that even before the 42nd Amendment (1976), secularism was an unalterable part of the Basic Structure woven into Articles 25 to 28.

Commonwealth Paradox: When India joined the Commonwealth of Nations in 1949 accepting the British Crown as head of the association, critics argued it compromised sovereignty; the Constituent Assembly clarified it was purely an extra-legal voluntary treaty that does not infringe constitutional supremacy.

valueAddition.title: Common Exam Trap: Textual Label vs. Living Spirit
bullets: Notice the trap: Secularism and socialism were already active through Fundamental Rights (Articles 25–28) and DPSP (Articles 38 & 39) in 1950.
However, the question specifically asks for the exact textual constitutional status on 26 January 1950.
Aspirants who memorize the current Preamble reflexively mark Option (d), missing that 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were absent in 1950.

inNews.source: The Hindu / Supreme Court of India
inNews.headline: Supreme Court Upholds Validity of Adding 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble via 42nd Amendment
inNews.relevance: Petitions challenging the 1976 insertion brought active judicial focus onto the historical baseline of the 1950 Preamble and reaffirmed that secularism and socialism are integral to the basic structure.

similarPyq.stem:
The Preamble to the Constitution of India is
(a) a part of the Constitution but has no legal effect
(b) not a part of the Constitution and has no legal effect either
(c) a part of the Constitution and has the same legal effect as any other part
(d) a part of the Constitution but has no legal effect independently of other parts
similarPyq.keyTakeaway: UPSC regularly returns to the Preamble across cycles—testing its legal enforceability (2020), its original historical text (2021), and the specific ideals of liberty and justice.

analysis.coreTakeaway: Remember: On 26 January 1950, India was declared a 'Sovereign Democratic Republic'—the words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were only added 26 years later by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

visualSuggestion.caption: Notice what UPSC did here: the examiner tested whether students knew which ideological qualifiers existed in the original 1950 text versus those inserted in 1976.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
With reference to India, consider the following statements:
1. When a prisoner makes out a sufficient case, parole cannot be denied to such prisoner because it becomes a matter of his/her right.
2. State Governments have their own Prisoner Release on Parole Rules.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: A conditional, temporary release of a prisoner for a specific exigency or reason, granted as an administrative concession rather than an absolute legal right.
keywords.concept: Parole: A conditional, temporary release of a prisoner for a specific exigency or reason, granted as an administrative concession rather than an absolute legal right.

keywords.shortNote: Under Entry 4 of the State List in the Seventh Schedule, 'Prisons, reformatories, Borstal institutions and other institutions of a like nature' are under exclusive State legislative competence.
keywords.concept: Prisons Jurisdiction (List II): Under Entry 4 of the State List in the Seventh Schedule, 'Prisons, reformatories, Borstal institutions and other institutions of a like nature' are under exclusive State legislative competence.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 falsely treats parole as an enforceable right rather than an administrative concession.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 is eliminated because parole is never an absolute right; Statement 2 is correct because States possess exclusive legislative power over prison rules.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Includes Statement 1, which contradicts settled criminal jurisprudence on parole.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 2 is factually and constitutionally sound under the Seventh Schedule.

valueAddition.title: Parole vs. Furlough: The Core Constitutional Matrix
bullets: Nature of Grant: Parole is a conditional release granted for a specific reason/exigency (e.g., death, marriage, grave medical condition in the family). Furlough is granted periodically without requiring any specific reason, primarily to maintain family/social ties and prevent institutionalization.
Legal Right Status: Neither is an absolute right, but furlough has a stronger statutory expectation based on good conduct, whereas parole is purely discretionary and case-specific.

Sentence Computation: In furlough, the period of release is counted as sentence served. In parole, the temporary release period is generally excluded from the total sentence term served (it operates as a temporary suspension of sentence).

valueAddition.title: Constitutional and Federal Architecture of Prisons
bullets: Seventh Schedule Entry 4 (State List): Vests 'Prisons, reformatories, Borstal institutions and other institutions of a like nature, and persons detained therein' exclusively with the States.

Model Prison Manual: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) issues model prison guidelines (such as the Model Prison Manual, 2016 and Model Prisons and Correctional Services Act, 2023) to provide a guiding framework, but States are not constitutionally bound to adopt them verbatim.

Article 21 Application: In *Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration (1980)*, the Supreme Court held that prisoners do not forfeit all constitutional rights upon entering prison walls; protection against torture, inhumane treatment, and denial of natural justice persists.

valueAddition.title: Key Precedents on Discretionary Release
bullets: Asfaq v. State of Rajasthan (2017): Clarified the distinct philosophical objectives of parole and furlough, reasserting that parole cannot be claimed as an absolute entitlement.

Home Secretary (Prison) v. H. Nilofer Nisha (2020): Confirmed that the grant of remission or parole is strictly governed by the rules framed by the respective State Government and administrative authorities must exercise discretion within those state-specific frameworks.

inNews.source: The Hindu / Supreme Court of India
inNews.headline: Supreme Court reasserts parole cannot be claimed as a matter of absolute right
inNews.relevance: Directly reaffirms that executive discretion to grant temporary conditional release depends on state-specific parole guidelines and public order assessments under Entry 4, List II.

During judicial custody, the police officer in charge of the case is not allowed to interrogate the suspect without the approval of the court. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

statementBreakdown.reference: Asfaq v. State of Rajasthan (2017) & H. Nilofer Nisha (2020)
statementBreakdown.explanation: The Supreme Court has consistently held that parole is a privilege and a discretionary administrative concession granted to a convict, not an absolute constitutional or statutory right. Even if a convict establishes a sufficient case (e.g., serious illness of a family member), the competent authority may deny parole based on concerns regarding public peace, threat to witnesses, or likelihood of absconding.

statementBreakdown.reference: Seventh Schedule (Entry 4, List II) & Prisons Act, 1894
statementBreakdown.explanation: Because 'Prisons' is a State subject under Entry 4 of List II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule, prison administration is governed by individual States. Consequently, State Governments frame their own specific rules for releasing prisoners on parole and furlough (e.g., The Rajasthan Prisoners Release on Parole Rules, The Maharashtra Management of Open Prisons and Parole Rules, etc.).

keywords.calloutNote: A classic absolute qualifier trap: the Supreme Court has consistently held parole is a privilege, not a right.

Prisons are on the State List, so State Governments formulate their own rules for releasing prisoners on parole.

subject: Indian Polity
stem: What is the position of the right to property in India?

options.text: Legal right available to citizens only
options.label: a

options.text: Legal right available to any person
options.label: b

options.text: Fundamental Right available to citizens only
options.label: c

options.text: Neither Fundamental Right nor legal right
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: Constitutional provision in Part XII stating that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.
keywords.concept: Article 300A: Constitutional provision in Part XII stating that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.

keywords.shortNote: An entitlement backed by statutory law or constitutional text outside Part III, enforceable through ordinary civil suits or High Court writs under Article 226.
keywords.concept: Legal / Constitutional Right: An entitlement backed by statutory law or constitutional text outside Part III, enforceable through ordinary civil suits or High Court writs under Article 226.

keywords.shortNote: Statutory amendment repealing Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 from Part III, re-inserting property rights into Chapter IV of Part XII as Article 300A.
keywords.concept: 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978: Statutory amendment repealing Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 from Part III, re-inserting property rights into Chapter IV of Part XII as Article 300A.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Confines protection strictly to citizens, ignoring that Article 300A uses the universal term 'person', thereby extending property protection to non-citizens, foreign nationals, and corporations.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (b) is correct. The 44th Amendment reclassified property from a Fundamental Right into a constitutional/legal right in Part XII, with Article 300A guaranteeing protection to 'any person'.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Retains the pre-1978 constitutional status; the 44th Amendment explicitly deleted the Right to Property from the Part III Fundamental Rights chapter.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: Part XII, Chapter IV of the Constitution of India
optionBreakdown.explanation: Dismisses constitutional protection entirely; Article 300A is an active constitutional and legal barrier against unauthorized expropriation by the executive.

valueAddition.title: Evolution of Property Rights: Part III to Part XII
bullets: Pre-1978 Triad: Property was originally protected by two distinct Fundamental Rights: Article 19(1)(f) (guaranteeing to citizens the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property) and Article 31 (prohibiting deprivation without lawful authority and compensation for all persons).

The 44th Amendment Shift (1978): Deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, enacting Article 300A under Part XII (Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits); property ceased to be a basic human entitlement guaranteed by Article 32 remedies.

Contemporary Judicial Resurrection (Vidya Devi 2020 & Bimal Kumar Shah 2024): The Supreme Court ruled that while property is not a Fundamental Right, it remains an inalienable human right and a constitutional right; the State cannot take possession of private land without statutory authority, fair compensation, and adherence to natural justice.

valueAddition.title: Citizen-Only vs. Universal Persons Trap
bullets: Lexical Wording of Article 300A: The provision explicitly reads: 'No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.' The word 'person' encompasses natural citizens, non-citizens, foreigners, and juristic entities (companies, trusts).

Remedial Constraint: Unlike violations of Part III where an aggrieved party can move the Supreme Court directly under Article 32, a violation of Article 300A allows invoking High Court writ jurisdiction under Article 226 or approaching ordinary civil courts.

Negative Protection Against the Executive: Article 300A protects the property holder solely against arbitrary executive confiscation; Parliament or a State Legislature can still enact a valid statute to acquire property for public purposes.

inNews.source: The Hindu / Supreme Court of India
inNews.headline: Supreme Court Sets Aside Land Acquisition Invocations Lacking Statutory Compensation Norms Under Article 300A
inNews.relevance: Supreme Court rulings reinforcing the seven sub-rights of property owners under Article 300A (duty to inform, hear objections, compensate, and rehabilitate) affirm the continued vitality of constitutional property jurisprudence.

analysis.coreTakeaway: Remember: The 44th Amendment demoted property from a Fundamental Right to a constitutional/legal right under Article 300A, which textually protects 'any person', not just citizens.

keywords.concept: Limited government: The foundational principle that government power is legally restricted to protect individual rights and prevent arbitrary rule.

optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because unitary states like the United Kingdom and Japan are constitutional governments without possessing a federal structure.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because nominal executive power is a characteristic of parliamentary systems, not the universal definition of constitutional government.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because a head enjoying real powers describes presidential systems like the United States, which also operates under a constitutional government.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: NCERT Class XI (Constitution: Why and How?) & Andrew Heywood
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (d) is correct. The universal definition of constitutional government is constitutionalism—a government legally limited and bounded by constitutional terms.

valueAddition.title: Constitutionalism as Limited Government
bullets: Philosophical Core: Rooted in John Locke's social contract and Montesquieu's separation of powers—state authority exists under prior legal constraints to protect fundamental rights.

Substantive vs. Nominal Check: The presence of a written constitution does not alone guarantee a constitutional government; genuine constitutionalism requires enforceable institutional limits and independent judicial review.

Supreme Court Reaffirmation: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and I.R. Coelho (2007), the Supreme Court emphasized that constitutional supremacy means no state organ possesses unlimited or arbitrary powers.

valueAddition.title: Common Exam Trap: Structural Forms vs. Defining Nature
bullets: Forms of Government Distractor: Options (a), (b), and (c) describe specific structural forms (federal vs. unitary, parliamentary vs. presidential), not the defining essence of constitutional governance.
The 'Federal' Fallacy: Many candidates confuse constitutionalism with federalism, forgetting that a centralized unitary state can be just as strictly limited by constitutional law.

keywords.shortNote: Chaired by Morarji Desai (later K. Hanumanthaiah); recommended a separate Department of Personnel under the Prime Minister and designating a minister/secretary solely for administrative reforms.
keywords.concept: First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966): Chaired by Morarji Desai (later K. Hanumanthaiah); recommended a separate Department of Personnel under the Prime Minister and designating a minister/secretary solely for administrative reforms.

keywords.shortNote: Report on Reorganisation of the Machinery of Government; focused on grouping central ministries into functional bureaus and establishing the O&M division, not creating a dedicated administrative reform minister.

valueAddition.title: N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar Committee (1949): Core Mandate & Findings
bullets: Mandate: Appointed to formulate a plan for the 'Reorganisation of the Machinery of Government' to streamline post-independence central administration.

Bureau Grouping: Recommended clustering 37 central departments and ministries into four fundamental bureaus: Bureau of Natural Resources and Agriculture, Bureau of Industry and Commerce, Bureau of Transport and Communications, and Bureau of Labour and Social Services.
Cabinet Committees: Proposed institutionalizing standing Cabinet Committees, notably the Defence Committee and the Economic Committee.
O&M Division: Recommended creating an Organization and Methods (O&M) wing in the Cabinet Secretariat to eliminate inter-departmental delays.
Central Secretariat Service (CSS): Blueprinted the restructuring and cadre-formation of the Central Secretariat Service.

valueAddition.title: First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966–70): Personnel & Machinery Mandate
bullets: Establishment & Leadership: Constituted on 5 January 1966 under Morarji Desai; chaired by K. Hanumanthaiah from 1967 following Desai's induction as Deputy PM.
Scope: Submitted 20 reports and 537 recommendations spanning public administration, personnel management, state administration, and redressal mechanisms.
Administrative Reforms Machinery: Recommended that a minister and a secretary be designated solely to pursue, evaluate, and promote administrative reform across ministries.

Department of Personnel: Explicitly advised taking personnel management away from the Ministry of Home Affairs to place a dedicated Department of Personnel under the Prime Minister's direct oversight.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
With reference to Indian Judiciary, consider the following statements:
1. Any retired judge of the Supreme Court of India can be called back to sit and act as a Supreme Court judge by the Chief Justice of India with prior permission of the president of India.
2. A High Court in India has the power to review its own judgement as the Supreme Court does.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: Constitutional mechanism under Article 128 allowing the Chief Justice of India, with prior Presidential assent, to request a retired Supreme Court or qualified High Court judge to temporarily sit and act as a judge of the Supreme Court.
keywords.concept: Attendance of Retired Judges: Constitutional mechanism under Article 128 allowing the Chief Justice of India, with prior Presidential assent, to request a retired Supreme Court or qualified High Court judge to temporarily sit and act as a judge of the Supreme Court.

keywords.shortNote: The judicial authority of a Court of Record to correct errors apparent on the face of the record and prevent miscarriage of justice, operating inherently even without an express replica of Article 137.
keywords.concept: Inherent Power of Review: The judicial authority of a Court of Record to correct errors apparent on the face of the record and prevent miscarriage of justice, operating inherently even without an express replica of Article 137.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks the established inherent review power of the High Court as a court of record.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks the constitutional mechanism enabling the CJI to recall retired judges under Article 128.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements accurately reflect constitutional provisions and judicial precedents governing the higher judiciary.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements are legally verified and constitutionally sound.

valueAddition.title: Article 128: Retired Judges at Sittings of the Supreme Court
bullets: Eligibility: A retired Supreme Court judge, or a retired High Court judge who is constitutionally qualified to be an SC judge.
Dual Consents Required: The CJI must obtain the previous consent of the President of India, AND the retired judge themselves must consent to sit and act.

Status and Privileges: While so sitting and acting, the judge is entitled to allowances determined by the President and possesses all the jurisdiction, powers, and privileges of an SC judge, but is not deemed to be a permanent judge of the Supreme Court.

valueAddition.title: Review Jurisdiction: Supreme Court vs. High Court
bullets: Supreme Court (Article 137): Express constitutional text empowers the SC to review any judgment pronounced or order made by it, subject to provisions of any law made by Parliament or rules under Article 145.

High Court (Article 215): No explicit counterpart to Article 137 exists in Part VI. However, as a Court of Record under Article 215, its plenary and inherent powers include reviewing its own judgments to correct patent mistakes.
Civil Procedure Code Linkage: Section 114 and Order 47 of the CPC also provide statutory recognition for review before High Courts in civil matters.

valueAddition.title: Ad-Hoc vs. Retired Judges in the Apex Court
bullets: Ad-Hoc Judges (Article 127): Appointed only when there is a lack of quorum of permanent judges; drawn exclusively from serving High Court judges qualified for the SC.
Retired Judges (Article 128): Invoked for clearing arrears or handling heavy caseloads; drawn from retired judges, not serving HC benches.

inNews.headline: Supreme Court invokes Article 128 to recall former judges for expedited pendency clearance
inNews.relevance: Directly highlights the contemporary practical application of Article 128 in addressing heavy judicial case backlogs via retired bench appointments.

similarPyq.keyTakeaway: UPSC systematically explores functional nuances, appointment checks, and structural powers shared or distinguished between the Supreme Court and High Courts.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Article 128 explicitly provides that the Chief Justice of India may at any time, with the previous consent of the President, request any person who has held the office of a Judge of the Supreme Court (or held the office of a Judge of a High Court and is duly qualified for appointment as an SC judge) to sit and act as a Judge of the Supreme Court.

statementBreakdown.reference: Article 215 & Shivdeo Singh v. State of Punjab (1963)
statementBreakdown.explanation: While Article 137 expressly confers review power on the Supreme Court, the Supreme Court has consistently held (notably in Shivdeo Singh v. State of Punjab and reaffirmed in Municipal Corp. of Greater Mumbai v. Pratibha Industries) that being a Court of Record under Article 215, a High Court has inherent jurisdiction to review its own orders to prevent miscarriage of justice or correct patent errors.

keywords.concept: Forest Rights Act, 2006 (FRA): An Act recognizing the pre-existing customary forest tenure and resource rights of forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers.

optionBreakdown.explanation: The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change enforces the Indian Forest Act, 1927 and the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, but Parliament explicitly bypassed MoEFCC to assign FRA nodal authority to the Ministry of Tribal Affairs.

optionBreakdown.explanation: The Ministry of Panchayati Raj coordinates general PRI governance and PESA implementation, not the overall execution of the Forest Rights Act.

valueAddition.title: Forest Rights Act, 2006: Core Statutory Anatomy
bullets: Enactment & Enforcement: Passed in December 2006; came into force on 31 December 2007 (Rules notified in 2008 and amended in 2012).
Constitutional Anchor: Enforces Article 21 (human dignity), Article 46 (promotion of educational and economic interests of SCs/STs), and Fifth/Sixth Schedule autonomy.

Cut-off Date & Eligibility: Occupation of forest land prior to 13 December 2005. FDSTs require proof of residence; OTFDs must prove continuous residence in the forest for at least three generations (75 years).

Substantive Rights & Ceilings: Individual Forest Rights (IFR) capped at a maximum of 4 hectares per family; Community Forest Rights (CFR) grants ownership of Minor Forest Produce (MFP) and rights to protect and regenerate community forests.

Three-Tier Implementation Machinery: Initiated by the Gram Sabha (via Forest Rights Committee); screened by the Sub-Divisional Level Committee (SDLC); finally approved by the District Level Committee (DLC chaired by District Collector).

valueAddition.title: FRA Adjudication Machinery Hierarchy
bullets: Gram Sabha: Highly empowered primary authority that receives claims, passes resolutions, and determines nature and extent of forest rights.

Sub-Divisional Level Committee (SDLC): Consists of revenue officers, forest officers, and three members of Panchayats (including two STs and one woman); hears petitions against Gram Sabha resolutions.
District Level Committee (DLC): Apex final appellate authority in the district; passes final orders approving the record of forest rights.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements in respect of Bharat Ratna and Padma Awards:
1. Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are titles under the Article 18 (1) of the Constitution of India.
2. Padma Awards, which were instituted in the year 1954, were suspended only once.
3. The number of Bharat Ratna Awards is restricted to a maximum of five in a particular year.
Which of the above statements are not correct?

keywords.shortNote: Article 18(1) prohibits the State from conferring titles; the Supreme Court held in Balaji Raghavan (1996) that National Awards are not 'titles' within the meaning of Article 18(1).
keywords.concept: Article 18(1) and National Civilian Honours: Article 18(1) prohibits the State from conferring titles; the Supreme Court held in Balaji Raghavan (1996) that National Awards are not 'titles' within the meaning of Article 18(1).
Bharat Ratna

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 3 is also incorrect because the formal ceiling is three, not five.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 is also incorrect as per the landmark ruling in Balaji Raghavan (1996).

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 2 is also incorrect because the awards were suspended twice.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: All three statements are not correct
optionBreakdown.explanation: Because the question stem explicitly asks for which statements are 'not correct', and all three statements (1, 2, and 3) are factually and legally incorrect, option (d) is the right answer.

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Jurisprudence of Article 18 & Balaji Raghavan (1996)
bullets: Constitution Bench Verdict: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Bharat Ratna and Padma Awards, ruling they represent state recognition of meritorious service and do not violate the principle of equality under Article 14 or Article 18.

Prefix/Suffix Forfeiture Rule: The Court ruled that recipients cannot use these honours as prefixes or suffixes to their names (e.g. on visiting cards, letterheads, or public books). If violated, the awardee forfeits the award.

Constitutional Committee Recommendation: Suggested the Prime Minister constitute a high-level committee in consultation with the President to streamline the selection process and maintain institutional credibility.

valueAddition.title: Award Architecture, Caps, and Suspensions
bullets: Genesis: Instituted by Presidential notifications on 2 January 1954; administered by the Ministry of Home Affairs.

Ceiling Limits: Bharat Ratna is formally capped at a maximum of 3 in a calendar year. Padma Awards (Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri) have an annual cap of 120 (excluding posthumous awards and awards given to NRI/PIO/Foreigners).

Two Historical Suspensions: (1) 1977-1980 by the Morarji Desai administration; (2) 1993-1997 pending public interest litigation in the Kerala and Madhya Pradesh High Courts challenging their constitutionality.
Monetary Grant: Neither the Bharat Ratna nor the Padma Awards carry any cash grant or monetary allowance; they carry a Sanad (certificate signed by the President) and a medallion.

inNews.headline: President approves conferment of Padma Awards honouring grassroots unsung achievers on Republic Day eve
inNews.relevance: Reflects the annual constitutional procedure under the Ministry of Home Affairs and the operationalization of the 120-recipient ceiling.

statementBreakdown.explanation: A Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court categorically held that the National Awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, and Padma Shri) do not amount to 'titles' within the contemplation of Article 18(1). However, they cannot be used as prefixes or suffixes to the recipient's name.

statementBreakdown.reference: Ministry of Home Affairs Chronology of National Awards
statementBreakdown.explanation: The Padma Awards were suspended more than once: first in July 1977 during the Janata Party government under Morarji Desai (revived in 1980), and again from 1993 to 1997 due to legal challenges questioning their constitutional validity pending before the High Courts and Supreme Court.
Under the governing statutory regulations of the award, the number of Bharat Ratna awards is restricted to a maximum of three in any particular calendar year, not five.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. In India, there is no law restricting the candidates from contesting in one Lok Sabha election from three constituencies.
2. In 1991 Lok Sabha Election, Shri Devi Lal contested from three Lok Sabha constituencies.
3. As per the existing rules, if a candidate contests in one Lok Sabha election from many constituencies, his/her party should bear the cost of bye-elections to the constituencies vacated by him/her in the event of him/her winning in all the constituencies.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: Statutory amendment introduced in 1996 capping the maximum number of constituencies a candidate can contest in any general or biennial election to two.
keywords.concept: Section 33(7) of RPA, 1951: Statutory amendment introduced in 1996 capping the maximum number of constituencies a candidate can contest in any general or biennial election to two.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Section 33(7) of the RPA, 1951 restricts a candidate to contesting a maximum of two constituencies.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Only statement 2 accurately reflects the historical reality of the 1991 Lok Sabha elections before the 1996 statutory cap was enacted.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 ignores Section 33(7), and statement 3 confuses an ECI recommendation with an existing legal rule.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: The public exchequer bears all expenses for parliamentary and assembly bye-elections.

valueAddition.title: Evolution of Multiple-Seat Candidature under RPA 1951
bullets: Pre-1996 Framework: There was no restriction on the number of constituencies a candidate could contest simultaneously in general or assembly elections.

1996 Amendment (Section 33(7)): Inserted by Act 21 of 1996, restricting an individual from contesting from more than two constituencies in a general election to Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Legislative Assembly, or State Legislative Council.

Section 70 (Resignation of Duplicate Seats): If a candidate is elected from both seats, they must resign from all but one seat within 14 days under Rule 91 of the Conduct of Elections Rules, failing which all seats become vacant.

Constitutional Validity (Ashwini Kumar Upadhyay v. Union of India, 2023): The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of Section 33(7), holding that permitting candidates to contest two seats is an issue of legislative policy belonging exclusively to Parliament.

valueAddition.title: ECI Reform Proposals & Law Commission Recommendations
bullets: One-Candidate-One-Seat (2004 & 2016): ECI proposed amending Section 33(7) to restrict candidates to a single constituency to curb expenditure and voter fatigue from avoidable bye-elections.

Reimbursement of Bye-Election Costs: In the alternative, ECI recommended that if two-seat contests continue, candidates vacating one seat should be required to deposit ₹5 lakh (Assembly) or ₹10 lakh (Lok Sabha), later proposed to be revised upwards, to partially defray bye-election costs.
Law Commission 255th Report (2015): Recommended a complete bar on multi-constituency contesting to eliminate resultant vacancies.

inNews.headline: Parliamentary panel reviews Law Commission suggestions on one-candidate-one-constituency electoral reforms
inNews.relevance: Directly relates to debates on amending Section 33(7) of the RPA 1951 to prevent state-funded bye-elections caused by candidates vacating duplicate seats.

statementBreakdown.reference: Representation of the People Act, 1951 · Section 33(7)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Section 33(7) explicitly bars a person from contesting a general election to the Lok Sabha from more than two constituencies. Therefore, an explicit statutory bar against contesting from three constituencies exists.

statementBreakdown.reference: ECI Statistical Report on General Elections, 1991
statementBreakdown.explanation: Prior to the 1996 amendment, candidates could contest from an unlimited number of seats. In the 1991 Lok Sabha election, former Deputy Prime Minister Shri Devi Lal contested simultaneously from three constituencies: Sikar (Rajasthan), Rohtak (Haryana), and Ferozepur (Punjab).

No existing statutory rule or law mandates that the political party or candidate bear the cost of the resultant bye-election. The entire expenditure is borne by the public exchequer; recovering expenses remains merely an un-enacted proposal by the ECI and Law Commission.

keywords.term: Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003
keywords.shortNote: The Parliamentary statute enacted to institutionalize financial discipline, reduce India's fiscal deficit, eliminate revenue deficit, and enforce multi-year fiscal transparency through mandatory annual policy statements.
keywords.concept: Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003: The Parliamentary statute enacted to institutionalize financial discipline, reduce India's fiscal deficit, eliminate revenue deficit, and enforce multi-year fiscal transparency through mandatory annual policy statements.

valueAddition.title: The Three Mandatory FRBM Statements Tabled with the Budget
bullets: Under Section 3(1) of the FRBM Act, 2003, the Finance Minister must lay three statutory statements before both Houses of Parliament every year along with the Annual Financial Statement and Demands for Grants:
1. Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement (setting three-year rolling targets for key fiscal indicators and explaining the assumptions behind revenue and expenditure projections).

2. Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement (outlining government policies on taxation, expenditure, market borrowings, and strategic fiscal priorities for the ensuing year) and 3. Macro-Economic Framework Statement (evaluating GDP growth, fiscal balance, and external sector trends).

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Budget Documents vs. FRBM Statutory Documents
bullets: Constitutional Mandate: Annual Financial Statement (Article 112), Demands for Grants (Article 113), Appropriation Bill (Article 114), and Finance Bill (Article 110 / Article 117).
Statutory Mandate (FRBM Act, 2003): Macro-Economic Framework Statement, Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement, Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement, plus quarterly review statements on fiscal trends.

2. The WPI does not capture changes in the prices of services, which CPI does.
3. Reserve Bank of India has now adopted WPI as its key measure of inflation and to decide on changing the key policy rates.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: Retail-level index tracking price changes of a representative basket of goods and services consumed by households.
keywords.concept: Consumer Price Index (CPI): Retail-level index tracking price changes of a representative basket of goods and services consumed by households.

keywords.shortNote: Producer-level index tracking price changes of tangible commodities at the first point of bulk bulk/wholesale commercial transaction.
keywords.concept: Wholesale Price Index (WPI): Producer-level index tracking price changes of tangible commodities at the first point of bulk bulk/wholesale commercial transaction.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements 1 and 2 are factually accurate regarding food basket weights and service inclusions.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Omits statement 1, which is also correct.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 3 is false because RBI tracks CPI-Combined, not WPI.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Incorrectly includes statement 3.

valueAddition.title: Comprehensive Architecture: Consumer Price Index (CPI)
bullets: Core Definition & Purpose: Measures changes over time in retail prices paid by households for final consumption.It  reflects the direct cost of living and domestic currency purchasing power.
Institutional Authority: Compiled and released on the 12th of every month by the National Statistical Office (NSO), Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI).

Base Year Progression: Standard reference in exam PYQ was 2012 = 100; upgraded to revised Base Year 2024 = 100 based on the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES 2023-24) aligning with Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose (COICOP) 2018 designed by United Nations Statistical Division to categorise individual consumption expenditure.

Basket Coverage: Tracks both manufactured goods and key consumer services (housing, medical care, transport, education, recreation). Food commands the single largest aggregate share (~45.86% in 2012 series).

Specialized Series: Labour Bureau (Ministry of Labour & Employment) maintains distinct worker indices: CPI-Industrial Workers (CPI-IW, Base 2016 = 100, used for Dearness Allowance), CPI-Agricultural Labourers (CPI-AL, Base 1986-87), and CPI-Rural Labourers (CPI-RL, Base 1986-87).

valueAddition.title: Comprehensive Architecture: Wholesale Price Index (WPI)
bullets: Core Definition & Purpose: Tracks price movements of merchandise at the first point of bulk commercial sale (ex-factory gate, ex-mine, wholesale mandi) before retail markups, freight costs, and retail taxes are applied.

Institutional Authority: Released on the 14th of every month by the Office of the Economic Adviser (OEA), Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
Base Year Progression: Exam-year series operated on Base Year 2011-12 = 100 (697 items); subsequently revised to Base Year 2022-23 = 100 to capture modern industrial production weights.

Basket Composition (2011-12 Series Weights): (1) Manufactured Products (64.23%), (2) Primary Articles (22.62%), and (3) Fuel & Power (13.15%). Food articles in Primary Articles (15.26%) plus manufactured food products bring total composite food weight to roughly 24.38%.

Scope Limitation: Strictly restricted to physical commodities (0% services coverage). Acts as a leading upstream indicator of cost-push pressures and serves as a deflator for national accounts (GVA/GDP).

valueAddition.title: Urjit Patel Committee & The Policy Paradigm Shift
bullets: Why WPI Was Dropped: Prior to 2014, RBI used WPI as its headline gauge. Because WPI completely excluded services and had a low food weight, it failed to reflect actual household cost of living and inflation expectations.
Recommendation (Jan 2014): The Urjit Patel Committee recommended adopting CPI-Combined as the sole nominal anchor for monetary policy.

Statutory Institutionalization: Formalized through the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement (2015) and Finance Act amendments to the RBI Act, 1934, establishing the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) mandated to target 4% CPI inflation with a +/- 2% tolerance band (2% to 6%).

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India Monetary Policy Report / The Hindu
inNews.headline: RBI highlights food price volatility in headline CPI while retaining calibrated stance under flexible inflation targeting
inNews.relevance: Directly reinforces CPI-Combined as the statutory anchor for Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) decisions, illustrating how food weighting continues to dictate domestic interest rate policy.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Food accounts for roughly 45.86% in the CPI-Combined series (and remains the dominant category in updated consumer surveys), whereas in WPI, composite food items (food articles in primary articles plus manufactured food products) total only around 24.38%.
WPI tracks only physical goods traded in bulk and completely omits services. In contrast, CPI includes major service categories such as transport, education, health, and housing.

RBI shifted from WPI to CPI-Combined as its headline inflation anchor in 2014 based on the Urjit Patel Committee report, formalizing Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) under Section 45ZA of the amended RBI Act, 1934.

stem:
With reference to the Indian economy after the 1991 economic liberalization, consider the following statements:
1. Worker productivity (Rs. per worker at 2004 -05 prices) increased in urban areas while it decreased in rural areas.
2. The percentage share of rural areas in the workforce steadily increased.
3. In rural areas, the growth in non -farm economy increased.
4. The growth rate in rural employment decreased
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: Net Domestic Product (NDP) or Gross Value Added (GVA) per employed worker measured at constant base-year prices to capture real output efficiency.
keywords.concept: Worker Productivity: Net Domestic Product (NDP) or Gross Value Added (GVA) per employed worker measured at constant base-year prices to capture real output efficiency.

keywords.shortNote: All economic activities in rural areas outside primary agriculture, forestry, and fishing—encompassing rural manufacturing, construction, trade, transport, and services.
keywords.concept: Rural Non-Farm Economy (RNFE): All economic activities in rural areas outside primary agriculture, forestry, and fishing—encompassing rural manufacturing, construction, trade, transport, and services.

keywords.shortNote: The long-run macroeconomic shift in which labor and output move away from low-productivity agriculture toward higher-productivity manufacturing, construction, and services alongside urbanization.
keywords.concept: Structural Transformation: The long-run macroeconomic shift in which labor and output move away from low-productivity agriculture toward higher-productivity manufacturing, construction, and services alongside urbanization.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both Statements 1 and 2 are factually false; rural productivity rose and rural workforce share declined.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminating Statement 1 immediately narrows the options to (b) and (c); Statement 4 holds true because rural employment growth slowed down post-1991.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Misses the well-documented slowdown in rural employment growth rate documented in NITI Aayog's 2017 rural economy paper.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly pairs false claims of falling rural productivity and rising rural workforce share.

valueAddition.title: NITI Aayog's Post-1991 Rural Economy Findings
bullets: The entire question is lifted verbatim from NITI Aayog's 2017 discussion paper by Ramesh Chand et al., analyzing structural shifts between 1993–94 and 2011–12 at constant 2004–05 prices.
While rural worker productivity rose nearly 2.7 times, the urban-to-rural productivity gap remained wide (roughly 2.8:1), driving migration toward urban centers.
By 2011–12, the non-farm sector already contributed nearly two-thirds of total rural Net Domestic Product (NDP), led by rural construction and services rather than agriculture.

valueAddition.title: Why Rural Employment Growth Slowed Despite Output Growth
bullets: Farm mechanization, rising educational enrollment among rural youth, and higher household incomes reduced distress labor participation in low-wage agriculture.
Because the expanding rural non-farm sector could not absorb every worker exiting farming, overall rural employment growth rate declined even as output per remaining worker increased.

inNews.source: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) / The Indian Express

inNews.relevance: MoSPI's Periodic Labour Force Survey released in September 2026 confirmed that non-farm activities—especially construction, trade, and transport—continue to absorb an expanding share of India's rural workforce.

statementBreakdown.reference: NITI Aayog Rural Economy Paper (2017) — Table 3
statementBreakdown.explanation: According to NITI Aayog data (at constant 2004–05 prices), real worker productivity increased in both urban areas (from Rs. 1,10,965 in 1993–94 to Rs. 2,82,515 in 2011–12) and rural areas (from Rs. 37,279 to Rs. 1,01,755)—it never decreased in rural areas.

statementBreakdown.reference: NITI Aayog Rural Economy Paper (2017) — Workforce Distribution
statementBreakdown.explanation: As India urbanized after 1991, the rural share in total national workforce steadily declined (falling from 77.8% in 1993–94 to 70.9% in 2011–12), while the urban workforce share correspondingly rose.

statementBreakdown.reference: NITI Aayog Rural Economy Paper (2017) — Rural NDP Composition
statementBreakdown.explanation: Post-1991, rural non-farm NDP growth accelerated sharply (rising from 6.72% annually during 1993–2005 to 9.21% during 2004–12), making construction, manufacturing, and services the dominant drivers of rural output.

statementBreakdown.reference: NITI Aayog Rural Economy Paper (2017) — Rural Employment Growth
statementBreakdown.explanation: Annual rural employment growth decelerated markedly after liberalization—slowing from 1.45% per annum (1993–94 to 2004–05) down to 0.35% per annum (2004–05 to 2011–12) as agricultural workforce absorption contracted.

With steady urbanization after 1991, the rural share of India's workforce fell from 77.8% to 70.9% rather than increasing.
Rural non-farm GDP growth accelerated from 6.7% to over 9.2% post-1991, driven by construction and rural services.
Rural employment growth slowed from 1.45% to 0.35% annually as workers left agriculture faster than non-farm jobs absorbed them.

answer.label: B

subject: Economy
stem: If you withdraw Rs. 1,00,000 in cash from your Demand Deposit Account at your bank, the immediate effect on aggregate money supply in the economy will be:

options.text: to increase it by more than Rs. 1,00,000
options.label: c

keywords.shortNote: The total volume of monetary assets circulating in the economy at a point in time, measured as: Currency with the Public (C) + Demand Deposits with the Banking System (DD) + Time Deposits with the Banking System (TD) + Other Deposits with the RBI.
keywords.concept: Aggregate Money Supply (M3 / Broad Money): The total volume of monetary assets circulating in the economy at a point in time, measured as: Currency with the Public (C) + Demand Deposits with the Banking System (DD) + Time Deposits with the Banking System (TD) + Other Deposits with the RBI.

keywords.term: Immediate Effect vs. Dynamic Multiplier Effect
keywords.shortNote: The prompt asks for the instantaneous accounting effect at the moment of cash withdrawal, where one component of money supply shifts into another without altering the net aggregate, as opposed to subsequent secondary credit contraction over time.
keywords.concept: Immediate Effect vs. Dynamic Multiplier Effect: The prompt asks for the instantaneous accounting effect at the moment of cash withdrawal, where one component of money supply shifts into another without altering the net aggregate, as opposed to subsequent secondary credit contraction over time.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Assuming a reduction ignores that the withdrawn cash enters directly into 'Currency with the Public', exactly counterbalancing the reduction in bank demand deposits.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: No new money is created by the central bank or banking system; it is merely an asset conversion within the existing money supply.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Confuses cash withdrawal with money creation. In fact, over time, cash withdrawals drain reserves and contract secondary credit creation, but never increase it.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: NCERT Class 12 Macroeconomics & RBI Monetary Aggregates
optionBreakdown.explanation: Aggregate money supply (M1 or M3) includes both 'Currency with the Public' and 'Demand Deposits'. Withdrawing ₹1,00,000 decreases Demand Deposits by ₹1,00,000 and simultaneously increases Currency with the Public by ₹1,00,000. The immediate net effect on aggregate money supply is exactly zero, leaving it completely unchanged.

valueAddition.title: Components of India's Monetary Aggregates
bullets: M1 (Narrow Money): Currency with the public (C) + Demand deposits with the banking system (DD) + 'Other' deposits with the RBI (OD).
M2: M1 + Post office savings bank deposits.
M3 (Broad Money / Aggregate Money Supply): M1 + Time deposits with the banking system (TD).
M4: M3 + Total post office deposits (excluding National Savings Certificates / NSC).

valueAddition.title: Immediate vs. Long-Term Impact of Cash Withdrawal
bullets: Immediate Accounting Effect (At $T_0$): $\Delta M3 = \Delta C + \Delta DD = (+₹1,00,000) + (-₹1,00,000) = 0$. The overall money stock is completely unchanged.

Long-Term Multiplier Impact (Dynamic over time): When cash leaves the banking system, bank cash reserves decline by ₹1,00,000. Because commercial banks lend on a fractional reserve basis, lower primary reserves shrink the capacity to generate secondary derivative deposits. Over time, the broad money supply will actually contract due to the reverse money multiplier effect ($1/rdr$).

valueAddition.title: Currency with the Public vs. Currency in Circulation
bullets: Currency in Circulation (CIC): Total physical currency notes and coins issued by the RBI and Government of India in the economy.
Currency with the Public (C): Currency in Circulation minus Cash held in commercial bank vaults. Vault cash does not count as money held by the public.
The Shift: Withdrawing cash moves funds out of the bank vault and bank deposit ledger straight into 'Currency with the Public'.

inNews.relevance: Directly reaffirms how liquidity transfers between bank ledgers and currency balances preserve aggregate monetary parity while altering banking system reserve ratios.

subject: Economy
stem:
If another global financial crisis happens in the near future, which of the following action/policies are most likely to give some immunity to India?
1. Not depending on short-term foreign borrowings
2. Opening up to more foreign banks account full
3. Maintaining capital convertibility
Select the correct answer using the code given below:

keywords.shortNote: Foreign borrowings with an original maturity of up to one year, which pose acute refinancing (rollover) and sudden stop risks during a cross-border liquidity freeze.
keywords.concept: Short-Term External Debt Vulnerability: Foreign borrowings with an original maturity of up to one year, which pose acute refinancing (rollover) and sudden stop risks during a cross-border liquidity freeze.

keywords.shortNote: The complete freedom to convert domestic financial assets into foreign financial assets at market-determined exchange rates without regulatory caps; during a global crisis, it permits catastrophic, unhindered capital flight.
keywords.concept: Full Capital Account Convertibility (FCAC): The complete freedom to convert domestic financial assets into foreign financial assets at market-determined exchange rates without regulatory caps; during a global crisis, it permits catastrophic, unhindered capital flight.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Only policy 1 provides genuine macroprudential insulation against a cross-border liquidity shock. Policies 2 and 3 act as direct conduits for transmitting external shocks into the domestic financial system.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Falsely treats expanding foreign bank presence as a stabiliser, whereas it acts as a primary transmission channel for cross-border banking contagion.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Recommends full capital convertibility, which removes the defensive capital flow friction protecting emerging market reserves during external panics.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Adopts all options without accounting for how unrestricted capital convertibility and global banking integration expose domestic economies to external shocks.

valueAddition.title: Why Short-Term Debt is Risky
bullets: Rollover Risk: Short-term debt requires continuous renewal; if global credit freezes, foreign creditors demand repayment in foreign exchange rather than renewing credit lines.

Greenspan-Guidotti Rule: Foreign exchange reserves of an emerging economy should at least equal 100% of its short-term external debt (residual maturity basis) to withstand an entire year without access to foreign borrowing.
India's Ratio: India's external debt management policy prioritizes long-term debt (ECBs with longer minimum average maturities) and keeps short-term debt within conservative prudential thresholds.

valueAddition.title: Why India Avoids Full Capital Account Convertibility
bullets: Prerequisite Deficits: S.S. Tarapore Committees recommended preconditions before pursuing full convertibility: gross fiscal deficit below 3.5% of GDP, gross NPAs below 5%, inflation mandated at 3–5%, and a substantial foreign exchange reserve cushion.

Capital Account Trilemma: India maintains calibrated, asymmetric capital account openness—near-complete freedom on foreign direct investment (FDI), managed quotas on debt (FPI/ECBs), and quantitative limits on retail outward remittances (LRS capped at $250,000 per financial year).

East Asian Crisis (1997) Lesson: Economies with fully open capital accounts and high short-term dollar borrowing (Thailand, Indonesia, South Korea) suffered systemic economic collapse when foreign capital pulled out overnight.

valueAddition.title: Contagion Transmission: The Cross-Border Banking Channel
bullets: Balance Sheet Retrenchment: Foreign banks facing domestic losses (e.g., in the US or Europe) cut foreign exposures first, suddenly drying up local working capital in host emerging markets.

Domestic Banking Cushion: India's predominance of domestic public and private sector banks funded primarily by sticky domestic retail deposits acts as a firebreak against external financial contagion.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India / Ministry of Finance
inNews.headline: India's External Sector Buffers Strengthen as Short-Term Debt-to-Reserves Ratio Remains at Historic Prudential Lows
inNews.relevance: Directly links to macroprudential defenses against global volatility, emphasizing low short-term debt dependency and substantial foreign reserve buffers.

statementBreakdown.reference: RBI External Debt Management Framework & Greenspan-Guidotti Rule
statementBreakdown.explanation: During an international credit crunch, global lenders pull back liquidity and refuse to roll over short-term debt obligations. Minimising reliance on short-term foreign commercial borrowings shields the domestic financial system from sudden-stop panics, sharp rupee depreciation, and foreign exchange depletion.

Opening up domestic credit to more foreign commercial banks increases vulnerability to international contagion. When parent foreign banks experience liquidity or solvency shocks in their home jurisdictions during a global panic, their overseas subsidiaries/branches rapidly deleverage and contract domestic credit lines, transmitting financial distress directly into India.

statementBreakdown.reference: Tarapore Committee Criteria & Macroprudential Capital Controls
statementBreakdown.explanation: Full capital account convertibility eliminates all barriers to outward capital outflows. In the event of a global liquidity panic, unrestricted convertibility triggers immediate, massive domestic and foreign capital flight (capital outflow shock), depleting foreign exchange reserves, collapsing the exchange rate, and destabilizing the banking architecture. Calibrated capital account controls provide India with structural insulation.

visualSuggestion.title: Policy Actions vs. Vulnerability to Global Financial Shocks

rows: Actively enforced by RBI via ECB guidelines
Eliminates sudden rollover defaults and shields forex reserves
Transmits parent bank deleveraging and credit freezes into domestic market
Enables unhindered capital flight, depleting reserves and collapsing the currency

hook.headline: How can India survive the next global financial crisis?
hook.teaser: Two popular economic ideas will actually worsen a crisis—here is why.

keywords.term: Not depending on short-term foreign borrowings
keywords.calloutNote: Short-term debt cannot be rolled over during a global freeze, triggering sudden sovereign default.
activePhrases: Not depending on short-term foreign borrowings

keywords.calloutNote: During a panic, free convertibility lets capital flee overnight, collapsing the domestic currency.
activePhrases: Maintaining full capital account convertibility
dimmedPhrases: Not depending on short-term foreign borrowings
contextPhrases: Opening up to more foreign banks

verdicts.source: Avoiding short-term foreign debt prevents liquidity freezes and currency runs when international markets panic.
When parent foreign banks suffer losses abroad, they cut domestic lending in India, spreading contagion.
Full convertibility removes exit barriers, allowing massive, unchecked capital outflows during panic.

answer.label: A
answer.text: Only statement 1 gives immunity; foreign bank expansion and full capital convertibility expose the economy to external contagion and capital flight.

keywords.shortNote: The primary 25% portion of a member country's IMF quota paid in hard currency or SDRs, which can be withdrawn unconditionally at any time without service charges.
keywords.concept: Reserve Tranche Position (RTP): The primary 25% portion of a member country's IMF quota paid in hard currency or SDRs, which can be withdrawn unconditionally at any time without service charges.

keywords.shortNote: A member country's financial commitment to the IMF based on its global economic weight, determining its voting power, maximum financing access, and SDR allocations.
keywords.concept: IMF Quota: A member country's financial commitment to the IMF based on its global economic weight, determining its voting power, maximum financing access, and SDR allocations.

keywords.shortNote: An international reserve asset created by the IMF to supplement member countries' official reserves, valued against a basket of five major global currencies.
keywords.concept: Special Drawing Rights (SDR): An international reserve asset created by the IMF to supplement member countries' official reserves, valued against a basket of five major global currencies.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: The World Bank provides long-term developmental and project loans, not quota-linked reserve tranche liquidity.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: While a central bank counts the Reserve Tranche inside its foreign exchange reserves, the facility itself is an IMF quota mechanism rather than a domestic central bank operation.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: The WTO is a multilateral trade rule-making and dispute settlement body; it does not extend balance-of-payments credit facilities to members.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: IMF Articles of Agreement · Quota Subscription
optionBreakdown.explanation: Historically called the Gold Tranche because members paid 25% of their IMF quota in gold, the Reserve Tranche lets members draw up to that subscribed amount unconditionally during balance-of-payments needs.

valueAddition.title: How the Reserve Tranche Works
bullets: Every IMF member pays 25% of its quota in reserve assets (Special Drawing Rights or widely accepted currencies like USD, EUR, JPY, GBP) and 75% in its own domestic currency.
Historically, that initial 25% subscription had to be paid in physical gold, giving rise to the legacy term 'Gold Tranche' before gold was demonetized in the 1970s.
A member can draw down its Reserve Tranche Position at short notice without facing IMF policy conditionalities, interest charges, or repayment schedules.

valueAddition.title: India's Foreign Exchange Reserves Basket
bullets: RBI tracks four distinct components under India's Forex Reserves: Foreign Currency Assets (FCA), Gold, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), and Reserve Tranche Position (RTP) in the IMF.
Drawing beyond the Reserve Tranche moves a country into 'Credit Tranches', where IMF structural reforms, interest rates, and phased disbursements apply.

hook.teaser: Notice the bracketed hint in the question—that single clue gives away the institution immediately.

A central bank holds the Reserve Tranche as an asset, but it is not a central bank monetary operation.
The WTO governs global trade rules and disputes; it has no credit window for members.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to Trade-Related Investment Measures (TRIMS), which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. Quantitative restrictions on imports by foreign investors are prohibited.
2. They apply to investment measures related to trade in both goods and services.
3. They are not concerned with the regulation of foreign investment.

keywords.shortNote: A WTO multilateral agreement prohibiting domestic investment rules that distort trade in goods by violating GATT principles of National Treatment or elimination of quantitative restrictions.
keywords.concept: Trade-Related Investment Measures (TRIMs): A WTO multilateral agreement prohibiting domestic investment rules that distort trade in goods by violating GATT principles of National Treatment or elimination of quantitative restrictions.

keywords.shortNote: A prohibited TRIMs policy mandating foreign or domestic firms to source a minimum percentage of inputs from local producers.
keywords.concept: Local Content Requirement (LCR): A prohibited TRIMs policy mandating foreign or domestic firms to source a minimum percentage of inputs from local producers.

keywords.shortNote: The WTO rule requiring imported goods to be treated no less favourably than domestically produced goods once they enter the local market.
keywords.concept: National Treatment (GATT Article III): The WTO rule requiring imported goods to be treated no less favourably than domestically produced goods once they enter the local market.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because TRIMs excludes services.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because TRIMs applies strictly to goods, not services.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Correctly captures both the ban on import restrictions under GATT Article XI and the fact that TRIMs disciplines trade distortions rather than regulating FDI entry rules.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because Statement 2 overstates coverage to services.

valueAddition.title: What TRIMs Prohibits (The Illustrative List)
bullets: Local Content Requirements: Forcing a firm to buy or use domestic inputs (violates GATT Article III:4 National Treatment).
Trade Balancing Requirements: Limiting a firm's imports to a proportion of its local exports (violates GATT Article XI:1 Quantitative Restrictions).
Foreign Exchange Restrictions: Restricting an enterprise's access to foreign exchange to the inflows attributable to that enterprise.

valueAddition.title: What TRIMs Does NOT Cover
bullets: Services Investment: Covered under Mode 3 (Commercial Presence) of the General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS), never TRIMs.
FDI Entry & Equity Caps: Countries remain free to cap foreign ownership (e.g., 49% or 74% FDI limits) or screen foreign investments under national law.

inNews.source: Ministry of Commerce & Industry / WTO Dispute Settlement Body
inNews.headline: India faces nine pending WTO disputes including challenges to PLI schemes under TRIMs
inNews.relevance: Parliamentary disclosures in August 2026 noted ongoing WTO disputes where trading partners challenged India's PLI schemes for automobiles, batteries, and solar modules for allegedly violating TRIMs local-sourcing rules.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Article 2 prohibits investment measures inconsistent with GATT Article XI (general elimination of quantitative restrictions), explicitly barring limits on the volume or value of imports an enterprise can bring in.
Article 1 explicitly states that the TRIMs Agreement applies to investment measures related to trade in goods only; trade in services is governed separately under GATS.
TRIMs does not regulate entry, ownership caps, or licensing of foreign direct investment; it strictly disciplines performance conditions that distort cross-border trade in goods.

activePhrases: both goods and services

Article 1 states clearly that the agreement applies to investment measures related to trade in goods only.

answer.text: Statements 1 and 3 are right—TRIMs bans import quotas on investors in goods, without regulating FDI entry itself.
