subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. The motion to impeach a Judge of the Supreme Court of Indian cannot be rejected by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha as per the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
2. The Constitution of India defines and gives details of what constitutes 'incapacity and proved misbehaviour' of the Judges of the Supreme Court of India.
3. The process of impeachment of the Judges of the Supreme Court of India is given in the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
4. If the motion for the impeachment of a Judge is taken up for voting, the law requires the motion to be backed by each House of the Parliament and supported by a majority of total membership of that House and by not less than two-thirds of total members of that House present and voting.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: Under Section 3(1) of the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha may either admit or refuse to admit a removal motion after consulting relevant material.
keywords.concept: Speaker's / Chairman's Discretion (Section 3(1)): Under Section 3(1) of the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha may either admit or refuse to admit a removal motion after consulting relevant material.

keywords.shortNote: The two exclusive constitutional grounds for the removal of a Supreme Court judge; neither term is defined, detailed, or illustrated anywhere in the Constitution of India.
keywords.concept: Proved Misbehaviour and Incapacity (Article 124(4)): The two exclusive constitutional grounds for the removal of a Supreme Court judge; neither term is defined, detailed, or illustrated anywhere in the Constitution of India.

keywords.shortNote: The statutory framework enacted under Article 124(5) regulating the procedure for the presentation of an address and for the investigation and proof of the misbehaviour or incapacity of a judge.
keywords.concept: The Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968: The statutory framework enacted under Article 124(5) regulating the procedure for the presentation of an address and for the investigation and proof of the misbehaviour or incapacity of a judge.

keywords.shortNote: Mandates that an address for removal must be supported by a majority of the total membership of each House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting in that same session.
keywords.concept: Special Majority (Article 124(4)): Mandates that an address for removal must be supported by a majority of the total membership of each House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting in that same session.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements 1 and 2 are factually incorrect: the Speaker has discretion to refuse admission, and the Constitution never defines the grounds.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 3 is correct, but this option incorrectly ignores Statement 4, which correctly cites the special majority required under Article 124(4).

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statements 3 and 4 are valid; Statement 1 is false regarding the Speaker's powers, and Statement 2 is false regarding constitutional definitions.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Incorrectly includes Statement 1, which denies the Speaker's explicit statutory power to reject a removal motion.

valueAddition.title: Judicial Removal Procedure Under the 1968 Act
bullets: Initiation Threshold: A removal notice must be signed by at least 100 members of the Lok Sabha or at least 50 members of the Rajya Sabha, and delivered to the Presiding Officer.
Presiding Officer's Gatekeeping: Under Section 3(1), the Speaker or Chairman may admit or refuse the motion after considering available evidence and consulting relevant authorities.

Three-Member Inquiry Committee: If admitted, a committee is constituted consisting of: (1) Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court Judge, (2) Chief Justice of a High Court, and (3) a distinguished jurist.
Consequences of Findings: If the committee acquits the judge, the motion drops permanently; if found guilty of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, the House takes up the motion for debate and voting.

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Safeguards & Removal Majorities
bullets: Twin Majority Rule (Art. 124(4)): Absolute majority of total membership (>50% of total seats) PLUS a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
Single Session Rule: The address must be passed by both Houses and presented to the President within the same parliamentary session.
Presidential Order: The President issues a formal order of removal only after both Houses adopt the address with the requisite special majorities.
High Court Parallel: Under Article 217(1) proviso (b) read with Article 218, High Court judges are removed by the exact same procedure, grounds, and majorities.

inNews.source: Supreme Court of India / The Hindu
inNews.headline: Supreme Court Bench Re-examines In-House Inquiry Procedures and Judicial Independence Protections for Constitutional Court Judges
inNews.relevance: Direct connection to the balance between internal peer review mechanisms, statutory inquiry frameworks under the 1968 Act, and parliamentary removal powers.

similarPyq.stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. A Judge of the Supreme Court can be removed from his office by an order of the President.
2. The President can issue the removal order only after an address by Parliament has been presented to him in the same session.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

statementBreakdown.explanation: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha (or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha) has absolute statutory discretion to either admit the motion or refuse to admit it. A prominent example occurred in 2018 when the Rajya Sabha Chairman rejected the notice of removal against the then CJI Dipak Misra.
While Article 124(4) lists 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity' as the sole grounds for removal, the Constitution nowhere defines, elaborates, or details what constitutes these terms.

Under Article 124(5), Parliament is empowered to regulate the procedure by law; accordingly, Parliament enacted the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, which lays down the step-by-step statutory process for investigation and removal.

Article 124(4) explicitly specifies that the address must be supported by a majority of the total membership of each House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting, and presented to the President in the same session.

hook.headline: Does the Constitution actually tell us what bad judge behaviour is?
hook.teaser: One common myth about judicial impeachment trips up almost every candidate.

keywords.term: cannot be rejected by the Speaker
keywords.calloutNote: Section 3(1) of the 1968 Act gives the Speaker full discretion to refuse admission.
activePhrases: motion to impeach a Judge of the Supreme Court of Indian cannot be rejected by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha

keywords.calloutNote: Look out for this recurring trap—the Constitution never defines 'misbehaviour' or 'incapacity'.
activePhrases: Constitution of India defines and gives details of what constitutes 'incapacity and proved misbehaviour'
dimmedPhrases: motion to impeach a Judge of the Supreme Court of Indian cannot be rejected by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha

verdicts.source: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha has statutory power to either admit or outright reject the motion.
The Constitution names 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity' as grounds, but never defines or elaborates on them.
Enacted under Article 124(5), the Judges (Inquiry) Act of 1968 outlines the entire statutory investigation and removal procedure.
The motion requires an absolute majority of total membership along with two-thirds of those present and voting in each House.

answer.label: C
answer.text: Statements 3 and 4 are correct: the 1968 Act prescribes the removal procedure and Article 124(4) mandates the dual special majority.

With reference to the provisions contained in Part IV of the Constitution of India, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. They shall be enforceable by courts.
2. They shall not be enforceable by any court.
3. The principles laid down in this part are to influence the making of laws by the State.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:

keywords.shortNote: Constitutional provisions comprising Articles 36 to 51 embodying socio-economic ideals to establish a welfare state.
keywords.concept: Part IV (DPSPs): Constitutional provisions comprising Articles 36 to 51 embodying socio-economic ideals to establish a welfare state.

keywords.shortNote: Core threshold provision declaring DPSPs non-enforceable by courts yet fundamental in the governance of the country.
keywords.concept: Article 37: Core threshold provision declaring DPSPs non-enforceable by courts yet fundamental in the governance of the country.

keywords.shortNote: Constitutional character denying citizens the power to compel state performance via judicial writs or court decrees.
keywords.concept: Non-justiciable: Constitutional character denying citizens the power to compel state performance via judicial writs or court decrees.

keywords.shortNote: Mandate under Article 37 binding the legislature and executive to apply Directive Principles when enacting and administering laws.
keywords.concept: Duty of the State: Mandate under Article 37 binding the legislature and executive to apply Directive Principles when enacting and administering laws.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (d) is correct. Article 37 balances two tenets: DPSPs are non-enforceable by any court, yet remain fundamental in the governance of the country and must guide state lawmaking.

valueAddition.title: Article 37 & The Dual Constitutional Mandate
bullets: Textual Milestones: Article 37 forms the gateway to Part IV; enacted 1949, enforces non-justiciability while establishing governance primacy.
Constitutional Duty: Enforces Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's Instrument of Instructions; directs Parliament and State Assemblies under Article 37 to apply DPSPs in lawmaking.
Judicial Balancing Ratio: In Minerva Mills (1980), the Supreme Court ruled that balance between Part III (Fundamental Rights) and Part IV (DPSPs) is an essential basic structure feature.
Interpretative Force: While non-enforceable directly, courts use DPSPs to interpret the scope of reasonable restrictions under Article 19 and expand personal liberty under Article 21.

valueAddition.title: The Binary Elimination Mechanism (Statement 1 vs. Statement 2)
bullets: Binary Incompatibility: Statements 1 and 2 are diametric opposites ('shall be enforceable' vs 'shall not be enforceable'); any option containing both or picking Statement 1 falls immediately.
Verbatim Bare Act Theft: UPSC drafted all three statements by lifting phrases directly from the two sentences of Article 37 without paraphrasing.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Other than the Fundamental Rights, which of the following parts of the Constitution of India reflect/reflects the principles and provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)?
1. Preamble
2. Directive Principles of State Policy
3. Fundamental Duties
Select the correct answer using the code given below:

keywords.shortNote: A milestone United Nations declaration adopted on 10 December 1948 enshrining 30 universal human rights and duties across civil, political, and socio-economic domains.
keywords.concept: UDHR (1948): A milestone United Nations declaration adopted on 10 December 1948 enshrining 30 universal human rights and duties across civil, political, and socio-economic domains.

keywords.shortNote: Part IV directives mirroring Articles 22 to 27 of UDHR concerning economic, social, and cultural rights (work, education, maternity relief, living wage).
keywords.concept: Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP): Part IV directives mirroring Articles 22 to 27 of UDHR concerning economic, social, and cultural rights (work, education, maternity relief, living wage).

keywords.shortNote: Part IV-A moral obligations directly aligned with Article 29(1) of UDHR, stating individuals owe duties to the community in which alone their full development is possible.
keywords.concept: Fundamental Duties: Part IV-A moral obligations directly aligned with Article 29(1) of UDHR, stating individuals owe duties to the community in which alone their full development is possible.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (d) is correct because the Preamble, DPSP, and Fundamental Duties each correspond directly to fundamental tenets of the UDHR 1948.

valueAddition.title: Mapping the UDHR (1948) to the Indian Constitutional Architecture
bullets: Civil & Political Rights (Articles 2 to 21 of UDHR): Translated primarily into Part III (Fundamental Rights), encompassing equality before law (Art 14), personal liberty (Art 21), and freedom of speech and expression (Art 19).

Economic, Social & Cultural Rights (Articles 22 to 27 of UDHR): Translated into Part IV (DPSP), including the right to social security, fair remuneration, health, and education (Arts 39, 41, 42, 43, 45).

Human Duties & Community Development (Article 29 of UDHR): UDHR Article 29(1) explicitly establishes that individuals bear duties to the community; this foundational moral premise was incorporated into Part IV-A via the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.

valueAddition.title: Judicial Harmony: UDHR as an Interpretative Conduit
bullets: Reading International Law into Domestic Jurisprudence: In Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrima Das (2000), the Supreme Court affirmed that the provisions of the UDHR are incorporated into the domestic law of India, giving them enforceability when read alongside constitutional guarantees.

Broad Conception of 'Human Rights': Candidates often restrict human rights strictly to enforceable 'Fundamental Rights', failing to recognize that the UDHR is an integrated charter covering rights, collective socio-economic goals, and civic duties.

Dignity as the Common Denominator: The Preamble is the moral gateway: in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Chief Justice Sikri noted that the Indian Constitution was framed in the light of the UDHR, with the Preamble reflecting its core commitment to individual dignity.

inNews.source: The Hindu / Supreme Court of India
inNews.headline: Supreme Court Invokes UDHR and Part IV Directives in Directing Universal Workplace Protections for Gig Workers
inNews.relevance: The Supreme Court's continuous reliance on UDHR Article 23 (just conditions of work) alongside Articles 21, 39, and 42 to extend social security benefits to informal sector workers highlights the active constitutional synthesis between international covenants and domestic provisions.

analysis.coreTakeaway: Remember: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) encompasses civil, political, economic, social, and civic duties; all three parts—Preamble, DPSP, and Fundamental Duties—mirror its provisions.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 is correct. The Preamble articulates Justice, Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity assuring the 'dignity of the individual', directly reflecting UDHR Article 1 ('All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights').

statementBreakdown.reference: UDHR Articles 22–27 vs. Constitution of India Part IV (Articles 38–43)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Statement 2 is correct. Part IV incorporates socio-economic guarantees matching the UDHR: right to work (Article 41 vs. UDHR Art 23), just and humane conditions of work (Article 42 vs. UDHR Art 23), and adequate standard of living (Article 47 vs. UDHR Art 25).

statementBreakdown.reference: UDHR Article 29(1) vs. Constitution of India Part IV-A (Article 51A)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Statement 3 is correct. Article 29(1) of UDHR states 'Everyone has duties to the community in which alone the free and full development of his personality is possible', which directly aligns with Part IV-A (Article 51A).

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. The President of India can summon a session of the Parliament at such place as he/she thinks fit.
2. The Constitution of India provides for three sessions of the Parliament in a year, but it is not mandatory to conduct all three sessions.
3. There is no minimum number of days that the Parliament is required to meet in a year.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: Empowers the President to summon each House of Parliament to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, ensuring six months do not intervene between sessions.
keywords.concept: Article 85(1): Empowers the President to summon each House of Parliament to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, ensuring six months do not intervene between sessions.

keywords.shortNote: The constitutional ceiling under Article 85(1) requiring Parliament to meet at least twice a year, without specifying sitting days or session names.
keywords.concept: Six-Month Rule: The constitutional ceiling under Article 85(1) requiring Parliament to meet at least twice a year, without specifying sitting days or session names.

valueAddition.title: Article 85: Summoning, Prorogation & Dissolution
bullets: Summoning Prerogative: Exercised by the President on the binding advice of the Union Cabinet (Article 74) via the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs (CCPA).
Inter-Session Interval: Six months is the maximum permissible gap between the last sitting in one session and the date appointed for its first sitting in the next session.
Convention vs. Constitution: The three-session framework (Budget, Monsoon, Winter) is a convention inherited from the British Westminster system and the Government of India Act, 1935.

valueAddition.title: Parliamentary Sittings: Regulatory Framework
bullets: No Statutory Floor: Unlike some state legislations or foreign legislatures, India has no constitutional or statutory requirement fixing a minimum number of sitting days per year.
Adjournment vs. Prorogation: Adjournment suspends sitting within an active session (exercised by the Presiding Officer); prorogation terminates the session itself (exercised by the President).

inNews.source: Lok Sabha Secretariat / The Hindu
inNews.headline: Parliamentary reforms committee proposes statutory floor of 100 annual sittings to arrest declining session durations
inNews.relevance: Directly highlights the constitutional absence of mandatory minimum sitting days under Article 85.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Article 85(1) explicitly provides that the President shall from time to time summon each House of Parliament to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit.
The Constitution does not mention three sessions; convening the Budget, Monsoon, and Winter sessions is purely a convention.
Neither the Constitution nor the statutory rules prescribe a minimum quota of calendar days or sittings that Parliament must convene in a year.

stem: In the context of India, which one of the following is the characteristic appropriate for bureaucracy?

options.text: An agency for widening the scope of parliamentary democracy
options.label: a

options.text: An agency for strengthening the structure of federalism
options.label: b

options.text: An agency for facilitating political stability and economic growth
options.label: c

options.text: An Agency for the implementation of public policy
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: The permanent, professional, non-elected administrative body tasked with translating legislative mandates and executive policies into field execution.
keywords.concept: Bureaucracy: The permanent, professional, non-elected administrative body tasked with translating legislative mandates and executive policies into field execution.

keywords.shortNote: A deliberate system of principles, laws, and regulatory measures adopted by the government to guide decisions and achieve socio-economic goals.
keywords.concept: Public policy: A deliberate system of principles, laws, and regulatory measures adopted by the government to guide decisions and achieve socio-economic goals.

keywords.shortNote: Civil servants appointed on merit for fixed tenure, distinct from the temporary political executive (ministers) who face periodic electoral change.
keywords.concept: Permanent executive: Civil servants appointed on merit for fixed tenure, distinct from the temporary political executive (ministers) who face periodic electoral change.

keywords.shortNote: A system where the political executive derives democratic legitimacy from and is held accountable to the legislature.
keywords.concept: Parliamentary democracy: A system where the political executive derives democratic legitimacy from and is held accountable to the legislature.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because widening parliamentary democracy is the constitutional role of elected legislatures, electoral commissions, and mass political participation, not bureaucratic machinery.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because strengthening federalism is an institutional function of constitutional bodies like Inter-State Council and GST Council; All-India Services operate federally but are not defined as federal-strengthening agencies.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because political stability stems from electoral mandates and executive leadership; economic growth is an outcome of macroeconomic policy, not the defining institutional characteristic of bureaucracy.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: NCERT Class XI (Executive, Section on Permanent Executive)
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (d) is correct. The universal and core characteristic of civil bureaucracy is serving as an administrative instrument for the direct execution and enforcement of public policies formulated by the political executive.

valueAddition.title: Weberian Ideal-Type & Constitutional Design in India
bullets: Max Weber's Classical Form: Bureaucracy is characterized by hierarchical authority, written rules, functional specialization, meritocratic recruitment, and political neutrality—its primary output is predictable, impersonal implementation of law.

Patel's Steel Frame (Article 312): Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel defended All-India Services in the Constituent Assembly as the indispensable instrument to maintain pan-Indian unity and carry out welfare state programs without regional or political bias.

Political Neutrality and Anonymity: Under the Westminster model, ministers remain politically accountable to Parliament for policy choices, while civil servants operate under civil service conduct rules to execute those choices faithfully regardless of party changes.

inNews.relevance: Judicial bench scrutiny regarding civil service boards, fixed tenures, and bureaucratic insulation from arbitrary executive interference highlights the permanent executive's constitutional mandate as a policy implementation arm.

subject: Indian Polity
stem: In India, separation of judiciary from the executive is enjoined by

options.text: a Directive Principle of State Policy
options.label: b

keywords.shortNote: Constitutional directive under Part IV obligating the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
keywords.concept: Article 50 (DPSP): Constitutional directive under Part IV obligating the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.

keywords.shortNote: A core feature of the Basic Structure ensuring judicial independence by insulating judicial functions and personnel from executive dominance.
keywords.concept: Separation of Powers Doctrine: A core feature of the Basic Structure ensuring judicial independence by insulating judicial functions and personnel from executive dominance.

keywords.shortNote: The major statutory realization of Article 50, which bifurcated magistrates into Judicial Magistrates (subordinate to High Courts) and Executive Magistrates (subordinate to State Governments).
keywords.concept: Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 (CrPC): The major statutory realization of Article 50, which bifurcated magistrates into Judicial Magistrates (subordinate to High Courts) and Executive Magistrates (subordinate to State Governments).

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: The Preamble secures Justice (social, economic, and political), Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity, but does not contain provisions enjoining the separation of judiciary from executive.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Direct match; Article 50 expressly enjoins the State to achieve the separation of the judiciary from the executive in public services.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: The Seventh Schedule allocates legislative subjects between the Union and States across three lists; it does not articulate inter-organ separation of powers.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: It is not merely an unwritten convention; separation is an express constitutional directive enshrined under Part IV and reinforced by basic structure jurisprudence.

valueAddition.title: Article 50: Constitutional Mandate & Historical Background
bullets: Colonial Heritage: Under the British Raj, District Collectors simultaneously wielded executive power and judicial magistracy, uniting the roles of revenue collector, police administrator, and trial judge.

Constituent Assembly Intent: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and K.T. Shah stressed that personal liberty under Article 21 would remain illusory if the investigating authority and the adjudicating judge were the same official.
Public Services Scope: Article 50 applies specifically to the 'public services of the State', targeting the separation of subordinate magistracy from general administrative officers.

valueAddition.title: Statutory Implementation: CrPC 1973 & Magistracy Bifurcation
bullets: Bifurcation of Magistracy: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (continued under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023) institutionalized Article 50 by creating two distinct magistrate cadres.
Judicial Magistrates: Placed under the direct administrative superintendence of the High Court and Sessions Judge; responsible for trial, appreciation of evidence, and sentencing.

Executive Magistrates: Retained under the administrative control of the State Government / District Magistrate; limited strictly to preventive actions, maintaining public order (e.g., Section 144), and administrative inquires.

inNews.headline: Supreme Court Bench Cites Article 50 While Barring Executive Bureaucrats from Heading Quasi-Judicial Appellate Tribunals
inNews.relevance: Direct modern manifestation of Article 50, where the apex court regularly strikes down tribunal recruitment rules allowing executive dominance over judicial functions.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Constitution of India defines its 'Basic Structure' in terms of federalism, secularism, fundamental rights and democracy.
2. The Constitution of India provides for 'Judicial review' to safeguard the citizens' liberties and to preserve the ideals on which the Constitution is based.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: A judicially crafted doctrine originating in Kesavananda Bharati (1973); neither defined nor mentioned anywhere in the text of the Constitution of India.
keywords.concept: Basic Structure Doctrine: A judicially crafted doctrine originating in Kesavananda Bharati (1973); neither defined nor mentioned anywhere in the text of the Constitution of India.

keywords.shortNote: The substantive constitutional basis conferring powers on the higher judiciary to invalidate laws and protect liberties, primarily rooted in Articles 13, 32, 136, 226, and 227.
keywords.concept: Constitutional Provision for Judicial Review: The substantive constitutional basis conferring powers on the higher judiciary to invalidate laws and protect liberties, primarily rooted in Articles 13, 32, 136, 226, and 227.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 is false because 'Basic Structure' is a judicial creation, not a constitutional definition.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 is eliminated due to the false claim that the Constitution defines basic structure; Statement 2 is correct as the Constitution explicitly provides mechanisms for judicial review.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Includes Statement 1, which falsely attributes the definition of Basic Structure to the Constitution.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 2 is valid, making this option incorrect.

valueAddition.title: Genesis and Evolution of Basic Structure
bullets: Shankari Prasad (1951) & Sajjan Singh (1965): Supreme Court held that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 includes the power to amend Fundamental Rights.
Golak Nath (1967): Reversing its earlier stand, the Court held that Fundamental Rights are given a transcendental position and Parliament cannot curtail them.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Overruled Golak Nath by holding that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, but cannot alter its 'Basic Structure' or essential framework.
Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975): Applied the doctrine for the first time to strike down a constitutional amendment (Clause 4 of the 39th Amendment).

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Roots of Judicial Review in India
bullets: Article 13(2): Prohibits the State from making any law taking away or abridging Fundamental Rights and declares any such law void to the extent of contravention.
Article 32 & Article 226: Empower the Supreme Court and High Courts to issue directions, orders, or writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
Articles 131–136 & Article 143: Confer original, appellate, and advisory jurisdictions that underpin the broader framework of judicial review.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997): Affirmed that judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 is an integral and essential feature forming part of the basic structure.

valueAddition.title: Frequent Examiner Traps: 'Defined in the Constitution'
bullets: Basic Structure: Not mentioned, not defined (Judicial innovation).
Judicial Review: The phrase itself is not explicitly defined in the text, but the Constitution provides for its substantive mechanisms via Articles 13, 32, 136, 226.
Contempt of Court, Martial Law, Office of Profit, Untouchability: Mentioned or referenced, but nowhere defined in the Constitution.

inNews.source: The Hindu / Supreme Court of India
inNews.headline: Supreme Court reiterates judicial review over legislative and executive actions is an unalterable basic feature
inNews.relevance: Directly reaffirms that while 'Basic Structure' is a judicial doctrine, the constitutional mandate for judicial review under Articles 13, 32, and 226 cannot be diluted by ordinary legislation or constitutional amendments.

statementBreakdown.explanation: The Constitution of India does NOT define or even mention the phrase 'Basic Structure'. The doctrine was propounded by the Supreme Court in the landmark Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) and evolved through subsequent judicial pronouncements.

The Constitution of India expressly provides for judicial review through provisions such as Article 13(2) (declaring laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void), Article 32 (remedies for enforcement of Fundamental Rights), and Article 226 (High Court writ jurisdiction) to safeguard citizens' liberties and preserve constitutional ideals.

visualSuggestion.title: Basic Structure vs Judicial Review: Constitutional Status

Inherent in constitutional supremacy and Articles 13, 32, 226
Is it part of Basic Structure?
It IS the Basic Structure doctrine

hook.headline: Does the Constitution of India define its 'Basic Structure'?
hook.teaser: Statement 1 looks like a standard textbook definition, but it is an examiner trap.

keywords.term: Constitution of India defines its 'Basic Structure'
keywords.calloutNote: A classic trap: 'Basic Structure' was invented by judges in 1973 and never appears in the constitutional text.
activePhrases: The Constitution of India defines its 'Basic Structure' in terms of federalism, secularism, fundamental rights and democracy.

keywords.calloutNote: Articles 13, 32, and 226 directly provide the mechanisms for judicial review.
activePhrases: The Constitution of India provides for 'Judicial review' to safeguard the citizens' liberties and to preserve the ideals on which the Constitution is based.
dimmedPhrases: The Constitution of India defines its 'Basic Structure' in terms of federalism, secularism, fundamental rights and democracy.

verdicts.source: The Constitution nowhere mentions or defines 'Basic Structure'; it was propounded in the Kesavananda Bharati ruling.
The Constitution expressly provides for judicial review under Articles 13, 32, and 226 to protect liberties.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Statement 1 is incorrect because the Constitution does not define Basic Structure; Statement 2 is correct because the Constitution provides for judicial review.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Constitutional Law notes

subject: Indian Polity
stem: A constitutional government by definition is a

keywords.shortNote: A political system where the authority of the state is defined, regulated, and limited by supreme constitutional law.
keywords.concept: Constitutional government: A political system where the authority of the state is defined, regulated, and limited by supreme constitutional law.

keywords.shortNote: The foundational principle that state power is legally circumscribed by institutional checks, balances, and individual rights.
keywords.concept: Limited government: The foundational principle that state power is legally circumscribed by institutional checks, balances, and individual rights.

keywords.shortNote: A government resting on the consent and electoral participation of the majority of the population.
keywords.concept: Popular government: A government resting on the consent and electoral participation of the majority of the population.

keywords.shortNote: A political framework featuring multiple political parties competing for power, often resulting in coalition rule.
keywords.concept: Multi-party government: A political framework featuring multiple political parties competing for power, often resulting in coalition rule.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because government by legislature describes parliamentary systems, whereas presidential regimes like the US are equally constitutional governments.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: Alexis de Tocqueville / Mill's Liberty Theory
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because popular government without constitutional limits enables majoritarian tyranny, the very opposite of constitutionalism.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because two-party democracies (like the US) are constitutional governments; a multi-party structure is not a definitive requirement.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: NCERT Class XI (Constitution: Why and How?) & Andrew Heywood
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (d) is correct. Constitutional government is by definition limited government, entrenching legal boundaries on state power to safeguard individual liberty.

valueAddition.title: Constitutionalism & The Mechanics of Legal Limitation
bullets: Philosophical Core (Locke & Madison): Power must be institutionally checked; merely holding popular elections does not create constitutionalism unless the government is legally restrained.

Substantive Restraint via Basic Structure: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980), the Supreme Court affirmed that limited government and judicial review are basic features that cannot be amended away under Article 368.

Institutional Levers: Limited government operates through three universal devices: written fundamental rights (negative state obligations), separation of powers (Article 50), and independent judicial review.

valueAddition.title: Common Exam Trap: Democratic Forms vs. Defining Nature

subject: Indian Polity
stem: One common agreement between Gandhism and Marxism is:

options.text: the final goal of a stateless society
options.label: a

keywords.shortNote: An ultimate social order where coercive state apparatus is rendered redundant through voluntary moral self-regulation or the elimination of class antagonisms.
keywords.concept: Stateless society: An ultimate social order where coercive state apparatus is rendered redundant through voluntary moral self-regulation or the elimination of class antagonisms.

keywords.shortNote: Marxist historical materialist doctrine positing that conflicting economic class interests inevitably drive revolutionary socio-political transitions.
keywords.concept: Class struggle: Marxist historical materialist doctrine positing that conflicting economic class interests inevitably drive revolutionary socio-political transitions.

keywords.shortNote: Marxist requirement for public collective ownership of the means of production, directly opposed to Gandhi's trusteeship concept.
keywords.concept: Abolition of private property: Marxist requirement for public collective ownership of the means of production, directly opposed to Gandhi's trusteeship concept.

keywords.shortNote: Marxist proposition that economic base structures (relations of production) decisively shape legal, ideological, and political superstructures.
keywords.concept: Economic determinism: Marxist proposition that economic base structures (relations of production) decisively shape legal, ideological, and political superstructures.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.reference: NCERT Class XI Political Theory & Andrew Heywood
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (a) is correct. Both philosophies converge on the end goal of a stateless society—Marx's ultimate communist stage (state withers away) and Gandhi's enlightened anarchy (Swaraj).

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because class struggle is unique to Marxism; Gandhi rejected class conflict, advocating class collaboration, harmony, and mutual interdependence.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because Marxism demands the total statutory abolition of private property, whereas Gandhi permitted private ownership under the moral umbrella of 'Trusteeship'.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ruled out because economic determinism is a foundational Marxist concept; Gandhi prioritized spiritual and moral consciousness over materialist economic drivers.

valueAddition.title: Ends vs. Means: The Philosophical Divide Between Marx and Gandhi
bullets: Convergence on the End (Stateless Society): Marx viewed the state as an executive committee of the bourgeoisie destined to 'wither away' after the dictatorship of the proletariat; Gandhi viewed the state as 'organized violence' and envisioned *Ramrajya* / enlightened anarchy where individuals are self-governing.

Irreconcilable Divergence on Means: Marx sanctioned violent class overthrow (proletarian revolution); Gandhi insisted on the indivisibility of means and ends, arguing impure, violent means could never yield a peaceful, just society.

Trusteeship vs. Expropriation: Marx advocated state expropriation of private property without compensation; Gandhi advocated that capitalists act as moral trustees holding excess wealth for the community.

valueAddition.title: Common Exam Trap: Conflating Convergence in 'Ends' with 'Means'
bullets: The 'Trusteeship' Trap: Candidates often confuse Gandhi's socialist inclinations with Marx's economic doctrines, forgetting Gandhi strongly opposed the forced abolition of private property (Option c).
Violence and Conflict: Options (b), (c), and (d) represent classical structural tenets of Marxist theory that Gandhi explicitly repudiated on moral and spiritual grounds.
Enlightened Anarchy Nuance: Gandhi described himself as a 'philosophical anarchist' because he considered the state's monopoly on coercive force fundamentally antithetical to moral autonomy.

analysis.coreTakeaway: Remember: Both Gandhi and Marx envisioned an ultimate stateless society, but diverged completely on the means—Marx through violent class revolution, Gandhi via non-violent moral transformation.

stem:
In India, Legal Services Authorities provide free legal services to which of the following type of citizens?
1. Person with an annual income of less than Rs. 1,00,000.
2. Transgender with an annual income of less than Rs. 2,00,000.
3. Member of Other Backward Classes (OBC) with an annual income of less than Rs. 3,00,000.
4. All Senior Citizens.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:

keywords.shortNote: The statutory provision of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 listing specific vulnerable categories entitled to free legal services regardless of means, alongside general income ceilings.
keywords.concept: Section 12 Eligibility Criteria: The statutory provision of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 listing specific vulnerable categories entitled to free legal services regardless of means, alongside general income ceilings.

keywords.shortNote: For general citizens, the statutory baseline is an annual income of less than ₹1,00,000 for cases before subordinate courts and High Courts, and ₹5,00,000 before the Supreme Court.
keywords.concept: Income Ceiling Thresholds (Sec. 12(h)): For general citizens, the statutory baseline is an annual income of less than ₹1,00,000 for cases before subordinate courts and High Courts, and ₹5,00,000 before the Supreme Court.

keywords.shortNote: Following the Supreme Court's landmark NALSA judgment (2014), several State Legal Services Authorities (such as Delhi SLSA) notified specific rules fixing a higher income ceiling of ₹2,00,000 per annum for transgender persons.
keywords.concept: Transgender Legal Aid Category: Following the Supreme Court's landmark NALSA judgment (2014), several State Legal Services Authorities (such as Delhi SLSA) notified specific rules fixing a higher income ceiling of ₹2,00,000 per annum for transgender persons.

keywords.shortNote: Members of Other Backward Classes (OBC) are not an enumerated category under Section 12, and senior citizens are not covered universally ('all')—their eligibility is subject to state-prescribed income caps.
keywords.concept: OBC & Senior Citizen Exclusions: Members of Other Backward Classes (OBC) are not an enumerated category under Section 12, and senior citizens are not covered universally ('all')—their eligibility is subject to state-prescribed income caps.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 correctly reflect the statutory income baseline and the special threshold notified for transgender persons.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because Statement 3 invents a non-existent OBC quota, and Statement 4 relies on the extreme word 'All'.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because Statement 3 is false; OBCs are not an enumerated beneficiary group under the 1987 Act.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because Statement 4 is incorrect; senior citizens are not entitled universally regardless of income.

valueAddition.title: Section 12: Statutory Beneficiaries of Free Legal Aid
bullets: Automatic Eligibility (No Income Test): Members of Scheduled Castes (SC) or Scheduled Tribes (ST); victims of human trafficking or begar (Art. 23); women and children (up to 18 years); persons with disabilities or mental illness; victims of mass disasters, ethnic violence, caste atrocities, floods, or industrial disasters; and industrial workmen.
Persons in Custody: Any person detained in a custody centre, protective home, juvenile home, or psychiatric hospital under Section 12(g).
Income-Based Eligibility: General individuals earning less than ₹1,00,000 per annum (higher limits in certain states); ₹5,00,000 per annum before the Supreme Court Legal Services Committee (SCLSC).

valueAddition.title: Three-Tier Architecture of Legal Services Authorities
bullets: National Level (NALSA): Chief Justice of India is Patron-in-Chief; serving or retired Judge of Supreme Court nominated by President acts as Executive Chairman.
State Level (SLSA): Chief Justice of High Court is Patron-in-Chief; serving or retired High Court Judge acts as Executive Chairman.
District & Taluk Level: District Judge acts as Chairman of the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA); senior civil judge heads the Taluka Legal Services Committee (TLSC).

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Foundations & Judicial Milestones
bullets: Article 39A (DPSP): Inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976; directs the State to secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice on a basis of equal opportunity, providing free legal aid by suitable legislation.

Article 21 Fundamental Right: In *Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar (1979)* and *M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra (1978)*, the Supreme Court held that the right to free legal aid for indigent accused is an implicit fundamental right under Article 21.
NALSA v. Union of India (2014): Recognized transgender persons as the 'third gender' and directed Centre and States to extend affirmative action, welfare measures, and dedicated legal aid mechanisms.

stem: A Parliamentary System of Government is one in which

options.text: all political parties in the Parliament are represented in the Government
options.label: a

options.text: the Government is responsible to the Parliament and can be removed by it
options.label: b

options.text: the Government is elected by the people and can be removed by them
options.label: c

options.text: the Government is chosen by the Parliament but cannot be removed by it before completion of a fixed term
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: The fundamental design merit of the parliamentary system where the executive is answerable to, scrutinized by, and dependent on the continuous confidence of the legislature.
keywords.concept: Continuous Executive Accountability: The fundamental design merit of the parliamentary system where the executive is answerable to, scrutinized by, and dependent on the continuous confidence of the legislature.

keywords.shortNote: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's rationale in the Constituent Assembly establishing that India preferred a daily and periodic assessment of executive responsibility over the tenure stability of the American presidential model.
keywords.concept: Accountability vs. Stability Trade-off: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's rationale in the Constituent Assembly establishing that India preferred a daily and periodic assessment of executive responsibility over the tenure stability of the American presidential model.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Strict independence between the executive and the legislature is the hallmark of the presidential system (strict separation of powers), whereas the parliamentary system is characterized by executive-legislative fusion and coordination.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Continuity of policy and high tenure stability are advantages attributed to the presidential system with fixed terms; parliamentary governments face risks of frequent cabinet falls, policy shifts, and coalition instability.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: The foremost advantage of the parliamentary system is continuous legislative oversight and collective responsibility, ensuring the executive remains accountable to the elected legislature on both a daily (debates, questions) and periodic (confidence votes) basis.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: In a parliamentary system, the head of the government (Prime Minister) can be changed without a general election whenever the ruling party or coalition elects a new leader or through a floor test.

valueAddition.title: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar on Parliamentary System (Constituent Assembly, 1948)
bullets: Constitutional Trade-off: 'A democratic executive must satisfy two conditions — it must be a stable executive and it must be a responsible executive. Unfortunately, it has not been possible so far to devise a system which can ensure both in equal degree.'
American vs. British Choice: 'The American system gives more stability but less responsibility. The British system, on the other hand, gives more responsibility but less stability.'

Daily & Periodic Assessment: 'The Draft Constitution in recommending the parliamentary system of Executive has preferred more responsibility to more stability... The assessment of responsibility is both daily (questions, resolutions, no-confidence motions) and periodic (elections).'

valueAddition.title: Merits vs. Demerits of Parliamentary Form
bullets: Merits: Harmony between legislature and executive; continuous accountability; prevention of authoritarianism; representation of diverse groups; availability of alternate government.
Demerits: Unstable government; no continuity of long-term policies; cabinet dictatorship (in brute majorities); violation of strict separation of powers; administration by generalists/politicians.

subject: Indian Polity
stem: Which part of the Constitution of India declares the ideal of Welfare State?

keywords.shortNote: A state committed to securing socio-economic justice, reducing inequalities, and providing basic economic security rather than acting merely as a police state.
keywords.concept: Welfare State: A state committed to securing socio-economic justice, reducing inequalities, and providing basic economic security rather than acting merely as a police state.

keywords.shortNote: Constitutional mandate directing the State to secure a social order for the promotion of the welfare of the people.
keywords.concept: Article 38: Constitutional mandate directing the State to secure a social order for the promotion of the welfare of the people.

keywords.shortNote: Instrument of socio-economic instructions establishing economic democracy and transforming India from a colonial police state into a modern welfare state.
keywords.concept: Part IV (DPSPs): Instrument of socio-economic instructions establishing economic democracy and transforming India from a colonial police state into a modern welfare state.

keywords.shortNote: Dr. Ambedkar's distinction establishing that Fundamental Rights secure political democracy, while Directive Principles secure social and economic democracy.
keywords.concept: Political vs. Socio-Economic Democracy: Dr. Ambedkar's distinction establishing that Fundamental Rights secure political democracy, while Directive Principles secure social and economic democracy.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.reference: Article 38(1), Part IV of the Constitution of India
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (a) is correct. Article 38 explicitly commands the State to promote the welfare of the people by securing a social order permeated by social, economic, and political justice.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: Part III of the Constitution of India
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fundamental Rights establish political democracy and negative restraints against state despotism, rather than the affirmative socio-economic architecture of a welfare state.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: While the Preamble resolves to secure socio-economic justice, Part IV is the operational and substantive constitutional chapter designed specifically to build the welfare state.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: The Seventh Schedule allocates legislative subjects between the Union and States across three lists, containing no declaration of philosophical state ideals.

valueAddition.title: Article 38: The Constitutional Foundation of the Welfare State
bullets: Official Identity & Textual Mandate: Article 38 directs the State to secure a social order for the promotion of the welfare of the people through social, economic, and political justice.
Constitutional Amendment Expansion: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 added Article 38(2), mandating the State to minimize inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities.
Dr. Ambedkar's Drafting Intent: Emphasized that Part IV aims to establish economic democracy, transforming India from a colonial 'police state' into an affirmative 'welfare state'.
Basic Structure Synthesis: In Minerva Mills (1980), the Supreme Court affirmed that the social revolution envisioned in Part IV is fundamental to the constitutional identity.

valueAddition.title: The Preamble vs. Part IV Jurisprudential Trap
bullets: The 'Justice Clause' Temptation: Candidates gravitate toward the Preamble due to its 'Social, Economic, and Political Justice' clause, but the explicit machinery of welfare resides in Part IV.
Superlative Constitutional Function: Fundamental Rights protect negative liberty against the State, whereas Directive Principles mandate positive affirmative welfare interventions.

inNews.relevance: Constitution Benches regularly reaffirm that Article 38 imposes an affirmative constitutional duty on governments to finance universal healthcare and basic social security architectures.

stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. According to the Constitution of India, a person who is eligible to vote can be made a minister in a State for six months even if he/she is not a member of the Legislature of that State.
2. According to the Representation of People Act, 1951, a person convicted of a criminal offence and sentenced to imprisonment for five years is permanently disqualified from contesting an election even after his release from prison.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: Article 326 sets the voting age at 18 years, whereas Article 173 mandates a minimum age of 25 years for the Legislative Assembly and 30 years for the Legislative Council to be eligible for appointment as a Minister.
keywords.concept: Voting Age vs. Ministerial Qualification: Article 326 sets the voting age at 18 years, whereas Article 173 mandates a minimum age of 25 years for the Legislative Assembly and 30 years for the Legislative Council to be eligible for appointment as a Minister.

keywords.shortNote: A person convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for two years or more is disqualified from the date of conviction and continues to be disqualified for a further period of six years since their release, not permanently.
keywords.concept: Section 8(3) Disqualification Period: A person convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for two years or more is disqualified from the date of conviction and continues to be disqualified for a further period of six years since their release, not permanently.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: An 18-year-old voter cannot be appointed a minister because Article 173 sets the minimum legislative qualification age at 25.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Section 8(3) imposes disqualification during the sentence plus 6 years after release, not a lifetime or permanent ban.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements contain distinct conceptual traps: age mismatch in statement 1 and duration exaggeration in statement 2.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Neither statement is legally or constitutionally valid, making (d) the correct answer.

valueAddition.title: Ministerial Appointment Without Legislative Membership
bullets: Article 164(4) Mechanism: A Minister who for any period of six consecutive months is not a member of the Legislature of the State shall at the expiration of that period cease to be a Minister.

Substantive Eligibility Benchmark: In B.R. Kapur v. State of Tamil Nadu (2001), the Supreme Court ruled that Article 164(4) is subject to the qualifications (Article 173) and disqualifications (Article 191) for legislative membership; an individual who lacks the basic age criterion or is disqualified cannot be sworn in even for a temporary six-month tenure.

Non-Consecutive Bar: In S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001), the Supreme Court ruled that a non-legislator who ceases to be a minister after six months cannot be reappointed without getting elected in the interim.

valueAddition.title: Criminal Disqualification Architecture under RPA 1951
bullets: Section 8(1): Covers specified offences (e.g., promoting enmity, bribery, rape, electoral offences). Any conviction carries a 6-year disqualification from the date of conviction (or 6 years from release if imprisoned).

Section 8(2): Convictions under specific laws (hoarding, adulteration, Dowry Prohibition Act) with imprisonment of not less than 6 months trigger disqualification during the term plus 6 years post-release.

Section 8(3) Residual Clause: A sentence of imprisonment for 2 years or more for any criminal offence triggers immediate disqualification, which lasts through the sentence and continues for exactly 6 years after release.
Permanent Ban Status: There is currently no provision for a lifetime or permanent ban on convicted politicians under the RPA, 1951.

inNews.relevance: Directly links to the ongoing constitutional debate on whether Section 8 of the RPA 1951 should be amended from a 6-year post-release bar to a lifetime ban.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

statementBreakdown.reference: Articles 164(4) & 173; B.R. Kapur v. State of Tamil Nadu (2001)
statementBreakdown.explanation: A person eligible to vote is at least 18 years of age (Article 326). However, to be a member of the State Legislature—and thus eligible to continue or be appointed as a Minister under Article 164(4)—a person must possess the qualifications prescribed under Article 173 (minimum 25 years of age for the Legislative Assembly and 30 years for the Legislative Council). As held by the Supreme Court in B.R. Kapur (2001), a person who is disqualified or not qualified under Article 173 cannot be appointed as a Minister even for six months.

statementBreakdown.reference: Representation of the People Act, 1951 · Section 8(3)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Under Section 8(3) of the RPA, 1951, a person convicted of an offence and sentenced to imprisonment for not less than two years is disqualified from the date of conviction and remains disqualified for a further period of six years following release from prison. Disqualification is not permanent.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. Coal sector was nationalized by the Government of India under Indira Gandhi.
2. Now, coal blocks are allocated on lottery basis.
3. Till recently, India imported coal to meet the shortages of domestic supply, but now India is self-sufficient in coal product.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: The legislation enacted under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi that brought private coal mines under state ownership in two phases (coking coal in 1971-72 and non-coking coal in 1973) to ensure scientific mining and worker welfare.
keywords.concept: Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973: The legislation enacted under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi that brought private coal mines under state ownership in two phases (coking coal in 1971-72 and non-coking coal in 1973) to ensure scientific mining and worker welfare.

keywords.shortNote: The statutory framework enacted after the Supreme Court cancelled 204 coal block allocations in 2014, mandating transparent electronic auctions for commercial and captive coal mining.
keywords.concept: Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015: The statutory framework enacted after the Supreme Court cancelled 204 coal block allocations in 2014, mandating transparent electronic auctions for commercial and captive coal mining.

keywords.shortNote: High-grade metallurgical coal with low ash and low moisture content essential for blast-furnace steel manufacturing, where India remains structurally import-dependent due to limited domestic reserves.
keywords.concept: Coking Coal: High-grade metallurgical coal with low ash and low moisture content essential for blast-furnace steel manufacturing, where India remains structurally import-dependent due to limited domestic reserves.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Only the historical fact of nationalization under Indira Gandhi is accurate; current allocation is via e-auction and India still imports coking and specialty coal.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because coal blocks are e-auctioned and India remains a major coal importer.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because domestic production still cannot replace coking coal imports.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because both contemporary policy claims in Statements 2 and 3 are factually wrong.

valueAddition.title: Evolution of Coal Governance in India
bullets: 1971–1973 (Nationalisation): Enacted under Indira Gandhi via the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972 and Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 to curb unscientific slaughter mining.

2014–2015 (Post-Coalgate Reset): In Manohar Lal Sharma v. Principal Secretary (2014), the Supreme Court cancelled 204 coal blocks allotted between 1993 and 2010, leading to the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 mandating e-auctions.
2020 (Commercial Mining): The Mineral Laws (Amendment) Act, 2020 opened commercial coal mining to private and foreign companies without end-use restrictions.

valueAddition.title: Why India Still Imports Coal Despite Record Output
bullets: Geological Constraint: Indian Gondwana coal has high ash content (30–45%) and low calorific value, making it unsuitable for steel blast furnaces.

Coking vs. Non-Coking Split: Roughly 85–90% of India's coking coal requirement for steelmaking is imported (mainly from Australia, Russia, and the US), alongside some non-coking coal for imported-coal-based coastal power plants.

inNews.source: Ministry of Coal / Press Information Bureau (PIB)
inNews.headline: India launches 11th round of commercial coal mine auctions while pushing Mission Coking Coal to trim steel sector imports
inNews.relevance: Ministry of Coal data in September 2026 showed domestic output passing the 1-billion-tonne milestone, yet coking coal imports remained above 55 million tonnes due to domestic washery and reserve constraints.

statementBreakdown.explanation: The Government of India under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi nationalized coking coal mines in 1971–72 and non-coking coal mines in 1973, leading to the formation of Coal India Limited (CIL) in 1975.
Following the 2014 Supreme Court ruling cancelling discretionary allocations, coal blocks are allocated through competitive transparent e-auctions—not on a lottery basis.

India is not self-sufficient in coal; while domestic thermal coal production has crossed one billion tonnes, India continues to import substantial quantities of high-grade coking coal for steel plants and specific coastal thermal plants.

Under the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015, blocks are awarded via competitive e-auctions, not lotteries.
Despite record domestic output, India remains heavily dependent on imported coking coal for its steel industry.

keywords.shortNote: A monetary expenditure threshold (Monthly Per Capita Consumption Expenditure or MPCE) required to purchase a minimum basket of essential goods and services.
keywords.concept: Poverty Line: A monetary expenditure threshold (Monthly Per Capita Consumption Expenditure or MPCE) required to purchase a minimum basket of essential goods and services.

keywords.shortNote: The spatial divergence in the cost of identical reference baskets across States, captured via state-specific price indices like CPI-AL (rural) and CPI-IW (urban).
keywords.concept: Inter-State Price Level Variation: The spatial divergence in the cost of identical reference baskets across States, captured via state-specific price indices like CPI-AL (rural) and CPI-IW (urban).

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Poverty rate (headcount ratio) is the resulting outcome or proportion of people living below the threshold, not the cause of setting the monetary cut-off.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Official poverty lines are calibrated to State-specific price levels using indices (CPI-AL for rural, CPI-IW for urban) to ensure the uniform purchasing power of the national reference basket.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Gross State Domestic Product measures aggregate macroeconomic output and economic size, not consumer price indices or minimum consumption expenditure norms.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: While PDS efficiency influences private expenditure, official state-level poverty line variation is mathematically determined by regional price indices rather than administrative PDS quality.

valueAddition.title: Evolution of Poverty Line Methodology
bullets: Y.K. Alagh Task Force (1979): Established minimum daily calorie intake norms—2,400 kcal (rural) and 2,100 kcal (urban)—valued using national prices.
Lakdawala Committee (1993): Disaggregated national estimation by introducing State-specific poverty lines, adjusting them with CPI-AL for rural and CPI-IW for urban areas.

Tendulkar Committee (2009): Shifted from pure calorie counting to a uniform basket across rural and urban areas based on the urban consumption pattern, explicitly incorporating private health and education spending and adjusting for Fisher price indices.

C. Rangarajan Committee (2014): Proposed an independent rural and urban basket incorporating nutrition (calories, protein, fats) and essential non-food expenditure, recommending MPCE of ₹972 (rural) and ₹1,407 (urban) at 2011-12 prices.

valueAddition.title: State-Specific Price Indices & Spatial Cost of Living
bullets: A uniform nominal poverty line across India would distort poverty figures because purchasing power parity varies significantly between states.
CPI for Agricultural Labourers (CPI-AL) and CPI for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) were historically compiled by the Labour Bureau to adjust state-level price baskets.
Higher living and transport costs in states like Goa or Nagaland naturally inflate their nominal poverty thresholds above the national average.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) exchange rates are calculated by comparing the prices of the same basket of goods and services in different countries.
2. In terms of PPP dollars, India is the sixth largest economy in the world.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: An exchange rate conversion method that equalizes the purchasing power of different currencies by comparing the cost of an identical standardized basket of goods and services across countries, eliminating distortions caused by non-tradable service price differences.
keywords.concept: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP): An exchange rate conversion method that equalizes the purchasing power of different currencies by comparing the cost of an identical standardized basket of goods and services across countries, eliminating distortions caused by non-tradable service price differences.

keywords.shortNote: The prevailing spot foreign exchange rate determined by cross-border trade and capital flows in currency markets, used to convert national GDPs into nominal US dollars.
keywords.concept: Market Exchange Rate (MER): The prevailing spot foreign exchange rate determined by cross-border trade and capital flows in currency markets, used to convert national GDPs into nominal US dollars.

keywords.shortNote: The global statistical initiative coordinated by the World Bank that surveys retail prices of comparable goods and services worldwide to compute Purchasing Power Parities and real GDP levels.
keywords.concept: International Comparison Program (ICP): The global statistical initiative coordinated by the World Bank that surveys retail prices of comparable goods and services worldwide to compute Purchasing Power Parities and real GDP levels.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accurately defines how PPP exchange rates are computed while catching the false sixth-place ranking in Statement 2.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Confuses India's historical nominal-GDP position (around 5th/6th in 2018–19) with its long-standing 3rd-place rank in PPP terms.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks that India has ranked as the world's third-largest economy in PPP dollars since surpassing Japan over a decade ago.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Rejects the standard textbook definition of Purchasing Power Parity.

valueAddition.title: Why India's GDP Is Much Larger in PPP Dollars Than in Nominal Dollars
bullets: Market exchange rates reflect only internationally traded goods and financial flows, ignoring that non-tradable local services (haircuts, healthcare, housing, local transport, food) are dramatically cheaper in developing countries like India than in advanced economies.

Because one US dollar buys far more goods and services inside India than in the United States, converting India's rupee GDP at the PPP exchange rate multiplies its measured economic size—placing India firmly at #3 globally behind China (#1) and the United States (#2).

valueAddition.title: Nominal GDP vs. PPP GDP: When Economists Use Each
bullets: GDP in PPP Dollars is preferred for comparing domestic living standards, real output volume, and poverty lines across countries.
Nominal GDP (at Market Exchange Rates) is used for measuring international financial clout, sovereign borrowing capacity, external trade shares, and global capital market weight.

In PPP dollars, India is the third-largest economy in the world behind China and the United States.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to India's Five-Year Plans, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. From the Second Five-Year Plan, there was a determined thrust towards substitution of basic and capital good industries.
2. The Fourth Five-Year Plan adopted the objective of correcting the earlier trend of increased concentration of wealth and economic power.
3. In the Fifth Five-Year Plan, for the first time, the financial sector was included as an integral part of the Plan.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.

keywords.shortNote: The growth strategy adopted in the Second Five-Year Plan (1956–61) prioritizing rapid industrialization through public-sector investment in heavy, basic, and capital goods industries alongside import substitution.
keywords.concept: Nehru–Mahalanobis Model: The growth strategy adopted in the Second Five-Year Plan (1956–61) prioritizing rapid industrialization through public-sector investment in heavy, basic, and capital goods industries alongside import substitution.

keywords.shortNote: A trade and industrial policy aimed at replacing foreign imports of heavy machinery and intermediate goods with domestic production using protective tariffs and import licensing.
keywords.concept: Import Substitution Industrialization (ISI): A trade and industrial policy aimed at replacing foreign imports of heavy machinery and intermediate goods with domestic production using protective tariffs and import licensing.

keywords.term: Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act, 1969
keywords.shortNote: Legislation enacted during the Fourth Five-Year Plan period following the Hazari and Dutt Committee findings to prevent concentration of economic power in a few large industrial houses.
keywords.concept: Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act, 1969: Legislation enacted during the Fourth Five-Year Plan period following the Hazari and Dutt Committee findings to prevent concentration of economic power in a few large industrial houses.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Basic/capital goods import substitution defined the Second Plan and curbing wealth concentration anchored the Fourth Plan, whereas financial-sector integration entered in the Ninth Plan.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because the Second Five-Year Plan is universally defined by the Mahalanobis heavy and capital goods thrust.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because the financial sector became an integral chapter of planning only in the Ninth Five-Year Plan (1997–2002).

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because Statement 3 misattributes a Ninth Plan milestone to the Fifth Plan.

valueAddition.title: Core Themes & Milestones Across Key Five-Year Plans
bullets: First Plan (1951–56): Harrod–Domar model prioritizing agriculture, irrigation, and price stability; Second Plan (1956–61): Nehru–Mahalanobis strategy targeting heavy, basic, and capital goods industries.
Fourth Plan (1969–74): 'Growth with stability and progressive achievement of self-reliance'—curbed corporate concentration via the MRTP Act (1969) and nationalization of 14 major banks.

Fifth Plan (1974–79): 'Garibi Hatao' (poverty eradication) and self-reliance; Ninth Plan (1997–2002): 'Growth with social justice and equity'—integrated the financial sector into the Plan framework for the first time.

valueAddition.title: Why Financial Sector Integration Happened Only in the Ninth Plan
bullets: Pre-1991 Era: Under administered interest rates and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) preemption, banking acted mainly as a passive fiscal financing channel rather than a market-driven sector.

Post-1991 Reforms: Following the Narasimham Committee-I (1991) and capital-market liberalization, the Ninth Plan (1997–2002) formally incorporated financial-sector reform as an integral part of macroeconomic planning.

inNews.source: NITI Aayog / Ministry of Finance
inNews.headline: NITI Aayog Vision Viksit Bharat 2047 working papers contrast post-1991 market-led industrial policy with early Five-Year Plan import substitution
inNews.relevance: October 2026 NITI Aayog industrial strategy notes evaluated how India transitioned from Second Plan heavy-industry import substitution toward export-competitive manufacturing and deep financial markets.

statementBreakdown.reference: Second Five-Year Plan (1956–61) · Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956
statementBreakdown.explanation: Guided by the P.C. Mahalanobis model, the Second Plan shifted India's investment focus toward domestic production (import substitution) of basic and capital goods such as steel, heavy engineering, and machine tools.

statementBreakdown.reference: Fourth Five-Year Plan (1969–74) · Growth with Stability & Distributive Justice
statementBreakdown.explanation: Responding to the Mahalanobis Committee on Income Distribution and the Monopolies Inquiry Commission, the Fourth Plan explicitly adopted the goal of curbing concentration of wealth and economic power (marked by bank nationalization and the MRTP Act in 1969).

statementBreakdown.reference: Ninth Five-Year Plan (1997–2002) · Financial Sector Integration
statementBreakdown.explanation: The financial sector was included as an integral part of the Plan document for the first time in the Ninth Five-Year Plan (1997–2002) following post-1991 banking and capital-market reforms—not in the Fifth Plan (1974–79).

The Fourth Plan (1969–74) explicitly targeted reducing concentration of wealth and economic power.
The financial sector was integrated into the Plan document for the first time in the Ninth Five-Year Plan, not the Fifth.

answer.label: A
answer.text: Statements 1 and 2 are correct—basic goods marked the Second Plan and anti-concentration marked the Fourth, while the financial sector entered in the Ninth Plan.
