subject: Economy
stem: With reference to land reforms in independent India, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The ceiling laws were aimed at family holdings and not individual holdings.
options.label: a

options.text: The major aim of land reforms was providing agricultural land to all the landless.
options.label: b

options.text: It resulted in cultivation of cash crops as a predominant form of cultivation.
options.label: c

options.text: Land reforms permitted no exemptions to the ceiling limits.
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: A comprehensive institutional framework aimed at restructuring agrarian relations through four core measures: abolition of intermediaries (zamindari), tenancy reforms, land ceilings and redistribution of surplus land to the landless, and consolidation of holdings.
keywords.concept: Land Reforms in Post-Independence India: A comprehensive institutional framework aimed at restructuring agrarian relations through four core measures: abolition of intermediaries (zamindari), tenancy reforms, land ceilings and redistribution of surplus land to the landless, and consolidation of holdings.

keywords.shortNote: Statutory limits imposed on the maximum quantum of agricultural land an entity could hold. Initially fixed on individual holdings in the 1950s/1960s, then revised in 1972 under national guidelines to focus on a family unit.
keywords.concept: Land Ceiling Acts: Statutory limits imposed on the maximum quantum of agricultural land an entity could hold. Initially fixed on individual holdings in the 1950s/1960s, then revised in 1972 under national guidelines to focus on a family unit.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Initially, ceiling laws were widely framed around individual holdings, allowing landowners to evade ceilings through family subdivisions.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: The primary socio-economic mandate of land reforms was redistributive justice—transferring ownership rights to the tiller and distributing surplus land to the landless.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Indian agriculture remained heavily foodgrain-centric; cash crop commercialization was not the driving result of land reforms.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Numerous exemptions (plantations, orchards, trusts, cooperative farms) were explicitly permitted under state ceiling legislations.

valueAddition.title: Four Pillars of Indian Land Reforms
bullets: Abolition of Intermediaries: Dismantled the parasitic Zamindari, Jagirdari, and Ryotwari rent-receiving layers; successfully brought roughly 20 million cultivators into direct relationship with the state.

Tenancy Reforms: Aimed at three targets—regulation of exorbitant rents (capped at 1/4th to 1/5th of produce), security of tenure against arbitrary eviction, and conferring ownership rights on long-term tenants.

Ceiling on Land Holdings: Imposition of upper statutory limits on agricultural holdings to mop up surplus land for redistribution to Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and landless agricultural labourers.

Consolidation of Land Holdings: Regrouping fragmented land parcels into contiguous operational plots to boost agricultural productivity and irrigation efficiency (most successful in Punjab, Haryana, and Western UP).

valueAddition.title: Evolution of Ceiling Legislation: 1950s vs. 1972 Guidelines
bullets: First Phase (1950s-1960s): Ceilings were enacted with wide variations between states. Most states fixed ceilings on an 'individual' rather than 'family' basis and permitted generous exemptions, resulting in massive benami transfers and fictitious partitions.

National Guidelines of 1972: Formulated to rectify systemic evasion. Key reforms included: (1) adopting a uniform 'family of five' (husband, wife, and three minor children) as the unit of application; (2) lowering ceilings to 10-18 acres for land with assured two-crop perennial irrigation, 27 acres for single-crop irrigated land, and 54 acres for dry/unirrigated land; (3) abolishing most exemptions, except for tea, coffee, and rubber plantations.

Constitutional Protection (Ninth Schedule): Article 31B protected land reform laws from judicial review on fundamental rights grounds (Articles 14, 19, 31), though later qualified by the Kesavananda Bharati (1973) basic structure test.

inNews.source: PIB / Ministry of Rural Development
inNews.headline: Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme (DILRMP) achieves 95% spatial record digitization, securing land title rights for marginal farmers
inNews.relevance: Reflects modern institutional follow-through on tenancy security and cadastral accuracy, completing the historical agenda of post-independence land reforms.

statementBreakdown.reference: First & Second Five-Year Plans / State Land Ceiling Legislations
statementBreakdown.explanation: During the first phase of land reforms in the 1950s and 1960s, ceiling legislation enacted across most states specified the individual as the unit of assessment, which allowed large landowners to transfer parcels to family members (benami transfers). Only after the 1972 National Guidelines was the family made the uniform basis of ceiling laws.

statementBreakdown.reference: Planning Commission · Five-Year Plans & Agrarian Policy
statementBreakdown.explanation: The overarching socio-economic objective of land reforms was redistributive equity: breaking feudal land monopolies, vesting land in the actual tiller, and acquiring surplus land above ceiling limits to distribute among landless agricultural labourers and marginal tenants.

statementBreakdown.reference: NCERT Class XI Indian Economic Development · Chapter 2
statementBreakdown.explanation: Land reforms did not make cash crop cultivation predominant. Food grains remained the overwhelming focus of Indian agriculture, particularly reinforced by the Green Revolution in the late 1960s to ensure national food security.

statementBreakdown.reference: Bipan Chandra (India Since Independence) · Agrarian Reforms
statementBreakdown.explanation: Ceiling laws contained extensive exemptions: plantations (tea, coffee, rubber), sugarcane farms operated by sugar factories, orchards, cattle-breeding farms, religious/charitable trusts, and efficiently managed mechanized farms. These loopholes severely diluted surplus land acquisition.

visualSuggestion.title: Land Reforms: Objectives vs. Implementation Reality

Security of tenure, fair rent, ownership rights
Massive informal evictions via 'voluntary surrenders' and personal cultivation claims
Distribute surplus land to landless agricultural labour
Evasion via benami transfers, individual-unit loopholes, and generous exemptions (plantations, trusts)
Reduce plot fragmentation to boost scale
Highly successful in NW India (Punjab, Haryana); sluggish in Eastern and Southern states

activePhrases: The major aim of land reforms was providing agricultural land to all the landless

The primary socio-economic aim was breaking feudal monopolies and granting surplus land to the landless.
Land reforms did not make cash crops predominant; foodgrains remained the primary national focus.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Providing land to the landless was the core objective of land reforms, making (b) the correct answer.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. Most of India's external debt is owed by governmental entities.
2. All of India's external debt is denominated in US dollars.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: Sovereign debt comprises external debt owed directly by the Government of India, while non-sovereign debt covers external commercial borrowings (ECBs), trade credits, and banking capital owed by private and commercial entities.
keywords.concept: Sovereign vs. Non-Sovereign External Debt: Sovereign debt comprises external debt owed directly by the Government of India, while non-sovereign debt covers external commercial borrowings (ECBs), trade credits, and banking capital owed by private and commercial entities.

keywords.shortNote: The currency composition of external debt indicates foreign exchange exposure; while the US dollar holds the largest share, significant debt is also denominated in Indian Rupee, Yen, SDRs, and Euro.
keywords.concept: Currency Denomination of Debt: The currency composition of external debt indicates foreign exchange exposure; while the US dollar holds the largest share, significant debt is also denominated in Indian Rupee, Yen, SDRs, and Euro.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Non-governmental entities owe roughly 80% of India's external obligations.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: India's debt is multi-currency, with substantial rupee-denominated and yen-denominated debt.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to identify the factual flaws in both statements.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: Neither statement 1 nor statement 2 is correct
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements are factually incorrect, making (d) the correct answer.

valueAddition.title: Components & Borrowing Channels of India's External Debt
bullets: External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs): The single largest component of India's external debt, accounting for roughly 32% to 34% of the total, borrowed directly by domestic corporates from foreign lenders.
Non-Resident Indian (NRI) Deposits: Constitutes approximately 22% to 24% of external debt (FCNR-B, NRE, and NRO accounts).
Short-Term Trade Credit: Accounts for around 18% to 20% of external debt, primarily consisting of supplier's and buyer's credit for merchandise imports.
Multilateral & Bilateral Sovereign Debt: Concessional and development loans from the World Bank, ADB, JICA, etc., which form the bulk of the government's external borrowings.

valueAddition.title: Currency Composition & External Vulnerability Indicators
bullets: Currency Breakdown: US Dollar-denominated debt is dominant (~54%), followed by Indian Rupee-denominated debt (~31%), SDRs (~5.5%), Japanese Yen (~5%), and Euro (~3%).

Significance of Rupee-Denominated Debt: External debt denominated in INR (like Masala Bonds or foreign portfolio investment in domestic G-Secs) carries zero direct foreign exchange exchange-rate risk for the domestic borrower, shielding the economy from currency depreciation shocks.

Prudential Vulnerability Ratios: External Debt-to-GDP ratio for India hovers comfortably between 18% and 20%, and foreign exchange reserves generally provide over 90% to 100% cover for total external debt, signifying strong external solvency.

inNews.source: RBI / Ministry of Finance
inNews.headline: India's external debt-to-GDP ratio remains resilient at 18.7% with non-sovereign commercial debt leading corporate capex borrowings
inNews.relevance: Directly reaffirms that private commercial borrowers account for the lion's share of India's external debt obligations, and highlights the ongoing dominance of the US dollar alongside rupee-denominated debt.

statementBreakdown.reference: RBI External Debt Statistics & MoF External Debt Status Report
statementBreakdown.explanation: Non-sovereign (commercial/private) debt constitutes the overwhelming majority of India's external debt (typically around 75% to 80%), driven by External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs), NRI deposits, and short-term trade credits. Sovereign (Government) external debt accounts for only about 20% to 22% of total external debt.

statementBreakdown.reference: RBI Currency Composition of External Debt
statementBreakdown.explanation: Not all external debt is in US dollars. While the US dollar is the largest single currency component (accounting for roughly 53% to 55%), substantial portions are denominated in Indian Rupee (~30% to 32%), Japanese Yen (~5% to 6%), SDRs, and Euro. The absolute word 'All' makes the statement factually incorrect.

subject: Economy
stem:
In the context of India, which ofthe following factors is/are contributor/ contributors to reducing the risk of a currency crisis?
1. The foreign currency earnings of India's IT sector
2. Increasing the government expenditure
3. Remittances from Indians abroad
Select the correct answer using the code given below.

keywords.shortNote: A severe and rapid depreciation in the external value of a domestic currency accompanied by acute depletion of foreign exchange reserves, typically triggered by unsustainable current account deficits or sudden capital outflows.
keywords.concept: Currency Crisis: A severe and rapid depreciation in the external value of a domestic currency accompanied by acute depletion of foreign exchange reserves, typically triggered by unsustainable current account deficits or sudden capital outflows.

keywords.shortNote: The non-merchandise balance of the Current Account comprising net services exports (such as IT/ITeS), private remittances (transfers), and net investment income, which offsets India's merchandise trade deficit.
keywords.concept: Net Invisibles: The non-merchandise balance of the Current Account comprising net services exports (such as IT/ITeS), private remittances (transfers), and net investment income, which offsets India's merchandise trade deficit.

keywords.shortNote: Unilateral foreign exchange inflows sent home by overseas Indian workers and diaspora, recorded as current transfers in the Current Account without creating any future repayment liability.
keywords.concept: Private Transfers (Remittances): Unilateral foreign exchange inflows sent home by overseas Indian workers and diaspora, recorded as current transfers in the Current Account without creating any future repayment liability.

keywords.shortNote: The macroeconomic vulnerability where an expansionary fiscal deficit spills over into higher domestic demand, inflation, and import growth, widening the Current Account Deficit and pressuring the domestic currency.
keywords.concept: Twin Deficit Problem: The macroeconomic vulnerability where an expansionary fiscal deficit spills over into higher domestic demand, inflation, and import growth, widening the Current Account Deficit and pressuring the domestic currency.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Misses the critical stabilizing role of overseas remittances, which consistently exceed $100 billion annually in India.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both IT service exports and diaspora remittances bring steady, non-debt foreign exchange into India, whereas higher government spending worsens fiscal and external balances.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Reverses basic open-economy macroeconomics—fiscal expansion increases inflation and import demand, putting downward pressure on the currency.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to recognize that unchecked fiscal expansion aggravates currency risk rather than reducing it.

valueAddition.title: Why IT Exports and Remittances Are India's Twin External Shields
bullets: India runs a chronic merchandise trade deficit driven by crude oil, gold, and electronics imports—left unchecked, a wide Current Account Deficit (CAD) triggers Rupee sell-offs.

Software/IT services exports and inward remittances together form the backbone of India's 'Net Invisibles' surplus, financing a major portion of the goods trade deficit without adding a single dollar of external debt.
Unlike volatile Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) 'hot money' that exits rapidly during global rate hikes, IT revenues and family remittances remain sticky and resilient during global downturns.

valueAddition.title: How Rising Government Expenditure Pressures the Currency
bullets: Higher government spending injects excess rupee liquidity and raises aggregate demand, stoking domestic inflation—which erodes the real competitiveness of Indian exports.
Simultaneously, higher domestic demand pulls in more imports, widening the Current Account Deficit and forcing the RBI to spend forex reserves to defend the Rupee.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) / World Bank
inNews.headline: India Retains Top Global Remittance Spot as Services Exports Cushion Merchandise Trade Gap
inNews.relevance: RBI Balance of Payments data released in September 2026 confirmed that record software service receipts and over $130 billion in inward remittances contained India's Current Account Deficit and stabilized the Rupee.

statementBreakdown.reference: RBI Balance of Payments — Services Exports
statementBreakdown.explanation: India's software and IT-enabled services exports generate a massive, stable net services surplus every year, supplying non-debt foreign exchange that cushions the Current Account Deficit and supports the Rupee.

Increasing government expenditure widens the fiscal deficit, fuels domestic inflation, and boosts import demand—weakening rather than strengthening the currency and heightening external vulnerability.

statementBreakdown.reference: RBI Balance of Payments — Secondary Income
statementBreakdown.explanation: Remittances from the Indian diaspora—the highest globally—provide steady, non-debt-creating foreign exchange inflows that bolster RBI's forex reserves and insulate the Rupee against external shocks.

visualSuggestion.title: Impact of Macroeconomic Flows on India's Currency Stability

rows: Current Account — Net Services Surplus (Non-debt FX inflow)
Reduces risk (builds forex reserves & offsets trade deficit)
Current Account — Private Transfers (Sticky non-debt FX inflow)
Reduces risk (provides steady dollar supply without debt obligation)
Widens Fiscal Deficit -> Higher inflation & import demand
Increases risk (aggravates Twin Deficit & weakens Rupee)

hook.headline: Does increasing government spending protect India from a currency crisis?
hook.teaser: Notice how spotting one basic fiscal-external link knocks out two options immediately.

keywords.calloutNote: Higher government spending widens the fiscal deficit, stokes inflation, and pulls in more imports—weakening the Rupee rather than protecting it.
activePhrases: Increasing the government expenditure

keywords.calloutNote: Alongside IT export earnings, diaspora remittances bring steady, non-debt dollars into India that cushion the Current Account Deficit.
activePhrases: Remittances from Indians abroad
dimmedPhrases: Increasing the government expenditure
contextPhrases: foreign currency earnings of India's IT sector

verdicts.source: Foreign currency earned by India's IT sector creates a massive services surplus that offsets our merchandise trade deficit and supports the Rupee.
Increasing government expenditure widens the fiscal deficit, fuels domestic inflation, and raises import demand—increasing currency pressure.
Remittances from Indians abroad supply sticky, debt-free foreign exchange that strengthens RBI reserves against external shocks.

answer.label: B
answer.text: IT exports and overseas remittances bring steady dollars while higher government spending worsens deficits—so 1 and 3 only is right.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your External Sector notes

items.title: Invisibles Offset Trade Gap
items.desc: IT services exports and remittances sit under Net Invisibles in the Current Account, financing India's oil and gold import gap.

items.title: Sticky vs. Hot Money
items.desc: Remittances and IT receipts are non-debt inflows that stay steady even when volatile FPI portfolio funds flee.

items.title: Twin Deficit Linkage
items.desc: An expansionary fiscal deficit spills over into higher imports and a wider Current Account Deficit, pressuring the exchange rate.

valueAddition.note: In Balance of Payments questions, always separate inflows that earn foreign exchange (exports, remittances, FDI) from domestic rupee spending that fuels imports.

options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: Flagship umbrella national initiative launched to cultivate innovation and an entrepreneurial ecosystem across schools, universities, and industry.
keywords.concept: Atal Innovation Mission (AIM): Flagship umbrella national initiative launched to cultivate innovation and an entrepreneurial ecosystem across schools, universities, and industry.

keywords.shortNote: The premier policy think-tank of the Government of India, acting as the nodal institutional host for national developmental initiatives.
keywords.concept: NITI Aayog: The premier policy think-tank of the Government of India, acting as the nodal institutional host for national developmental initiatives.

valueAddition.title: What is Atal Innovation Mission (AIM)?
bullets: Origin & Custodian: Announced in the 2015 Union Budget and set up under NITI Aayog to create an umbrella innovation framework spanning schools, startups, and research institutions.
Dual Core Mandate: Promoting entrepreneurship through self-employment and talent utilization (SETU), and creating innovation hubs that foster problem-solving from classrooms to industry.

Atal New India Challenges (ANIC) & ARISE: Targeted grant-in-aid challenges aimed at developing market-ready tech solutions for national challenges and MSMEs.
Mentor India & AIM iCREST: Ecosystem capacity-building initiatives pairing corporate leaders with innovators and strengthening incubator management.

subject: Economy
stem: Which of the following is issued by registered foreign portfolio investors to overseas investors who want to be part of Indian stock market without registering themselves directly?

keywords.shortNote: An Offshore Derivative Instrument (ODI) issued overseas by a SEBI-registered Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI) against underlying Indian securities, enabling unregistered foreign investors to gain economic exposure to Indian equities or debt.
keywords.concept: Participatory Note (P-Note): An Offshore Derivative Instrument (ODI) issued overseas by a SEBI-registered Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI) against underlying Indian securities, enabling unregistered foreign investors to gain economic exposure to Indian equities or debt.

keywords.shortNote: Any financial instrument issued outside India by a registered FPI that derives its value from underlying securities listed or proposed to be listed on an Indian stock exchange.
keywords.concept: Offshore Derivative Instrument (ODI): Any financial instrument issued outside India by a registered FPI that derives its value from underlying securities listed or proposed to be listed on an Indian stock exchange.

keywords.shortNote: A negotiable, unsecured short-term money market instrument issued in dematerialized form by scheduled commercial banks and All-India Financial Institutions against funds deposited for a fixed maturity.
keywords.concept: Certificate of Deposit (CD): A negotiable, unsecured short-term money market instrument issued in dematerialized form by scheduled commercial banks and All-India Financial Institutions against funds deposited for a fixed maturity.

keywords.shortNote: An unsecured, short-term corporate promissory note issued at a discount by creditworthy companies, primary dealers, and financial institutions to raise working capital for tenors between 7 days and 1 year.
keywords.concept: Commercial Paper (CP): An unsecured, short-term corporate promissory note issued at a discount by creditworthy companies, primary dealers, and financial institutions to raise working capital for tenors between 7 days and 1 year.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Certificates of Deposit are short-term wholesale money market instruments issued by scheduled commercial banks and financial institutions to raise domestic liquidity, not offshore equity derivatives.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Commercial Paper is an unsecured short-term debt instrument issued by highly rated domestic corporates for working capital, unrelated to foreign portfolio access.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: A Promissory Note is a generic written unconditional promise to pay a specified sum of money—a distractor phrased to sound visually similar to Participatory Note.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Participatory Notes are issued offshore by SEBI-registered FPIs to foreign investors seeking returns from Indian equities without undergoing direct SEBI KYC and registration.

valueAddition.title: How Participatory Notes Work on the Ground
bullets: A foreign hedge fund or high-net-worth investor wanting exposure to Indian stocks without setting up local tax, compliance, and SEBI registration infrastructure buys a P-Note offshore from a registered FPI (such as a global investment bank).

The registered FPI buys the actual shares on the NSE or BSE in its own name and passes the economic returns (dividends and capital gains) to the P-Note holder while retaining legal title and voting rights.

Because P-Notes historically masked the ultimate beneficial owner, SEBI tightened norms—mandating strict KYC/AML disclosures, banning P-Notes with naked derivatives as underlying assets, and levying regulatory fees on ODI subscribers.

valueAddition.title: Separating Money Market Notes from Offshore Equity Instruments
bullets: Certificates of Deposit (CDs) and Commercial Papers (CPs) are domestic short-term money market debt instruments with maturities of up to 1 year, regulated by the RBI.
Participatory Notes are offshore capital market derivative instruments linked to Indian shares or bonds, regulated by SEBI through the issuing FPI.

inNews.relevance: SEBI tightened granular ultimate beneficial owner reporting for P-Note and ODI holders exceeding concentration thresholds in August 2026 to prevent regulatory arbitrage around FPI disclosure rules.

verdicts.source: Certificates of Deposit are short-term debt instruments issued by Indian banks to raise domestic liquidity, not offshore equity instruments.
Commercial Paper is issued by Indian companies for short-term working capital up to one year.
A Promissory Note is just a general legal promise to pay under the Negotiable Instruments Act—placed here only to look like Participatory Note.
Participatory Notes are issued overseas by SEBI-registered FPIs so foreign investors can participate in Indian markets without direct SEBI registration.

keywords.concept: selected by: Denotes the screening and recommendatory headhunting bureau, not the final notifying body (ACC).

keywords.concept: Banks Board Bureau: Set up in 2016 on P.J. Nayak Committee recommendations; replaced in July 2022 by the Financial Services Institutions Bureau (FSIB).

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Banks Board Bureau (BBB) was set up in 2016 to shortlist whole-time directors and non-executive chairpersons for PSBs. Since July 1, 2022, FSIB performs this exact selection role.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: RBI grants mandatory regulatory approval for private bank MD/CEO appointments, but does not select public sector bank heads.

optionBreakdown.label: c

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Public sector bank boards cannot appoint their own leadership; candidate selection is centralized through the autonomous bureau.

valueAddition.title: BBB to FSIB Transition
bullets: Genesis: Recommended by the P.J. Nayak Committee (2014) to depoliticize state-run bank appointments; operationalized in 2016 under Mission Indradhanush.
Legal Challenge: In 2021, Delhi HC held BBB lacked statutory authority to select directors for state-run general insurers under its original notification.
FSIB Overhaul (2022): Government replaced BBB with the Financial Services Institutions Bureau (FSIB) on July 1, 2022 via a DFS resolution.
Current Scope: Recommends whole-time directors and non-executive chairpersons for PSBs, public sector insurers (LIC, GIC Re), and FIs (NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, EXIM).

valueAddition.title: Selection vs Appointment Pipeline
bullets: Recommending Authority: FSIB screens, interviews, and forwards candidate panels to the Department of Financial Services (DFS).
Final Approving Body: Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC), headed by the Prime Minister, issues the formal appointment orders.
Governing Framework: Banking Companies (Acquisition & Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, 1970 & 1980; SBI Act, 1955 for State Bank of India.
Private Bank Contrast: Private boards select candidates via Nomination & Remuneration Committees, subject to prior RBI approval under Sec 35B of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

stem: The Service Area Approach was implemented under the purview of

options.text: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme
options.label: c

keywords.shortNote: An operational strategy introduced by the RBI in April 1989 where each semi-urban and rural commercial bank branch was allocated 15 to 25 contiguous villages to plan and monitor credit delivery.
keywords.concept: Service Area Approach (SAA): An operational strategy introduced by the RBI in April 1989 where each semi-urban and rural commercial bank branch was allocated 15 to 25 contiguous villages to plan and monitor credit delivery.

keywords.shortNote: Introduced in late 1969 on the recommendations of the Gadgil Study Group and Nariman Committee, assigning specific districts to designated banks to act as lead institutions for coordinated district credit planning.
keywords.concept: Lead Bank Scheme (LBS): Introduced in late 1969 on the recommendations of the Gadgil Study Group and Nariman Committee, assigning specific districts to designated banks to act as lead institutions for coordinated district credit planning.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: IRDP was a government subsidy-cum-bank-credit anti-poverty scheme for self-employment; while bank branches financed IRDP beneficiaries within allocated villages, SAA was not an administrative arm of IRDP.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Introduced with effect from April 1, 1989, the Service Area Approach was designed as an operational modification of the Lead Bank Scheme to forge a direct, purposeful link between rural bank branches and village-level credit planning.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: MGNREGA is a statutory wage-employment guarantee enacted over 15 years after SAA was launched; its banking interface is limited to direct benefit transfer (DBT) wage payments.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (2015)
optionBreakdown.explanation: NSDM was launched in 2015 to converge skill training initiatives across sectors, having no historical or institutional connection to rural credit zoning.

valueAddition.title: Lead Bank Scheme & SAA Mechanics
bullets: Genesis of SAA: Recommended in 1988 by an RBI committee chaired by Deputy Governor P.D. Ojha; made operational on April 1, 1989 under the Lead Bank Scheme umbrella.

Core Mechanism: Each rural and semi-urban branch of commercial banks and Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) was assigned a designated service area of 15–25 contiguous villages for economic survey, credit planning, and end-use monitoring.

Relaxation of SAA (2004): Following recommendations of the Vyas Committee, the mandatory exclusivity of the service area was dispensed with in December 2004 for all loans except government-sponsored schemes, allowing farmers to borrow from any bank branch of their choice.

valueAddition.title: Committees on Rural Credit & Banking Cadre
bullets: Gadgil Study Group (1969) & Nariman Committee (1969): Recommended area approach to banking, which gave birth to the Lead Bank Scheme (districts allocated to specific commercial banks).

District Coordination Framework: Lead Bank Scheme institutionalized the District Consultative Committee (DCC), chaired by the District Collector/Magistrate, to review the Annual Credit Plan prepared by the Lead District Manager (LDM).
Bhasin Committee (2009) & Usha Thorat Committee (2009): Reviewed the Lead Bank Scheme to reorient it from mere physical branch allocation to full financial inclusion and digital payment connectivity.

subject: Economy
stem: Which of the following is not included in the assets of a commercial bank in India?

options.text: Money at call and short notice
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: Resources owned or claims held by the bank that generate interest or income, including loans given, government securities, cash reserves, and interbank lending.
keywords.concept: Assets of a commercial bank: Resources owned or claims held by the bank that generate interest or income, including loans given, government securities, cash reserves, and interbank lending.

keywords.shortNote: Funds placed by customers (demand and time deposits) that the bank owes back on demand or maturity, making them the primary liability of a bank.
keywords.concept: Deposits: Funds placed by customers (demand and time deposits) that the bank owes back on demand or maturity, making them the primary liability of a bank.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.reference: Schedule 9, Form A, Banking Regulation Act, 1949
optionBreakdown.explanation: Advances (loans, cash credits, and overdrafts extended to borrowers) are assets because the borrower owes that principal and interest back to the bank.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: Schedule 3, Form A, Banking Regulation Act, 1949
optionBreakdown.explanation: Deposits represent money owed by the bank to its depositors; under bank accounting, they sit strictly on the liabilities side of the balance sheet.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: Schedule 8, Form A, Banking Regulation Act, 1949
optionBreakdown.explanation: Investments in government securities (SLR requirements), PSU bonds, and commercial paper earn interest/dividends and are listed as assets.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: Schedule 7, Form A, Banking Regulation Act, 1949
optionBreakdown.explanation: Money at call (repayable in 1 day) and short notice (up to 14 days) lent in the interbank market represents short-term claims against other banks, categorized as assets.

valueAddition.title: Bank Balance Sheet: Assets vs Liabilities
bullets: Statutory Format: Regulated under Section 29 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949; Form A of the Third Schedule lays down standard schedules.
Liabilities (What bank owes): Capital (Sched 1), Reserves & Surplus (Sched 2), Deposits (Sched 3), Borrowings (Sched 4), and Other Liabilities/Provisions (Sched 5).
Assets (What bank owns/claims): Cash with RBI (Sched 6), Balances with other banks & Call/Short Money (Sched 7), Investments (Sched 8), Advances (Sched 9), and Fixed Assets (Sched 10).

valueAddition.title: Liquidity Order of Bank Assets
bullets: Liquidity Ladder: Assets are arranged in descending order of liquidity—from Cash in hand/with RBI (highest liquidity, zero yield) to Advances (lowest liquidity, highest yield).
Money at Call & Short Notice: Serves as a bank's immediate liquidity buffer right after physical cash, deployed in the overnight and interbank call-money market.
Core Examiner Trap: Aspirants often confuse customer perception with bank accounting; money deposited is an asset for the individual, but a strict liability for the bank.

subject: Economy
stem: Which one of the following is not the most likely measure the Government/RBI takes to stop the slide of Indian rupee?

options.text: Curbing imports of non-essential goods and promoting exports
options.label: a

options.text: Encouraging Indian borrowers to issue rupee denominated Masala Bonds
options.label: b

options.text: Easing conditions relating to external commercial borrowing
options.label: c

keywords.shortNote: Depreciation of the rupee driven by high demand for foreign currency (dollars) relative to domestic currency supply in the forex market.
keywords.concept: Depreciation of Indian rupee: Depreciation of the rupee driven by high demand for foreign currency (dollars) relative to domestic currency supply in the forex market.

keywords.shortNote: Central bank policy of cutting policy rates and infusing liquidity, which lowers interest rates, reduces foreign yield differentials, and accelerates capital outflows.
keywords.concept: Expansionary monetary policy: Central bank policy of cutting policy rates and infusing liquidity, which lowers interest rates, reduces foreign yield differentials, and accelerates capital outflows.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Curbing non-essential imports reduces dollar outflows, while boosting exports increases dollar inflows; this directly stabilizes the rupee.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Masala bonds are rupee-denominated overseas borrowings where currency risk sits with foreign investors; issuing them brings foreign capital without creating rupee-depreciation exchange risk for Indian firms.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: RBI Master Direction on ECB Framework
optionBreakdown.explanation: Liberalizing ECB rules (raising borrowing caps, lowering hedging costs) encourages companies to bring dollars into India, boosting dollar supply and arresting the rupee's slide.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: An expansionary monetary policy cuts repo rates and pumps domestic liquidity, narrowing the interest rate differential between India and the US; this triggers capital flight and depreciates the rupee further.

valueAddition.title: Forex Stabilization
bullets: Monetary Defense: To halt currency depreciation, central banks implement monetary tightening (hiking interest rates or draining domestic liquidity) to prevent carry-trade flight.
Capital Account Interventions: RBI opens special windows for FPI debt limits, eases External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) limits, and relaxes FCNR(B) deposit caps to pull in dollars.
Direct Market Intervention: Selling foreign exchange from forex reserves while soaking up domestic currency directly combats speculative depreciation runs.

valueAddition.title: Masala Bonds & Currency Risk Shift
bullets: Concept: Rupee-denominated debt papers floated by Indian entities in overseas capital markets (pioneered by IFC in 2013 and HDFC in 2016).
Exchange Risk Allocation: Foreign investors shoulder the currency risk; if the rupee weakens, repayment liability for the Indian issuer does not expand.
Core Trap: Candidates often assume issuing bonds abroad always increases domestic currency risk; Masala bonds explicitly transfer exchange volatility to overseas buyers.

inNews.relevance: Directly applies the exact macro-stabilization playbook tested in this PYQ, using liberalized foreign debt avenues and selective forex market operations to anchor rupee volatility.

Rupee-denominated Masala bonds attract foreign capital without transferring exchange risk to domestic borrowers.
Relaxing external borrowing rules increases dollar inflows into Indian markets, strengthening the rupee.
Rate cuts lower returns for foreign investors, triggering capital flight and worsening the currency slide.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
As per the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central (Amendment) Rules, 2018
1. if rules for fixed-term employment are implemented, it becomes easier for the firms/companies to lay off workers
2. no notice of termination of employment shall be necessary in the case of temporary workman
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: A direct contractual engagement of a workman for a predetermined duration with statutory parity in wages and social security, but expiring automatically without retrenchment compensation or mandatory prior notice.
keywords.concept: Fixed-Term Employment (FTE): A direct contractual engagement of a workman for a predetermined duration with statutory parity in wages and social security, but expiring automatically without retrenchment compensation or mandatory prior notice.

keywords.shortNote: A category of worker engaged for work essentially temporary in nature, whose employment can be terminated upon cessation of the job without advance notice, provided it is not by way of punishment.
keywords.concept: Temporary Workman: A category of worker engaged for work essentially temporary in nature, whose employment can be terminated upon cessation of the job without advance notice, provided it is not by way of punishment.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Ignores the statutory rule under Paragraph 13(2) exempting employers from serving termination notice to temporary workmen.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks the structural flexibilities introduced by the 2018 rules where contract expiry avoids retrenchment hurdles.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements accurately reflect the provisions: FTE facilitates contract expiration without retrenchment burdens, and temporary workmen require no advance termination notice.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both provisions are verbatim interpretations of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central Rules framework.

valueAddition.title: Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central Rules, 2018
bullets: Universal Coverage: Extended Fixed-Term Employment (FTE) across all industrial sectors; previously, it was restricted only to the apparel and garment manufacturing sector in 2016.
Statutory Parity: Mandated that hours of work, wages, allowances, and statutory benefits of FTE workers cannot be lower than those of permanent workmen doing identical work.
Gratuity Eligibility: Fixed-term employees are eligible for pro-rata statutory benefits, including gratuity even if they do not complete the continuous 5-year service threshold under standard rules.

valueAddition.title: Codification under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020
bullets: Subsumed Acts: The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes the Trade Unions Act (1926), Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act (1946), and Industrial Disputes Act (1947).
Section 2(o) Definition: Formally codified 'fixed term employment' into the substantive Code with full statutory backing.
Threshold Elevation: Raised the threshold for mandatory prior government permission for lay-off, retrenchment, and closure from 100 to 300 workers.

statementBreakdown.reference: Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central (Amendment) Rules, 2018 — Item 7A & Rule 5
statementBreakdown.explanation: Fixed-term employment allows contracts to expire automatically at the end of the stipulated period. Under Section 2(oo)(bb) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, non-renewal of an FTE contract does not constitute 'retrenchment', exempting companies from notice periods, retrenchment compensation, or government permissions for separation.

statementBreakdown.reference: Schedule I, Paragraph 13(2) of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central Rules, 1946 / 2018 Amendment
statementBreakdown.explanation: Paragraph 13(2) specifically provides that no temporary workman—whether monthly-rated, weekly-rated, or piece-rated—shall be entitled to any notice or pay in lieu of notice if their services are terminated, unless agreed otherwise under contract.

hook.headline: Can companies fire contract workers without giving notice?
hook.teaser: Look at the fine print of India's labour rules—this trap tripped hundreds of aspirants.

activePhrases: easier for the firms/companies to lay off workers

verdicts.source: Non-renewal of a fixed contract isn't treated as retrenchment under Section 2(oo)(bb), giving firms significant flexibility.
Schedule I states verbatim that no notice of termination is required for temporary workmen unless specified in the contract.

answer.label: C
answer.text: Both statements are correct under the 2018 Standing Orders Rules.

subject: Economy
stem: What was the purpose of Inter-Creditor Agreement signed by Indian banks and financial institutions recently?

options.text: To lessen the Government of India's perennial burden of fiscal deficit and current account deficit
options.label: a

options.text: To support the infrastructure projects of Central and State Governments
options.label: b

options.text: To act as independent regulator in case of applications for loans of Rs. 50 crore or more
options.label: c

options.text: To aim at faster resolution of stressed assets of Rs. 50 crore or more which are under consortium lending
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: A contractual pact signed among lenders under Project SASHAKT to establish majority voting rules for time-bound resolution of stressed consortium loans without waiting for unanimous consent.
keywords.concept: Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA): A contractual pact signed among lenders under Project SASHAKT to establish majority voting rules for time-bound resolution of stressed consortium loans without waiting for unanimous consent.

keywords.shortNote: An arrangement where several banks collectively finance a large borrower to spread credit risk, governed by coordinated joint decision-making.
keywords.concept: Consortium lending: An arrangement where several banks collectively finance a large borrower to spread credit risk, governed by coordinated joint decision-making.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Twin deficit management involves fiscal consolidation and export-import balance, not inter-bank resolution protocols for commercial bad loans.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: National Infrastructure Pipeline & Development Finance Institutions
optionBreakdown.explanation: Infrastructure funding is channeled through long-term specialized institutions like NaBFID and NIIF, whereas the ICA dealt specifically with recovering bad loans.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: The ICA is a lender contract, not an independent statutory regulator; statutory banking regulation is the exclusive domain of the RBI.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Signed in July 2018 following the Sunil Mehta Committee recommendations, the ICA aimed at expediting out-of-court resolution of stressed assets worth ₹50 crore or more under multi-banking or consortium arrangements.

valueAddition.title: Project SASHAKT & ICA Framework
bullets: Origin: Recommended by the Sunil Mehta Committee (July 2018) under Project SASHAKT to resolve non-performing loans outside the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).

Threshold Matrix: Under Project SASHAKT, loans up to ₹50 crore were resolved at the bank level within 90 days; ₹50 crore to ₹500 crore were tackled via the Inter-Creditor Agreement; loans above ₹500 crore involved Asset Management Companies (AMCs).

Majority Rule vs Holdout Problem: Overcame the traditional bottleneck where small dissenting lenders blocked resolutions; the lead lender implements the plan once approved by lenders representing 66% in aggregate value and 75% by number (under the revised RBI June 7, 2019 Prudential Framework).

valueAddition.title: RBI Prudential Framework (June 7, 2019)
bullets: Supreme Court Trigger: In Dharani Sugars (April 2019), the Supreme Court quashed the RBI's February 12, 2018 circular; RBI then issued the comprehensive June 7, 2019 Prudential Framework.
Mandatory ICA Execution: RBI made it legally mandatory for all regulated lenders to enter into an Inter-Creditor Agreement within a 30-day review period of default.
Timeline & Penalty: Imposes a 180-day resolution timeline from the default review period; failure to resolve or refer to IBC attracts additional bank provisioning of up to 35%.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India / Ministry of Finance
inNews.headline: Lenders sign revised Inter-Creditor Agreements under updated pre-IBC corporate debt resolution guidelines
inNews.relevance: Directly updates the inter-creditor mechanism tested in this PYQ, streamlining the binding majority voting framework between commercial banks and NBFCs for resolving large stressed accounts before formal NCLT admission.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB) is the first regulatory body set up by the Government of India.
2. One of the tasks of PNGRB is to ensure competitive markets for gas.
3. Appeals against the decisions of PNGRB go before the Appellate Tribunals for Electricity.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

keywords.term: Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB)
keywords.shortNote: A statutory downstream energy regulator established under the PNGRB Act, 2006 to regulate the refining, processing, storage, transportation, distribution, marketing, and sale of petroleum, petroleum products, and natural gas (excluding upstream crude oil and natural gas production).
keywords.concept: Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB): A statutory downstream energy regulator established under the PNGRB Act, 2006 to regulate the refining, processing, storage, transportation, distribution, marketing, and sale of petroleum, petroleum products, and natural gas (excluding upstream crude oil and natural gas production).

keywords.shortNote: A statutory appellate body established under Section 110 of the Electricity Act, 2003 that also serves as the designated appellate tribunal for orders and decisions passed by the PNGRB under Section 30 of the PNGRB Act, 2006.
keywords.concept: Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL): A statutory appellate body established under Section 110 of the Electricity Act, 2003 that also serves as the designated appellate tribunal for orders and decisions passed by the PNGRB under Section 30 of the PNGRB Act, 2006.

keywords.shortNote: An interconnected pipeline network authorized and regulated by PNGRB to supply Piped Natural Gas (PNG) to households and industries and Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) to vehicles within designated Geographical Areas.
keywords.concept: City Gas Distribution (CGD) Network: An interconnected pipeline network authorized and regulated by PNGRB to supply Piped Natural Gas (PNG) to households and industries and Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) to vehicles within designated Geographical Areas.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated immediately because SEBI, TRAI, CERC, and IRDAI all predate the 2006 PNGRB Act.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: PNGRB promotes competitive downstream gas markets and routes its appeals to the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), while being far from India's first regulatory body.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because PNGRB was established in 2007, not as India's first regulatory authority.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because Statement 1 makes a false 'first regulatory body' superlative claim.

valueAddition.title: Upstream vs. Downstream Regulatory Split in Oil & Gas
bullets: Downstream Regulated by PNGRB: Refining, processing, storage, pipelines, City Gas Distribution (CNG/PNG), and retail marketing—excluding crude oil and natural gas production.

Upstream Overseen by DGH: Exploration, licensing (HELP/OALP blocks), and production of crude oil and natural gas fall under the Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH) under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, not PNGRB.

valueAddition.title: Why APTEL Hears PNGRB Appeals
bullets: Shared Energy Appellate Forum: Rather than creating a separate tribunal for natural gas disputes, Parliament designated the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL, set up under the Electricity Act, 2003) as the common appellate body for PNGRB decisions, with further appeal lying to the Supreme Court.

statementBreakdown.reference: PNGRB Act, 2006 · Chronology of Indian Regulators
statementBreakdown.explanation: PNGRB was established in 2007 under the PNGRB Act of 2006—decades after earlier statutory regulators such as SEBI (1992), TRAI (1997), IRDAI (1999), and CERC (1998).

statementBreakdown.reference: PNGRB Act, 2006 · Section 11(a) (Functions of the Board)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Section 11 of the PNGRB Act explicitly mandates the Board to protect consumer interests by fostering fair trade and competition amongst entities in downstream petroleum and natural gas markets.

Under Section 30 of the PNGRB Act, 2006, the Appellate Tribunal established under Section 110 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (APTEL) acts as the Appellate Tribunal for hearing appeals against PNGRB orders.

visualSuggestion.title: India's Energy & Infrastructure Regulators vs. Appellate Bodies

rows: Downstream refining, pipelines, CGD & gas marketing

hook.headline: Do appeals against India's gas regulator really go to the Electricity Tribunal?
hook.teaser: Yes—and eliminating Statement 1's 'first regulatory body' claim solves this question in seconds.

keywords.term: first regulatory body set up by the Government of India
keywords.calloutNote: PNGRB was set up under the 2006 Act—long after statutory regulators like SEBI (1992), TRAI (1997), and CERC (1998).
activePhrases: first regulatory body set up by the Government of India

keywords.calloutNote: Under Section 30 of the PNGRB Act, 2006, APTEL serves as the designated appellate forum for PNGRB decisions.
activePhrases: Appellate Tribunals for Electricity
dimmedPhrases: first regulatory body set up by the Government of India
contextPhrases: Appeals against the decisions of PNGRB

verdicts.source: PNGRB was created under a 2006 law, well after SEBI (1992), TRAI (1997), and IRDAI (1999).
Section 11 of the PNGRB Act mandates the Board to protect consumers and foster competitive markets for gas.
Appeals against PNGRB orders go before the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), with further appeal to the Supreme Court.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Statements 2 and 3 are correct—PNGRB fosters competitive gas markets and its appeals go to APTEL, while it was set up in 2006–07.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Energy & Regulators notes

items.title: PNGRB vs DGH Split
items.desc: PNGRB regulates refining, pipelines, and City Gas Distribution, while upstream oil and gas exploration sits with DGH.

items.title: Shared Energy Tribunal
items.desc: APTEL hears appeals from both power regulators (CERC/SERCs) and the petroleum-gas regulator (PNGRB).

items.title: Gas-Based Economy
items.desc: PNGRB's unified pipeline tariff and CGD rounds aim to raise natural gas in India's energy mix to 15% by 2030.

valueAddition.note: Notice how Statement 3 looks counterintuitive—gas appeals going to an electricity tribunal—while Statement 1 hides the actual false superlative.

subject: Economy
stem:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017?
1. Pregnant women are entitled for three months pre-delivery and three months post-delivery paid leave.
2. Enterprises with creches must allow the mother minimum six creche visits daily.
3. Women with two children get reduced entitlements.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.

keywords.shortNote: Central labour welfare legislation amending the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (applicable to establishments employing 10 or more persons) that enhanced paid maternity leave from 12 weeks to 26 weeks for the first two surviving children and mandated workplace creche facilities.
keywords.concept: Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017: Central labour welfare legislation amending the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (applicable to establishments employing 10 or more persons) that enhanced paid maternity leave from 12 weeks to 26 weeks for the first two surviving children and mandated workplace creche facilities.

keywords.shortNote: The statutory division of the 26-week paid maternity leave allowing a woman to take not more than 8 weeks (roughly two months, not three months) preceding the expected date of delivery, with the remaining 18 weeks taken post-delivery.
keywords.concept: Pre-Delivery vs. Post-Delivery Leave Split: The statutory division of the 26-week paid maternity leave allowing a woman to take not more than 8 weeks (roughly two months, not three months) preceding the expected date of delivery, with the remaining 18 weeks taken post-delivery.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because pre-delivery leave is capped at 8 weeks (not 3 months) and creche visits are 4 per day (not 6).

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because the statutory daily creche visit entitlement is four visits, not six.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Women having two or more surviving children get a reduced 12-week paid maternity leave (6 weeks pre-delivery + 6 weeks post-delivery), whereas Statements 1 and 2 distort the 8-week pre-delivery cap and 4 daily creche visits.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because only Statement 3 accurately states the statutory provisions of the 2017 Act.

valueAddition.title: Exact Statutory Numbers Under the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017
bullets: Leave Entitlement & Split: 26 weeks total paid leave for women with fewer than two surviving children (maximum 8 weeks pre-delivery + minimum 18 weeks post-delivery); for women with two or more surviving children, entitlement drops to 12 weeks (maximum 6 weeks pre-delivery + 6 weeks post-delivery).

Adoptive & Commissioning Mothers: Women legally adopting a child below 3 months of age and commissioning mothers (biological mothers using a surrogate) are entitled to 12 weeks of paid maternity leave from the date the child is handed over.

Creche & Work-From-Home: Establishments employing 50 or more workers must provide a creche facility with 4 daily visits allowed (including rest intervals), and employers may permit work-from-home after the 26-week period on mutually agreed terms.

valueAddition.title: Continuity Under the Code on Social Security, 2020
bullets: Subsumed Without Dilution: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (as amended in 2017) is one of the nine central labour laws consolidated into the Code on Social Security, 2020—retaining the exact 26-week/12-week leave split, 8-week pre-delivery ceiling, and 50-employee creche threshold.

inNews.source: Ministry of Labour and Employment / Press Information Bureau (PIB)
inNews.headline: Labour Ministry issues compliance advisory reinforcing mandatory 26-week paid maternity leave and workplace creche norms across private and public establishments
inNews.relevance: October 2026 Ministry of Labour advisories reiterated strict enforcement of the 26-week paid maternity benefit, 50-employee workplace creche mandate, and non-discrimination rules across formal-sector employers.

statementBreakdown.reference: Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 · Section 5(3) (8 Weeks Pre-Delivery Cap)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Total paid maternity leave was raised to 26 weeks (roughly 6 months), but pre-delivery leave cannot exceed 8 weeks (about 2 months), with the remaining 18 weeks post-delivery—not an equal 3-month pre-delivery and 3-month post-delivery split.

statementBreakdown.reference: Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 · Section 11A (Four Creche Visits Daily)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Establishments with 50 or more employees must provide a creche facility and allow the mother four visits a day to the creche (including the rest interval)—not six visits daily.

statementBreakdown.reference: Section 5(3) Proviso · Reduced 12-Week Entitlement Beyond Two Surviving Children
statementBreakdown.explanation: A woman who already has two or more surviving children receives a reduced paid maternity leave entitlement of 12 weeks (of which not more than 6 weeks can precede expected delivery) instead of the 26 weeks granted for the first two children.

hook.headline: Does India's Maternity Benefit law give 3 months pre-delivery leave and 6 creche visits daily?
hook.teaser: Both numbers are tweaked—see the exact 8-week and 4-visit limits in the 2017 Act.

keywords.term: three months pre-delivery and three months post-delivery
keywords.calloutNote: Total paid leave is 26 weeks, but pre-delivery leave is capped at 8 weeks (about 2 months)—not 3 months.
activePhrases: three months pre-delivery and three months post-delivery

keywords.term: Women with two children get reduced entitlements
keywords.calloutNote: For a woman who already has two or more surviving children, paid maternity leave drops from 26 weeks to 12 weeks.
activePhrases: Women with two children get reduced entitlements
dimmedPhrases: three months pre-delivery and three months post-delivery

verdicts.source: Out of 26 weeks of paid leave, pre-delivery leave cannot exceed 8 weeks (about 2 months), with 18 weeks post-delivery.
Establishments with 50 or more workers must allow the mother 4 visits a day to the creche, not 6.
Women who already have two or more surviving children receive a reduced entitlement of 12 weeks instead of 26 weeks.

answer.label: C
answer.text: Only Statement 3 is correct—women who already have two surviving children get 12 weeks instead of 26 weeks, while pre-delivery leave is capped at 8 weeks and creche visits at 4 daily.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Social Security & Labour Laws notes

items.title: Asymmetric Leave Split
items.desc: 26 weeks splits into a maximum of 8 weeks before delivery and at least 18 weeks after childbirth.

items.title: Creche & 4 Visits
items.desc: Mandatory for establishments with 50 or more employees, granting 4 daily visits inclusive of rest breaks.

items.title: Adoptive & Surrogacy Leave
items.desc: Adoptive mothers (child under 3 months) and commissioning mothers also receive 12 weeks of paid leave.

valueAddition.note: In questions on statutory welfare laws, examiners routinely swap exact figures—turning 8 weeks into 3 months and 4 creche visits into 6.

subject: Economy
stem: Which one of the following is not a sub-index of the World Bank's 'Ease of Doing Business Index'?

keywords.shortNote: A former World Bank benchmark (published 2003–2020) that ranked 190 economies across 10 regulatory life-cycle indicators affecting small and medium domestic firms.
keywords.concept: Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) Index: A former World Bank benchmark (published 2003–2020) that ranked 190 economies across 10 regulatory life-cycle indicators affecting small and medium domestic firms.

keywords.shortNote: The World Bank's successor flagship benchmarking project launched after discontinuing Doing Business, evaluating the business climate across regulatory framework, public services, and operational efficiency.
keywords.concept: Business Ready (B-READY): The World Bank's successor flagship benchmarking project launched after discontinuing Doing Business, evaluating the business climate across regulatory framework, public services, and operational efficiency.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: General policing and maintenance of public law and order is not among the 10 regulatory indicators of the Ease of Doing Business Index (which measures commercial contract enforcement rather than general policing).

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Paying taxes was one of the 10 core sub-indices, tracking total tax and contribution rate, number of payments, and time spent complying with tax laws.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Registering property was one of the 10 core sub-indices, measuring procedures, time, and cost to transfer commercial real estate title.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Dealing with construction permits was one of the 10 core sub-indices, assessing steps, time, and cost to legally build a commercial warehouse.

valueAddition.title: All 10 Sub-Indices of Doing Business (Firm Life-Cycle)
bullets: Starting & Building: (1) Starting a Business, (2) Dealing with Construction Permits, (3) Getting Electricity, (4) Registering Property.
Finance & Operations: (5) Getting Credit, (6) Protecting Minority Investors, (7) Paying Taxes, (8) Trading Across Borders.
Disputes & Exit: (9) Enforcing Contracts, (10) Resolving Insolvency (Note: 'Employing Workers' was tracked separately without scoring weight).

valueAddition.title: From Doing Business to World Bank B-READY
bullets: The World Bank discontinued the Doing Business report in September 2021 following data irregularity audits in the 2018 and 2020 editions.

Its replacement, Business Ready (B-READY), evaluates 10 life-cycle topics (including Business Entry, Business Location, Utility Services, Labor, Financial Services, International Trade, Taxation, Dispute Resolution, Market Competition, and Business Insolvency) across three pillars: Regulatory Framework, Public Services, and Operational Efficiency.

inNews.headline: World Bank expands Business Ready (B-READY) 2026 rollout covering over 100 economies including India
inNews.relevance: The World Bank's 2026 Business Ready expansion brings India into its successor assessment cycle, evaluating digital public services and commercial dispute resolution alongside DPIIT's Business Reforms Action Plan (BRAP).

hook.teaser: Spot the broad policing metric hiding among three technical business compliance indicators.

subject: Economy
stem: In the context of any country, which one of the following would be considered as part of its social capital?

options.text: The proportion of literates in the population
options.label: a

options.text: The stock of its buildings, other infrastructure and machines
options.label: b

options.text: The size of population in the working age group
options.label: c

options.text: The level of mutual trust and harmony in the society
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: The internal social and cultural coherence of a society, embodied in shared norms, values, mutual trust, civic networks, and interpersonal harmony that facilitate collective action and reduce transaction costs.
keywords.concept: Social Capital: The internal social and cultural coherence of a society, embodied in shared norms, values, mutual trust, civic networks, and interpersonal harmony that facilitate collective action and reduce transaction costs.

keywords.shortNote: Human capital represents individual skills, knowledge, and health embodied in the workforce, while physical capital consists of man-made tangible durable assets like buildings, roads, and machinery.
keywords.concept: Human Capital vs. Physical Capital: Human capital represents individual skills, knowledge, and health embodied in the workforce, while physical capital consists of man-made tangible durable assets like buildings, roads, and machinery.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: The proportion of literates, educational attainment, and technical skills define Human Capital, not Social Capital.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Buildings, transport infrastructure, factories, and machinery constitute tangible Physical Capital.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: The size of the population in the working-age cohort (15–64 years) represents the potential labour supply and demographic dividend.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Mutual trust, shared civic reciprocity, and communal harmony directly embody the relational fabric defining Social Capital.

valueAddition.title: Taxonomy of Capital in Economic Development
bullets: Physical Capital: Man-made tangible assets used in production, such as plants, factories, machinery, roads, and telecommunications infrastructure.
Human Capital: The stock of individual knowledge, education, competencies, cognitive skills, and health embodied in people.
Natural Capital: The world's stock of natural resources and environmental assets, including geology, soil, air, water, and living organisms.
Social Capital: The norms, shared values, institutions, and relational networks that foster cooperation within or among groups, substantially lowering contract enforcement and transaction costs.

valueAddition.title: The Dimensions of Social Capital
bullets: Bonding Social Capital: Inward-looking ties between people of similar background (family, close friends, homogeneous community groups) that provide emotional and close support.
Bridging Social Capital: Outward-looking ties connecting diverse social, ethnic, or socio-economic groups, fostering broad civic trust and national cohesion.
Linking Social Capital: Ties between people and formal institutions or individuals in positions of authority, critical for leveraging resources, state protection, and economic mobility.

Economic Significance: High social capital correlates with lower corruption, stronger contract enforcement, higher compliance with voluntary taxation, and accelerated economic growth (as outlined by Francis Fukuyama).

statementBreakdown.reference: Sociological and Economic Taxonomy of Capital
statementBreakdown.explanation: Social capital refers to the networks of relationships among people who live and work in a particular society, enabling that society to function effectively through generalized trust, shared reciprocity norms, and social cohesion.

valueAddition.title: Payment Data Localisation
bullets: Statutory Basis: Issued under Section 10(2) read with Section 18 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 (PSS Act).

Scope of Data: Covers end-to-end transaction details—customer data, payment credentials, authentication data, and balance logs. Cross-border processing is permitted, but foreign data must be deleted and brought back to India within 24 hours.
Supervisory Mechanism: Compliance requires a System Audit Report (SAR) by a CERT-IN empaneled auditor submitted directly to the RBI.

valueAddition.title: Institutional & Legislative Evolution
bullets: Enforcement Measures: In 2021, RBI temporarily barred major global card networks (Mastercard, American Express, Diners Club) from onboarding new domestic customers until full data localization compliance was verified.

Broader Legal Interface: Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 allows cross-border data transfers based on a government blacklist approach, but preserves sectoral localization mandates like RBI's payment data diktat.
Examiner Trap: CAG audits only government accounts and state-funded bodies under Article 149; private and commercial payment audits are routed strictly to the sectoral regulator (RBI).

stem: With reference to the Constitution of India, prohibitions or limitations or provisions contained in ordinary laws cannot act as prohibitions or limitations on the constitutional powers under Article 142. It could mean which one of the following?

options.text: The decisions taken by the Election Commission of India while discharging its duties cannot be challenged in any court of law.
options.label: a

options.text: The Supreme Court of India is not constrained in the exercise of its powers by laws made by the Parliament.
options.label: b

options.text: In the event of grave financial crisis in the country, the President of India can declare Financial Emergency without the counsel from the Cabinet.
options.label: c

options.text: State Legislatures cannot make laws on certain matters without the concurrence of Union Legislature.
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: An inherent constitutional reservoir empowering the Supreme Court to pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it.
keywords.concept: Article 142(1) — 'Complete Justice': An inherent constitutional reservoir empowering the Supreme Court to pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it.

keywords.shortNote: The constitutional doctrine holding that non-obstante powers under Article 142 cannot be clipped, curtailed, or prohibited by provisions contained in ordinary parliamentary legislation.
keywords.concept: Subordination of Ordinary Statutes: The constitutional doctrine holding that non-obstante powers under Article 142 cannot be clipped, curtailed, or prohibited by provisions contained in ordinary parliamentary legislation.

keywords.shortNote: Under Article 142(1), decrees and orders passed to do complete justice are enforceable throughout the territory of India in such manner as prescribed by Parliament or by the President.
keywords.concept: Enforceability of Decrees: Under Article 142(1), decrees and orders passed to do complete justice are enforceable throughout the territory of India in such manner as prescribed by Parliament or by the President.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Election Commission orders are subject to judicial review under Articles 32, 136, and 226; Article 142 has no bearing on immunizing ECI decisions.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Captures the exact judicial interpretation of Article 142: ordinary legislative bars enacted by Parliament cannot circumscribe or fetter the plenary constitutional power of the Supreme Court to do complete justice.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Financial Emergency is declared under Article 360 and is strictly governed by the aid and advice of the Union Cabinet under Article 74, unrelated to Article 142.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Relates to the legislative distribution of powers and repugnancy under Part XI, not judicial powers under Article 142.

valueAddition.title: Article 142: Constitutional Anatomy & Plenary Scope
bullets: Plenary Jurisdiction: Article 142(1) empowers the Supreme Court to make such order as is necessary for doing 'complete justice' in any cause or matter pending before it.
Territorial Enforceability: Any decree or order so passed is enforceable throughout the territory of India in the manner prescribed by Parliament, and until then, as prescribed by the President.

Discovery & Contempt Powers: Under Article 142(2), the Supreme Court has all powers to secure the attendance of any person, require the discovery or production of documents, or investigate and punish any contempt of itself.

valueAddition.title: Evolution of Article 142: How the Power Grew
bullets: Phase 1 — The Strict Era (1962, Prem Chand Garg): The Court held it cannot bypass laws made by Parliament. If an Act says 'No', Article 142 cannot say 'Yes'.
Phase 2 — The Superpower Era (1991, Union Carbide / Bhopal Gas): The Court reversed its stand. It ruled that ordinary parliamentary laws cannot tie its hands when doing complete justice.

Phase 3 — The Guardrail Era (1998, SC Bar Association): The Court set limits. Article 142 can fill gaps in the law, but it cannot completely rewrite statutes or create brand-new punishments out of thin air.
Modern Use (2023, Shilpa Sailesh): The Court used this power to grant immediate divorce in cases of 'irretrievable breakdown of marriage', waiving the mandatory 6-month statutory waiting period.

valueAddition.title: Article 142 vs High Courts (Article 226)
bullets: Supreme Court Exclusivity: The power to pass orders to do 'complete justice' under Article 142 is available solely to the Supreme Court; High Courts have no parallel constitutional provision.

Inherent Powers of High Courts: High Courts exercise inherent powers under Section 482 of the CrPC/BNSS (criminal) and Section 151 of the CPC (civil), but these are subordinate statutory powers, whereas Article 142 is a plenary constitutional power.

valueAddition.title: Fifth Schedule, Paragraph 5: Regulatory Framework

Hanumanthaiah, emphasized that a person appointed as Governor should have a long experience in public life and administration and an open mind, but it did not frame the verbatim criteria regarding a detached figure without intense political links.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Appointed by the DMK-led Tamil Nadu government under P.V. Rajamannar, this committee primarily recommended omitting Articles 356 and 357, making the Inter-State Council effective, and mandating consultation with the State Cabinet before appointing a Governor, rather than defining these specific personal detachment benchmarks.

optionBreakdown.explanation: The Sarkaria Commission explicitly laid down that a Governor should be an eminent person in some walk of life, an outsider to the State, a detached figure without intense political links who has not taken part in politics in the recent past, and selected in effective consultation with the Chief Minister of the State.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: The Venkatachaliah Commission (NCRWC) largely endorsed the Sarkaria Commission's formulation in 2002 and proposed a committee comprising the Prime Minister, Home Minister, Speaker of Lok Sabha, and the State Chief Minister for selecting Governors, but the original doctrinal benchmark was formulated by the Sarkaria Commission.

valueAddition.title: Sarkaria Commission: Four Criteria for Governor's Appointment (Para 4.16.01)
bullets: Eminence Criterion: The appointee should be an eminent person in some walk of life.
Outsider Criterion: The appointee must be a person from outside the State concerned.
Detachment Criterion: The appointee should be a detached figure and not too intimately connected with the local politics of the State.
Political Inactivity Criterion: The appointee should not have taken too great a part in politics generally, and particularly in the recent past.
Consultation Mandate: The State Chief Minister must be effectively consulted by the Prime Minister before finalising the appointment.

valueAddition.title: Punchhi Commission Recommendations on the Governor (2010)
bullets: Selection Committee: Proposed a committee comprising the Prime Minister, Home Minister, Speaker of Lok Sabha, and the concerned Chief Minister (with Vice President as an optional chair) to appoint Governors.

Tenure Security: Recommended that the phrase 'during the pleasure of the President' under Article 156(1) be deleted and replaced with a fixed five-year term, removable only via a procedure analogous to the impeachment of the President by the State Legislature.
Chancellorship Role: Recommended amending relevant statutes to relieve Governors of university chancellorship roles to prevent governance conflict with state ministers.
