stem: India enacted the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 in order to comply with the obligations

keywords.shortNote: An intellectual property sign used on agricultural, natural, or manufactured goods originating from a specific geographical territory whose quality, reputation, or characteristics are essentially attributable to that origin.
keywords.concept: Geographical Indication (GI): An intellectual property sign used on agricultural, natural, or manufactured goods originating from a specific geographical territory whose quality, reputation, or characteristics are essentially attributable to that origin.

keywords.shortNote: The WTO multilateral agreement setting minimum standards for intellectual property protection, obligating member states to provide legal means to prevent misleading geographical origin claims.
keywords.concept: TRIPS Agreement (Articles 22–24): The WTO multilateral agreement setting minimum standards for intellectual property protection, obligating member states to provide legal means to prevent misleading geographical origin claims.

keywords.shortNote: The statutory authority headquartered in Chennai under the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (DPIIT) that administers GI registration in India.
keywords.concept: Geographical Indications Registry: The statutory authority headquartered in Chennai under the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (DPIIT) that administers GI registration in India.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: The ILO sets international labour standards and workplace conventions; it has no mandate over intellectual property rights or geographical indications.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: The IMF governs international monetary cooperation, exchange rate stability, and balance-of-payments financing—not trade-related intellectual property laws.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD)
optionBreakdown.explanation: UNCTAD is a UN research and policy-advocacy body supporting developing countries in trade and investment; it does not enforce binding IP treaty obligations.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: As a founding WTO member, India enacted the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 (enforced from September 2003) to fulfill its binding obligations under the TRIPS Agreement.

valueAddition.title: Indian GI Act, 1999: Key Statutory Mechanics
bullets: Validity & Renewal: A GI registration is valid for 10 years and can be renewed indefinitely for successive 10-year periods (unlike patents, which expire permanently after 20 years).
Collective Ownership: A GI is a community right registered to an association of producers or statutory body—it cannot be assigned, licensed, or mortgaged to an individual private owner.
First Indian GI: Darjeeling Tea became the first product registered under the Act in 2004–05; the GI Registry operates from Chennai.

valueAddition.title: India's Post-WTO Intellectual Property Overhaul
bullets: To meet its January 1, 2005 TRIPS transition deadline as a developing economy, India overhauled multiple IP statutes alongside the 1999 GI Act.

Key enactments included the Trade Marks Act (1999), Designs Act (2000), Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act (2001), Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act (2000), and the Patents (Amendment) Act, 2005 introducing product patents in pharmaceuticals.

stem: Which one of the following links all the ATMs in India?

keywords.shortNote: The foundational backbone network that interconnects shared ATMs across banks in India to enable nation-wide interoperable cash withdrawals.
keywords.concept: National Financial Switch (NFS): The foundational backbone network that interconnects shared ATMs across banks in India to enable nation-wide interoperable cash withdrawals.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Indian Banks' Association is a voluntary representative association of Indian banks; it co-promoted NPCI but does not operate payment networks.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: NSDL is a securities depository holding financial securities (shares, bonds) in electronic demat form under SEBI regulation.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: Section 4, Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007
optionBreakdown.explanation: NPCI operates the National Financial Switch (NFS), which links and routes interbank ATM transactions across commercial banks, RRBs, and cooperative banks in India.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: RBI acts as the regulator and overseer of payment systems and manages high-value settlements like RTGS, but delegated retail switches like NFS to NPCI.

valueAddition.title: NPCI & National Financial Switch (NFS)
bullets: Genesis of NFS: Developed in 2004 by the Institute for Development and Research in Banking Technology (IDRBT); handed over to NPCI in December 2009 to scale domestic interbank retail switches.
Legal Status of NPCI: Incorporated under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013 (not-for-profit company), founded by RBI and IBA under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.
Ecosystem Umbrella: Besides NFS (ATMs), NPCI operates UPI, IMPS, RuPay, NACH, AePS (Aadhaar-enabled Payment System), and NETC FASTag.

valueAddition.title: ATM Classification & Interoperability
bullets: ATM Ownership Types: Bank-owned ATMs (on/off-premise), Brown Label ATMs (hardware owned by 3rd party vendor, cash management and connectivity sponsored by a bank), and White Label ATMs (owned and operated by non-bank NBFCs licensed by RBI under PSS Act).
Interoperability Engine: NFS provides real-time switching, card authentication, and multi-currency processing for domestic and international card schemes.
Core Trap: Candidates often confuse the regulator (RBI) or industry association (IBA) with the dedicated operational switch operator (NPCI).

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. As per the Right to Education (RTE) Act, to be eligible for appointment as a teacher in a State, a person would be required to possess the minimum qualification laid down by the concerned State Council of Teacher Education.
2. As per the RTE Act, for teaching primary classes, a candidate is required to pass a Teacher Eligibility Test conducted in accordance with the National Council of Teacher Education guidelines.
3. In India, more than 90% of teacher education institutions are directly under the State Governments.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: A statutory body established under the NCTE Act, 1993 under the Ministry of Education, designated as the Central Government's academic authority under Section 23(1) of the RTE Act, 2009 to prescribe minimum qualifications for school teachers nationwide.
keywords.concept: National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE): A statutory body established under the NCTE Act, 1993 under the Ministry of Education, designated as the Central Government's academic authority under Section 23(1) of the RTE Act, 2009 to prescribe minimum qualifications for school teachers nationwide.

keywords.shortNote: A mandatory qualifying examination introduced pursuant to NCTE's August 2010 notification under Section 23(1) of the RTE Act, 2009—conducted centrally as CTET by CBSE or by State Governments as STET—for appointment as a teacher in Classes I to VIII.
keywords.concept: Teacher Eligibility Test (TET): A mandatory qualifying examination introduced pursuant to NCTE's August 2010 notification under Section 23(1) of the RTE Act, 2009—conducted centrally as CTET by CBSE or by State Governments as STET—for appointment as a teacher in Classes I to VIII.

keywords.term: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009
keywords.shortNote: Parliamentary legislation enacting Article 21A of the Constitution to guarantee free and compulsory elementary education (Classes I to VIII, ages 6 to 14) along with statutory norms for pupil-teacher ratios, teacher qualifications, and school infrastructure.
keywords.concept: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009: Parliamentary legislation enacting Article 21A of the Constitution to guarantee free and compulsory elementary education (Classes I to VIII, ages 6 to 14) along with statutory norms for pupil-teacher ratios, teacher qualifications, and school infrastructure.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because minimum teacher qualifications under the RTE Act are prescribed uniformly by NCTE (authorized by the Central Government), not by State bodies.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Passing TET per NCTE guidelines is mandatory under the RTE framework, whereas NCTE (not State Councils) sets minimum qualifications and over 90% of teacher education colleges are private rather than State-run.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because neither State-determined minimum qualifications nor 90% State ownership of teacher education institutions is accurate.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because the ownership ratio is inverted—over 90% of teacher education institutions are private, not State Government-run.

valueAddition.title: Section 23 of the RTE Act & National Teacher Qualification Norms
bullets: Centralized Academic Authority: Section 23(1) empowers the Central Government to notify an academic authority (NCTE) to set uniform minimum teacher qualifications across India; only the Central Government can temporarily relax these norms for a State up to five years under Section 23(2).

TET Validity & NEP 2020 Link: TET qualifying certificates now carry lifetime validity (extended from 7 years), and National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 extends TET requirements across all stages of school education (Foundational, Preparatory, Middle, and Secondary) alongside the 4-year Integrated Teacher Education Programme (ITEP).

valueAddition.title: Why Teacher Education Ownership Skewed Private
bullets: Private Dominance in TEIs: Following rapid deregulation in the 1990s and 2000s, standalone private self-financed institutions grew to account for over 90% of all B.Ed. and D.El.Ed. institutions in India—prompting the Justice J.S. Verma Commission and NEP 2020 to mandate phasing out standalone TEIs into multidisciplinary universities.

stem:
With reference to the provisions made under the National Food Security Act, 2013, consider the following statements:
1. The families coming under the category of 'below poverty line (BPL)' only are eligible to receive subsidised food grains.
2. The eldest woman in a household, of age 18 years or above, shall be the head of the household for the purpose of issuance of a ration card.
3. Pregnant women and lactating mothers are entitled to a 'take-home ration' of 1600 calories per day during pregnancy and for six months thereafter.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: The two statutory beneficiary categories under Section 3 of the National Food Security Act, 2013 replacing the earlier APL/BPL classification—covering up to 75% of the rural population and up to 50% of the urban population.
keywords.concept: Priority Households (PHH) & Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY): The two statutory beneficiary categories under Section 3 of the National Food Security Act, 2013 replacing the earlier APL/BPL classification—covering up to 75% of the rural population and up to 50% of the urban population.

keywords.shortNote: The statutory grain-distribution framework under NFSA 2013 delivering 5 kg of food grains per person per month to Priority Households and 35 kg per household per month to Antyodaya Anna Yojana families.
keywords.concept: Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS): The statutory grain-distribution framework under NFSA 2013 delivering 5 kg of food grains per person per month to Priority Households and 35 kg per household per month to Antyodaya Anna Yojana families.

keywords.shortNote: The statutory table annexed to NFSA 2013 specifying minimum daily energy and protein standards for supplementary nutrition—prescribing 600 calories and 18–20 grams of protein per day (not 1600 calories) for pregnant women and lactating mothers.
keywords.concept: Schedule II Nutritional Norms (NFSA, 2013): The statutory table annexed to NFSA 2013 specifying minimum daily energy and protein standards for supplementary nutrition—prescribing 600 calories and 18–20 grams of protein per day (not 1600 calories) for pregnant women and lactating mothers.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because NFSA replaced the BPL criterion with broader 75% rural and 50% urban coverage under PHH and AAY.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Designating the eldest woman aged 18 or above as household head for ration cards is an explicit statutory mandate under Section 13(1), whereas Statements 1 and 3 misstate beneficiary eligibility and calorie norms.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because neither BPL-only eligibility nor a 1600-calorie supplementary ration norm exists in NFSA 2013.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because Schedule II prescribes 600 calories per day for pregnant and lactating women, not 1600 calories.

valueAddition.title: Core Statutory Entitlements Under NFSA, 2013 & PMGKAY
bullets: Population Coverage & Grain Quota: Covers up to 75% rural and 50% urban population (~81.35 crore beneficiaries); Priority Households receive 5 kg per person per month, while poorest-of-the-poor Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) households receive 35 kg per household per month (provided completely free of cost under Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana since January 2023).

Eldest Woman as Household Head (Section 13): The eldest woman aged 18 years or above is designated head of household for ration cards; if a household has no woman aged 18 or above, the eldest male member acts as head temporarily until a female member attains 18 years of age.

Maternity & Child Nutrition (Sections 4–6 & Schedule II): Pregnant women and lactating mothers receive free supplementary nutrition of 600 calories (18–20g protein) per day through Anganwadi centres plus maternity benefit of not less than Rs. 6,000.

valueAddition.title: Grievance Redressal & Food Security Allowance
bullets: Two-Tier Redressal & Cash Compensation: NFSA mandates District Grievance Redressal Officers (DGROs) and State Food Commissions, and requires State Governments to pay a Food Security Allowance in cash under Section 8 whenever entitled food grains or meals are not supplied.

inNews.source: Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution / Press Information Bureau (PIB)
inNews.headline: Centre continues free food grain distribution to over 80 crore NFSA beneficiaries under PMGKAY alongside One Nation One Ration Card portability
inNews.relevance: October 2026 Food Ministry operational updates highlighted nationwide biometric portability under One Nation One Ration Card across all 36 States and UTs, serving over 80 crore PHH and AAY beneficiaries under NFSA 2013.

statementBreakdown.explanation: NFSA 2013 moved away from the 'Below Poverty Line (BPL)' classification to cover up to 75% of the rural population and up to 50% of the urban population under Priority Households (PHH) and Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) households identified by State Governments.
Section 13(1) of NFSA 2013 mandates that the eldest woman who is not less than 18 years of age in every eligible household shall be head of the household for the purpose of issue of ration cards.

statementBreakdown.reference: NFSA, 2013 · Section 4 & Schedule II (600 Calories Nutritional Standard)
statementBreakdown.explanation: Under Section 4 read with Schedule II of NFSA 2013, pregnant women and lactating mothers are entitled to free meals or take-home rations providing 600 calories and 18–20 grams of protein per day—inflated by 1,000 calories in the statement to 1600 calories.

visualSuggestion.title: Key Provisions of the National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013

rows: Up to 75% rural & 50% urban population (PHH & AAY categories)
Restricted falsely to 'below poverty line (BPL) only'
Eldest woman aged 18 years or above (Section 13)
Inflated by 1,000 calories to '1600 calories per day'

hook.headline: Does the National Food Security Act restrict subsidised grains to BPL families only?
hook.teaser: No—it covers 75% of rural and 50% of urban India, and cuts that 1600-calorie figure down to 600.

keywords.calloutNote: NFSA 2013 replaced BPL targeting with Priority Households (PHH) and AAY, covering up to 75% of rural and 50% of urban citizens.
activePhrases: 'below poverty line (BPL)' only

keywords.term: eldest woman in a household, of age 18 years or above
keywords.calloutNote: Section 13(1) of NFSA 2013 designates the eldest woman aged 18 or above as the head of household for issuing ration cards.
activePhrases: eldest woman in a household, of age 18 years or above
dimmedPhrases: 'below poverty line (BPL)' only

verdicts.source: NFSA 2013 moved beyond BPL lists to cover up to 75% rural and 50% urban population under Priority Households and AAY.
Section 13(1) mandates that the eldest woman aged 18 or above in a household shall be the head for issuing a ration card.
Schedule II of NFSA 2013 entitles pregnant and lactating women to 600 calories per day, not 1600 calories.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Only Statement 2 is correct—NFSA names the eldest adult woman as household head on ration cards, while coverage extends far beyond BPL and maternity rations provide 600 calories daily.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Food Security & Welfare Acts notes

items.title: PHH & AAY Entitlements
items.desc: Priority Households receive 5 kg per person monthly, while Antyodaya Anna Yojana families get 35 kg per household monthly.

items.title: Food Security Allowance
items.desc: If entitled food grains or meals are not supplied, State Governments must pay a statutory cash allowance.

items.title: Daily Calorie Norms
items.desc: Prescribes 600 kcal for pregnant/lactating women, 500 kcal for children aged 6m–6y, and 800 kcal for malnourished children.

valueAddition.note: Notice two classic examiner tricks in one question: the restrictive word 'only' on BPL eligibility and a digit tweak turning 600 calories into 1600.

subject: Economy
stem: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the meaning of legal tender money?

options.text: The money which is tendered in courts of law to defray the fee of legal cases
options.label: a

options.text: The money which a creditor is under compulsion to accept in settlement of his claims
options.label: b

options.text: The bank money in the form of cheques, drafts, bills of exchange etc.
options.label: c

options.text: The metallic money in circulation in a country
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: Currency notes and coins backed by statutory guarantee that cannot be lawfully refused by a creditor in discharge of financial obligations or debt.
keywords.concept: Legal Tender Money: Currency notes and coins backed by statutory guarantee that cannot be lawfully refused by a creditor in discharge of financial obligations or debt.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Plays on the literal word 'legal'; money paid in courts consists of court fees or judicial stamps, which is not the economic definition of legal tender.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: Section 26(1), RBI Act, 1934 & Section 6, Coinage Act, 2011
optionBreakdown.explanation: Legal tender is currency which every creditor is legally obligated to accept in settlement of debt or dues; refusing it extinguishes the claim to interest and legal recourse.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Cheques, drafts, and bills of exchange are fiduciary/optional bank money; a creditor can lawfully refuse them and insist on legal tender cash.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Legal tender encompasses both metallic coins and paper currency notes issued by the sovereign/central bank, not solely metallic currency.

valueAddition.title: Legal Tender & Currency Framework
bullets: Statutory Backing: Currency notes are unlimited legal tender across India under Section 26(1) of the RBI Act, 1934, guaranteed by the Central Government.
Coinage Act, 2011 (Section 6): Coins are legal tender up to statutory ceilings—coins of ₹1 and above are legal tender up to ₹1,000; 50-paise coins up to ₹10 (making them limited legal tender).

Demonetization Mechanism: Under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act, 1934, the Central Government, on the recommendation of the RBI Central Board, can declare any series of bank notes to cease to be legal tender.

valueAddition.title: Legal Tender vs Fiduciary Money
bullets: Fiat Money: Currency backed by sovereign decree without intrinsic commodity backing; all legal tender is fiat money.
Fiduciary Money: Instruments (cheques, drafts, letters of credit) accepted based on mutual trust between payer and payee, without legal compulsion to accept.
Central Bank Digital Currency (e-Rupee): Issued under the RBI Act (amended in 2022) as a sovereign digital token holding full legal tender status on par with paper cash.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India
inNews.headline: RBI expands retail e-Rupee pilot and clarifies legal tender status of digital token currency
inNews.relevance: Directly links to the definition tested in this PYQ, cementing sovereign central bank digital currency (CBDC) under Section 26 of the RBI Act with identical legal tender obligations as physical paper notes.

visualSuggestion.title: Money Classifications: Legal Compulsion & Backing

rows: RBI Bank Notes (₹10, ₹500, etc.) & Digital Rupee
Compulsory (Cannot be refused up to any value)

hook.headline: Can a shopkeeper or creditor legally refuse your cash?
hook.teaser: The term 'legal tender' has nothing to do with courts or legal proceedings.

keywords.calloutNote: Look for the concept of sovereign compulsion where refusal by a creditor is legally prohibited.
activePhrases: meaning of legal tender money

keywords.calloutNote: By law, a creditor cannot refuse legal tender to settle a debt without forfeiting legal claims.
activePhrases: creditor is under compulsion to accept in settlement of his claims
dimmedPhrases: meaning of legal tender money

verdicts.source: Court fees are payments for legal administration, playing on the word 'legal' without defining the monetary term.
Legal tender is sovereign-backed currency that a creditor is legally bound to accept for settling claims.
Cheques and drafts are optional fiduciary money; a payee can legally refuse them and demand cash.
Legal tender includes paper bank notes and digital fiat currency, not just metallic coins.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Legal tender is money that a creditor is legally obligated to accept in settlement of debts and obligations.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Money & Banking notes

items.title: RBI Act, 1934
items.desc: Bank notes issued by RBI are unlimited legal tender guaranteed by the Central Government.

items.title: Coinage Act, 2011
items.desc: Coins are limited legal tender: ₹1+ coins are legal tender up to ₹1,000; 50-paise up to ₹10.

items.title: Cheques & Drafts
items.desc: Accepted purely on trust without statutory compulsion; creditors can lawfully decline them.

valueAddition.note: Don't confuse sovereign legal tender (mandatory acceptance) with fiduciary bank instruments (voluntary acceptance).

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) is the amount that banks have to maintain in the form of their own funds to offset any loss that banks incur if the account-holders fail to repay dues.
2. CAR is decided by each individual bank.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: The proportion of a bank's core and supplementary capital to its risk-weighted assets, functioning as an equity buffer against borrower default.
keywords.concept: Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR): The proportion of a bank's core and supplementary capital to its risk-weighted assets, functioning as an equity buffer against borrower default.

keywords.shortNote: A bank's assets and off-balance sheet exposures weighted according to their credit and default risk profile.
keywords.concept: Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA): A bank's assets and off-balance sheet exposures weighted according to their credit and default risk profile.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.reference: Statement 1 is true; Statement 2 is false.
optionBreakdown.explanation: Only Statement 1 accurately captures the economic definition and loss-absorption purpose of CAR.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because banks do not set their own statutory capital ratios; RBI dictates the floor.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails due to the incorrect inclusion of Statement 2.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because Statement 1 is the valid standard definition of CAR.

valueAddition.title: CAR Calculation & Regulatory Norms
bullets: Formula: CAR = (Tier 1 Capital + Tier 2 Capital) / Risk-Weighted Assets * 100. Tier 1 covers primary loss-absorbing equity, while Tier 2 acts as supplementary capital.

RBI vs Basel Norms: Basel III prescribes a minimum CAR of 8%. The RBI enforces a stricter 9% baseline for scheduled commercial banks, rising to 11.5% with the mandatory 2.5% Capital Conservation Buffer.
Supervisory Enforcement: Under the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework, breaching minimum CAR triggers RBI curbs on lending, branch expansion, and dividend payouts.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India / Financial Stability Report
inNews.headline: Scheduled commercial banks report multi-year high CRAR of 16.8% under RBI Basel III monitoring
inNews.relevance: Directly tracks the regulatory ratio tested in this PYQ, showing Indian commercial banks maintaining a capital cushion well above RBI's statutory 11.5% mandate.

statementBreakdown.reference: RBI Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations
statementBreakdown.explanation: CAR ensures that a bank holds enough own funds (equity and reserves) to absorb losses when borrowers default, protecting depositors against insolvency.
Statutory minimum CAR thresholds are fixed and enforced centrally by the Reserve Bank of India in line with Basel standards, not decided by individual banks.

visualSuggestion.title: Capital Adequacy: Global Basel III vs RBI Mandate

hook.headline: Can your bank decide its own safety cushion against loan defaults?
hook.teaser: Statement 2 gives banks way too much power—and costs aspirants two easy marks.

keywords.calloutNote: This is the core purpose of CAR: forcing banks to keep equity to absorb bad loans before depositors lose a rupee.
activePhrases: offset any loss that banks incur if the account-holders fail to repay dues

keywords.calloutNote: A classic authority trap. Minimum safety ratios are strictly dictated by the RBI, never by the bank itself.
activePhrases: CAR is decided by each individual bank
dimmedPhrases: offset any loss that banks incur if the account-holders fail to repay dues

verdicts.source: CAR is equity capital set aside to absorb default losses and protect depositors against bank insolvency.
The minimum CAR is mandated centrally by the Reserve Bank of India under Basel III norms, not decided independently by each bank.

answer.label: A
answer.text: Only Statement 1 is correct; CAR absorbs loan losses, but its minimum limit is set by the RBI, not individual banks.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Banking Regulation notes

items.title: Capital / RWA
items.desc: CAR = (Tier 1 + Tier 2 Capital) / Risk-Weighted Assets * 100.

items.title: RBI Baseline
items.desc: RBI enforces a 9% minimum CAR (stricter than Basel's 8%), reaching 11.5% with the 2.5% buffer.

items.title: Prompt Corrective Action
items.desc: Breaching minimum CAR triggers RBI lending and branch expansion curbs under PCA.

valueAddition.note: Never let an exam statement convince you that commercial banks set their own regulatory safety ratios—the central bank dictates them.

subject: Economy
stem: Which one of the following best describes the term "Merchant Discount Rate" sometimes seen in news?

options.text: The incentive given by a bank to a merchant for accepting payments through debit cards pertaining to that bank.
options.label: a

options.text: The amount paid back by banks to their customers when they use debit cards for financial transactions for purchasing goods or services.
options.label: b

options.text: The charge to a merchant by a bank for accepting payments from his customers through the bank's debit cards.
options.label: c

options.text: The incentive given by the Government to merchants for promoting digital payments by their customers through Point of Sale (PoS) machines and debit cards.
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: The percentage fee charged to a merchant by a bank for facilitating digital payment acceptance via debit or credit cards.
keywords.concept: Merchant Discount Rate (MDR): The percentage fee charged to a merchant by a bank for facilitating digital payment acceptance via debit or credit cards.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: MDR is a cost or fee levied on the merchant, not an incentive or subsidy granted by the bank.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Amounts returned to customers are reward points or cashbacks, not MDR.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: MDR is the commission a merchant pays to the bank for providing infrastructure to accept digital card payments from customers.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Government budgetary subsidies compensate banks for low-value digital transactions, but that fiscal support is not the definition of MDR.

valueAddition.title: MDR Framework & Zero-MDR Regime
bullets: Fee Sharing: MDR collected from a merchant is split between the card-issuing bank (via the interchange fee), the acquiring bank (PoS terminal provider), and the payment network (RuPay, Visa, Mastercard).

Zero-MDR Mandate: Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 (inserted via Finance Act, 2019) mandates zero MDR on RuPay debit cards and UPI for businesses with annual turnover exceeding Rs 50 crore.

Government Reimbursement: To offset bank revenue losses from zero MDR, MeitY provides an annual budgetary incentive scheme to subsidize acquiring banks for processing low-value BHIM-UPI and RuPay debit transactions.

inNews.source: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) / NPCI
inNews.headline: Cabinet approves financial incentive scheme to promote low-value BHIM-UPI and RuPay debit card transactions
inNews.relevance: Directly links to the Zero-MDR mandate tested in this PYQ, compensating banks for processing costs on digital payment rails where merchant charges remain legally capped at zero.

visualSuggestion.title: Digital Payment Terminology: Clarifying Common Confusions

rows: Commission charged for accepting digital card payments
Fee paid to compensate the card-issuing bank for credit/liquidity risk
Incentive paid to encourage digital payments at point of sale
Fiscal compensation for handling zero-fee UPI and RuPay transactions

hook.headline: Why do some small shopkeepers refuse card payments?
hook.teaser: The culprit is the Merchant Discount Rate—and it is not a discount for the buyer.

keywords.calloutNote: Despite the word 'discount', this is actually a commission charged to the merchant.
activePhrases: Merchant Discount Rate

keywords.term: charge to a merchant by a bank
keywords.calloutNote: This identifies MDR as an operational fee levied on retailers for accepting card payments.
activePhrases: charge to a merchant by a bank for accepting payments
dimmedPhrases: Merchant Discount Rate

verdicts.source: MDR is a cost borne by the retailer, not an incentive given by banks.
Amounts returned to customers are reward points or cashbacks, not MDR.
MDR is the percentage fee charged to a merchant by a bank for processing customer debit card payments.
Government schemes may reimburse payment costs, but the core economic definition of MDR is the merchant fee.

answer.label: C
answer.text: Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) is the fee charged to a merchant by the bank for accepting digital card payments.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Digital Economy notes

items.title: 3-Way Distribution
items.desc: MDR proceeds are split between the card-issuing bank (interchange fee), the acquiring bank, and the payment network.

items.title: Zero-MDR Regime
items.desc: Mandates zero merchant fees on RuPay debit cards and UPI transactions under the PSS Act, 2007.

items.title: Discount Misnomer
items.desc: In banking, 'discount' refers to a fee deducted at source, not a consumer sales promotion.

valueAddition.note: Never mistake the banking term 'discount' for a promotional consumer offer—in finance, it refers to a fee deducted at source.

subject: Economy
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Reserve Bank of India manages and services Government of India Securities but not any State Government Securities.
2. Treasury bills are issued by the Government of India and there are no treasury bills issued by the State Governments.
3. Treasury bills are issued at a discount from the par value.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: Zero-coupon, short-term debt instruments issued by the central government via RBI auction to bridge temporary fiscal cash-flow mismatches.
keywords.concept: Treasury Bills (T-Bills): Zero-coupon, short-term debt instruments issued by the central government via RBI auction to bridge temporary fiscal cash-flow mismatches.

keywords.shortNote: A debt security that pays no periodic interest but is issued at a discount to its face value and redeemed at par upon maturity.
keywords.concept: Zero-Coupon Bond: A debt security that pays no periodic interest but is issued at a discount to its face value and redeemed at par upon maturity.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because RBI routinely manages and services State Government Securities under Section 21A of the RBI Act.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to include Statement 2, which correctly identifies that State Governments cannot issue T-Bills.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: Statement 1 is false; Statements 2 and 3 are true.
optionBreakdown.explanation: Correctly pairs the prohibition on State T-Bills with the discounted zero-coupon nature of T-Bills.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because it incorporates the false premise of Statement 1.

valueAddition.title: Sovereign Debt Instruments & Tenors
bullets: Tenors of T-Bills: Issued in three standard maturity tenors via periodic RBI auctions—91-day, 182-day, and 364-day.
Cash Management Bills (CMBs): Non-standard maturity instruments (less than 91 days) issued by the Central Government and RBI to meet sudden, temporary cash requirements.

State Government Financing: States issue dated securities called State Development Loans (SDLs) for medium-to-long term borrowing, and use RBI's Ways and Means Advances (WMA) and Overdraft (OD) facilities for short-term mismatch management.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India
inNews.headline: RBI notifies enhanced Ways and Means Advances (WMA) limits for State Governments and Union Territories
inNews.relevance: Directly links to how States handle short-term liquidity needs in the absence of power to issue Treasury bills, relying on RBI-calibrated WMA ceilings.

statementBreakdown.explanation: RBI is statutorily bound to manage Central Government public debt under Section 20/21, and it also manages the public debt and securities of State Governments under bilateral agreements pursuant to Section 21A.

statementBreakdown.reference: Government Securities Act, 2006 & RBI Debt Management Guidelines
statementBreakdown.explanation: Treasury bills are issued exclusively by the Central Government; State Governments cannot issue T-Bills and instead meet short-term liquidity needs via Ways and Means Advances (WMA) and issue State Development Loans (SDLs) for market borrowing.

statementBreakdown.reference: Standard Money Market Practice (RBI Master Circular)
statementBreakdown.explanation: T-Bills are zero-coupon debt securities issued at a discount to their face (par) value and redeemed at full face value at maturity, with the discount margin serving as the investor's return.

visualSuggestion.title: Centre vs State Government Borrowing Instruments

rows: No T-Bills; rely on WMA / Special WMA from RBI
Reserve Bank of India (Mandatory by Statute)
Reserve Bank of India (Under Sec 21A Agreements)

hook.headline: Can your State Government issue Treasury Bills?
hook.teaser: Statement 2 catches almost every beginner off guard—and changes the entire answer.

keywords.calloutNote: An extreme negative trap. RBI manages debt for both the Centre and all agreeing States.
activePhrases: but not any State Government Securities

keywords.term: no treasury bills issued by the State Governments
keywords.calloutNote: This absolute statement is surprisingly true—only the Central Government can issue T-Bills.
activePhrases: there are no treasury bills issued by the State Governments
dimmedPhrases: but not any State Government Securities
contextPhrases: Treasury bills are issued by the Government of India

verdicts.source: Under Section 21A of the RBI Act, RBI manages public debt for all State Governments through formal agreements.
State Governments are not permitted to issue Treasury Bills; they manage short-term liquidity through RBI's WMA facility.
T-Bills pay no periodic coupon; they are sold at a discount and redeemed at full face value at maturity.

answer.label: C
answer.text: Statements 2 and 3 are correct; RBI manages debt for both Centre and States, while T-Bills are issued only by the Centre at a discount.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your G-Sec Market notes

items.title: State Debt Management
items.desc: RBI manages the issuance and servicing of State Development Loans (SDLs) via bilateral pacts with States.

items.title: Discount Mechanism
items.desc: T-Bills carry zero interest rate; investor return equals face value minus discounted purchase price.

items.title: State Short-Term Cash
items.desc: Because States cannot issue T-Bills, they manage temporary revenue mismatches through RBI Ways and Means Advances.

valueAddition.note: Don't fall for the trap that an absolute qualifier ('no treasury bills issued by States') is always incorrect—here it is legally accurate.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana, consider the following statements:
1. It is the flagship scheme of the Ministry of Labour and Employment.
2. It, among other things, will also impart training in soft skills, entrepreneurship, financial and digital literacy.
3. It aims to align the competencies of the unregulated workforce of the country to the National Skill Qualification Framework.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: The flagship outcome-based skill training scheme launched in 2015 by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) and implemented through the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC) to certify youth with industry-relevant skills.
keywords.concept: Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY): The flagship outcome-based skill training scheme launched in 2015 by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) and implemented through the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC) to certify youth with industry-relevant skills.

keywords.shortNote: A nationally integrated competency-based framework notified by the Government of India that organizes qualifications across levels 1 to 10 according to knowledge, skills, and aptitude, enabling vertical and horizontal mobility between vocational and general education.
keywords.concept: National Skill Qualification Framework (NSQF): A nationally integrated competency-based framework notified by the Government of India that organizes qualifications across levels 1 to 10 according to knowledge, skills, and aptitude, enabling vertical and horizontal mobility between vocational and general education.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated immediately because PMKVY belongs to the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, not the Ministry of Labour and Employment.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because aligning unregulated workforce competencies to the NSQF via Recognition of Prior Learning is a core statutory pillar of PMKVY.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: PMKVY is administered by MSDE while imparting soft, financial, digital, and entrepreneurship skills and certifying informal workers against NSQF standards.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because Statement 1 misattributes the scheme to the Ministry of Labour and Employment.

valueAddition.title: Three Core Pillars of PMKVY Implementation
bullets: Short-Term Training (STT): Conducted at PMKVY Training Centres (PMKKs) for school/college dropouts and unemployed youth, combining NSQF-aligned technical trades with soft skills, entrepreneurship, financial, and digital literacy.

Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) & Special Projects: RPL assesses and certifies existing informal skills of workers in unorganized sectors (construction, agriculture, handicrafts) without requiring full classroom courses, while Special Projects target vulnerable groups and customized industry needs.

valueAddition.title: Evolution to PMKVY 4.0 & Future-Ready Trades
bullets: Demand-Driven On-the-Job Training: PMKVY 4.0 (part of the Skill India Programme) shifts away from supply-driven training targets toward on-the-job training (OJT), industry partnerships, and new-age Industry 4.0 courses in AI, robotics, mechatronics, drones, and green hydrogen.

inNews.source: Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) / Press Information Bureau (PIB)
inNews.headline: Cabinet-approved restructured Skill India Programme scales PMKVY 4.0 with AI, drone, and green-skill training tracks across districts
inNews.relevance: October 2026 MSDE progress reviews highlighted expanded PMKVY 4.0 short-term training and Recognition of Prior Learning certifications across Industry 4.0, renewable energy, and digital trades.

statementBreakdown.reference: Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) · Nodal Ministry
statementBreakdown.explanation: PMKVY is the flagship scheme of the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE)—not the Ministry of Labour and Employment.

statementBreakdown.reference: PMKVY Short-Term Training Curriculum · Employability & Digital Modules
statementBreakdown.explanation: Alongside domain-specific technical trades, PMKVY short-term training explicitly incorporates mandatory modules in soft skills, entrepreneurship, financial literacy, and digital literacy.

statementBreakdown.reference: PMKVY Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) · NSQF Alignment
statementBreakdown.explanation: Through its Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) component, PMKVY assesses and certifies the informal competencies of workers in the unregulated sector and aligns them with the National Skill Qualification Framework (NSQF).

visualSuggestion.title: Skill Development vs. Employment Schemes: Nodal Ministries & Core Focus

stem: If the President of India exercises his power as provided under Article 356 of the Constitution in respect of a particular state, then

options.text: the Assembly of the State is automatically dissolved.
options.label: a

options.text: the powers of the Legislature of that state shall be exercisable by or under the authority of the Parliament.
options.label: b

options.text: Article 19 is suspended in that State.
options.label: c

options.text: the President can make laws relating to that state.
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: Mandates that upon the proclamation of President's Rule, the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament.
keywords.concept: Article 356(1)(b): Mandates that upon the proclamation of President's Rule, the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament.

keywords.shortNote: The constitutional status of the State Legislative Assembly immediately following an Article 356 proclamation, preserving it from dissolution until Parliament approves the proclamation.
keywords.concept: Suspended Animation: The constitutional status of the State Legislative Assembly immediately following an Article 356 proclamation, preserving it from dissolution until Parliament approves the proclamation.

keywords.shortNote: Governs the exercise of legislative powers of the State, enabling Parliament to confer law-making authority on the President.
keywords.concept: Article 357: Governs the exercise of legislative powers of the State, enabling Parliament to confer law-making authority on the President.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.reference: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
optionBreakdown.explanation: The State Legislative Assembly is placed under suspended animation upon the initial proclamation and is not dissolved automatically; as ruled in S.R. Bommai, dissolution can occur only after both Houses of Parliament approve the proclamation.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Article 356(1)(b) directly declares that the President may declare that the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fundamental Rights under Article 19 are automatically suspended only during a National Emergency declared under Article 352 on grounds of war or external aggression, bearing no application to President's Rule under Article 356.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: The President does not inherently acquire direct law-making powers upon the proclamation; under Article 357(1)(a), Parliament must first pass a law explicitly delegating its legislative power to the President before the President can enact President's Acts.

valueAddition.title: Article 356: Legal Anatomy & Direct Consequences
bullets: Twin Trigger Provisions: Article 356 (failure of constitutional machinery based on Governor's report or suo motu) and Article 365 (failure of a State to comply with or give effect to lawful executive directions from the Union).

Executive Powers: The President assumes to himself all or any functions of the State Government and all or any powers vested in or exercisable by the Governor or any body or authority in the State (the State Council of Ministers is dismissed).

Legislative Powers: Powers of the State Legislature vest in Parliament [Article 356(1)(b)]. Under Article 357(1)(a), Parliament may delegate this power to the President, who may then enact 'President's Acts' for that State.

Immunity of High Courts: Article 356(1) proviso explicitly prohibits the President from assuming any powers vested in or exercisable by a High Court or suspending any constitutional provision relating to High Courts.

Judicial Safeguards (S.R. Bommai, 1994): Proclamation is subject to judicial review; the Assembly cannot be dissolved before Parliamentary approval (only suspended); burden of proof lies on the Union to produce material justifying the breakdown.

valueAddition.title: National Emergency (Art. 352) vs. President's Rule (Art. 356)
bullets: Approval Timelines: Article 352 requires approval within one month by special majority; Article 356 requires approval within two months by simple majority of both Houses.

State Government Status: Under Article 352, State executive and legislature continue to function concurrently under Central control; under Article 356, the State executive is dismissed and legislative powers are taken over by Parliament.

Impact on Fundamental Rights: Article 352 suspends Article 19 (via Art. 358) and allows presidential suspension of right to enforce other FRs (via Art. 359, excluding Arts. 20 & 21); Article 356 has zero effect on Fundamental Rights.
Maximum Tenure: Article 352 has no constitutional maximum limit (can continue indefinitely with periodic approvals); Article 356 has a strict maximum ceiling of three years.

inNews.headline: Supreme Court reiterates Bommai guidelines on judicial review of gubernatorial reports leading to Article 356 recommendations
inNews.relevance: Reaffirms that the breakdown of constitutional machinery cannot be invoked arbitrarily for political instability where floor tests remain available.

keywords.shortNote: In the 1st Lok Sabha (1952), the Communist Party of India (CPI) won 16 seats and emerged as the single largest opposition party; the Swatantra Party was founded much later, in 1959.
keywords.concept: First Lok Sabha Opposition: In the 1st Lok Sabha (1952), the Communist Party of India (CPI) won 16 seats and emerged as the single largest opposition party; the Swatantra Party was founded much later, in 1959.

keywords.shortNote: The Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha was formally recognized for the first time in December 1969, when Ram Subhag Singh of Congress (O) was recognized following the Indian National Congress split.
keywords.concept: Leader of Opposion: The Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha was formally recognized for the first time in December 1969, when Ram Subhag Singh of Congress (O) was recognized following the Indian National Congress split.

keywords.shortNote: Under Direction 121 of the Speaker, an opposition party must possess at least 10% of the total strength of the House (55 members out of 543/545, not 75) to be recognized as an official Parliamentary Party and have its leader designated as Leader of the Opposition.
keywords.concept: 10% Quorum Benchmark (Mavalankar Rule): Under Direction 121 of the Speaker, an opposition party must possess at least 10% of the total strength of the House (55 members out of 543/545, not 75) to be recognized as an official Parliamentary Party and have its leader designated as Leader of the Opposition.

optionBreakdown.label: b

valueAddition.title: Leader of the Opposition: Legal & Institutional Framework
bullets: Statutory Recognition: Accorded formal statutory status under the Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977; holds the rank, salary, and perks equivalent to a Cabinet Minister.

Threshold Criteria: Section 2 of the 1977 Act defines the Leader of the Opposition as that member who is the Leader of the party in opposition to the Government having the greatest numerical strength and recognized as such by the Speaker/Chairman.

Direction 121 (The 10% Quorum Rule): Mandates that a group or party must have a strength not less than the quorum fixed to constitute a sitting of the House (one-tenth or 10% of total seats, i.e., 55 members in Lok Sabha and 25 members in Rajya Sabha).
Shadow Cabinet Origin: Modeled on the British Westminster convention where the Leader of the Opposition heads the Shadow Cabinet and prepares an alternative government.

valueAddition.title: Role in High-Level Statutory Selection Committees
bullets: Lokpal: Prime Minister, Speaker of Lok Sabha, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, Chief Justice of India (or nominee), and an eminent jurist (Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013).
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC): Prime Minister, Union Minister of Home Affairs, and Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha (CVC Act, 2003).
Central Information Commission (CIC): Prime Minister, Union Cabinet Minister, and Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha (RTI Act, 2005).
CBI Director: Prime Minister, CJI (or nominee), and Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha (DPSE Act, 1946). When no LoP is recognized, the leader of the single largest opposition party is included.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. No criminal proceedings shall be instituted against the Governor of a State in any court during his term of office.
2. The emoluments and allowances of the Governor of a State shall not be diminished during his term of office.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: Grants absolute criminal immunity, providing that no criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted or continued against the President or a Governor during their term of office.
keywords.concept: Article 361(2): Grants absolute criminal immunity, providing that no criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted or continued against the President or a Governor during their term of office.

keywords.shortNote: Protects gubernatorial independence by mandating that the emoluments and allowances of the Governor shall not be diminished during his term of office.
keywords.concept: Article 158(4): Protects gubernatorial independence by mandating that the emoluments and allowances of the Governor shall not be diminished during his term of office.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Confirms that both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are accurate constitutional provisions.

valueAddition.title: Article 158: Conditions of Governor's Office
bullets: Article 158(1) Legislative Incompatibility: The Governor cannot be a member of either House of Parliament or a House of the Legislature of any State; if an MP or MLA is appointed, they are deemed to have vacated their seat on the date of assuming office.
Article 158(2) Office of Profit: The Governor shall not hold any other office of profit.

Article 158(3) Official Residence & Allowances: Entitled without payment of rent to the use of official residences (Raj Bhavan) and such emoluments, allowances, and privileges as determined by Parliament by law (Governors (Emoluments, Allowances and Privileges) Act, 1982).

Article 158(3A) Dual Charge Apportionment: When the same individual is appointed Governor of two or more States (7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956), the emoluments and allowances are allocated among the States in such proportion as the President may by order determine.
Article 158(4) Non-Diminution: Emoluments and allowances cannot be reduced during the incumbency, safeguarding institutional independence from legislative hostility.

valueAddition.title: Article 361: Fourfold Executive Protection Matrix
bullets: Article 361(1) Non-Answerability: Personal immunity from answering to any court for official acts and duties (the Union or State government can still be sued under Article 300).
Article 361(2) Criminal Immunity: Complete shield against criminal prosecutions, charges, or FIR registrations during incumbency.
Article 361(3) Arrest Bar: Absolute prohibition on the issuance of any court process or warrant for arrest or imprisonment.

Article 361(4) Civil Suit Procedural Carve-out: Civil suits in respect of acts done in a personal capacity (before or after taking office) are permitted only after delivering a two-month advance written notice.

inNews.source: Supreme Court of India / The Hindu
inNews.headline: Supreme Court examines gubernatorial immunity under Article 361 in light of civil court petitions regarding pre-tenure liabilities
inNews.relevance: Directly reinforces the strict distinction between absolute criminal immunity under Article 361(2) and conditional civil liability under Article 361(4).

options.text: A bill shall be deemed to be a Money Bill if it contains only provisions relating to imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax.

options.text: A Money Bill has provisions for the custody of the Consolidated Fund of India or the Contingency Fund of India.
options.label: b

options.text: A Money Bill is concerned with the appropriation of moneys out of the Contingency Fund of India.
options.label: c

options.text: A Money Bill deals with the regulation of borrowing of money or giving of any guarantee by the Government of India.
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: The seven exhaustive sub-clauses (a to g) specifying matters that qualify a bill as a Money Bill if it contains 'only' those provisions.
keywords.concept: Article 110: The seven exhaustive sub-clauses (a to g) specifying matters that qualify a bill as a Money Bill if it contains 'only' those provisions.

keywords.shortNote: An imprest placed at the disposal of the President to facilitate immediate advances for unforeseen expenditure pending parliamentary authorization via supplementary demands or appropriation from the Consolidated Fund.
keywords.concept: Contingency Fund of India (Article 267): An imprest placed at the disposal of the President to facilitate immediate advances for unforeseen expenditure pending parliamentary authorization via supplementary demands or appropriation from the Consolidated Fund.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accurately quotes sub-clause (a) defining taxation provisions.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accurately quotes sub-clause (c) governing custody and payments into/out of both funds.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Substitutes 'Contingency Fund' where the Constitution strictly mandates 'Consolidated Fund of India'. Appropriation bills (under Art. 114) apply solely to the Consolidated Fund.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accurately quotes sub-clause (b) regarding sovereign borrowing and financial guarantees.

valueAddition.title: Article 110(1): Complete Seven-Clause Anatomy
bullets: (a) Tax: Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration, or regulation of any tax.
(b) Borrowing: Regulation of government borrowing or sovereign debt guarantees.
(c) Custody & Withdrawal: Custody of Consolidated Fund OR Contingency Fund, payments in or withdrawals out.
(d) Appropriation: Appropriation of moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India ONLY.
(e) Charged Expenditure: Declaring any expenditure to be expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund, or increasing its amount.
(f) Receipt & Audit: Receipt of money on account of Consolidated Fund or Public Account, or custody/issue/audit of such accounts.
(g) Incidental: Any matter incidental to any of the matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (f).

inNews.relevance: Direct examination of whether legislative enactments containing non-financial administrative clauses violate the restrictive definitional threshold of Article 110(1).

similarPyq.keyTakeaway: UPSC tests Article 110 and 109 both at the micro-textual level (exact fund names in clauses) and at the procedural macro-level (powers of Rajya Sabha).

statementBreakdown.explanation: Reflects the exact verbatim wording of Article 110(1)(a): 'the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax'.

Reflects the exact verbatim text of Article 110(1)(c): 'the custody of the Consolidated Fund of India or the Contingency Fund of India, the payment of moneys into or the withdrawal of moneys from any such Fund'.

This statement is factually and constitutionally wrong, hence the correct answer to this 'not correct' question. Under Article 110(1)(d), 'appropriation of moneys' applies exclusively out of the Consolidated Fund of India. Moneys are never 'appropriated' out of the Contingency Fund; rather, advances are made from it by the President under Article 267(1).
Reflects the verbatim text of Article 110(1)(b): 'the regulation of the borrowing of money or the giving of any guarantee by the Government of India'.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly shall vacate his/her office if he/she ceases to be a member of the assembly.
2. Whenever the Legislative Assembly is dissolved, the Speaker shall vacate his/her office immediately.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.concept: Office of Speaker

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 is the verbatim text of Article 179(a), while Statement 2 directly contradicts the express protection in the second proviso.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 2 is false because the Speaker remains in office despite the dissolution of the House.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Incorrectly accepts Statement 2 by missing the constitutional proviso on continuity.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Incorrectly rejects Statement 1, which is a fundamental condition of holding the office.

valueAddition.title: Office of Speaker: Vacation, Resignation & Removal
bullets: Vacation & Resignation (Art. 179): Vacates on losing membership (Art. 179(a)); resigns by writing under their hand addressed to the Deputy Speaker, NOT the Governor (Art. 179(b)).
Removal Procedure (Art. 179(c)): Removed by a resolution passed by all the then members of the Assembly (effective majority); requires at least 14 days' advance notice.

Presiding During Removal (Art. 181): When a removal resolution is under consideration, the Speaker cannot preside, but retains the right to speak, take part in proceedings, and vote in the first instance (no casting vote in case of equality of votes).
Parallel Constitutional Mirror: Article 178–181 for the State Legislative Assembly exactly mirror Articles 93–96 for the Lok Sabha.

inNews.headline: Constitutional Bench Deliberates Scope of Speaker's Powers During Assembly Dissolution and Interregnum
inNews.relevance: Direct examination of institutional continuity under Article 179 and the Speaker's administrative role until a newly elected Assembly convenes.

similarPyq.stem:
Regarding the office of the Lok Sabha Speaker, consider the following statements:
1. He/She holds the office during the pleasure of the President.
2. He/She need not be a member of the House at the time of his/her election but has to become a member of the House within six months from the date of his/her election.
3. If he/she intends to resign, the letter of his/her resignation has to be addressed to the Deputy Speaker.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

statementBreakdown.explanation: Article 179(a) provides that a member holding office as Speaker or Deputy Speaker of an Assembly shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the Assembly.

The second proviso to Article 179 explicitly states: 'Provided further that, whenever the Assembly is dissolved, the Speaker shall not vacate his office until immediately before the first meeting of the Assembly after the dissolution.' The Speaker continues in office to maintain institutional continuity.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Right to Privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of Right to Life and Personal Liberty.
Which of the following in the Constitution of India correctly and appropriately imply the above statement?

options.text: Article 14 and the provisions under the 42nd Amendment to the Constitution
options.label: a

options.text: Article 17 and the Directive Principles of State Policy in Part IV
options.label: b

options.text: Article 21 and the freedoms guaranteed in Part IlI
options.label: c

options.text: Article 24 and the provisions under the 44th Amendment to the Constitution
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: An intrinsic constitutional entitlement protecting bodily integrity, informational self-determination, and personal spatial autonomy under Article 21.
keywords.concept: Right to Privacy: An intrinsic constitutional entitlement protecting bodily integrity, informational self-determination, and personal spatial autonomy under Article 21.

keywords.shortNote: The fundamental guarantee that no person shall be deprived of their life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
keywords.concept: Article 21: The fundamental guarantee that no person shall be deprived of their life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

keywords.shortNote: The foundational matrix of Fundamental Rights, particularly Articles 14, 19, and 21, within which privacy operates as a structural core.
keywords.concept: Part III: The foundational matrix of Fundamental Rights, particularly Articles 14, 19, and 21, within which privacy operates as a structural core.

keywords.shortNote: Unanimous 9-judge Constitution Bench ruling establishing privacy as a Fundamental Right, formally overruling M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962).
keywords.concept: Puttaswamy Verdict (2017): Unanimous 9-judge Constitution Bench ruling establishing privacy as a Fundamental Right, formally overruling M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962).

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Pairs equality before law with the 42nd Amendment, which inserted socialist principles and duties rather than establishing personal privacy protections.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Combines the abolition of untouchability with non-justiciable socio-economic governance directives, missing the essential seat of personal liberty.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (c) is correct. Chief Justice J.S. Khehar's leading opinion held that privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and forms part of the freedoms guaranteed in Part III.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: References the prohibition of hazardous child labour and the Janata-era amendment focused on property demotion and emergency safeguards, bearing no link to privacy.

valueAddition.title: Verbatim Judicial Dictum: Paragraph 3-R in Puttaswamy
bullets: Verbatim Judgment Phrasing: Chief Justice Khehar's order for the nine-judge bench concluded: 'The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.' UPSC lifted the question and correct option verbatim from this conclusion.

The 'Penumbral Radiance' Principle: Justice J. Chelameswar noted that privacy is not an isolated island but a penumbral right that radiates across Article 19(1)(a) (speech and thought), Article 19(1)(d) (movement), and Article 25 (freedom of conscience).

Dignity as an Inalienable Core: Justice D.Y. Chandrachud emphasized that privacy is the constitutional core of human dignity, without which individual autonomy and self-determination cannot meaningfully exist.

valueAddition.title: Historical Juxtaposition: The Decoy Amendments
bullets: Part III vs. Part IV Decoy: Option (b) pairs Article 17 with Directive Principles; while DPSPs inform constitutional interpretation, the Supreme Court specifically grounded privacy as an enforceable fundamental entitlement within Part III.
Three-Year Testing Cycle: UPSC formulated this verbatim test in 2018 immediately following the August 2017 judgment, then retested its direct anchor in 2021 and 2024.

inNews.source: The Hindu / Supreme Court of India
inNews.headline: Supreme Court Invokes Puttaswamy Part III Standards to Evaluate State Health Database Surveillance Safeguards
inNews.relevance: Constitution Benches consistently apply the Puttaswamy doctrine (Article 21 read with Part III freedoms) to ensure digital welfare architectures maintain strict proportionality and statutory data protections.

subject: Indian Polity
stem:
Which of the following are regarded as the main features of the "Rule of Law"?
1. Limitation of Powers
2. Equality before law
3. People's responsibility to the Government
4. Liberty and civil rights
Select the correct answer using the code given below:

keywords.shortNote: Constitutional doctrine demanding government action be bounded by established laws, ensuring non-arbitrariness, legal equality, and individual liberty.
keywords.concept: Rule of Law: Constitutional doctrine demanding government action be bounded by established laws, ensuring non-arbitrariness, legal equality, and individual liberty.

keywords.shortNote: Constitutionalism principle restricting governmental authority to prevent arbitrary executive action and protect citizens' fundamental freedoms.
keywords.concept: Limitation of Powers: Constitutionalism principle restricting governmental authority to prevent arbitrary executive action and protect citizens' fundamental freedoms.

keywords.shortNote: A.V. Dicey's second pillar stating that all individuals, irrespective of rank or status, remain equally subject to the ordinary jurisdiction of the courts.
keywords.concept: Equality before law: A.V. Dicey's second pillar stating that all individuals, irrespective of rank or status, remain equally subject to the ordinary jurisdiction of the courts.

keywords.shortNote: Legal entitlements and fundamental protections guaranteed to individuals against arbitrary state encroachments and private tyranny.
keywords.concept: Civil rights and liberties: Legal entitlements and fundamental protections guaranteed to individuals against arbitrary state encroachments and private tyranny.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (c) is correct. Limitation of powers, legal equality, and civil liberties constitute the core elements of the Rule of Law, while Statement 3 describes authoritarian regimes.

valueAddition.title: A.V. Dicey's Triad & Basic Structure Status
bullets: Dicey's Three Pillars: (1) Absence of arbitrary power; (2) Equality before law; (3) The constitution as the result of the ordinary law of the land.
Basic Structure Anchor: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) firmly entrenched the Rule of Law as an unamendable feature of the Indian Constitution.

valueAddition.title: Inverted Accountability Distractor
bullets: Inverted Accountability Trap: Statement 3 subtly swaps 'Government's responsibility to the people' with 'People's responsibility to the Government'.
Authoritarian Decoy: Citizen responsibility to the state characterizes totalitarian doctrines, whereas liberal constitutionalism prioritizes civil rights over executive prerogatives.

inNews.relevance: Direct judicial warnings that executive actions must follow due process and statutory procedures reinforce that limitation of powers remains the operational core of Article 14.

subject: Indian Polity
stem: Which one of the following reflects the most appropriate relationship between law and liberty?

options.text: If there are more laws, there is less liberty.
options.label: a

options.text: If there are no laws, there is no liberty.
options.label: b

options.text: If there is liberty, laws have to be made by the people.
options.label: c

options.text: If laws are changed too often, liberty is in danger.
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: The fundamental political theory relationship establishing that just laws do not abolish or restrain liberty, but preserve and enlarge it.
keywords.concept: Law and Liberty: The fundamental political theory relationship establishing that just laws do not abolish or restrain liberty, but preserve and enlarge it.

keywords.shortNote: The classical formulation from the Second Treatise: 'where there is no law, there is no freedom'.
keywords.concept: John Locke's Maxim: The classical formulation from the Second Treatise: 'where there is no law, there is no freedom'.

keywords.shortNote: Freedom from arbitrary external restraint, which requires legal boundaries to prevent stronger individuals from coercing weaker ones.
keywords.concept: Negative Liberty: Freedom from arbitrary external restraint, which requires legal boundaries to prevent stronger individuals from coercing weaker ones.

keywords.shortNote: The constitutional principle ensuring that governance is anchored in established, foreseeable laws rather than arbitrary individual wills.
keywords.concept: Rule of Law: The constitutional principle ensuring that governance is anchored in established, foreseeable laws rather than arbitrary individual wills.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Presents an inverse mechanical relationship rooted in extreme laissez-faire or anarchism; in constitutional jurisprudence, protective laws (such as labour or anti-discrimination statutes) enhance rather than diminish aggregate human liberty.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: John Locke's 'Second Treatise of Government' (Sec. 57) & NCERT Class XI
optionBreakdown.explanation: Option (b) is correct. Locke demonstrated that the true end of law is not to abolish or restrain, but to preserve and enlarge freedom; in the absence of enforceable legal rules, the weak remain at the mercy of the strong, destroying liberty.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: Democratic Process vs. Substantive Liberty Nexus
optionBreakdown.explanation: Reflects Rousseau's doctrine of popular sovereignty and democratic legislation; while participatory lawmaking is a hallmark of representative democracy, it describes the procedural origin of laws rather than the foundational relationship between law and liberty.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: Legal Stability & Rule of Law Precepts
optionBreakdown.explanation: Captures an observation regarding statutory volatility and institutional instability; frequent legal amendments threaten legal certainty and predictability, but this does not define the essential relationship between law and liberty.

valueAddition.title: Lockean Constitutionalism: Law as the Enabler of Freedom
bullets: Locke's Exact Thesis: In Chapter VI of the Second Treatise of Government (1689), John Locke wrote: 'The end of law is not to abolish or restrain, but to preserve and enlarge freedom... where there is no law, there is no freedom. For liberty is to be free from restraint and violence from others, which cannot be where there is no law.'

Distinction from Hobbesian Absolutism: Thomas Hobbes argued in Leviathan that law is a command that curbs natural freedom to prevent a violent state of nature. In contrast, Locke and modern constitutionalists view law as the protective framework that transforms precarious natural license into secure civil liberty.

Harmonization with Part III of the Indian Constitution: Articles 14 to 22 demonstrate that liberty is not an unregulated void; the State enacts laws (such as Article 15(3) protections or Article 21A free education) specifically to guarantee real, substantive freedom to vulnerable citizens.

valueAddition.title: Superlative Relational Bait: Locke vs. Rousseau vs. Montesquieu
bullets: The 'Most Appropriate' Superlative: The stem asks for the 'most appropriate relationship'. Options (a), (c), and (d) all represent recognizable political aphorisms, but Option (b) captures the indispensable ontological prerequisite of liberty.

The Rousseau Decoy: Option (c) embodies Rousseau's concept of moral freedom (obeying a law that people prescribe to themselves). However, a democratically enacted law can still be tyrannical (the tyranny of the majority) if it lacks constitutional limits.

The Libertarian Fallacy: Option (a) treats every law as an automatic subtraction from liberty. In reality, a traffic law or a penal prohibition against assault does not reduce freedom—it guarantees the freedom of all road users and citizens to live without violence.

keywords.concept: Rules Committee: A procedure-regulating panel in each House (15 LS / 16 RS) chaired ex-officio by the Presiding Officer (Speaker/Chairman) to review and amend the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business.

optionBreakdown.label: a

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Directly matches the verbatim statutory function of overseeing subordinate legislation, statutory orders, and rule-making authority.

optionBreakdown.label: c

valueAddition.title: Comparing Committees
bullets: Bicameral Architecture: All four are separate single-House committees, not joint bodies (e.g., Subordinate Legislation has 15 LS / 15 RS; Assurances has 15 LS / 10 RS; Rules has 15 LS / 16 RS; BAC has 15 LS / 11 RS).

Chairmanship Distinction: Business Advisory Committee and Rules Committee are ex-officio chaired by the Speaker in Lok Sabha and Chairman in Rajya Sabha; Subordinate Legislation and Assurances chairs are nominated by the Presiding Officer from among members.

Ministerial Bar vs Inclusion: Ministers are strictly ineligible for Subordinate Legislation and Assurances; conversely, the Minister for Parliamentary Affairs is a key member in the Business Advisory Committee.
Ultra Vires Audit: Subordinate Legislation checks whether executive rules contain retrospective clauses, bar judicial review, or impose unauthorized fees/taxes without explicit parent Act approval.
