subject: Economy
stem:
Which of the following is/are included in the capital budget of the Government of India?
1. Expenditure on acquisition of assets like roads, buildings, machinery, etc.
2. Loans received from foreign governments
3. Loans and advances granted to the States and Union Territories
Select the correct answer using the code given below.

keywords.shortNote: The component of the Union Budget comprising Capital Receipts (transactions that create liabilities or reduce financial assets) and Capital Expenditure (outlays that create physical/financial assets or reduce liabilities).
keywords.concept: Capital Budget: The component of the Union Budget comprising Capital Receipts (transactions that create liabilities or reduce financial assets) and Capital Expenditure (outlays that create physical/financial assets or reduce liabilities).

keywords.shortNote: Government outlays resulting in the creation of physical or financial assets—such as roads, buildings, machinery, equity investments, and loans granted to States—or reduction in financial liabilities.
keywords.concept: Capital Expenditure (CapEx): Government outlays resulting in the creation of physical or financial assets—such as roads, buildings, machinery, equity investments, and loans granted to States—or reduction in financial liabilities.

keywords.shortNote: Loans raised by the Central Government from foreign governments and multilateral institutions under Article 292, recorded as debt-creating capital receipts because they create a future repayment liability.
keywords.concept: External Borrowings (Capital Receipts): Loans raised by the Central Government from foreign governments and multilateral institutions under Article 292, recorded as debt-creating capital receipts because they create a future repayment liability.

keywords.term: Loans and Advances by Central Government
keywords.shortNote: Credit extended by the Union to State Governments, Union Territories, and CPSEs, classified as capital expenditure because it creates a financial asset (loan receivable) on the Centre's balance sheet.
keywords.concept: Loans and Advances by Central Government: Credit extended by the Union to State Governments, Union Territories, and CPSEs, classified as capital expenditure because it creates a financial asset (loan receivable) on the Centre's balance sheet.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Overlooks that the Capital Budget encompasses both Capital Receipts (foreign loans) and Capital Expenditure (loans granted to States).

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Excludes physical infrastructure creation (roads, buildings, machinery), which is the most recognizable form of capital expenditure.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to recognize that loans received from foreign governments are capital receipts inside the Capital Budget.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: All three items belong to the Capital Budget: items 1 and 3 are Capital Expenditure (creating physical and financial assets), while item 2 is a Capital Receipt (creating a debt liability).

valueAddition.title: Why Both Sides of a Loan sit in the Capital Budget
bullets: The Capital Budget has two sides—Capital Receipts and Capital Expenditure—and any transaction that alters the government's balance sheet of assets or liabilities belongs here.
When the Centre receives a loan from a foreign government, its debt liability rises (Capital Receipt); when the Centre grants a loan to a State or UT, its financial asset rises (Capital Expenditure).

By contrast, annual interest paid on foreign loans (Revenue Expenditure) and annual interest received from States (Revenue Receipt) sit in the Revenue Budget because they neither create nor extinguish principal assets or liabilities.

valueAddition.title: Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment
bullets: In recent Union Budgets, the Centre has expanded 50-year interest-free loans to States under the 'Scheme for Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment'—booked directly as Central Capital Expenditure.

inNews.source: Ministry of Finance / PIB
inNews.headline: Centre Releases Fresh Tranche of 50-Year Interest-Free Capital Assistance Loans to States for FY27
inNews.relevance: The Finance Ministry approved additional 50-year interest-free loans to States in November 2026 to accelerate state-level infrastructure capex, illustrating how loans to States operate as Central capital expenditure.

statementBreakdown.reference: NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics — Capital Expenditure
statementBreakdown.explanation: Spending on acquiring physical infrastructure and capital goods such as roads, buildings, and machinery directly creates durable public assets, making it core capital expenditure.

statementBreakdown.reference: Union Budget Receipt Budget — External Debt
statementBreakdown.explanation: Loans received from foreign governments create a future sovereign repayment obligation (liability), placing them squarely under debt-creating capital receipts within the Capital Budget.

statementBreakdown.reference: NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics — Financial Asset Creation
statementBreakdown.explanation: Loans and advances granted by the Centre to States and Union Territories create a financial asset (a claim to future principal repayment) for the Union Government, making them capital expenditure.

visualSuggestion.title: Anatomy of the Union Capital Budget

rows: Loans & advances granted to States and UTs

hook.headline: Do loans given by the Centre to States count as Capital Expenditure?
hook.teaser: Notice how UPSC combines both sides of the Capital Budget—receipts and expenditure—into one three-statement check.

keywords.term: capital budget of the Government of India
keywords.calloutTerm: “capital budget of the Government of India”
keywords.calloutNote: Remember that the Capital Budget includes BOTH Capital Receipts (items that create liabilities) and Capital Expenditure (items that create assets).
activePhrases: capital budget of the Government of India

keywords.term: Loans and advances granted to the States and Union Territories
keywords.calloutTerm: “Loans and advances granted to the States and Union Territories”
keywords.calloutNote: When the Centre lends money to States, it gains a financial asset—so lending is Capital Expenditure, while borrowing abroad is a Capital Receipt.
activePhrases: Loans and advances granted to the States and Union Territories
dimmedPhrases: capital budget of the Government of India
contextPhrases: acquisition of assets like roads, buildings, machinery

verdicts.source: Spending on roads, buildings, and machinery creates long-term physical assets, which is textbook capital expenditure.
Loans received from foreign governments create a future repayment liability, placing them under capital receipts in the Capital Budget.
Loans granted to States and UTs create a financial asset (loan receivable) for the Centre, making them capital expenditure.

answer.label: D
answer.text: Every single item either creates an asset or creates a liability inside the Capital Budget—so 1, 2 and 3 is right.

valueAddition.title: Value addition
valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your Union Budget notes

items.title: Asset or Liability Test
items.desc: Any transaction creating/reducing an asset or liability enters the Capital Budget; everything else enters the Revenue Budget.

items.title: Principal vs. Interest Split
items.desc: Giving or receiving loan principal sits in the Capital Budget, while paying or receiving interest sits in the Revenue Budget.

items.title: Grants Are Revenue Outlay
items.desc: Unlike loans to States (Capital Expenditure), non-repayable grants given to States are booked as Revenue Expenditure.

valueAddition.note: Never confuse 'loans granted to States' (repayable, creates a financial asset -> Capital Expenditure) with 'grants given to States' (non-repayable -> Revenue Expenditure).

subject: Economy
stem: Recently, which one of the following currencies has been proposed to be added to the basket of IMF's SDR?

keywords.shortNote: An international reserve asset created by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in 1969 to supplement member countries' official reserves, whose daily value is determined by a weighted basket of five major world currencies.
keywords.concept: Special Drawing Rights (SDR): An international reserve asset created by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in 1969 to supplement member countries' official reserves, whose daily value is determined by a weighted basket of five major world currencies.

keywords.shortNote: The dual IMF benchmark required for inclusion in the SDR basket—requiring a currency to be both widely used to make payments for international transactions and widely traded in the principal foreign exchange markets.
keywords.concept: Freely Usable Currency Criterion: The dual IMF benchmark required for inclusion in the SDR basket—requiring a currency to be both widely used to make payments for international transactions and widely traded in the principal foreign exchange markets.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: The Russian Rouble has never been part of or formally approved for addition to the IMF's Special Drawing Rights currency basket.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: The South African Rand does not meet the global trade share or freely usable currency thresholds required for the SDR valuation basket.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Because the Indian Rupee lacks full capital account convertibility and carries a smaller share in global FX settlement turnover, it is not included in the SDR basket.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.reference: IMF Executive Board SDR Review (November 2015 / October 2016)
optionBreakdown.explanation: Following its five-yearly review in November 2015, the IMF Executive Board added the Chinese Renminbi (RMB) as the fifth currency in the SDR basket effective October 1, 2016.

valueAddition.title: The Five-Currency IMF SDR Basket & Dual Inclusion Criteria
bullets: Current Five-Currency Basket: US Dollar (USD), Euro (EUR), Chinese Renminbi (CNY/RMB), Japanese Yen (JPY), and British Pound Sterling (GBP)—reviewed by the IMF Executive Board every five years (most recently in 2022, where the Renminbi's weight rose to 12.28%, behind only the US Dollar and Euro).

Two Mandatory Criteria: To enter the SDR basket, an economy must be among the world's top exporters (Export Criterion) and its currency must be judged 'freely usable'—widely used in international payments and widely traded in major foreign exchange markets.

valueAddition.title: What SDRs Actually Are (And What They Are Not)
bullets: An SDR is neither a physical currency nor a direct claim on the IMF; rather, it is a potential claim on the freely usable currencies of IMF members, allowing countries to exchange SDRs for hard currency (USD, EUR, JPY, GBP, RMB) during Balance of Payments liquidity needs.
SDRs form one of the four components of India's Foreign Exchange Reserves alongside Foreign Currency Assets (FCA), Gold Reserves, and the Reserve Tranche Position (RTP) with the IMF.

inNews.source: International Monetary Fund (IMF) / Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
inNews.headline: IMF Prepares Groundwork for 2027 Quinquennial SDR Valuation Review Amid Rising Asian Currency Settlement Volumes
inNews.relevance: October 2026 IMF reserve-currency tracking confirmed the five-currency SDR basket—US Dollar, Euro, Chinese Renminbi, Japanese Yen, and British Pound—anchoring member SDR allocations and India's foreign exchange reserve holdings.

visualSuggestion.title: Composition & Criteria of the IMF SDR Currency Basket

rows: Top global export share + Freely usable currency
First emerging-market currency to meet export & freely usable tests
Deep, liquid global foreign exchange settlement markets

hook.headline: Which emerging-market currency joined the IMF's exclusive SDR basket in 2016?
hook.teaser: Notice how the IMF's 'freely usable currency' rule narrows all four emerging-market options down to one.

keywords.calloutNote: Special Drawing Rights are valued daily using a five-currency basket—US Dollar, Euro, Japanese Yen, British Pound, and the newly added fifth currency.
activePhrases: basket of IMF's SDR

keywords.calloutNote: China's Renminbi became the first emerging-market currency to join the SDR basket in October 2016 after meeting the IMF's export and freely usable criteria.
activePhrases: Renminbi
dimmedPhrases: basket of IMF's SDR

verdicts.source: The Russian Rouble has never been included in or proposed for addition to the IMF's SDR currency basket.
The South African Rand does not meet the IMF's global export and freely usable currency thresholds.
The Indian Rupee lacks full capital account convertibility and is not part of the SDR valuation basket.
The IMF Executive Board approved adding China's Renminbi (RMB) as the fifth currency in the SDR basket effective October 2016.

answer.label: D
answer.text: China's Renminbi joined the US Dollar, Euro, Yen, and Pound as the fifth SDR currency—so Option D is right.

valueAddition.subtitle: Add these to your External Sector & IMF notes

items.title: Current SDR Basket
items.desc: US Dollar, Euro, Chinese Renminbi, Japanese Yen, and British Pound—reviewed every 5 years by the IMF.

items.title: SDR Entry Criteria
items.desc: A currency must belong to a top global exporter and be 'freely usable' in international payments and FX trading.

items.desc: India's Forex Reserves hold Foreign Currency Assets, Gold, IMF SDRs, and the Reserve Tranche Position (RTP).

valueAddition.note: Remember that SDR is a reserve asset backed by five freely usable currencies, not a printed currency—and the Renminbi is the only non-G7 currency inside it.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to 'Financial Stability and Development Council, consider the following statements:
1. It is an organ of NITI Aayog.
2. It is headed by the Union Finance
3. It monitors macroprudential supervision of the economy.
Which of the statements given above is/are

keywords.shortNote: An apex non-statutory body set up under the Ministry of Finance to ensure macroeconomic stability and inter-regulatory coordination.
keywords.concept: Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC): An apex non-statutory body set up under the Ministry of Finance to ensure macroeconomic stability and inter-regulatory coordination.

keywords.shortNote: System-wide financial oversight aimed at mitigating systemic risks across interconnected financial sectors rather than individual institutions alone.
keywords.concept: Macroprudential Supervision: System-wide financial oversight aimed at mitigating systemic risks across interconnected financial sectors rather than individual institutions alone.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect because FSDC is under the Ministry of Finance, not NITI Aayog.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Omits statement 2, which is correct.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statements 2 and 3 accurately describe the leadership and mandate of the FSDC.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Incorrectly includes statement 1.

valueAddition.title: What is the Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC)?
bullets: Genesis & Nature: Proposed by the Raghuram Rajan Committee on Financial Sector Reforms (2008) and constituted in December 2010. It is an apex, non-statutory executive body functioning under the Ministry of Finance.

Core Purpose: Resolves inter-regulatory friction, addresses jurisdictional overlaps, and maintains systemic stability across banking, capital markets, insurance, and pensions without eroding the statutory autonomy of individual regulators.

valueAddition.title: FSDC Composition & Dual-Tier Structure
bullets: FSDC Apex Council: Chaired by the Union Finance Minister. Members include Governor of RBI, Chairpersons of SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, and IFSCA, along with Finance Secretary, Secretaries of DEA, DFS, MeitY, MCA, Revenue, and the Chief Economic Adviser (CEA).
FSDC Sub-Committee: Chaired by the Governor of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). It handles frequent operational meetings, continuous technical risk assessments, and background preparatory work.

valueAddition.title: Core Mandate & Functional Domains
bullets: Macroprudential Oversight: Monitors systemic financial risks, contagion pathways, and the health of interconnected Financial Conglomerates (FCs).
Financial Inclusion & Literacy: Drives nationwide strategies for expanding banking access, consumer awareness, and credit penetration.
Coordination with Global Bodies: Manages India's interface with international bodies like the Financial Stability Board (FSB) and Financial Action Task Force (FATF).

inNews.source: Ministry of Finance / PIB / The Hindu
inNews.headline: Union Finance Minister chairs FSDC meeting to review systemic financial resilience and inter-regulatory framework for cross-border fintech flows
inNews.relevance: Directly reaffirms the leadership of the Union Finance Minister and the core macroprudential oversight mandate tested in Statements 2 and 3.

statementBreakdown.explanation: FSDC is not an organ of NITI Aayog. It was established by an executive order of the Government of India in December 2010 under the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance.

The Council is chaired by the Union Finance Minister. Its members include the heads of all financial sector regulators (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, IFSCA), key Finance Ministry secretaries, and the Chief Economic Adviser.
Monitoring macroprudential supervision of the entire economy—including the functioning of large financial conglomerates and addressing systemic risks—is a primary mandate of the FSDC.

visualSuggestion.title: FSDC Apex Council vs. FSDC Sub-Committee

rows: Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance

hook.headline: Who really heads the Financial Stability Council?

subject: Economy
stem: In the context of which of the following do you sometimes find the terms 'amber box, blue box and green box' in the news?

keywords.shortNote: A WTO multilateral treaty negotiated during the 1986–1994 Uruguay Round that disciplines agricultural trade across three pillars: market access, domestic support, and export competition.
keywords.concept: Agreement on Agriculture (AoA): A WTO multilateral treaty negotiated during the 1986–1994 Uruguay Round that disciplines agricultural trade across three pillars: market access, domestic support, and export competition.

keywords.shortNote: The annual monetary value of trade-distorting Amber Box domestic agricultural subsidies calculated by the WTO, subject to de minimis caps of 5% of agricultural production value for developed countries and 10% for developing countries.
keywords.concept: Aggregate Measurement of Support (AMS): The annual monetary value of trade-distorting Amber Box domestic agricultural subsidies calculated by the WTO, subject to de minimis caps of 5% of agricultural production value for developed countries and 10% for developing countries.

keywords.shortNote: The permissible threshold of trade-distorting Amber Box domestic support exempted from reduction commitments—capped at 5% of total agricultural production value for developed nations and 10% for developing nations.
keywords.concept: De Minimis Ceiling: The permissible threshold of trade-distorting Amber Box domestic support exempted from reduction commitments—capped at 5% of total agricultural production value for developed nations and 10% for developing nations.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.reference: WTO Agreement on Agriculture · Domestic Support Boxes
optionBreakdown.explanation: Under the WTO's Agreement on Agriculture, domestic farm subsidies are classified into Amber, Blue, and Green Boxes—much like traffic lights—based on how much they distort international agricultural trade.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation
optionBreakdown.explanation: SAARC deals with South Asian regional cooperation and SAFTA tariff schedules, not the multilateral agricultural subsidy box classification.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: UN Framework Convention on Climate Change
optionBreakdown.explanation: UNFCCC governs climate mitigation, adaptation, and climate finance mechanisms (such as the Green Climate Fund), not agricultural trade subsidy boxes.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: While agricultural market access comes up in India–EU FTA talks, the Amber, Blue, and Green Box terminology originates strictly from the multilateral WTO Agreement on Agriculture.

valueAddition.title: The Traffic-Light Logic of WTO Farm Subsidies
bullets: Amber Box (Slow Down / Reduce): All domestic support measures considered to distort production and trade—such as Minimum Support Price (MSP) procurement and input subsidies on power, fertilizers, and irrigation. Capped under Aggregate Measurement of Support (AMS) at 5% (developed) and 10% (developing) de minimis limits.

Blue Box (Amber Box with Conditions): Subsidies tied to acreage or livestock numbers that require farmers to limit production (production-limiting quotas or land set-aside programs), currently exempt from spending caps.

Green Box (Go / Unlimited): Subsidies causing zero or minimal trade distortion—must be government-funded (not through higher consumer prices) and decoupled from current production or prices. Includes agricultural research, pest control, disaster relief, environmental conservation, and decoupled income support (such as PM-KISAN).

valueAddition.title: Why India Clashes at the WTO Over Amber Box Rules
bullets: Outdated 1986–88 Reference Price: WTO calculates Amber Box price support by comparing current administered prices (MSP) against a frozen 1986–88 external reference price, artificially inflating India's subsidy figures due to decades of inflation.

Bali Peace Clause (2013): Protects developing countries' public stockholding (PSH) food-security programmes from legal challenges if they breach the 10% de minimis limit, pending a permanent solution at the WTO.

inNews.source: WTO Committee on Agriculture / Ministry of Commerce & Industry
inNews.headline: India and G-33 coalition press WTO Agriculture Committee for permanent solution on Public Stockholding and Amber Box inflation adjustment
inNews.relevance: WTO Agriculture Committee negotiations in October 2026 saw India and the G-33 coalition demand updating the 1986–88 external reference price used to compute Amber Box ceilings for public food procurement programmes.

With reference to the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC), consider the following statements:
1. IMFC discusses matters of concern affecting the global economy, and advises the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on the direction of its work.
2. The World Bank participates as observer in IMFC's meetings.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: The primary ministerial-level advisory body to the IMF Board of Governors that deliberates on global economic stability and guides the Fund's policy work program twice a year.
keywords.concept: International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC): The primary ministerial-level advisory body to the IMF Board of Governors that deliberates on global economic stability and guides the Fund's policy work program twice a year.

keywords.shortNote: NA
keywords.concept: International Monetory Fund (IMF): NA

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because Statement 2 is also accurate.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because Statement 1 is also accurate.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both the advisory mandate of the IMFC to the IMF and the World Bank's participation as an observer are core institutional features of IMFC meetings.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Eliminated because both statements come directly from the official IMF governance description of the IMFC.

valueAddition.title: Structure & Functioning of the IMFC
bullets: Composition: Comprises 24 members (finance ministers or central bank governors) drawn from the 191 IMF Governors, mirroring the exact 24 constituencies of the IMF Executive Board so every member country is represented.

Consensus Operation: The IMFC has no formal voting power; it meets twice a year (during the Spring and Annual Meetings) and operates by consensus, issuing a communiqué that guides the IMF's half-yearly work agenda.
Historical Origin: Created in September 1999 to replace the Interim Committee of the Board of Governors on the International Monetary System (established in 1974).

valueAddition.title: IMFC vs. Joint Development Committee
bullets: IMFC (IMF-only Advisory): Focuses on macroeconomic stability, exchange rates, sovereign debt, and systemic financial risks; the World Bank attends as an observer.

Development Committee (Joint World Bank–IMF Body): Formally titled the Joint Ministerial Committee of the Boards of Governors of the Bank and the Fund on the Transfer of Real Resources to Developing Countries—advises both institutions jointly on poverty reduction and development finance.

inNews.relevance: At the October 2026 IMFC meeting in Bangkok, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman represented India's four-country constituency alongside World Bank President Ajay Banga attending as an official observer.

statementBreakdown.explanation: The IMFC advises and reports to the IMF Board of Governors on the supervision and management of the international monetary and financial system, setting strategic guidance for the IMF's work program.
Several international institutions—including the World Bank Group, WTO, BIS, UN, UNCTAD, OECD, FSB, and ILO—participate as official observers in IMFC meetings.

subject: Economy
stem: Which of the following best describes the term 'import cover', sometimes seen in the news?

options.text: It is the ratio of value of imports to the Gross Domestic Product of a country.
options.label: a

options.text: It is the total value of imports of a country in a year.
options.label: b

options.text: It is the ratio between the value of exports and that of imports between two countries.
options.label: c

options.text: It is the number of months of imports that could be paid for by a country's international reserves.
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: An external sector adequacy metric measuring the number of months of projected merchandise imports a country can finance solely using its existing foreign exchange reserves.
keywords.concept: Import Cover: An external sector adequacy metric measuring the number of months of projected merchandise imports a country can finance solely using its existing foreign exchange reserves.

keywords.shortNote: An international reserve adequacy benchmark stating that a country's foreign exchange reserves should at least equal 100% of its short-term external debt maturing within one year.
keywords.concept: Guidotti–Greenspan Rule: An international reserve adequacy benchmark stating that a country's foreign exchange reserves should at least equal 100% of its short-term external debt maturing within one year.

keywords.shortNote: External assets held and controlled by a country's central bank—comprising Foreign Currency Assets, Gold, SDRs, and the IMF Reserve Tranche Position—to back liabilities and stabilize currency markets.
keywords.concept: Foreign Exchange Reserves: External assets held and controlled by a country's central bank—comprising Foreign Currency Assets, Gold, SDRs, and the IMF Reserve Tranche Position—to back liabilities and stabilize currency markets.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: The ratio of total imports to GDP measures an economy's trade openness and import intensity, not its reserve adequacy.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Total annual import value is simply the gross import bill on the current account, without comparing it against foreign exchange reserves.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.reference: Bilateral Export-Import Ratio / Terms of Trade
optionBreakdown.explanation: Comparing exports against imports between two countries reflects bilateral trade balance or terms of trade, unrelated to import cover.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Import cover divides total foreign exchange reserves by the average monthly merchandise import bill, showing how many months a nation can pay for essential imports if all foreign inflows suddenly stop.

valueAddition.title: Calculation & Policy Benchmark of Import Cover
bullets: Formula: Import Cover (in months) = Total Foreign Exchange Reserves / Average Monthly Merchandise Imports.

Adequacy Threshold: International financial institutions and the RBI generally treat an import cover of 3 to 4 months as the minimum safety floor, while 10 to 12 months signals strong external resilience against sudden capital outflows or oil price shocks.

Historical Contrast: During India's 1991 Balance of Payments crisis, import cover plunged to barely 2 weeks (~$1.2 billion in reserves), whereas strong reserve accumulation pushed it above 11 months in recent years.

valueAddition.title: Key External Sector Vulnerability Indicators Tracked by RBI
bullets: Import Cover of Reserves: Measures current-account shock absorption capacity (months of goods imports covered).
Short-Term Debt to Reserves Ratio: Tracks capital-account rollover risk (residual maturity short-term debt as a percentage of forex reserves).
Net International Investment Position (NIIP): Shows the gap between a country's external financial assets and external liabilities as a percentage of GDP.

inNews.headline: India's foreign exchange reserves provide over 11 months of import cover amid steady merchandise trade flows
inNews.relevance: RBI's October 2026 reserve management report confirmed that India's forex buffer covers more than 11 months of projected merchandise imports, insulating the rupee against global rate and oil volatility.

stem:
What is/are the purpose/purposes of Government's 'Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme' and 'Gold Monetization Scheme'?
1. To bring the idle gold lying with Indian households into the economy.
2. To promote FDI in the gold and jewellery sector.
3. To reduce India's dependence on gold imports.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.

keywords.shortNote: Government securities denominated in grams of gold issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India as a paper/demat substitute for holding physical bullion, paying a fixed annual coupon alongside market-linked gold price appreciation.
keywords.concept: Sovereign Gold Bond (SGB): Government securities denominated in grams of gold issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India as a paper/demat substitute for holding physical bullion, paying a fixed annual coupon alongside market-linked gold price appreciation.

keywords.shortNote: A scheme launched in 2015 replacing the earlier Gold Deposit Scheme that enables resident households, trusts, and institutions to deposit idle physical gold with designated banks in exchange for interest-bearing metal-account returns.
keywords.concept: Gold Monetization Scheme (GMS): A scheme launched in 2015 replacing the earlier Gold Deposit Scheme that enables resident households, trusts, and institutions to deposit idle physical gold with designated banks in exchange for interest-bearing metal-account returns.

keywords.shortNote: The external trade shortfall occurring when a country's total imports of goods, services, and transfers exceed its exports, historically widened in India by large physical bullion imports.
keywords.concept: Current Account Deficit (CAD): The external trade shortfall occurring when a country's total imports of goods, services, and transfers exceed its exports, historically widened in India by large physical bullion imports.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Misses the primary macroeconomic goal of curbing bullion imports to contain the Current Account Deficit.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Wrongly attributes FDI promotion to domestic gold financialization schemes.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both schemes work together to mobilize idle domestic gold and substitute physical bullion demand, reducing import dependence without involving FDI.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to recognize that SGB and GMS are exclusively domestic resident schemes with zero FDI mandate.

valueAddition.title: How SGB and GMS Attack the Same Problem from Two Angles
bullets: Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs) target new investment demand—instead of buying physical gold bars or coins, investors buy RBI-backed bonds denominated in grams of gold, earning 2.5% annual interest plus capital gains tax exemption if held to the 8-year maturity.

Gold Monetization Scheme (GMS) targets existing stock—households and trusts deposit idle physical jewellery or bullion (minimum 10 grams of raw gold) with banks for short-term (1–3 years), medium-term (5–7 years), or long-term (12–15 years) tenors to earn tax-free interest.

Together, they reduce unproductive locking of household savings and lower India's merchandise import bill, since gold is consistently among India's top three import items alongside crude oil and electronics.

valueAddition.title: Eligibility Boundary: Strictly Resident Indians
bullets: Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) and foreign investors cannot subscribe to fresh Sovereign Gold Bonds or open Gold Monetization Scheme accounts—making any claim of 'promoting FDI' structurally impossible.
Under GMS, short-term bank deposits are held on the bank's own balance sheet, while medium- and long-term deposits are accepted on behalf of the Central Government.

inNews.source: Ministry of Finance / Business Standard
inNews.headline: Government Reviews Sovereign Gold Bond Tranche Calendar Amid Elevated Global Bullion Prices
inNews.relevance: The Finance Ministry reassessed fresh Sovereign Gold Bond issuances and rationalized gold customs duties in July 2026 to balance sovereign borrowing costs against domestic bullion import demand.

statementBreakdown.explanation: The Gold Monetization Scheme directly targets the estimated 20,000+ tonnes of idle gold held by Indian households and temples, mobilizing it through banks so refiners and jewellers can recycle domestic gold for productive economic use.

Neither SGB nor GMS is an FDI promotion policy; SGBs are restricted strictly to resident Indian entities (individuals, HUFs, trusts, universities, charitable institutions), and GMS accepts deposits exclusively from resident Indians.

statementBreakdown.reference: Ministry of Finance External Sector Rationale
statementBreakdown.explanation: By shifting investor demand from physical bars/coins into paper SGBs and recycling existing household gold via GMS, both schemes aim to curb physical gold imports and ease pressure on India's Current Account Deficit.

stem:
The establishment of 'Payment Banks' is being allowed in India to promote financial inclusion. Which of the following statements is/are correct in this context?
1. Mobile telephone companies supermarket chains that are owned and controlled by residents are eligible to be promoters of Payment Banks.
2. Payment Banks can issue both credit cards and debit cards.
3. Payment Banks cannot undertake lending activities.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.

keywords.shortNote: A differentiated bank category licensed under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 to provide remittance services and accept demand deposits, but prohibited from lending.
keywords.concept: Payments Banks: A differentiated bank category licensed under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 to provide remittance services and accept demand deposits, but prohibited from lending.

keywords.shortNote: Funds held in current and savings accounts that are payable on demand, subject to a statutory regulatory cap of Rs 2 lakh per individual customer.
keywords.concept: Demand Deposits: Funds held in current and savings accounts that are payable on demand, subject to a statutory regulatory cap of Rs 2 lakh per individual customer.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because Payments Banks cannot issue credit cards.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: Statements 1 and 3 are true; Statement 2 is false.
optionBreakdown.explanation: Correctly pairs eligible promoter categories with the statutory ban on credit cards and lending.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because issuing credit cards is prohibited.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because Statements 2 and 3 are mutually contradictory (issuing credit cards is a credit/lending activity).

valueAddition.title: Payments Bank Operational Framework
bullets: Deposit Limits: Permitted to accept only demand deposits (savings and current accounts), capped at Rs 2 lakh per individual customer (enhanced from Rs 1 lakh in April 2021). Cannot accept time/fixed deposits (FD/RD).
Reserve Requirements: Must invest a minimum of 75% of demand deposit balances in Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) eligible Government securities/Treasury Bills with maturity up to one year.
Operating Balances: Maximum 25% of deposits can be held in current and time/fixed deposits with other scheduled commercial banks for operational and liquidity management.

valueAddition.title: Capital Adequacy & Promoter Lock-in
bullets: Minimum Capital: Required to have a minimum paid-up equity capital of Rs 100 crore and maintain a minimum Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 15%.
Promoter Stake: The promoter must hold at least 40% of the paid-up voting equity capital for the initial 5 years from commencement of operations.

Cross-Selling: While prohibited from direct lending, Payments Banks can distribute non-risk sharing financial products like mutual fund units, insurance products, and third-party bank loans as an agent.

subject: Economy
stem:
With reference to 'Bitcoins', sometimes seen in the news, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. Bitcoins are tracked by the Central Banks of the countries.
2. Anyone with a Bitcoin address can send and receive Bitcoins from anyone else with a Bitcoin address.
3. Online payments can be sent without either side knowing the identity of the other.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.

keywords.shortNote: A decentralized, peer-to-peer digital currency operating on a distributed blockchain ledger without central bank backing or intermediary control.
keywords.concept: Bitcoin: A decentralized, peer-to-peer digital currency operating on a distributed blockchain ledger without central bank backing or intermediary control.

keywords.shortNote: A privacy property where transactions are publicly anchored to cryptographic public keys (addresses) rather than real-world personal identities.
keywords.concept: Pseudonymity: A privacy property where transactions are publicly anchored to cryptographic public keys (addresses) rather than real-world personal identities.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because central banks do not track or control decentralized Bitcoin transactions.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.reference: Statement 1 is false; Statements 2 and 3 are true.
optionBreakdown.explanation: Correctly eliminates central bank tracking while confirming permissionless peer-to-peer transfers and pseudonymous payments.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to include Statement 2, which accurately reflects the permissionless nature of Bitcoin addresses.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because it incorporates the false premise of central bank oversight.

valueAddition.title: Bitcoin Architecture & Regulatory Reality
bullets: Decentralized Ledger: Operates via Proof-of-Work (PoW) consensus on an immutable public blockchain; no sovereign or central bank exercises issuance, surveillance, or supervisory control over the base protocol.

Pseudonymity vs Anonymity: While transacting parties do not see each other's personal identities, every transaction is permanently recorded on the public ledger; forensic blockchain analytics can map wallet addresses to IP addresses or KYC-verified crypto exchanges.

Legal Status in India: Not recognized as legal tender. The Supreme Court struck down RBI's 2018 banking ban in IMAI v. RBI (2020). Gains from Virtual Digital Assets (VDAs) are taxed at a flat 30% under Section 115BBH of the Income Tax Act, plus a 1% TDS under Section 194S.

inNews.source: Financial Stability Board (FSB) / Reserve Bank of India
inNews.headline: G20-FSB crypto roadmap reviews cross-border compliance on Virtual Digital Assets and anti-money laundering standards
inNews.relevance: Directly links to the pseudonymous, borderless nature tested in this PYQ, coordinating global regulatory baselines between national regulators and FATF Travel Rule monitoring on crypto transactions.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Bitcoin operates on a decentralized peer-to-peer network where transactions are validated by distributed network nodes and miners, not tracked, regulated, or issued by any central bank.
Bitcoin is permissionless; anyone who generates a cryptographic public-private key pair possesses a Bitcoin address and can directly transfer or receive tokens globally without intermediary approval.

Transactions reveal only alphanumeric wallet addresses and transfer amounts on the public ledger, allowing parties to settle payments without disclosing their legal or real-world identities to each other.

Decentralized public blockchain (No central bank tracking)
Requires KYC verification and commercial bank accounts

keywords.calloutNote: This is fundamentally wrong. Bitcoin was created specifically to eliminate central bank tracking and control.

answer.label: B
answer.text: Statements 2 and 3 are correct; Bitcoin is a decentralized, permissionless, pseudonymous network free from central bank tracking.

subject: Economy
stem:
What is/are the purpose/purposes of the 'Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR)' announced by RBI?
1. These guidelines help improve the transparency in the methodology followed by banks for determining the interest rates on advances.
2. These guidelines help ensure availability of bank credit at interest rates which are fair to the borrowers as well as the banks.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.

keywords.term: Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR)
keywords.shortNote: An internal benchmark lending rate introduced by the RBI in April 2016 that links loan interest rates to the marginal (incremental) cost of raising new funds rather than average historical costs.
keywords.concept: Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR): An internal benchmark lending rate introduced by the RBI in April 2016 that links loan interest rates to the marginal (incremental) cost of raising new funds rather than average historical costs.

keywords.shortNote: The speed and extent to which changes in the central bank's policy repo rate are passed through by commercial banks to their lending and deposit rates.
keywords.concept: Monetary Transmission: The speed and extent to which changes in the central bank's policy repo rate are passed through by commercial banks to their lending and deposit rates.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to include Statement 2, which is an explicit statutory objective of the guidelines.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails to include Statement 1, which represents the core rationale for replacing the opaque Base Rate regime.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements are verbatim quotes from the preamble objectives laid down in the RBI's December 2015 MCLR circular.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Fails because both statements correctly state the official objectives of the MCLR framework.

valueAddition.title: MCLR Formula & Four Core Components
bullets: MCLR Structure: MCLR = Marginal Cost of Funds + Negative Carry on CRR + Operating Costs + Tenor Premium.
Marginal Cost of Funds: Calculated using 92% weightage on the marginal cost of fresh borrowings/deposits and 8% on return on net worth.
Reset Clause: Loans linked to MCLR carry a mandatory reset clause (typically 6 months or 1 year), meaning interest rate changes reflect on borrower EMIs only on the scheduled reset date.

valueAddition.title: Evolution of RBI Lending Benchmarks
bullets: Benchmark Timeline: Prime Lending Rate (BPLR, 2003) -> Base Rate (July 2010) -> MCLR (April 2016) -> External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR, October 2019).
Shortcoming of MCLR: Transmission remained slow and asymmetric because banks adjusted the spread or delayed resetting rates during repo rate cuts.

Transition to EBLR: From October 1, 2019, RBI mandated all floating-rate retail and MSME loans be tied to external benchmarks (such as the Repo Rate or 91/182-day T-Bill yields), superseding MCLR for new retail credit.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India / Financial Stability Report
inNews.headline: RBI highlights persistent transmission divergence between EBLR-linked retail loans and legacy MCLR corporate advances
inNews.relevance: Directly links to the lending benchmarks tested in this PYQ, analyzing how monetary policy changes pass through quickly to retail borrowers under EBLR but face reset lags under the MCLR framework.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Improving transparency in the methodology followed by commercial banks for arriving at lending rates on advances is an explicitly codified regulatory objective of the MCLR framework.
Ensuring the availability of bank credit at interest rates that are fair to both borrowers and banks is explicitly stated as the second fundamental purpose in the RBI's operative guidelines.

rows: Average cost of all existing deposits
Immediate (resets mandatory at least once in 3 months)
Mandatory for all fresh floating retail & MSME loans

hook.headline: Why did RBI replace the Base Rate with MCLR in 2016?
hook.teaser: Banks used to cut deposit rates instantly, but held back on cutting home loan rates.

keywords.calloutNote: MCLR forced banks to use a standardized, formula-driven calculation based on fresh deposit costs.
activePhrases: help improve the transparency in the methodology followed by banks

keywords.term: fair to the borrowers as well as the banks
keywords.calloutNote: Ensuring borrowers benefit from rate cuts while banks maintain viable lending margins.
activePhrases: interest rates which are fair to the borrowers as well as the banks.
dimmedPhrases: help improve the transparency in the methodology followed by banks
contextPhrases: purposes of the 'Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR)'

verdicts.source: The RBI circular explicitly states improving transparency in bank interest determination as a core objective.
Ensuring credit availability at interest rates fair to both borrowers and banks is directly written into the RBI guidelines.

answer.label: C
answer.text: Both statements are correct; MCLR was introduced to make lending rates transparent, objective, and fair to both borrowers and lenders.

subject: Economy
stem:
The term ‘Core Banking Solution’ is sometimes seen in the news. Which of the following statements best describes/describe this term?

1. It is a network of a bank’s branches which enables customers to operate their accounts from any branch of the bank on its network regardless of where they open their accounts. 
2. It is an effort to increase RBI’s control over commercial banks through computerization. 
3. It is a detailed procedure by which a bank with huge non-performing assets is taken over by another bank.

Select the correct answer using the code given below:

keywords.shortNote: Centralized online real-time software system connecting a bank's branches so that a customer becomes a client of the bank rather than a specific branch.
keywords.concept: Core Banking Solution (CBS): Centralized online real-time software system connecting a bank's branches so that a customer becomes a client of the bank rather than a specific branch.

keywords.shortNote: A regulatory framework applied by the RBI to monitor and stabilize financially stressed banks, distinct from commercial software solutions.
keywords.concept: Prompt Corrective Action (PCA): A regulatory framework applied by the RBI to monitor and stabilize financially stressed banks, distinct from commercial software solutions.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Only statement 1 accurately captures the operational nature of Core Banking Solutions.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Both statements 2 and 3 are incorrect distractors.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Incorrectly includes statement 3.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Incorrectly includes statements 2 and 3.

valueAddition.title: What is Core Banking Solution (CBS)?
bullets: Acronym Meaning: CORE stands for 'Centralized Online Real-time Exchange'.
Decoupling the Branch: Shifts banking from 'customer of the branch' to 'customer of the bank', enabling anywhere-banking for deposits, withdrawals, and remittances.
Common Platforms: Includes software suites such as Finacle (Infosys), BaNCS (TCS), and Flexcube (Oracle).
RBI Integration: RBI maintains its own centralized core banking portal called 'e-Kuber', used by government departments and commercial banks for clearing and settlement.

valueAddition.title: NPA Resolution Mechanisms vs. CBS
bullets: Prompt Corrective Action (PCA): RBI framework monitoring capital ratios (CRAR), asset quality (NNPA), and leverage to intervene in fragile banks.
Amalgamation / Mergers: Carried out under Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, or through government-notified consolidation schemes, having no connection to CBS.

inNews.source: Reserve Bank of India / The Hindu
inNews.headline: RBI directs cooperative and regional rural banks to ensure seamless cloud-based CBS integration
inNews.relevance: Directly links the core technical infrastructure of banking networks (CBS) to modern financial inclusion and digital payment clearing pipelines.

statementBreakdown.explanation: Core Banking Solutions (CBS) link all branches of a bank to a central database server, allowing customers to conduct transactions across any interconnected branch regardless of where the account was originally opened.

CBS is operational software deployed by individual banks to network branches and streamline retail customer operations; it is not a tool designed to increase central bank control over commercial banks.
Takeovers and resolutions of banks with high NPAs are handled through statutory mechanisms (e.g., Prompt Corrective Action, Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act, or the IBC), not via CBS.

visualSuggestion.title: Decentralized Branch Banking vs. Core Banking Solution (CBS)

rows: Local ledger maintained at home branch
Centralized real-time server across entire bank network
Restricted mostly to base account branch
Transactions accessible from any branch, ATM, or portal

hook.headline: What does 'Core Banking Solution' really mean?
hook.teaser: Let's uncover why CORE banking turned you into a customer of the entire bank.

keywords.calloutNote: Centralized database that makes branch location irrelevant for customers.
activePhrases: networking of a bank's branches which enables customers to operate their accounts from any branch

keywords.calloutNote: Common examiner trap: CBS is customer software, not a central bank control tool.

verdicts.source: CBS networks all branches to a central database, enabling transactions across any branch regardless of where the account opened.
CBS is operational software for bank customers, not a tool to enhance central bank control over commercial banks.
NPA takeovers occur under statutory frameworks like PCA or the Banking Regulation Act, not through CBS.

answer.label: a
answer.text: Statement 1 accurately describes Core Banking Solution, making (a) the correct answer.

subject: Economy
stem: The term 'Base Erosion and Profit Shifting' is sometimes seen in the news in the context of

options.text: mining operation by multinational companies in resource-rich but backward areas
options.label: a

options.text: curbing of the tax evasion by multinational companies
options.label: b

options.text: exploitation of genetic resources of a country by multinational companies
options.label: c

options.text: lack of consideration of environmental costs in the planning and implementation of developmental projects
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: Corporate tax-planning strategies used by multinational enterprises (MNEs) that exploit gaps and mismatches in national tax rules to artificially shift taxable profits out of high-tax jurisdictions where economic value is created into low- or no-tax jurisdictions ('tax havens'), eroding the domestic tax base.
keywords.concept: Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS): Corporate tax-planning strategies used by multinational enterprises (MNEs) that exploit gaps and mismatches in national tax rules to artificially shift taxable profits out of high-tax jurisdictions where economic value is created into low- or no-tax jurisdictions ('tax havens'), eroding the domestic tax base.

keywords.shortNote: The 15-point international tax reform framework launched by the OECD and G20 (including India) to curb cross-border tax avoidance through Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR), anti-treaty shopping rules, and updated transfer pricing norms.
keywords.concept: OECD/G20 BEPS Action Plan: The 15-point international tax reform framework launched by the OECD and G20 (including India) to curb cross-border tax avoidance through Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR), anti-treaty shopping rules, and updated transfer pricing norms.

keywords.shortNote: The pricing of goods, services, intellectual property royalties, or intra-group loans transferred between related subsidiaries of a multinational corporation across borders—frequently manipulated to shift profits unless benchmarked at 'arm's-length price'.
keywords.concept: Transfer Pricing: The pricing of goods, services, intellectual property royalties, or intra-group loans transferred between related subsidiaries of a multinational corporation across borders—frequently manipulated to shift profits unless benchmarked at 'arm's-length price'.

keywords.shortNote: The practice of routing cross-border investments through shell entities in intermediate countries with favourable Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAAs) solely to minimize withholding and capital gains taxes.
keywords.concept: Treaty Shopping: The practice of routing cross-border investments through shell entities in intermediate countries with favourable Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAAs) solely to minimize withholding and capital gains taxes.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.text: mining operation by multinational companies in resource-rich but backward areas
optionBreakdown.explanation: Plays on the word 'erosion' to sound environmental or geological—BEPS deals strictly with fiscal tax bases, not soil erosion or mineral extraction.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.text: curbing of the tax evasion by multinational companies
optionBreakdown.explanation: Accurately identifies BEPS as the global initiative led by the OECD and G20 to stop multinational corporations from eroding national tax bases and shifting profits to tax havens.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.text: exploitation of genetic resources of a country by multinational companies
optionBreakdown.explanation: Exploitation of genetic resources relates to biopiracy and Access and Benefit Sharing under the Convention on Biological Diversity (Nagoya Protocol), not BEPS.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.text: lack of consideration of environmental costs in the planning and implementation of developmental projects
optionBreakdown.reference: Environmental Impact Assessment / Green Accounting Distractor
optionBreakdown.explanation: Environmental externalities and green GDP accounting have no connection to Base Erosion and Profit Shifting.

valueAddition.title: How Multinationals Erode Tax Bases (And How India Counters It)
bullets: Profit-Shifting Channels: MNEs deduct excessive interest payments on intra-group loans or pay inflated royalties for patents/trademarks held by shell subsidiaries in zero-tax jurisdictions—shrinking taxable profits in countries like India where actual sales and R&D happen ('Base Erosion') and booking them in tax havens ('Profit Shifting').

India's Counter-Measures: Enactment of General Anti-Avoidance Rules (GAAR), Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR) for large MNEs under Section 286 of the Income-tax Act, Thin Capitalization rules (Section 94B capping intra-group interest deductions at 30% of EBITDA), and signing the OECD Multilateral Instrument (MLI) to insert Principal Purpose Tests into bilateral DTAAs.

valueAddition.title: From BEPS 1.0 to the OECD/G20 Two-Pillar Solution (BEPS 2.0)
bullets: Pillar One reallocates a portion of residual profits of the largest and most profitable MNEs to market jurisdictions where users and consumers are located, even without a physical presence.

Pillar Two establishes a 15% Global Minimum Corporate Tax (GloBE rules) on MNEs with consolidated annual revenues above EUR 750 million, ensuring large multinationals pay at least 15% effective tax regardless of where they book profits.

inNews.source: OECD / Ministry of Finance
inNews.headline: Over 140 Inclusive Framework Jurisdictions Advance Global Minimum Tax Implementation Under OECD BEPS Pillar Two
inNews.relevance: International tax coordination updates in October 2026 highlighted wider rollout of the 15% Global Minimum Tax and Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-Up Taxes (QDMTT) under the OECD/G20 BEPS Inclusive Framework to curb profit shifting by multinationals.

visualSuggestion.title: Anatomy of BEPS: How Profit Shifting Works vs. Policy Counter-Measures

rows: Overcharging Indian subsidiaries for IP, brand fees, or intra-group services
Loading high-tax subsidiaries with heavy intra-group debt to deduct interest
Section 94B cap on interest deduction at 30% of EBITDA
Routing investments through low-tax treaty jurisdictions without substance
GAAR & Principal Purpose Test under OECD Multilateral Instrument (MLI)

hook.headline: What does 'Base Erosion' actually erode—soil, minerals, or tax revenue?
hook.teaser: Notice how UPSC plants two environmental distractors to bait candidates who take the word 'erosion' literally.

keywords.calloutNote: Break the phrase in two: 'Base Erosion' shrinks a country's taxable income base, while 'Profit Shifting' moves those profits on paper to low-tax havens.
activePhrases: Base Erosion and Profit Shifting

keywords.term: curbing of the tax evasion by multinational companies
keywords.calloutTerm: “curbing of the tax evasion by multinational companies”
keywords.calloutNote: Led by the OECD and G20, the BEPS Action Plan closes cross-border tax loopholes used by multinationals.
activePhrases: curbing of the tax evasion by multinational companies
dimmedPhrases: Base Erosion and Profit Shifting

verdicts.source: Uses 'mining' and 'resource-rich' to trick candidates into confusing tax base erosion with land or mineral degradation.
BEPS refers to the OECD/G20 framework curbing cross-border tax avoidance and profit shifting by multinational companies.
Exploitation of genetic resources falls under the Nagoya Protocol and biodiversity laws, not BEPS.
Environmental cost accounting in projects has nothing to do with corporate profit shifting.

answer.label: B
answer.text: BEPS is the OECD/G20 initiative to stop multinationals from shifting taxable profits into tax havens—making Option B right.

subject: Economy
stem: Recently, India's first 'National Investment and Manufacturing Zone' was proposed to be set up in

keywords.shortNote: Mega greenfield integrated industrial townships of at least 5,000 hectares (50 sq. km) conceptualized under the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011 with autonomous governance, single-window clearances, and world-class infrastructure.
keywords.concept: National Investment and Manufacturing Zone (NIMZ): Mega greenfield integrated industrial townships of at least 5,000 hectares (50 sq. km) conceptualized under the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011 with autonomous governance, single-window clearances, and world-class infrastructure.

keywords.shortNote: India's flagship industrial policy framework aimed at raising the share of manufacturing in GDP to 25% and creating 100 million additional jobs by eliminating regulatory bottlenecks and clustering industries inside NIMZs.
keywords.concept: National Manufacturing Policy (NMP), 2011: India's flagship industrial policy framework aimed at raising the share of manufacturing in GDP to 25% and creating 100 million additional jobs by eliminating regulatory bottlenecks and clustering industries inside NIMZs.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.reference: DPIIT Final Approval · Prakasam District, Andhra Pradesh (2015)
optionBreakdown.explanation: In October 2015, the Government of India granted final approval to India's first National Investment and Manufacturing Zone outside the Delhi–Mumbai Industrial Corridor in Prakasam district, Andhra Pradesh.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: While Gujarat hosts major Delhi–Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC) nodes like Dholera Special Investment Region, the first standalone NIMZ granted final central approval was in Prakasam, Andhra Pradesh.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: Maharashtra hosts DMIC industrial nodes such as Shendra-Bidkin (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar), not India's first notified NIMZ.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Uttar Pradesh hosts industrial corridor nodes along the DMIC and Amritsar–Kolkata Industrial Corridor, rather than the first NIMZ.

valueAddition.title: Design & Governance Architecture of NIMZs
bullets: Minimum Area Threshold: Each NIMZ requires a minimum contiguous land area of 5,000 hectares (50 sq. km), with at least 30% earmarked strictly for manufacturing units.

Institutional Governance: Declared by State Governments as Industrial Townships under Article 243Q(1) proviso of the Constitution, managed by a State-led Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) offering single-window clearances, simplified labour compliance, and common effluent treatment.

valueAddition.title: NIMZ vs. Special Economic Zone (SEZ): Key Distinctions
bullets: Market Orientation: SEZs are treated as foreign territory for customs duties with a primary focus on export earnings, whereas NIMZs serve both domestic tariff area (DTA) sales and exports without customs-enclave fencing.

Scale & Focus: SEZs can be small sector-specific enclaves (even 10–50 hectares for IT/biotech), whereas NIMZs are multi-sector mega industrial cities of at least 5,000 hectares built around integrated urban-industrial infrastructure.

inNews.source: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) / National Industrial Corridor Development Corporation (NICDC)
inNews.headline: NICDC and DPIIT accelerate plug-and-play industrial smart cities across Andhra Pradesh and national industrial corridors to lift manufacturing GDP share
inNews.relevance: September 2026 industrial corridor reviews highlighted progress across Andhra Pradesh's Kopparthy, Orvakal, and Prakasam industrial hubs, carrying forward the NIMZ cluster strategy for export-ready manufacturing.

keywords.shortNote: Prorogation terminates a session without ending the House's life; dissolution ends the very life of the Lok Sabha and triggers the rules of lapsing under Article 107.
keywords.concept: Prorogation vs Dissolution: Prorogation terminates a session without ending the House's life; dissolution ends the very life of the Lok Sabha and triggers the rules of lapsing under Article 107.

keywords.shortNote: Explicitly provides that a Bill pending in Parliament shall not lapse by reason of the prorogation of the Houses.
keywords.concept: Article 107(3): Explicitly provides that a Bill pending in Parliament shall not lapse by reason of the prorogation of the Houses.

keywords.shortNote: Provides that a Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha which has not been passed by the Lok Sabha shall not lapse on a dissolution of the House of the People.
keywords.concept: Article 107(4): Provides that a Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha which has not been passed by the Lok Sabha shall not lapse on a dissolution of the House of the People.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect because prorogation never kills a pending bill.

optionBreakdown.label: b

optionBreakdown.label: c

valueAddition.title: Position of Bills on Dissolution (Art. 107 & 108)
bullets: Lapses: Any bill pending in Lok Sabha (originating in LS or transmitted to LS), and any bill passed by Lok Sabha but pending in Rajya Sabha.
Does NOT Lapse: Bill pending in Rajya Sabha not passed by Lok Sabha; Bill passed by both Houses pending President's assent; Bill returned by President for reconsideration.
Joint Sitting Exception: If the President has notified an intention to summon a joint sitting under Art. 108 before dissolution, the bill does not lapse.

keywords.shortNote: Prescribes that a person is eligible to contest Panchayat elections upon attaining 21 years of age, setting a lower qualification bar than the State Legislative Assembly.
keywords.concept: Article 243F (Disqualifications for Membership): Prescribes that a person is eligible to contest Panchayat elections upon attaining 21 years of age, setting a lower qualification bar than the State Legislative Assembly.

keywords.shortNote: Fixes a 5-year term for every Panchayat and mandates that a body reconstituted upon premature dissolution serves only the remainder of the original term.
keywords.concept: Article 243E (Duration of Panchayats): Fixes a 5-year term for every Panchayat and mandates that a body reconstituted upon premature dissolution serves only the remainder of the original term.

valueAddition.title: Article 243E: Dissolution, Tenure & Election Timelines
bullets: Fixed Five-Year Term: Every Panchayat continues for five years from the date appointed for its first meeting and no longer [Article 243E(1)].

Mandatory Election Windows: Elections to constitute a Panchayat must be completed either (i) before the expiry of its five-year duration, or (ii) before the expiration of a period of six months from the date of its premature dissolution [Article 243E(3)].

Remainder Period Rule: A newly elected Panchayat following premature dissolution does not enjoy a fresh five-year term; it operates strictly for the unexpired remainder of the original tenure [Article 243E(4)].

Six-Month Remainder Exemption: Proviso to Article 243E(3) dictates that if the remainder of the period is less than six months, it is not necessary to hold any intermediate bye-election before constituting the regular Panchayat for a fresh five-year term.

valueAddition.title: Constitutional Age Hierarchy Across Indian Representative Bodies
bullets: 21 Years Threshold: Panchayats (Part IX, Article 243F) and Municipalities (Part IXA, Article 243V).
25 Years Threshold: Lok Sabha (House of the People, Article 84(b)) and State Legislative Assemblies (Vidhan Sabha, Article 173(b)).
30 Years Threshold: Rajya Sabha (Council of States, Article 84(b)) and State Legislative Councils (Vidhan Parishad, Article 173(b)).
35 Years Threshold: President of India (Article 58(1)(b)), Vice-President of India (Article 66(3)(b)), and State Governors (Article 157).

stem: The Parliament of India acquires the power to legislate on any item in the State List in the national interest if a resolution to that effect is passed by the

options.text: Lok Sabha by a simple majority of its total membership.
options.label: a

options.text: Lok Sabha by a majority of not less than two-thirds of its total membership.
options.label: b

options.text: Rajya Sabha by a simple majority of its total membership.
options.label: c

options.text: Rajya Sabha by a majority of not less than two-thirds of its members present and voting.
options.label: d

keywords.shortNote: Empowers Parliament to legislate with respect to a matter in the State List if the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) declares by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest.
keywords.concept: Article 249: Empowers Parliament to legislate with respect to a matter in the State List if the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) declares by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest.

keywords.shortNote: Exclusive constitutional prerogatives vested in the Upper House as the institutional representative of the States, notably under Article 249 (State List legislation) and Article 312 (All-India Services creation).
keywords.concept: Special Powers of Rajya Sabha: Exclusive constitutional prerogatives vested in the Upper House as the institutional representative of the States, notably under Article 249 (State List legislation) and Article 312 (All-India Services creation).

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Article 249 vests this initiative exclusively in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha), not the Lok Sabha, to ensure constituent States consent before their legislative sphere is accessed in the national interest.

optionBreakdown.label: b
optionBreakdown.explanation: Lok Sabha has no constitutional competence to initiate or pass the authorizing resolution under Article 249, regardless of the majority invoked.

optionBreakdown.label: c
optionBreakdown.explanation: A simple majority of total membership is legally insufficient; Article 249 explicitly mandates a special majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.

optionBreakdown.label: d
optionBreakdown.explanation: Article 249(1) explicitly provides that if the Council of States has declared by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest that Parliament should make laws with respect to any matter enumerated in the State List, it shall be lawful for Parliament to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India with respect to that matter.

valueAddition.title: Article 249: Constitutional Mechanics & Duration Limits
bullets: Verbatim Threshold: Supported by 'not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting' in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha).

Validity of Resolution: The resolution remains in force for such period not exceeding one year as may be specified therein, but can be renewed indefinitely for one year at a time through subsequent resolutions.

Cessation of Law: A law made by Parliament under this provision ceases to have effect on the expiration of six months after the resolution has ceased to be in force (except regarding things done or omitted to be done).

Concurrent State Competence Preserved: Article 249 does not restrict the legislature of a State from passing any law on the same subject; however, in the event of repugnancy between the State law and the parliamentary law, the parliamentary law prevails under Article 251.

valueAddition.title: Five Extraordinary Scenarios for Parliamentary Legislation on List II
bullets: Article 249 (National Interest): Initiated exclusively by Rajya Sabha via two-thirds present and voting resolution; effective for 1 year at a time; laws lapse 6 months after resolution expires.
Article 250 (National Emergency): Operates automatically when a Proclamation of Emergency under Article 352 is in force; laws lapse 6 months after the emergency ceases to operate.

Article 252 (Agreement Between States): Initiated when the legislatures of two or more States pass resolutions requesting Parliament to legislate; applicable only to consenting States and those that subsequently adopt it (can be amended or repealed only by Parliament, not by the States).
Article 253 (International Agreements): Enables Parliament to legislate on any State List subject to implement international treaties, conventions, or agreements without requiring State consent.
Article 356 (President's Rule): Powers of the State legislature become exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament.

1. The Chief Secretary in a State is appointed by the Governor of that State.
2. The Chief Secretary in a State has a fixed tenure.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

keywords.shortNote: Senior-most civil servant in a State, head of the state administrative machinery, ex-officio Secretary to the State Cabinet, and principal advisor to the Chief Minister.
keywords.concept: Chief Secretary: Senior-most civil servant in a State, head of the state administrative machinery, ex-officio Secretary to the State Cabinet, and principal advisor to the Chief Minister.

optionBreakdown.label: a
optionBreakdown.explanation: Identifies Statement 1 as the sole correct statement.

valueAddition.title: Office of the Chief Secretary: Constitutional & Administrative Framework
bullets: Genesis: Created in 1799 by Lord Wellesley (Governor-General of Bengal), first held by G.H. Barlow.
Appointment Mechanism: Selected by the Chief Minister from senior IAS officers of the Apex Scale (Level 17); formally appointed and notified by order of the Governor.
Ex-Officio Capacities: Secretary to the State Cabinet, Head of the Civil Services of the State, Chairman of the State Civil Services Board (CSB), and Chief Coordinator across all State departments.

Tenure & Extension: Retires at 60 years of age under Rule 16(1) of AIS (DCRB) Rules, 1958; central government concurrence is required to extend service beyond superannuation (normally capped up to 6 months under Rule 16(1A)).

valueAddition.title: Cabinet Secretary (Centre) vs. Chief Secretary (State)
bullets: Tenure Distinction: The Cabinet Secretary has a minimum fixed tenure of 2 years (extendable up to a total of 4 years under Rule 56(d) of Fundamental Rules); the Chief Secretary has no statutory fixed tenure.

Administrative Span: A Chief Secretary exercises residual authority over subjects not allocated to any specific department; the Cabinet Secretary does not hold residual departmental charges at the Centre.
Protocol Standing: The Cabinet Secretary ranks 11th in the Central Table of Precedence; Chief Secretaries within their respective States rank 23rd.

inNews.source: Supreme Court of India / The Hindu
inNews.headline: Supreme Court reiterates primacy of elected State Government in the selection and transfer of Chief Secretary
inNews.relevance: Directly highlights the selection, appointment, and tenure dynamics of the Chief Secretary under constitutional rules of business.

statementBreakdown.reference: Article 166(1), Constitution of India & State Rules of Business
statementBreakdown.explanation: Executive actions of the State are expressed to be taken in the name of the Governor (Article 166(1)). Formally, the Chief Secretary is appointed by the Governor of the State, acting on the advice of the Chief Minister.

There is no minimum or fixed tenure mandated for the post of Chief Secretary in a State. While the IAS (Cadre) Amendment Rules, 2014 established minimum two-year tenures for specified cadre posts, the post of Chief Secretary is not bound by a fixed tenure and serves subject to superannuation or premature transfer/reassignment by the State Government.
